Britain should be a leader in long-range high-speed aircraft, but routine hypersonic transport by the mid-1970s is probably too far.

Hypersonic flight imposes severe problems of heat, fuel consumption, materials and range. It is plausible for experimental reconnaissance aircraft, rocketplanes or prestige prototypes. It is less plausible as the normal method for moving ministers, troops or passengers around the Commonwealth.

Britain’s practical aviation strengths should instead be:

- very long-range high-subsonic transports;
- supersonic passenger and military transports;
- aerial-refueling aircraft;
- high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft;
- maritime patrol aircraft with exceptional endurance;
- experimental hypersonic research vehicles.

Geography also gives Britain alternatives to flying across German Europe.

Britain reaches Canada and the Caribbean directly across the Atlantic. It reaches southern Africa and the Indian Ocean through Atlantic islands, West African routes, the Cape and British-controlled stepping stones. Australia can be reached through Canada and the Pacific or through the Cape and Indian Ocean.

The result is an expensive but genuinely global air network whose routes deliberately avoid dependence upon German, Italian or American goodwill.

By 1972, the Philippines should no longer be merely “slowly drifting” toward Japan. The timeline already places its entry into Japan’s associated sphere around 1958. fileciteturn0file1

- preferential trade;

The mid-1970s should be the point when automation stops appearing experimental and begins appearing economically transformative.

- heavy engineering;
- mines;
- steel;
- automotive production;
- chemical plants;
- dangerous work formerly performed by coerced labor;
- highly standardized state industries.

- automobiles;
- consumer goods;
- electronics;
- ports;
- warehouses;
- shipyards;
- food processing;
- precision assembly.

The Japanese motive is not merely novelty. Its imperial economy possesses immense resources and markets but insufficient skilled Japanese labor to administer and manufacture everything. - terminals;

- banking networks;
- government databases;
- airline and railway reservation systems;
- industrial process control.

## The American view of the world

By 1975, the average politically attentive American sees the United States as **a continental republic trapped in a world of empires**.

America has not been conquered. Its economy is large, its population prosperous and its military formidable. Yet it has never experienced the world-historical victory that defined the real United States after 1945.

Instead, Americans remember:

- remaining neutral while Germany and Japan won;
- failing in the Philippines;
- Germany launching the first satellite;
- Germany landing first on the Moon;
- Kennedy’s interventions in Honduras and Venezuela;
- the Atlantic Accord dividing the ocean without treating Britain as an American partner;
- Cuba becoming an armed foreign-supported fortress;
- Argentina receiving German weapons;
- Japan entering Peru;
- Canada preparing for an American invasion;
- Rockwell winning a plurality and being denied the presidency;
- Rockwell then being murdered.

The dominant emotion is not defeat. It is **frustrated power**.

America believes it ought to be able to dictate events in its hemisphere, yet repeatedly discovers that foreign powers can act through advisers, companies, arms shipments, bases, loans and local allies without technically violating the Atlantic Accord.

### Germany in American eyes

Germany is the principal military-technological threat.

It is admired for engineering, feared for its army, resented for the Moon landing and treated as dangerously opaque. The American public knows about German tanks, rockets and U-boats. It does not fully understand the colonial labor system or the scale of the submarine fleet.

To the American Navy, Germany is the nightmare enemy: a power capable of closing the Atlantic without needing to invade the United States.

To American industry, Germany is a competitor in machinery, chemicals, nuclear power, aerospace and armaments.

To American moralists, reports from Africa reveal the true character behind the polished German facade.

### Japan in American eyes

Japan is the economic and Pacific threat.

The Philippines is America’s great humiliation. Japanese domination of Asian trade, robotics and microelectronics suggests that the future may belong not to Germany’s continental military machine but to Japan’s disciplined industrial empire.

American attitudes contain a potent mixture of:

- admiration;
- racial anxiety;
- commercial fear;
- resentment over the Philippines;
- fascination with Japanese efficiency;
- concern for Australia and the Pacific.

Germany frightens the Pentagon. Japan frightens businessmen, workers and parents wondering what kind of economy their children will inherit.

### Britain in American eyes

Britain is the most emotionally complicated power.

It remains culturally familiar and historically related, but it is no longer reliably friendly. Britain fortifies Canada and Atlantic possessions partly against the United States. London believes Washington abandoned it to the German sphere in 1968.

Some Americans regard Britain as an aging imperial rival clinging to Canada. Others see it as the only European civilization capable of balancing Germany. Still others fear that Britain could give German or Latin-bloc influence indirect access to North America through the Commonwealth.

Canada becomes the uncomfortable question that neither country can ignore.

### The Latin bloc

The Latin bloc is less alien to many Americans than Germany or Japan, particularly to Catholic and Hispanic constituencies. Italy, Spain, Portugal and Occitania share religious and civilizational connections with large parts of American society.

But strategically they remain competitors.

Their volunteers and advisers appear in Cuba. Their cultural diplomacy operates throughout Latin America. Their monarchies and Catholic-corporatist institutions attract Americans dissatisfied with both National Renewal and liberal constitutionalism.

Buchanan can acknowledge them as civilizational relatives while insisting that America must never become their dependent.

### Africa

Africa remains remote to much of the American electorate until photographs, refugee accounts and foreign broadcasts expose the scale of German repression.

The issue cuts unpredictably across American politics.

Black churches, civil-rights organizations and some Democratic-Republicans make German Africa a central moral cause. The government uses atrocities to distinguish the American order from National Socialism, although the Free Association regime weakens America’s moral credibility.

National Renewal divides. Its most racialist elements defend German colonial firmness or deny reports. Buchanan has strong reasons to reject this. He can condemn German exterminatory colonialism from a Catholic, nationalist and American position without adopting liberal egalitarianism:

> Germany’s empire is German. Its crimes are German. America has no obligation to imitate foreign racial theories merely because Berlin opposes communism and liberalism.

This helps Buchanan detach National Renewal from being perceived as Germany’s American imitation.

## American military priorities

The world of 1975 produces a different American defense establishment from our own.

Without nuclear weapons, great-power war remains imaginable. It would be catastrophic, but not automatically civilization-ending. That makes conventional planning more urgent rather than less.

American priorities become:

- anti-submarine warfare;
- fixed Atlantic acoustic networks;
- long-range patrol aircraft;
- convoy escorts;
- attack submarines;
- satellite ocean surveillance;
- carrier aviation;
- conventional cruise and ballistic missiles;
- rapid reinforcement of the Caribbean and South America;
- space-based reconnaissance;
- defense of ports and naval bases against submarine missile attack.

The central American nightmare is not a German tank army crossing the Atlantic. It is the sudden discovery that German submarines have already taken station off Norfolk, New York, Boston, the Panama Canal and major Gulf ports.

## The domestic political meaning of 1972–76

The Democratic-Republicans and National Renewal describe the same world in opposite ways.

The Democratic-Republican argument is:

> Rockefeller preserved peace, repaired the economy, continued nuclear and space modernization, avoided a ruinous Cuban invasion, and prevented America from stumbling into war with Germany, Japan or Britain.

National Renewal’s argument is:

> The establishment lost the Philippines, lost the space race, tolerated German penetration of Argentina, allowed Japan into Peru, permitted Cuba to become a fortress, drove Canada into British militarization, stole the presidency in 1968, barely held it in 1972, and then failed to protect George Lincoln Rockwell.

The assassination transforms all these separate grievances into one narrative of national dispossession.

Buchanan can ask a devastating question during the 1976 campaign:

> How can the government promise to find every German submarine in the Atlantic when it cannot even truthfully identify the man who murdered George Rockwell on American soil?

That is the emotional convergence of the period.

## A workable chronology

### 1972

The Democratic-Republican fusion wins narrowly. National Renewal captures the House. Cuba passes its national-defense and conscription reforms. German, Latin and Japanese missions begin standardizing Cuban forces. Argentina expands licensed German armaments production.

### 1973

The Free Association constitutional order is upheld. Cuba begins licensed FA-60 rifle manufacture and expands its first naval yard. African insurgencies intensify. Britain issues a major Commonwealth industrial and defense reorganization program.

### 1974

Germany publicly unveils its missile cruiser, indirectly revealing technologies already used by guided-missile U-boats. Argentina receives or commissions its German cruiser and begins operating older German submarines. Japanese industrial automation becomes a major subject in American politics and business journalism.

### 1975

German African counterinsurgency escalates into mass atrocities. Cuba launches its first domestically assembled military craft. British reconstruction is publicly declared complete or nearly complete. Rockwell begins his presidential tour and is assassinated. Buchanan inherits National Renewal.

### 1976

America enters the election under the surface calm of peace, but surrounded by visible evidence that every rival power has spent the preceding four years preparing for war.

That is the central character of the era:

> **1972–1976 is when the postwar world stops improvising and becomes permanent.**

The empires have recovered, the client states have industrialized, the oceans have been divided into hidden patrol zones, the colonies have begun to rebel, and America must finally decide whether it remains a constitutional continental power or becomes the militant hemispheric empire National Renewal believes history requires.

The existing setting leaves the Palestine settlement open while establishing that Germany has used forced Jewish emigration into the Mandate as a means of destabilizing Britain. fileciteturn0file0

A workable settlement is a **smaller Israel beside a much larger Hashemite Jordan**, rather than either total Jewish victory or total Hashemite control.

### The Palestine War, 1947–1950

When Britain’s wider war ends in defeat, it can no longer indefinitely police communal conflict in Palestine. German-sponsored or compelled Jewish emigration adds a large refugee population to an already militarized Jewish community.

Britain tries to terminate the Mandate through a negotiated division, but neither side accepts the initial boundaries. Fighting breaks out among Jewish forces, Arab Palestinian formations, the Transjordanian Arab Legion and irregular forces from neighboring states.

The crucial difference from reality is that there is:

- no Soviet support for the Jewish state;
- no victorious United States willing to make Israel a central strategic commitment;

The Arab Legion therefore performs better and takes more territory than it did historically.

### The Amman Settlement

Around 1950 or 1951, Britain brokers an imposed settlement.

**Israel** survives as a narrow but sovereign state centered upon the Tel Aviv–Haifa coastal corridor and portions of western Galilee. It is smaller, more crowded and more strategically vulnerable than the historical state. It does not receive most of the Negev.

**Jordan** annexes the Arab highlands, Jerusalem, the Jordan Valley, the Negev and Gaza, becoming a much larger Hashemite kingdom with access both to Aqaba and the Mediterranean vicinity. The formal name may remain the **Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan**, but “Jordan and Palestine” becomes common diplomatic language.

**Jerusalem** remains under Hashemite civil sovereignty, while Christian holy places and access rights are guaranteed by a treaty involving Britain, the Vatican, Italy and the local religious communities.

**Britain** retains long-term air, naval and communications rights in Jordan, at Aqaba and possibly through a leased facility near Haifa.

The historical UN partition proposal envisaged separate Arab and Jewish states with internationalized Jerusalem; the alternative here is that the military balance and British defeat produce a more explicitly Hashemite settlement. citeturn241734search7turn241734search22

### Palestine by the 1970s

I would place the war in **1974**, with the crisis building through 1973.

### Iraqi reasoning

- historically attached to the Basra province;
- an artificial British creation;
- governed by a dynasty protected by foreign arms;
- denying Iraq adequate access to the Gulf;
- withholding Arab oil wealth from the Arab national project.

The Iraqi leadership also makes several serious miscalculations.

It believes Britain remains psychologically broken by 1947. It sees London dispersed across Canada, Africa, India, the Atlantic and the Gulf. It assumes that nuclear energy has reduced Kuwait’s importance. Most importantly, Iraqi planners study the Britain of the 1950s rather than the reconstructed Commonwealth military of 1974.

The opening Iraqi operation is initially successful.

Armored and motorized formations cross the frontier, overwhelm border positions and move toward Kuwait City. Iraqi airborne or commando units attempt to seize the airport, radio stations and the ruling family. Kuwaiti units fight but cannot stop the invasion alone.

The emir formally invokes Britain’s defense guarantee.

London responds with a speed that shocks Baghdad:

- Royal Marines arrive from Gulf and Indian Ocean stations.
- RAF aircraft deploy through Bahrain, Oman, southern India and Ceylon.
- A British carrier group enters the Gulf of Oman.
- Airborne troops reinforce Kuwait City.
- Long-range aircraft attack Iraqi airfields and transport nodes.
- British and Kuwaiti forces establish a defensive line south of the city.
- Saudi Arabia permits staging and sends forces to protect Kuwait’s southern approaches.
- Iran mobilizes opposite Basra and closes the possibility of an uncontested Iraqi rear.

Britain achieves air superiority, isolates the Iraqi spearheads and begins destroying their supply columns. Iraqi forces discover that capturing desert territory is much easier than sustaining mechanized formations beneath British air and naval power.

Britain does not stop at restoring the border.

A British-Commonwealth force counterattacks into southern Iraq, takes **Umm Qasr and the Faw Peninsula**, and threatens to encircle Basra. Royal Navy and RAF strikes destroy Iraqi naval facilities, bridges, fuel stores and rail infrastructure.

The British do not need to occupy Baghdad. Once British artillery and aircraft can threaten Basra, the Iraqi government must choose between an armistice and the destruction of the country’s principal southern port and oil-export infrastructure.

This remains a limited war of perhaps six to ten weeks rather than a prolonged occupation.

### The settlement

The imposed treaty includes:

- permanent Iraqi recognition of Kuwait;
- a demilitarized border zone;
- Kuwaiti sovereignty over disputed islands and approaches;
- British basing and reinforcement rights in Kuwait;
- reparations paid through long-term oil deliveries;
- preferential contracts for British and Kuwaiti firms in southern Iraqi production;
- restrictions on Iraqi naval forces in the northern Gulf;
- a Shatt al-Arab agreement favorable to Iran;
- withdrawal of British forces from Iraqi territory once the conditions are implemented.

The oil concessions should not amount to Britain simply confiscating Iraqi fields. They are better structured as indemnities, export guarantees and forced commercial contracts. That lets London claim it fought for Kuwaiti independence while still extracting material compensation.

## What the victory does for Britain

This is precisely the sort of war Britain needs.

It is not a second world war and not a restoration of nineteenth-century supremacy. It is a clear, limited expeditionary victory in defense of a recognized client, achieved with British planning, British ships, British aircraft and Commonwealth logistics.

At home, it becomes known either as the **Kuwait Campaign** or the **Second Basra Campaign**.

Its psychological importance is greater than its territorial scale:

- Britain proves that its reconstructed armed forces work.
- The Royal Marines become national heroes.
- The RAF demonstrates global reach.
- The Royal Navy validates the Commonwealth base system.
- Britain forces a hostile regional power to retreat.
- The country experiences its first uncomplicated victory since its 1947 defeat.

The old wound does not disappear, but—as you put it—it scabs over.

Victory also helps Britain reclaim limited great-power status. America, Germany, Japan and Italy can no longer treat it merely as a defeated island serving as the administrative center of a declining empire.

## What the defeat does to Iraq

Britain wins the war but does not defeat Arab nationalism.

Instead, the defeat transforms it.

The first revolutionary government is blamed for amateurism, divided command and reckless optimism. A harder internal faction—more disciplined, more authoritarian and more security-minded—takes power after the armistice.

The new Iraqi mythology claims:

- Kuwait was preserved only by British imperial violence;
- Iran stabbed the Arab nation in the back;
- Saudi Arabia collaborated with foreigners against Arab unity;
- Jordan’s Hashemites betrayed their Iraqi cousins;
- Iraq was defeated because the Arab world was divided, not because the cause was wrong.

Thus, Britain wins the campaign and creates a much more dangerous Iraq.

By 1976, Baghdad is rebuilding its military, funding subversion in Jordan and the Gulf, cultivating Palestinian radicals and demanding the removal of every European base from Arab territory.

That is the real **Arab nationalist spring**: not an immediate wave of successful unifications, but a political awakening spreading outward from Iraq after a humiliating but mythologized defeat.

## Oil is less dominant, but still vital

Mass nuclear power substantially changes the stakes, but it does not make petroleum unimportant.

Nuclear reactors reduce the need to burn oil or coal for grid electricity and permit nuclear propulsion for the largest warships. Nevertheless, oil remains indispensable for:

- aircraft;
- automobiles and trucks;
- tanks and armored vehicles;
- most merchant shipping;
- smaller naval vessels;
- lubricants;
- plastics and chemicals;
- fertilizer feedstocks;
- export revenue and foreign exchange.

The Gulf therefore matters less as the place whose closure would immediately darken every European city. The Kuwait War is consequently fought as much for **prestige, treaty credibility, strategic geography and imperial access** as for electricity or raw barrels of oil.

## The American spaceplane system

The 1971 American lunar landing works, but one technical clarification improves it considerably:

> The spaceplane should not itself land on the Moon.

Wings and aerodynamic control surfaces are useless on the airless lunar surface and become dead mass during the translunar journey. Instead, the American system consists of:

1. A reusable spaceplane carrying crew and cargo from Earth to low orbit.
2. A reusable or semireusable orbital tug carrying the lunar mission from Earth orbit toward the Moon.
3. A dedicated lunar lander descending from lunar orbit.
4. The returning crew transferring back into the waiting spaceplane for runway recovery on Earth.

The public still calls it “the American spaceplane Moon mission,” just as a naval campaign may be named after its carrier even though aircraft perform the actual attack.

This architecture is genuinely superior to the German 1970 mission in long-term logistical terms. Germany wins the race with a powerful, calculation-heavy expendable rocket system. America arrives second but possesses reusable Earth-to-orbit transportation and the beginnings of a permanent orbital logistics network.

Historical American lifting-body experiments from 1963 through 1975 demonstrated controlled atmospheric flight and runway landing by wingless or low-wing spacecraft, while contemporary Shuttle planning explicitly envisaged a reusable vehicle carrying people and cargo to orbit and returning like an aircraft. citeturn241734search9turn443261search25

## The 1971 American lunar landing

The American mission occurs roughly seven months after Germany’s.

It does not erase the humiliation of coming second, but it changes the strategic interpretation of the race.

Germany has proven that it can reach the Moon first. America has proven that it can construct a **transportation system**.

The American crew returns to a runway rather than descending beneath parachutes in a disposable capsule. Much of the orbital equipment is retained for future missions. The lunar ferry or tug can be refueled and reused after refurbishment.

Kennedy’s aerospace program is vindicated posthumously, while Rockefeller inherits the question of what to do with it.

## Space development, 1972–1976

### 1972: operational crewed flight

The spaceplane moves beyond one- and two-pilot proving missions. Standard flights now carry:

- a commander;
- a pilot;
- one or two mission specialists;
- occasionally a payload or military specialist.

The vehicle performs satellite inspection, orbital experiments and long-duration systems tests. America begins standardizing the cargo compartment and orbital docking equipment.

A second lunar expedition may occur, but the administration does not authorize a permanent base.

### 1973: routine cargo deployment

A dedicated cargo configuration enters service. Some missions carry only two crewmen; others are fully automated developmental flights.

The spaceplane begins launching:

- weather satellites;
- communications satellites;
- reconnaissance systems;
- ocean-surveillance satellites;
- navigation prototypes;
- scientific observatories.

The vehicle also retrieves failed or experimental satellites. American engineers increasingly design satellites to be repaired, refueled or returned rather than simply abandoned.

Historical Shuttle studies already contemplated satellite deployment, retrieval, refurbishment and reusable payloads, so an accelerated American program reaching these functions by the mid-1970s is reasonable in this timeline. citeturn443261search19turn443261search22

### 1974: automated orbital flight

The United States conducts its first completely uncrewed orbital spaceplane mission.

Ground control and onboard computers manage:

- launch sequencing;
- orbital insertion;
- navigation;
- cargo deployment;
- deorbit;
- atmospheric entry;
- approach;
- runway landing.

This is technologically ambitious but supportable within the setting’s accelerated computing and reusable-flight program. NASA was historically conducting automatic unpowered approach-and-landing research by 1975, including dozens of automatic approaches using digital flight-control computers. citeturn443261search0

The military immediately sees the value. Automated flights can risk vehicles without risking trained astronauts and can launch sensitive reconnaissance payloads without a large crew.

### 1975: the orbital network

The spaceplane is no longer merely a prestige craft. It becomes the service vehicle for an expanding American orbital infrastructure.

The United States establishes the first elements of:

- continuous hemispheric communications;
- improved hurricane and weather surveillance;
- military navigation;
- global ship tracking;
- electronic-intelligence collection;
- early warning against conventional missile attack;
- orbital reconnaissance of German, Japanese and Latin-bloc bases.

These systems cannot locate deeply submerged German U-boats directly, but they can observe submarine bases, tenders, communications ships, patrol aircraft and unusual naval movements.

Lunar activity concentrates on reconnaissance rather than settlement. Automated landers survey possible base sites, test long-duration power systems and cache supplies. Crewed expeditions remain occasional.

### 1976: transportation rather than exploration

By the election year, America possesses perhaps **two or three operational spaceplanes** and conducts roughly six to ten flights annually. The exact number should remain modest enough that each mission is still nationally significant but frequent enough that the program is clearly operational.

Spaceplanes have largely supplanted expendable rockets for routine small and medium payloads into low orbit. They have not eliminated rockets completely.

Expendable or partly reusable launchers remain preferable for:

- very heavy payloads;
- high geosynchronous orbit;
- deep-space probes;
- large lunar cargo;
- missions whose orbit cannot be economically reached by the spaceplane.

The orbital tug allows spaceplane-delivered cargo to reach higher orbits, but it does not repeal the energy requirements of spaceflight.

## Civilian aviation effects

The civilian consequence should not be “the invention of the autopilot.” Commercial and military aircraft already possess autopilots.

The spaceplane program instead accelerates:

- digital fly-by-wire;
- automatic landing;
- inertial and satellite navigation;
- computerized flight management;
- automatic engine control;
- fault-tolerant computers;
- electronic cockpit displays;
- terrain and weather integration.

A 1970s airliner might still carry two or three pilots because passengers, unions and regulators demand human command. Yet the aircraft can fly nearly the entire route automatically and land safely in conditions that would previously have closed the airport.

By the 1980s, American spaceflight avionics can produce civilian aircraft whose pilots supervise integrated systems rather than manually controlling every stage of flight.

## Why no lunar base yet?

Rockefeller has no clear political incentive to spend heavily upon a permanent settlement.

America has already answered Germany’s landing, Congress remains divided, Cuba is fortifying, submarine defense is expensive and National Renewal controls much of the domestic political initiative.

Between 1972 and 1976, the space agency therefore does the less dramatic but more useful work:

- mapping landing sites;
- testing automated cargo delivery;
- studying lunar dust and construction;
- developing closed life-support systems;
- testing compact reactors;
- building Earth-orbit infrastructure;
- proving reusable operations.

By 1976, America is technically capable of beginning a permanent lunar outpost but has not made the political decision.

That becomes an obvious election issue. Buchanan can argue that Rockefeller has built “a railway to the Moon and refused to lay the final mile.” The Democratic-Republicans can answer that orbital communications, navigation and surveillance are more valuable than planting another flag beside an expensive hut.

## The mid-1970s Middle East and space in one chronology

**1947–1951:** Britain loses Egypt but retains Gulf interests. Palestine descends into war. A reduced Israel survives; Jordan annexes Arab Palestine and Jerusalem.

**1950s–1960s:** Egypt remains an Italian-influenced monarchy or conservative military-monarchical state. Syria remains within Italy’s sphere. Hashemite Iraq cultivates Arab leadership but fails to fulfill it.

**1968–1970:** A delayed Iraqi revolution overthrows Faisal II and establishes the Arab National Republic.

**1970:** Germany lands the first man on the Moon.

**1971:** America lands a crew through its reusable spaceplane–orbital tug–lunar lander system.

**1972–1973:** Iraq becomes the ideological center of Arab restoration. America operationalizes crewed and cargo spaceplane flights. Tension rises around Kuwait.

**1974:** Iraq invades Kuwait. Britain drives it out, enters southern Iraq and imposes the Basra settlement. America flies its first fully automated orbital mission.

**1975:** A harder Iraqi regime consolidates after defeat. British confidence revives. Arab nationalism spreads underground through Jordan, Palestine, Syria and the Gulf. America builds orbital satellite networks and surveys lunar-base sites.

**1976:** The Middle East is temporarily stable but sharply polarized among Baghdad, the Saudi-Gulf monarchies, Iran, Britain, Italy and the Hashemite Jordanian order. America possesses the world’s most advanced reusable space transportation system but still lacks a permanent lunar presence.

The larger pattern matches the rest of 1972–1976:

> **The great powers are not conquering new continents. They are constructing the military, industrial and ideological systems from which the next age of wars will emerge.**

The most coherent chronology is therefore:

- Britain’s continued occupation of Kuwait;
- any attempt by either power to determine Kuwait’s future without an Arab settlement.

Privately, Saudi Arabia helps Britain and the Kuwaiti administration in limited but important ways.

It closes the frontier to Iraqi infiltrators and supply movements. It mobilizes near the Kuwait–Saudi border, forcing Iraq to guard its southern flank. It quietly shares information gathered by tribal networks, merchants, and Japanese-supported communications systems. British aircraft in distress may receive emergency landing rights, although Britain is denied public basing privileges.

Saudi commercial firms provide fuel, water, vehicles, and medical supplies through intermediaries. Selected Kuwaiti tribal and security formations receive Saudi assistance. Saudi troops may occupy disputed border posts or the old Neutral Zone under the pretext of preventing the war from spreading.

Riyadh avoids direct offensive operations against Iraqi formations unless Iraqi troops cross into Saudi territory.

Britain understands what the Saudis are doing. The Saudis understand that Britain understands. Neither government publicly acknowledges cooperation.

## The British campaign

The war might unfold in four stages.

### Iraqi opening success

Iraq crosses the frontier with several mechanized divisions, takes northern defensive positions, and advances toward Kuwait City and the British installations.

The local Kuwaiti forces are too small to stop them. British advisers organize delaying actions while the emir and administration remain in Kuwait City or relocate temporarily to a secure British base.

Iraqi propaganda declares the restoration of the Province of Kuwait.

### British containment

RAF units arrive from Bahrain, Qatar, Aden, and Indian Ocean stations. Royal Marines and airborne troops secure Kuwait City, the airport, ports, and oil facilities. The Royal Navy closes the northern Gulf.

The Iraqi advance slows because of poor logistics, British air attack, demolitions, and resistance around prepared installations.

Saudi mobilization prevents Iraq from widening the front southward.

### Counteroffensive

British and Commonwealth troops counterattack northward. Rather than a single effortless armored sweep, the campaign involves several difficult actions around roads, oil installations, defensive berms, and urban approaches.

The Iraqis fight effectively in some prepared positions. Elsewhere, formations collapse when fuel, communications, or senior headquarters are destroyed.

Britain clears Kuwait and crosses into Iraq.

### Limited invasion of southern Iraq

Britain takes or isolates Umm Qasr, the Faw Peninsula, and perhaps Safwan. RAF and naval strikes threaten Basra’s port, bridges, oil terminals, and rail connections.

London does not seek to overthrow the Iraqi government. The objective is to force Baghdad to accept terms and demonstrate that another invasion will place Basra itself at risk.

The campaign lasts weeks or perhaps several months—not days—but ends in a clear British operational victory.

## The settlement

Because Kuwait is not independent, the treaty cannot require Iraq to recognize a sovereign Kuwaiti republic.

Instead, the armistice imposes:

- Iraqi recognition of the established Kuwait boundary;
- Iraqi renunciation of force for a defined period, perhaps twenty-five years;
- a demilitarized strip north of the frontier;
- British inspection or surveillance rights;
- reparations through oil deliveries and commercial concessions;
- restrictions on Iraqi naval forces near the northern Gulf;
- British retention of its bases and protective treaty with the emir;
- exchange of prisoners and withdrawal from southern Iraq.

Iraq may carefully avoid recognizing Britain’s permanent *right* to rule Kuwait. It recognizes only the existing boundary and agrees not to alter it by force.

That allows Baghdad to sign the treaty while later claiming that the national question remains open.

## Saudi diplomacy after the war

The moment Iraq is defeated, Saudi policy turns sharply against Britain.

Riyadh demands:

- withdrawal of temporary British reinforcements;
- reduction of the permanent British garrison;
- Arabization of Kuwait’s officer corps and administration;
- an eventual conference on the status of the Gulf protectorates;
- guarantees that Britain will not transform Kuwait into a platform for attacks on other Arab states.

Saudi Arabia presents itself as the power that prevented both Iraqi annexation and indefinite British military expansion.

The British government knows this is opportunistic. London may nevertheless grant limited cosmetic concessions because it needs Saudi neutrality more than it needs Saudi friendship.

Kuwait receives more internal autonomy, a larger local army, and perhaps a consultative council. Britain retains defense and foreign affairs.

Thus, the British victory slightly loosens the imperial system without ending it.

## Who claims victory?

Britain possesses the only unambiguous military victory.

But politically, everyone constructs a partial victory.

Britain says it defeated aggression and proved the restored Commonwealth can defend its obligations.

The Kuwaiti emir says his dynasty and people survived both annexation and war.

Saudi Arabia says it prevented a revolutionary Iraqi empire while refusing to recognize European ownership of Arab soil.

Iraq says it was defeated only because Britain, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Jordan, and the Latin bloc conspired against Arab reunification.

Jordan’s exile government says the National Socialist regime sacrificed Iraqi soldiers in a reckless foreign adventure.

Germany says the Iraqis misused German equipment and denies responsibility for the invasion.

Japan praises Saudi independence and uses the crisis to argue that only Asian and Arab solidarity can end European rule without replacing it with Baghdad’s tyranny.

## The strategic consequences

The war heals part of Britain’s psychological wound while deepening its Middle Eastern problem.

Britain has proven that:

- its surface fleet remains useful;
- its expeditionary army can fight;
- its Commonwealth logistics system works;
- its aircraft can sustain distant operations;
- German weapons do not guarantee German-quality performance.

But Britain has also revealed that nearly every regional actor opposes its Gulf system.

Saudi Arabia helped it only because Iraq was worse. Iran cooperated because Iraqi expansion threatened the Gulf balance. Jordan assisted because the Iraqi regime had overthrown the Hashemites. The Kuwaiti dynasty supports Britain because London guarantees its survival.

There is no deep pro-British coalition.

The imperial structure remains standing, but it now resembles a fortress held together by local rulers who fear their neighbors more than they resent London.

## The stronger ideological triangle

By 1975–76, the region therefore has three Arab positions:

**National Socialist Iraq:** Kuwait must be restored to the Arab Iraqi nation, and the monarchies must eventually be swept away.

**Saudi Arabia:** all European control of Arabia is illegitimate, but Arab territories must not be swallowed by a revolutionary centralized Iraq.

**Hashemite Jordan and the Iraqi government in exile:** Arab unity must come through legitimate monarchy and federation, not either British protectorates or National Socialist conquest.

Britain is opposed by all three but remains indispensable to two of them.

That is the core irony of the Kuwait War:

> **Saudi Arabia assists Britain in preserving a territory that Saudi Arabia itself eventually intends to take from Britain.**

The war is therefore a British victory, an Iraqi humiliation, a Saudi diplomatic maneuver, and the beginning—not the end—of the struggle over Britain’s Arabian empire.

The German program should **not** simply be NASA beginning in 1945 with a twelve-year head start. The stronger path is:

> Germany begins ahead, wastes several years pursuing military boost-glide weapons, adopts von Braun’s grandiose station-first architecture, suffers one major heavy-launch disaster, and reaches the Moon in 1970 with a much deeper orbital infrastructure than Apollo—but without America’s reusable spaceplane.

That preserves German technical leadership while explaining why it does not land someone on the Moon in 1962.

## First: the A9/A10 should not be operational in 1947

A complete, dependable A9/A10 system before the war ends is too ambitious.

The actual A9 lineage had barely entered flight testing. The A4b—essentially the winged A9 under a designation that protected its priority—first flew in December 1944 and crashed after its guidance failed. A second flight in January 1945 reached roughly Mach 4 and demonstrated controlled ascent, but a wing failed when it entered the glide phase. The larger A10 booster remained much further from an operational vehicle. citeturn758648view0

By the end of 1947, this Germany can realistically possess:

- a mature A4/V-2 family;
- a substantially improved A4b/A9 with successful boost-glide tests;
- full-scale A10 structural articles;
- clustered-engine and large-combustion-chamber static tests;
- advanced staging, guidance and telemetry experiments;
- no dependable transatlantic operational A9/A10 yet.

The uninterrupted program matters enormously, but **uninterrupted does not mean unhindered**. Germany remains at war until 1947, with bombing damage, competing weapons priorities, raw-material shortages, transportation problems and pressure to field weapons immediately.

I would put the first complete A9/A10 test around **1949–1950**, not 1947. It achieves something approximating transatlantic range, but its accuracy and reliability are poor. It becomes an impressive demonstration and an engineering bridge, not an economical weapon.

Without nuclear warheads, an intercontinental missile carrying one or two tons of conventional explosive is a spectacularly expensive way to destroy one building. This deprives Germany of the same urgent ICBM-to-space-launcher pipeline that drove much real-world Cold War rocketry.

## Von Braun does eventually become undisputed—but not immediately

During the war, von Braun was technical director, while Walter Dornberger was the military director and institutional patron. That division should continue through the immediate postwar years. The historical Peenemünde program was already an enormous organization rather than the product of one solitary inventor. citeturn931061view1

A believable leadership progression would be:

**1945–1952:** Dornberger remains overall military director. Von Braun controls technical design but does not control budgets, military requirements or production priorities.

**1952–1958:** The missile and space programs begin separating. Dornberger becomes the senior ministerial and procurement figure, while von Braun becomes director-general of heavy rockets and orbital development.

**After the first satellite:** Von Braun’s prestige becomes politically untouchable. Dornberger retires upward into an honorary or advisory office, and von Braun becomes president of a consolidated **Reichsraumfahrtamt**, or equivalent.

**During the regency:** Competing military, SS, industrial and party bodies attempt to seize pieces of the program. Von Braun’s technical authority is made formally supreme because the regents cannot agree upon anyone else. He becomes one of the few figures whose personal prestige transcends the factions.

“Undisputed head” should therefore mean that von Braun possesses the final architectural veto—not that he personally designs every engine, guidance package and spacecraft.

## Von Braun was not really a laboratory recluse

One correction to the characterization: von Braun was unusually effective as a public advocate.

He wrote extensively for popular audiences, promoted spaceflight through *Collier’s*, appeared in Walt Disney television programs and became one of America’s most visible scientific celebrities. NASA’s own history describes him as both a major rocket developer and a prominent champion of space exploration. citeturn931061view0turn915940view2

He was less a bench scientist by the 1950s than:

- a systems architect;
- an engineering manager;
- a political advocate;
- a budgetary strategist;
- a public evangelist for spaceflight.

In this Reich, he would probably dislike compulsory provincial tours, party banquets and theatrical rallies. But he would understand perfectly that publicity protects his program.

His preferred public role would be carefully controlled:

- illustrated lectures;
- technical documentaries;
- school broadcasts;
- interviews beside models;
- explanations of orbital mechanics;
- occasional appearances with Hitler’s son or the regency;
- little direct partisan or ideological polemic.

He would allow the regime to make him a hero because that heroism purchases rockets.

After 1970, he becomes something close to a national scientific patriarch: decorated, given the highest civil honors, placed on postage stamps and schoolroom portraits, and called upon to explain that the Moon is only the beginning.

## His grandiosity is one of the reasons the Moon takes until 1970

Von Braun historically imagined spaceflight as an ascending system:

1. large launch vehicles;
2. an orbital station;
3. reusable or semireusable ferry craft;
4. lunar expeditions;
5. permanent lunar activity;
6. Mars.

His popular plans emphasized a wheel-shaped station and elaborate lunar expeditions rather than a minimalist one-off landing. His original Mars study was similarly vast, treating an interplanetary expedition as a fleet operation rather than one small spacecraft. citeturn915940view2turn394408search0

If he has final authority, Germany initially rejects the cheapest “flags and footprints” route.

Von Braun’s preferred lunar architecture is based upon **Earth-orbit assembly**:

- launch crew vehicle separately;
- launch lunar ship components separately;
- assemble and fuel them beside an orbital station;
- send a substantial expedition rather than a tiny direct-ascent capsule;
- retain equipment that can support later missions.

This is technologically richer but slower.

America later chooses its spaceplane system because it wants frequent, reusable access to orbit. Germany builds an orbital harbor because von Braun wants the Moon and Mars to become destinations in a permanent transport network.

Neither side simply duplicates Apollo.

The German program would contain several recognizable courts within the larger von Braun establishment.

Rees is the practical manager who turns von Braun’s ambitions into hardware. In this setting, Rees is:

- deputy director of the entire program;
- head of systems integration;
- the man who tells von Braun which dreams cannot yet be built;
- von Braun’s likely successor after retirement or death.

Von Braun is the architect. Rees is the master builder.

Debus historically specialized in test stands, electrical installations, guidance support and launch operations. He later became the first director of Kennedy Space Center. citeturn915940view3

Here he runs:

- Peenemünde launch operations;
- construction of the postwar operational spaceport;
- countdown and range safety;
- mobile and fixed launch infrastructure;
- astronaut-launch integration.

By the 1960s, Debus is effectively lord of the launch range.

Stuhlinger began in guidance and control, later organized space-science work and became chief scientist within von Braun’s organization. citeturn931061view2

His alternate role should include:

- scientific satellites;
- radiation and upper-atmosphere studies;
- space medicine;
- nuclear-electric propulsion;
- ion engines;
- Mars probes;
- long-duration station science.

He is one of the figures who turns the program from a missile enterprise into an actual scientific establishment.

Gröttrup was a Peenemünde guidance-and-control expert historically taken into the Soviet program. With no Soviet occupation of Germany, he remains inside the Reich and becomes one of the central links between rocketry and German computing. citeturn167380search0

- inertial guidance;
- digital flight control;
- telemetry;
- onboard calculation;
- ground tracking networks;
- automated rendezvous;
- military payload integration.

Rudolph remains the industrial-production organizer, including the morally darkest side of mass production and coerced labor.

Dannenberg becomes a major propulsion and stage-integration figure. Historically he helped develop Redstone and Jupiter and later served as deputy manager of Saturn. citeturn167380search5

Ehricke becomes the younger visionary who pushes beyond von Braun’s already ambitious program. He was historically both a propulsion engineer and a prominent philosopher of astronautics and space colonization. citeturn915940view5

- industrial activity in orbit;
- permanent lunar settlements;

Oberth is not running engineering teams by the 1960s. He is the revered founder, theoretician and ceremonial intellectual ancestor.

## The space-program geography

Germany should eventually operate three distinct layers of facilities.

### Peenemünde

Peenemünde remains the sacred birthplace and principal research complex:

- propulsion laboratories;
- aerodynamic facilities;
- guidance research;
- prototype assembly;
- training;
- early launch tests;
- public museum and ceremonial center by the 1960s.

The first successful A4 launch on **3 October 1942** becomes retrospectively celebrated as the beginning of the German space age. The actual A4 first flew successfully on that date. citeturn931061view1

Peenemünde is not ideal for every orbital mission. Germany possesses an enormous conquered eastern interior, so the operational heavy-launch center should be built in the sparsely populated **Kalmyk–Lower Volga steppe**, perhaps between Elista and Astrakhan.

This gives Germany:

- large exclusion zones;
- eastward launch corridors;
- room for falling stages;
- secrecy;
- rail connections to the industrial west;
- distance from foreign observation;
- access to Caspian tracking stations.

Its official name can remain bureaucratic—something like **Reichsversuchsstelle Wolga**—while foreigners call it the Volga Spaceport.

The moral dimension matters. Its construction involves deportation, coerced labor and the clearing of local populations. The gleaming center of German space triumph is built inside the colonial east.

### Imperial tracking stations

The Reich establishes telemetry, radio and observation stations across:

- Norway and the Arctic;
- Iceland after German entry;
- the Caucasus;
- equatorial Africa;
- Atlantic islands;
- Indian Ocean territories or friendly facilities.

The African sites are primarily tracking and communications installations, avoiding the geographical awkwardness of a major west-coast African launch complex.

## A canon-ready German chronology

### 1945–1947: the extended weapons phase

The A4 family continues improving throughout the final war years.

The A4b/A9 receives better guidance, stronger wings and improved reentry control. The A10 remains a ground-development project involving large engines, clustering, tanks and staging.

By the 1947 armistice, Germany has not flown an operational transatlantic missile, but it has solved enough of the underlying problems that continued development is inevitable.

Von Braun privately begins circulating plans for:

- satellites;
- orbital observatories;
- crew capsules;
- stations;
- lunar expeditions.

The military regards most of this as postwar fantasy.

### 1948–1951: A9/A10 culmination

**1948:** A successful A9 boost-glide flight demonstrates controlled high-speed atmospheric return over several hundred miles.

**1949:** The first A10 booster flight tests clustered propulsion and stage separation. It does not carry a live A9.

**1950:** The first complete A9/A10 vehicle flies. It achieves extreme range but misses its intended impact zone badly and suffers structural damage during the A9 glide.

**1951:** A second integrated test succeeds well enough to prove the concept but confirms that the weapon is extravagantly costly for its conventional payload.

The military retains a small long-range-missile program. Von Braun takes the large-stage technology into orbital development.

The A9/A10 is therefore **not Germany’s Saturn**. It is the bridge that teaches staging, high-speed reentry, large propulsion and guidance.

### 1952–1956: the hidden orbital program

The Reich creates a dual establishment:

- a classified military missile directorate;
- a nominally scientific orbital office under von Braun.

Germany develops a new postwar launch-vehicle nomenclature rather than pretending that A11 and A12 were already finished designs. I recommend technical designations such as:

- **Raumträger I**
- **Raumträger II**
- **Raumträger III**

Propaganda nicknames can be assigned later.

The early launchers use:

- alcohol/LOX and later kerosene/LOX lower stages;
- clusters of proven engines;
- small solid or liquid upper stages;
- increasingly digital guidance.

Germany launches sounding rockets, recoverable biological payloads and high-altitude cameras, but says little publicly.

A satellite by 1957 is entirely plausible. Stuhlinger later recalled that the displaced historical von Braun team believed it could have launched a satellite in 1956 had it received authorization; the team had a suitable modified rocket in readiness well before Explorer 1. citeturn915940view1turn931061view3

Germany’s date is therefore restrained rather than excessively early.

### 3 October 1957: the first satellite

Germany launches **Sternbote I** on the fifteenth anniversary of the first successful A4.

This is the first launch announced live or near-live to the world. All earlier heavy-rocket tests were military secrets or announced only after the fact.

Sternbote is modest:

- radio transmitter;
- temperature and pressure instruments;
- radiation detector;
- perhaps 80–150 kilograms;
- elliptical orbit.

The propaganda effect is immense.

The date becomes **German Spaceflight Day**, although the regime deemphasizes that the historical path began with bombardment weapons and forced labor.

### 1958–1960: satellites and recovery

**1958:** Weather, communications and photographic-reconnaissance satellites follow. The reconnaissance purpose remains classified.

**1959:** Germany places an animal capsule in orbit and successfully recovers it.

**1960:** A German pilot completes a suborbital flight in a ballistic capsule. The flight is announced only after recovery.

Germany begins construction of the full Lower Volga space center and commits to human orbital operations.

### 1961: first person in orbit

Germany places the first human into orbit in **1961**.

The spacecraft is small, heavily automated and intended more as proof of national mastery than as a pilot-controlled vehicle.

This should be another universally remembered event, but it is culturally subordinate to the Moon landing. The astronaut becomes a major celebrity, though never as central to the program’s mythology as von Braun.

### 1962–1963: regency disruption

Hitler’s incapacity or death creates a bureaucratic struggle over the program.

The Luftwaffe wants military control. The Navy wants reconnaissance and ocean-surveillance satellites. The SS wants an ideologically reliable directorate. Industrial ministries want commercial and nuclear applications. The party wants prestige spectacles.

For roughly eighteen months, large-project approvals slow.

The compromise is to make von Braun formally supreme as **President of the Reich Space Office**, with separate military customers purchasing services from his organization.

This is the moment he becomes genuinely undisputed.

### 1963–1965: orbital technique

Germany deliberately masters the techniques required by von Braun’s architecture.

**1963:** Multi-person and multi-day orbital mission.

**1964:** First rendezvous and docking between separately launched vehicles.

**1965:** First German extravehicular activity and first long-duration orbital laboratory module.

Germany also sends increasingly capable robotic probes toward Venus and Mars. Von Braun had begun writing his detailed Mars concepts in the late 1940s and consistently treated Mars as the eventual objective. citeturn394408search0turn394408search2

Germany assembles its first genuine modular orbital station in early 1966.

It is not von Braun’s enormous rotating wheel. It is a narrow cylindrical complex with:

- two or three modules;
- three-person crew;
- ninety-day endurance;
- docking ports;
- optical and radar observation systems;
- military and scientific sections.

Later in 1966, the first full lunar-class **Raumträger III** is destroyed during a static firing or fueled launch rehearsal at the Lower Volga complex.

A turbopump or combustion-instability failure triggers a cascading propellant explosion. The launch stand is destroyed, dozens of engineers and workers are killed, and the only lunar-capable pad is rendered unusable.

Von Braun survives because he is in the remote control bunker.

The regime announces a “serious industrial accident” but suppresses:

- the full casualty count;
- the number of coerced eastern workers killed;
- the lunar purpose of the vehicle;
- the degree to which launch management had been pressured to meet a political date.

The disaster delays the Moon program by approximately eighteen to twenty-four months. Without it, Germany might plausibly attempt a landing in 1968.

It also allows von Braun and Rees to impose a much stricter centralized safety and systems-management regime.

### 1967–1968: robotic Moon and circumlunar flight

**1967:** Germany successfully soft-lands an automated craft on the Moon and returns close imagery. A later mission returns a small sample robotically.

**1968:** A German crew circles the Moon and returns.

This is the first time human beings see the far side directly. The mission is publicly triumphant but produces enormous internal pressure: America’s spaceplane is approaching operational status, and the regency demands a landing before the United States can steal the prestige prize.

### 1969: lunar orbit and American spaceplane shock

Germany conducts:

- a crewed lunar-orbit mission;
- a full unmanned landing rehearsal;
- orbital assembly and refueling tests;
- final validation of the lunar lander.

America achieves its first orbital spaceplane flight in 1969.

This profoundly disturbs von Braun. Germany is still ahead in heavy lift, stations and lunar operations, but America has demonstrated the beginnings of routine reusable Earth-to-orbit transportation.

The contest is no longer simply “who reaches the Moon.” It is now between two architectures.

### 20 December 1970: the German Moon landing

I would fix the first German landing to **20 December 1970**.

That permits the American landing to occur on **20 July 1971**, preserving the established seven-month gap exactly.

The German mission consists of:

- three crewmen;
- one remaining in lunar orbit;
- two descending;
- one or two surface excursions;
- scientific equipment;
- a German flag and Reich banner;
- extensive film and live radio;
- the infamous salute beside the swastika.

The lunar ship has been assembled or at least fueled using multiple launches and orbital infrastructure. It is less elegant than Apollo but leaves more equipment in useful orbit.

The event is the absolute summit of German postwar prestige.

## What Germany does after the landing

Von Braun does not regard the landing as completion.

### 1971–1972

Germany conducts follow-up expeditions with:

- longer surface stays;
- a rover;
- improved geological equipment;
- unmanned cargo landers;
- experiments in nuclear surface power.

### 1973–1974

A small prefabricated lunar shelter is emplaced.

This is not yet a permanently occupied base. It is a **seasonal outpost** used for missions lasting several weeks or months. Supplies and equipment remain between expeditions.

Germany also expands its orbital station and experiments with nuclear-electric tugs under Stuhlinger’s influence.

### 1975–1976

Germany possesses:

- expendable heavy lift;
- an established orbital station;
- rendezvous and orbital assembly experience;
- a periodically occupied lunar outpost;
- sophisticated robotic Mars and Venus probes;
- a formal study for a crewed Mars expedition in the late 1980s or early 1990s.

America possesses:

- reusable spaceplanes;
- higher potential flight frequency;
- better satellite deployment and servicing;
- automated runway-return technology;
- a transportation system that may eventually become cheaper than Germany’s rockets.

Thus Germany wins the first age of spaceflight, while America may be building the system that wins the second.

## What the public knows—and what it does not

The German public knows:

- 3 October 1942 as the ancestral rocket date;
- 3 October 1957 as the first satellite;
- the first German in orbit;
- the first orbital station;
- the 1968 circumlunar mission;
- 20 December 1970 as the Moon landing.

It does not know:

- how many orbital launches failed before Sternbote;
- the actual military satellite program;
- the precision of German long-range missiles;
- the full 1966 disaster;
- the use of forced and coerced labor;
- the scale of orbital ocean surveillance;
- how much the space and submarine missile programs share;
- which “scientific” spacecraft are military reconnaissance systems.

Germany announces launches once success is assured. Its program therefore appears almost uncannily reliable compared with the publicly visible American program.

## Von Braun’s final position

After the Moon landing, von Braun is at the height of his authority.

He is useful to the regency because he embodies continuity:

- he served Hitler’s wartime state;
- survived the transition into imperial victory;
- built the postwar technical order;
- now stands beside Hitler’s son as proof that the Reich’s destiny continues beyond its founder.

But he is not merely a propaganda puppet. His technical establishment has become one of the Reich’s internal powers, comparable to the military, party bureaucracy and major industrial combines.

Historically, von Braun died in 1977. Keeping approximately the same health trajectory works well. He sees the Moon landing, directs the first post-lunar phase, retires or becomes honorary president around 1974–75, and dies in **1977 or 1978**. citeturn931061view0

Rees succeeds him operationally. Ehricke becomes the leading public advocate of expansion. Stuhlinger controls advanced science and propulsion. The regime turns von Braun into a permanent national myth.

There is also no American denazification or reinvention of his biography in this world. His historical involvement with, knowledge of and benefit from the forced-labor system remains embedded in his career, and the victorious Reich has no reason to conceal it domestically as wrongdoing—only to sanitize it for foreign audiences. citeturn931061view0turn931061view1

The finished German story is therefore not simply “von Braun was allowed to pursue his dream.”

It is:

> **Von Braun converts the Reich’s most terrible wartime weapon into the machinery of planetary expansion, becomes one of the regime’s greatest heroes, and reaches the Moon—while carrying the institutions, labor system and moral compromises of Peenemünde with him all the way there.**
