iturn789923image0turn789923image1turn789923image2turn789923image4

The Falklands War should become the moment when Britain discovers that **winning at Kuwait did not prove that the Commonwealth expeditionary system could defeat a mature peer-equipped state at the far end of the Atlantic**.

Kuwait was a difficult but favorable war:

- Britain possessed nearby bases and regional allies.
- Iraq had only recently received its German systems.
- Iraqi maintenance, staff work, and combined-arms coordination were poor.
- Britain could threaten Basra and force a decision on land.

Argentina is almost the opposite case. It has spent fifteen years building its forces around German equipment, developing licensed production, training technicians, and planning for one specific theater. It fights close to its own airfields against a British fleet operating thousands of miles from home. The setting already establishes Argentina as a sovereign but overwhelmingly German-equipped arsenal state, while Britain has fortified the Falklands since the Atlantic Accord and rebuilt itself as the command-and-design center of the wider Commonwealth. fileciteturn25file0 fileciteturn25file1

The war therefore should not be a seventy-four-day expedition. By Reagan’s inauguration on **January 20, 1985**, it is a genuine, unresolved regional war.

# First: Operation Torch is the correct British analogy

We have already established that Operation Torch either fails or never secures a durable Western return to the European theater. Normandy remains less definite—it may never be attempted in recognizable form, or may fail to produce a continental foothold.

British critics can therefore speak of:

> **“A second Torch in the South Atlantic.”**

They mean a politically ordered amphibious operation conducted at the limits of British air cover, against an enemy whose strength has been underestimated, because the government believes prestige requires a landing.

That phrase becomes bitterly relevant after Britain’s first failed attempt to establish a major East Falkland beachhead.

# The long buildup, 1975–1983

Argentina does not suddenly decide to invade in a fit of desperation.

The Falklands become its principal long-range national military project.

## Argentina’s argument

The public Argentine case rests upon four claims:

1. Britain seized the islands from an existing Argentine settlement in 1833.
2. The islands sit upon Argentina’s continental and maritime approaches.
3. Britain has lost nearly every convincing basis for claiming a civilizing or strategic necessity in South America.
4. The Atlantic Accord itself recognizes that the Americas form a distinct strategic hemisphere.

Buenos Aires therefore argues that Britain is trying to preserve an imperial exception that neither Washington nor Argentina would tolerate from Germany, Italy, or Japan.

Argentine propaganda carefully avoids describing the islanders as a legitimate separate people possessing an unlimited veto. They are described as:

- British settlers;
- a transplanted colonial population;
- residents whose property and local customs will be protected;
- but not a nation capable of transferring sovereignty away from Argentina.

## Britain’s argument

Britain’s public case is simpler:

- the islanders overwhelmingly want to remain British;
- London cannot transfer citizens against their will;
- surrender under military threat would imperil every remaining Commonwealth possession;
- Argentina’s German armament makes the dispute part of the wider Atlantic balance.

Privately, British officials understand that the islands are extremely difficult to defend indefinitely. In real history, British governments considered negotiations and leaseback in part because officials judged that stopping a determined Argentine attack would require an expensive diversion of military resources. citeturn461201view0

Alternate Britain has responded to that danger more aggressively than historical Britain, but not enough to create an impregnable fortress.

## The British garrison before invasion

By early 1984, the islands possess approximately:

- 800–1,000 regular British and Commonwealth personnel;
- 200–300 local defense volunteers and reservists;
- coastal and air-search radar;
- several short-range air-defense batteries;
- helicopters and light reconnaissance aircraft;
- a small number of vertical-takeoff fighters deployed rotationally;
- two patrol vessels;
- prepared demolitions and coastal observation posts;
- a runway improved enough for transports and patrol aircraft, but not a sustained major fast-jet force.

This is far stronger than the historical Royal Marine detachment.

It is still too small to defeat an Argentine operation involving ten or fifteen thousand troops, overwhelming local air power, submarines, naval missiles, and airborne reinforcement.

The British deterrent rests upon the belief that Argentina will not risk the Royal Navy’s eventual arrival.

That belief is the central miscalculation.

# The Argentine military project

Argentina’s armed forces are not German formations wearing Argentine badges.

They have their own weaknesses:

- interservice rivalry;
- politicized senior appointments;
- uneven conscript quality;
- maintenance bottlenecks;
- exaggerated confidence;
- dependence upon German components and technical assistance.

But by 1984 they are no longer Iraq with unfamiliar German equipment.

Argentina has:

- licensed German-pattern rifles, radios, trucks, and armored vehicles;
- aircraft crews trained for maritime strike;
- shore-based anti-ship missiles;
- a German-built light missile cruiser;
- several older but quiet German U-boats;
- mobile air-defense batteries;
- night-vision equipment;
- modern artillery fire-direction computers;
- engineers who have rehearsed rapid airfield construction;
- fifteen years of institutional experience with German maintenance doctrine.

Most importantly, the Malvinas mission gives the force cohesion.

An Argentine infantryman may dislike his officers, government, or living conditions. He nevertheless broadly believes that the islands belong to Argentina.

Britain is confronting troops who believe they are liberating national territory, not merely preserving a client dictator.

# The final diplomatic cycle

I would give the crisis three failed settlement attempts.

## The Lisbon talks, 1981–1982

Portugal serves as a useful intermediary because it belongs loosely to the Latin bloc, retains old connections with Britain, and does not want either Germany or Spain dominating South American diplomacy.

Britain offers:

- expanded Argentine commercial access;
- shared fisheries;
- joint petroleum and seabed exploration;
- easier travel;
- eventual discussions concerning dependencies.

Argentina demands an explicit sovereignty timetable.

The talks fail.

## The Rio formula, 1983

Brazil, supported by Buchanan’s administration and the Vatican, proposes:

- joint administration for twenty years;
- Argentine symbols and representation on the islands;
- British responsibility for local law and islander rights;
- demilitarization;
- shared resources;
- a final sovereignty conference after the transitional period.

The islanders reject it because it places them upon a road whose probable destination is Argentine sovereignty.

The Argentine military rejects it because twenty more years of discussion appears indistinguishable from indefinite delay.

## The Argentine final initiative

In late 1983, Buenos Aires announces that negotiations must produce a transfer framework by **March 31, 1984**.

Britain offers renewed talks, economic concessions, and perhaps a form of nominal condominium—but refuses to set a transfer date without islander consent.

Argentina concludes that Britain intends to negotiate forever while extending the runway, improving air defenses, and making invasion progressively harder.

German diplomats recommend restraint publicly. German firms quietly accelerate deliveries of spares, electronics, runway equipment, and maritime stores.

# The invasion: April 1984

Argentina does not issue a traditional declaration of war.

That would concede that it is attacking foreign territory and would strengthen Britain’s legal argument for strikes against Argentina itself.

Instead, Buenos Aires announces a **recovery operation**.

The final Argentine diplomatic note is delivered in London almost simultaneously with the opening of military operations. It declares that:

- Argentine sovereignty is being restored;
- British forces will be treated honorably if they surrender;
- local civil administration and private property will be protected;
- Argentina does not consider itself at war with the British people;
- any British counterattack will constitute aggression against Argentine territory.

The military operation can retain the historical name:

> **Operación Rosario**

The symbolism works particularly well in this more Catholic Argentine society.

## The battle for the islands

Unlike the historical seizure, this is a real local battle lasting approximately three days.

Argentina attacks through:

- special-forces reconnaissance;
- marine landings;
- airborne seizure of key ground;
- suppression of British radar and communications;
- naval blockade;
- strikes against the airfield and defensive positions.

The British garrison fights effectively and inflicts meaningful losses.

Argentina avoids unrestricted bombardment of Stanley because it expects to govern the island and wants an intact airfield. British defenders withdraw toward prepared positions, but once Argentine troops threaten to divide the garrison and artillery begins ranging the civilian settlement, the governor authorizes surrender.

The outcome gives both sides an enduring story.

Argentina remembers:

> The armed forces recovered the islands in combat.

Britain remembers:

> The garrison was overwhelmed, not dishonored.

# What Argentina does after the seizure

Argentina has prepared for the British response.

Within weeks, it moves perhaps **12,000–16,000 personnel** into the islands, disproportionately concentrated on East Falkland.

The occupation force includes:

- experienced marines and mountain troops;
- engineers;
- artillery;
- mobile surface-to-air missiles;
- anti-ship batteries;
- radar and electronic-warfare teams;
- helicopter and transport units;
- military police;
- large stores of food, ammunition, fuel, and prefabricated shelter.

The runway near Stanley is lengthened and reinforced using German-designed modular systems. It still cannot become a mainland-quality air base overnight, but it can support transports, interceptors under restricted conditions, drones, reconnaissance craft, and sustained helicopter operations.

West Falkland receives a smaller force, intended to provide warning and depth rather than serve as the principal fortress.

Argentina prepares specifically for:

- British submarine blockade;
- night raids;
- amphibious landings;
- attacks upon Stanley;
- isolation of individual garrisons.

This is why the British cannot simply repeat the historical campaign at greater scale.

# Britain’s initial reaction

I recommend retaining **Margaret Thatcher** as prime minister, but as a substantially altered political figure.

She comes to power around 1980 as an Imperial Conservative and Commonwealth modernizer, not as the architect of a wholesale privatization revolution. She favors:

- disciplined public corporations;
- naval rebuilding;
- technological industry;
- fiscal restraint;
- Commonwealth cohesion;
- a hard line against further imperial retreat.

The Kuwait victory reinforces her belief that Britain has recovered the ability to use force overseas.

The Falklands reveal the limits of that conclusion.

## The original British assumption

The cabinet believes that dispatching a major task force may be sufficient.

The reasoning is:

- Argentina cannot defeat the Royal Navy;
- the economic cost of mobilization will frighten Buenos Aires;
- German support cannot become overt without violating the Atlantic Accord;
- the Argentine officer corps will seek negotiations once British carriers arrive;
- a short blockade followed by one well-chosen landing will collapse the occupation.

Every element contains some truth.

Taken together, they produce a dangerously optimistic plan.

# The task force becomes a war fleet

Britain initially dispatches:

- carriers and escorts;
- amphibious ships;
- Royal Marines and airborne troops;
- submarines;
- support and repair ships;
- requisitioned liners and cargo vessels;
- Commonwealth auxiliaries.

As losses and requirements grow, the operation expands into a broad Commonwealth mobilization.

Canada provides electronics, transport, and intelligence support but avoids a highly visible combat role because of American sensitivities.

Australia and New Zealand provide ships, crews, supplies, and replacement units, although fear of Japan limits what can be removed from the Pacific.

South Africa provides repair, airfields, fuel, weather support, and Cape transit.

Britain’s distributed Commonwealth system proves essential. It also proves slow and politically complicated.

# The operational difference from Kuwait

British commanders rapidly identify five problems.

## No nearby secure air umbrella

In Kuwait, Britain could operate from friendly bases.

In the South Atlantic, carrier aircraft must simultaneously:

- defend the fleet;
- escort strike aircraft;
- suppress Argentine positions;
- protect transports;
- patrol against submarines.

Every aircraft assigned to one mission is unavailable for another.

## Argentina controls the nearer shore

Mainland Argentine aircraft can attack, return, rearm, and fly again.

British aircraft operate from moving ships exposed to missiles, weather, and mechanical failure.

## The submarines are real

Argentina’s U-boats are not merely prestige objects.

They have trained crews, modern torpedoes, coatings, and German-derived sonar. Even unsuccessful contacts force the British fleet to maneuver, delay, and consume enormous anti-submarine resources.

## The equipment is integrated

An Argentine missile battery is not a recently delivered foreign curiosity.

It is tied to Argentine radar, doctrine, communications, and rehearsed targeting procedures.

## Argentina can replace losses

Britain must bring every replacement across the Atlantic.

Argentina must cross several hundred miles.

That is the war’s fundamental arithmetic.

# The first year of fighting

## May 1984: South Georgia

Britain retakes South Georgia.

This provides a necessary early victory and proves the task force can fight.

Argentina does not heavily defend it because the principal objective is the Falklands themselves. The British government presents the operation as the beginning of liberation.

The Argentine government presents it as a peripheral raid.

Both descriptions are partly correct.

## June: the naval approaches

The first major fleet encounters destroy the assumption of a painless blockade.

British submarines force most Argentine major surface ships close to the mainland.

Argentina responds through:

- missile aircraft;
- U-boats;
- long-range reconnaissance;
- shore-based targeting;
- small fast naval units.

Britain loses or sees badly damaged several escorts and at least one major transport or amphibious vessel.

A British carrier is damaged seriously enough to reduce flight operations, though not necessarily sunk. Sinking one immediately could make continued offensive operations nearly impossible; damaging and withdrawing one forces Britain to reinforce rather than simply abandon the campaign.

Argentina also loses aircraft, ships, and at least one submarine. Its missile cruiser survives by remaining close enough to mainland air cover that Britain cannot attack it without appearing to expand the war.

## July: the first East Falkland landing

The government presses for an early landing in the San Carlos region or another sheltered western inlet.

The location is geographically sensible. Argentina has anticipated it.

British landing craft enter under:

- radar surveillance;
- artillery fire;
- missile threat;
- mines;
- night-equipped Argentine infantry.

The landing is not an annihilation, but it fails to establish a sustainable major beachhead.

A transport or landing ship is sunk or crippled. Several battalion elements reach shore but are withdrawn after the fleet concludes that reinforcement cannot be maintained under the existing Argentine fire envelope.

This becomes the event compared to Operation Torch.

The phrase **“No Second Torch”** enters Parliament.

## August–September: the West Falkland decision

After the failed East Falkland attempt, the military changes strategy.

Rather than assaulting the principal Argentine fortress directly, Britain lands on **West Falkland**, where Argentine forces are thinner and air-defense coverage is less dense.

This operation succeeds after prolonged reconnaissance and bombardment.

Britain captures or isolates:

- Port Howard;
- Fox Bay;
- adjacent high ground;
- several smaller Argentine positions.

By autumn, Britain possesses a viable island lodgment with:

- artillery;
- air-defense systems;
- helicopters;
- a temporary airstrip;
- repair and supply facilities.

The Union flag again flies over part of the Falklands.

This prevents Argentina from claiming an uncontested victory and gives Britain a physical base for further operations.

## October 1984–January 1985: the divided archipelago

By Reagan’s inauguration, the position is roughly:

### Britain holds

- South Georgia;
- most or all of West Falkland;
- surrounding waters intermittently;
- limited positions or raiding access around western East Falkland;
- the strategic initiative at sea, but not complete sea control.

### Argentina holds

- Stanley;
- the major East Falkland settlements and airfield;
- the principal defensive ridges;
- a large and increasingly entrenched garrison;
- the ability to resupply by air and occasional naval penetration;
- the advantage of proximity.

This is no longer an expedition.

It is an island siege combined with a naval-air war.

# Could Britain simply starve the islands?

Britain absolutely considers it.

The argument for siege is strong:

- Argentina cannot supply a large garrison indefinitely without tremendous cost.
- British submarines can make surface reinforcement dangerous.
- British possession of West Falkland tightens the ring.
- time allows Britain to build airstrips and bring additional aircraft south.
- every month strains Argentine fuel, spares, and transport.

But it is not a complete solution.

Argentina can still use:

- transport aircraft;
- low-altitude flights;
- submarines;
- fast vessels during poor weather;
- dispersed mainland airfields;
- local food and requisitioning;
- stored supplies accumulated before the invasion.

A genuine starvation strategy might take a year or longer. It would also expose the islanders and Argentine conscripts to hunger, disease, and severe winter conditions.

The government faces the additional problem that a British general election is due during 1985.

The Navy and Army increasingly favor a methodical reduction:

> Build West Falkland, strangle Stanley, suppress the airfield, and assault only after Argentine capability has been degraded.

Political ministers want a decisive victory before the electorate concludes that the empire has become trapped in an unwinnable war.

# British domestic politics

The invasion initially creates overwhelming national unity.

The first casualties create debate.

The failed landing creates factions.

## The government position

The government argues that abandoning the islands would:

- reward aggression;
- destroy Commonwealth confidence;
- hand Germany a strategic victory;
- demonstrate that Britain can defend only territories near friendly bases;
- reopen every imperial and maritime dispute.

## The “No Second Torch” faction

This group includes:

- anti-imperial Labour members;
- fiscally conservative MPs;
- liberal constitutionalists;
- veterans who distrust amphibious optimism;
- politicians from regions suffering from mobilization and shipping requisitions.

They argue that the islands cannot justify sacrificing major portions of the Royal Navy.

Their preferred settlement includes:

- cease-fire;
- international administration;
- removal of both major garrisons;
- protection for islanders;
- delayed sovereignty negotiations;
- perhaps permanent local autonomy under nominal Argentine sovereignty.

The government calls them defeatists.

The hard imperial press calls some of them traitors.

After the failed landing, ordinary voters begin listening to them.

## The hard-war faction

The opposite group demands attacks on:

- mainland Argentine air bases;
- missile sites;
- naval bases;
- fuel depots;
- military industry.

Their argument is operationally powerful:

> Britain is trying to defeat an army on the islands while leaving the system supplying that army untouched.

The problem is political. Attacking Argentina proper could transform a contained island war into a hemispheric conflict and provide Germany with a justification for greater involvement.

# The chemical-weapons panic

This should be a genuine misunderstanding rather than an Argentine plan.

An Argentine general gives a speech declaring that the armed forces possess:

> “the means to render any enemy bridgehead untenable and, if necessary, uninhabitable.”

He is referring to:

- artillery;
- mines;
- fuel-air weapons;
- destruction of facilities;
- denial of water and shelter.

A rushed English translation renders the statement as Argentina’s willingness to **“make the islands uninhabitable by any means.”**

British newspapers interpret this as a chemical or biological threat.

The Americans react strongly.

Argentina may possess old chemical stocks or the industrial ability to manufacture agents, but has no intention of using them. Buenos Aires understands that chemical warfare would:

- unite America and Britain;
- destroy Argentine diplomatic support;
- invite retaliation;
- expose Argentine mainland cities;
- make German support politically poisonous.

Argentina privately reassures Brazil, the Vatican, and Washington that no chemical or biological weapons have been deployed.

The United States nevertheless announces that any such use would result in immediate hemispheric intervention.

This creates a clear red line without making America a British ally.

# Buchanan’s final policy

Buchanan’s position through January 1985 is **armed mediation**.

He establishes four limits:

1. Germany may not deploy state military forces into the American hemisphere.
2. Britain may fight for the islands but not invade or strategically bomb Argentina proper.
3. Argentina may not use chemical or biological weapons.
4. Neither side may interfere with neutral American or hemispheric shipping.

American ships and aircraft enter the wider South Atlantic, but not as an extension of the British task force.

Their mission is to observe, separate, and contain.

The British dislike this because it effectively protects Argentine mainland bases.

The Argentines dislike it because it prevents Germany from openly balancing British sea power.

That mutual dissatisfaction is evidence that the policy is genuinely separate from either belligerent.

# Reagan inherits the war

Reagan takes office on January 20, 1985.

He retains Buchanan’s containment rules because they are strategically sound, but changes the language.

Buchanan spoke about hemispheric order.

Reagan speaks about preventing an island dispute from becoming a war among civilizations.

His public formula is:

> “No conquest by proxy, no imperial escalation, and no foreign fleet will turn the South Atlantic into the opening battlefield of a world war.”

Britain does not formally ask Reagan for combat assistance.

There are several reasons:

- Britain considers itself a great power.
- A formal request would strengthen America’s claim to supervise British operations.
- Reagan would condition aid upon restraint against the mainland.
- British political culture still resents the Atlantic Accord.
- A visibly American-supplied victory would reduce the Commonwealth’s prestige.

There are quiet contacts concerning:

- rescue;
- navigation;
- weather;
- deconfliction;
- identification of neutral shipping;
- German treaty compliance.

But there is no public American-British combat partnership comparable to our historical Anglo-American relationship.

In the real Falklands crisis, the Reagan administration attempted mediation and contemplated renewed negotiations if fighting became prolonged; it also distinguished material assistance from direct operational participation. citeturn461201view2 Argentine officials themselves believed American pressure was necessary to keep Britain from pursuing the conflict to its “bitter end.” citeturn461201view1

# Reagan and American arms exports

The Falklands profoundly affects Reagan’s defense policy.

He sees that Germany’s greatest geopolitical weapon is not necessarily its own army.

It is the ability to provide another state with:

- doctrine;
- training;
- rifles;
- vehicles;
- aircraft;
- missiles;
- radar;
- submarines;
- licensed industry;
- decades of technical dependence.

Reagan therefore begins developing an **American Arsenal Initiative** in 1985.

Its purpose is to make American weapons the attractive alternative to German and Japanese systems.

It emphasizes:

- reliable export models;
- training packages;
- spare-parts guarantees;
- licensed assembly under American supervision;
- communications compatibility;
- patrol aircraft and ships;
- affordable fighters;
- air-defense systems;
- helicopters;
- armored vehicles suited to regional forces.

Historically, Reagan’s administration explicitly regarded conventional arms transfers as an essential instrument of foreign policy, alliance capability, deterrence, and American defense production. citeturn461201view4 That instinct fits this alternate world even more strongly.

Reagan does **not** sell major systems to either Falklands belligerent while the war continues.

He targets states such as:

- Brazil;
- Chile;
- Colombia;
- Mexico;
- selected Caribbean associates;
- non-German Arab and African partners.

The policy’s implicit message is:

> A country need not become industrially dependent upon Berlin merely because it needs modern weapons.

# Why Japan stays out

Japan has access and influence in Peru, but direct Japanese involvement produces little gain.

Tokyo would risk:

- confrontation with the United States;
- conflict with Britain and Australia;
- disruption of Pacific trade;
- association with a German client;
- stretching its fleet into a distant theater of marginal importance.

Japan may sell Argentina civilian electronics or permit private commercial transactions. It does not dispatch a carrier group to the South Atlantic.

The Falklands are strategically important to Germany and America because of the Atlantic boundary. They are not important enough for Japan to risk a global naval crisis.

# The German role

Germany follows the Atlantic Accord with legal precision.

No serving German combat formation lands in Argentina.

No openly German warship crosses into the American side of the agreed hemisphere.

Instead, Argentina receives:

- commercial spares;
- civilian technicians;
- retired German personnel;
- volunteers formally released from service;
- encrypted communications assistance;
- corporate intelligence;
- satellite imagery sold through intermediaries;
- neutral-flag shipping;
- credit;
- diplomatic advice.

Berlin does not call Argentina a puppet.

Argentina is too proud and too autonomous for that.

Germany regards it as:

> a sovereign strategic partner whose strength prevents American monopoly in the Western Hemisphere.

Americans frequently collapse that distinction and speak of “the Germans in Argentina,” even when the individuals involved are Argentine officers using Argentine-produced versions of German equipment.

# The alternate Able Archer crisis

This should occur later in **1985**, not before Reagan’s inauguration.

The historical Able Archer scare arose because a routine exercise incorporated unusual alert transitions and communications during a period of heightened political tension, causing Soviet forces to react with exceptional readiness. citeturn461201view3

The alternate version should combine an exercise with a real naval confrontation.

## The setup

Britain prepares a possible long-range strike against Argentine air bases around Río Grande and the southern mainland.

Washington warns London that an attack on the mainland would violate American containment policy.

At the same time, Germany dispatches a **South Atlantic Navigation Protection Group**:

- one missile cruiser;
- several escorts;
- an oiler;
- an intelligence vessel;
- unacknowledged submarines.

The group sails south along the **European side** of the Mid-Atlantic boundary.

Germany claims it is:

- protecting commercial shipping;
- monitoring threats to neutral vessels;
- preparing to evacuate German civilians;
- exercising its lawful freedom of navigation.

The formation never openly crosses the treaty line.

The timing is deliberately intimidating.

## The American exercise

Reagan authorizes **Hemispheric Shield 85**, a major command and naval exercise intended to demonstrate that America can close the western Atlantic to a foreign fleet.

It includes:

- carrier dispersal;
- submarine alerts;
- long-range patrol aircraft;
- live command transitions;
- satellite tasking;
- simulated attacks on submarine and missile threats;
- reinforcement of Atlantic bases.

German intelligence observes actual American deployments accompanying exercise messages.

Berlin cannot determine whether the exercise is:

- a warning;
- preparation to attack the German group;
- cover for intervention against Argentina;
- or the beginning of a wider Atlantic offensive.

German submarines increase readiness.

American commanders detect unusual German movements and conclude Berlin may be preparing to cross the line.

For perhaps thirty-six hours, both sides believe the other is using an exercise or navigation mission to disguise an actual operation.

No nuclear weapons exist to end civilization in an afternoon.

The feared war is still catastrophic:

- German submarines against Atlantic shipping;
- American carrier strikes;
- conventional missiles against ports and airfields;
- attacks upon orbital systems;
- British entry against Germany;
- Argentine attacks upon American patrols;
- a conflict that could continue for a decade.

## Resolution

The crisis ends through direct communications.

Reagan suspends the final phase of the exercise.

Germany turns the surface group northeast.

Britain cancels the mainland strike.

Argentina moves no additional strategic systems toward the islands.

The event becomes known as:

> **The Ridge Line Scare**

It produces a later Atlantic incidents protocol governing:

- naval exercises near the boundary;
- submarine notifications in crisis zones;
- missile-targeting radar;
- emergency communications;
- movements of large formations.

This is the setting’s Able Archer moment: not a misunderstanding over nuclear release, but a terrifying recognition that a routine sequence of alerts could begin a general conventional war before political leaders understood what their commanders were doing.

# Britain in January 1985

At Reagan’s inauguration, the British public understands three things.

## Britain is still a great power

It has moved and sustained a major fleet across the Atlantic, retaken South Georgia, seized West Falkland, and continued fighting despite serious losses.

## Britain is not omnipotent

Its carriers, ships, and landing forces can be damaged by a regional state equipped and prepared by Germany.

Kuwait did not prove that every imperial expedition would be easy.

## The war cannot remain politically indefinite

The government must eventually choose among:

- another major assault on East Falkland;
- a long blockade;
- strikes against Argentina proper;
- or negotiations that fall short of complete restoration.

None offers an easy victory.

# Canon-ready first-year chronology

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **1981–83** | Portuguese, Brazilian, American, and Vatican-supported negotiations fail over sovereignty timing and islander consent. |
| **Late 1983** | Argentina issues a final deadline and accelerates military preparations. Germany increases indirect technical and commercial assistance. |
| **Early April 1984** | Argentina launches *Operación Rosario* without a traditional declaration of war. The reinforced British garrison surrenders after several days of combat. |
| **April–May 1984** | Britain mobilizes a Commonwealth task force. Argentina heavily reinforces and fortifies the islands. |
| **May 1984** | Britain retakes South Georgia. |
| **June 1984** | Serious naval-air combat demonstrates that Argentine German-pattern missiles, submarines, aircraft, and radar are operationally mature. British losses force reinforcements. |
| **July 1984** | Britain’s first major East Falkland landing attempt fails or is withdrawn under heavy attack—the “Second Torch” controversy. |
| **August–September 1984** | Britain successfully establishes a large lodgment on West Falkland. |
| **Autumn 1984** | The war becomes a blockade, air-sea attrition campaign, and preparation for a second landing. |
| **January 1985** | Reagan inherits an unresolved war. Britain holds West Falkland and South Georgia; Argentina holds Stanley and most of East Falkland. |
| **Later 1985** | A proposed British mainland strike, German fleet movement along the Atlantic boundary, and an American containment exercise produce the Ridge Line Scare. |

# The correct stopping point

We should not yet decide whether Argentina ultimately wins or loses.

At this stage each side has proved something and failed to prove something.

Argentina has proved that:

- it can seize the islands;
- its German-equipped military is not a hollow imitation;
- Britain cannot simply appear offshore and command surrender.

It has not proved that:

- it can break a sustained British blockade;
- Germany will openly rescue it;
- America will accept permanent German-aligned control of the islands.

Britain has proved that:

- it can sustain a genuine long-range war;
- the Commonwealth system remains militarily meaningful;
- it will absorb substantial casualties rather than automatically retreat.

It has not proved that:

- it can retake East Falkland at acceptable cost;
- its fleet can operate indefinitely within Argentine missile range;
- the United States will let it widen the war.

That leaves January 1985 in exactly the proper position:

> **Argentina has won the seizure. Britain has prevented the seizure from becoming a settlement. The United States has prevented the war from becoming a world war—but has not found a way to end it.**

# The Falklands campaign, January–June 1985

The most plausible course is a British campaign that **does make steady progress**, but never produces the clean breakthrough Thatcher wants before the election.

By the opening of the campaign season:

- Britain has shown that it can return to East Falkland and defeat Argentine formations in prepared battle.
- Argentina has shown that it can absorb losses, counterattack, and impose serious naval casualties.
- Stanley remains Argentine.
- The British electorate is not prepared to abandon the war, but it is increasingly hostile to operations conducted primarily to meet political deadlines.

That produces a competitive wartime election rather than either a patriotic landslide or an antiwar collapse.

The campaign builds naturally upon the setting’s Siege Commonwealth logistics, Argentina’s long familiarity with German weapons, and Britain’s post-Kuwait overconfidence. fileciteturn27file0

## The position on January 20, 1985

At Reagan’s inauguration, the front looks approximately like this:

### Britain controls

- South Georgia;
- most of West Falkland;
- Port Howard and Fox Bay;
- a developing West Falkland airstrip and logistical base;
- much of the open sea around the islands, intermittently rather than absolutely.

### Argentina controls

- Stanley;
- Mount Pleasant airfield;
- Darwin and Goose Green;
- nearly all of East Falkland;
- the principal radar, missile, and fixed defensive network;
- approximately 18,000–22,000 troops on the islands.

Britain has perhaps 12,000–15,000 ground personnel ashore across West Falkland and South Georgia, with tens of thousands more aboard ships, at Ascension-like staging points, and throughout the Cape and Atlantic supply network.

The ground forces are therefore much closer in strength than the relative national populations or economies would suggest.

Britain cannot send a continental army. Every battalion requires:

- a ship berth;
- food and fuel carried thousands of miles;
- air-defense cover;
- landing capacity;
- medical evacuation;
- ammunition storage;
- spare parts;
- protection from submarines and missiles.

Argentina must cross only the water from Patagonia, although the British blockade makes even that increasingly dangerous.

# A note on tanks

The Falklands cannot support sweeping armored warfare.

Historically, the British employed only a handful of Scorpion and Scimitar light vehicles because their low ground pressure made them among the few armored vehicles capable of operating across the rough, marshy terrain. citeturn848706search13turn848706search23

In the alternate war:

- light tracked reconnaissance vehicles;
- armored personnel carriers;
- engineering vehicles;
- helicopters;
- infantry;
- and artillery

do most of the actual maneuver.

Full-sized tanks are confined to:

- prepared roads;
- airfield surfaces;
- gravel tracks;
- engineered matting;
- temporarily frozen ground;
- the Stanley–Mount Pleasant–Darwin corridor.

There **is** an iconic Panzer-versus-British-tank battle, but it involves perhaps a dozen vehicles on each side, not hundreds crossing the countryside.

# The television war

This becomes the world’s first true **same-day television war**.

It is not uninterrupted live broadcasting from foxholes. The British government imposes delays, censorship, and geographic restrictions. But portable electronic cameras, satellite relays, aircraft reconnaissance recordings, shipboard cameras, and military video feeds mean that footage can reach Britain within hours rather than after the campaign.

Every evening viewers may see:

- burning ships;
- missile-camera footage;
- exhausted infantry returning from patrol;
- prisoners;
- damaged tanks;
- helicopters flying casualties out;
- maps showing hills gained and lost.

Graphic material is generally reserved for late broadcasts, but the distinction between Mature Exhibition cinema and television news becomes politically contentious. A fictional death in a war film is controlled; a real sailor on fire aboard a destroyer may appear on the evening news.

The Ministry of Defence calls this necessary public information.

Opposition politicians call it selective war editing.

Soldiers call it strange that the country sometimes sees a battle before their families receive official casualty notices.

# Monthly campaign summary

| Month | Principal operation | Overall result |
|---|---|---|
| January | **Operation Winter Quay** | Britain strengthens West Falkland, but Argentina inflicts a major naval-logistical loss |
| February | **Operation Lantern** | British raids damage Argentine surveillance and missile positions, but cannot hold exposed ground |
| March | **Operation Crown Gate** | Britain establishes a permanent San Carlos bridgehead at severe cost |
| April | **Operation Blackthorn** | Britain captures Darwin and Goose Green—the first major land victory |
| May | **Operación Cóndor del Sur** | Argentina nearly severs the British lodgment; Britain holds, but the front stalls |
| June | **Operation Sceptre** | Britain captures Mount Pleasant and wins the war’s principal tank battle; Stanley remains untaken |

# January 1985: Operation Winter Quay

## British objective

Before attempting another crossing of Falkland Sound, Britain must turn West Falkland from a temporary lodgment into a genuine campaign base.

Operation Winter Quay expands:

- the Port Howard landing complex;
- fuel and ammunition storage;
- field hospitals;
- helicopter maintenance;
- air defense;
- naval repair facilities;
- an all-weather runway near Fox Bay or Port Howard;
- modular roads across the worst peat ground.

Commonwealth engineers work alongside British formations.

Australian heavy equipment, Canadian communications systems, South African fuel, and New Zealand transport support become visible proof that this is a Commonwealth war rather than an isolated Royal Navy expedition.

## Argentine response: Operación Tridente

Argentina understands what the runway means.

Once Britain can base fighters, reconnaissance aircraft, transports, and strike helicopters on West Falkland, British dependence upon carriers decreases and the invasion of East Falkland becomes much easier.

Argentina therefore launches a coordinated attack:

- mainland aircraft strike the runway and fuel facilities;
- submarines approach British supply lanes;
- missile aircraft target support shipping;
- special forces raid observation posts;
- electronic warfare attempts to blind British radar during the attack.

The runway is damaged but not destroyed.

The Argentine success comes at sea. A quiet Argentine submarine reaches the support area and torpedoes a major British auxiliary carrying engineering stores, fuel equipment, and several hundred personnel.

The ship either sinks in shallow water or is abandoned after fire spreads through the vehicle deck.

The attack kills perhaps 150–200 British and Commonwealth personnel and delays the runway program by two weeks.

## British response

British submarines and patrol aircraft retaliate by intercepting an Argentine resupply convoy.

One transport is sunk and another forced to surrender or beach itself. Argentine losses are substantial, but the British public sees its own burning ship more vividly than distant enemy freighters.

## Political effect

January teaches Britain that the war has no safe rear area.

The government’s language changes from:

> “The islands will be liberated.”

to:

> “The campaign will be completed methodically and without timetable.”

Nobody believes the second half.

# February 1985: Operation Lantern

## Purpose

Britain cannot return to San Carlos Water while Argentina controls:

- radar at Fanning Head;
- observation posts overlooking Falkland Sound;
- mobile anti-ship missiles;
- artillery registration points;
- northern air-defense positions;
- reconnaissance facilities around Pebble Island.

Operation Lantern is a month-long sequence of raids rather than one large landing.

## The raids

Royal Marines, Special Air Service units, Commonwealth commandos, and naval helicopters strike several positions.

The most important attacks are:

### Pebble Island

British commandos destroy:

- reconnaissance aircraft;
- fuel stores;
- radar equipment;
- helicopter facilities.

### Fanning Head

A larger night assault destroys the radar and missile-control site that helped defeat the 1984 landing attempt.

The position is briefly occupied, photographed, stripped of intelligence material, and then abandoned before Argentina can concentrate artillery against it.

### Northern sound

Mine-clearance teams and small naval craft begin secretly marking safer approaches for the future landing fleet.

## Argentine counteraction

Argentina reacts aggressively.

Heliborne troops pursue withdrawing commandos, and one British helicopter formation is ambushed by radar-directed anti-aircraft fire.

Several helicopters are lost, together with experienced pilots and commandos.

An Argentine force reoccupies Fanning Head within forty-eight hours, but it returns to ruined equipment, false positions, and British-planted sensors.

## Result

Operation Lantern is a genuine British success, but not a territorial one.

It gives Britain:

- radar frequencies;
- missile procedures;
- defensive maps;
- prisoners familiar with the Argentine plan;
- safer channels toward San Carlos.

Argentina claims victory because it still controls the ground.

Britain claims victory because the ground no longer sees as far as it did.

## Television effect

This is the month in which commando footage enters popular culture.

The public sees green-tinted night-camera images, helicopters skimming the water, and explosions at radar positions.

Recruitment rises.

So does public expectation that British special forces can solve problems which actually require divisions, artillery, engineers, and ships.

# March 1985: Operation Crown Gate

Operation Crown Gate is the second British attempt to establish a permanent bridgehead on East Falkland.

Unlike the rushed 1984 operation, it is preceded by:

- weeks of reconnaissance;
- deception landings;
- attacks on Argentine radar;
- false radio traffic suggesting a landing farther north;
- submarine interdiction of mainland reinforcements;
- concentrated naval bombardment;
- electronic jamming;
- helicopter insertions behind the coast.

## The landing

The first waves enter San Carlos Water before dawn.

Argentina has prepared defenses, but the destruction of its surveillance network delays recognition of the main landing.

British forces seize:

- Port San Carlos;
- Ajax Bay;
- defensive heights overlooking the anchorage;
- several Argentine artillery positions.

By daylight, Argentina identifies the operation and begins a sustained air and missile campaign.

## The air-sea battle

This becomes one of the most visually horrifying weeks of the war.

Argentina attacks the confined British shipping with:

- low-level aircraft;
- anti-ship missiles;
- guided bombs;
- drones or remotely piloted reconnaissance aircraft;
- artillery directed from inland observers.

Britain loses:

- one landing ship;
- two escorts sunk or rendered total losses;
- numerous landing craft;
- several helicopters;
- large quantities of fuel and ammunition.

A carrier is damaged again but remains operational.

British air defenses and fighters inflict severe Argentine aircraft losses, but Argentina accepts those losses to attack the transports.

## The ground battle

Argentine troops counterattack toward the beaches but encounter:

- naval gunfire;
- British artillery landed in the first waves;
- anti-tank missiles;
- helicopters moving reserves;
- defensive positions prepared by engineers.

The Argentines fail to drive the British into the water.

By the end of March, Britain has perhaps 7,000–9,000 troops in the San Carlos perimeter.

That is the strategic achievement:

> Britain is permanently back on East Falkland.

It is not yet advancing toward Stanley.

## Political effect

Support for the war rises because the operation succeeds.

Confidence in the government does not rise as much, because the public has watched ships burn for the price of the lodgment.

The emerging public position is:

> “We cannot withdraw now—but why were the losses necessary?”

# April 1985: Operation Blackthorn

The British bridgehead cannot survive indefinitely as an isolated pocket.

Its first major land objective is the Darwin–Goose Green position, which protects Argentina’s southern flank and threatens British movement out of San Carlos.

## The operational plan

Britain attacks with:

- Royal Marines and paratroopers;
- a Commonwealth infantry brigade;
- artillery firing from San Carlos;
- helicopter-borne flanking forces;
- light tracked armor;
- naval gunfire from Falkland Sound;
- a small number of expeditionary tanks restricted to the road corridor.

Argentina has deeply fortified:

- Darwin Hill;
- Goose Green;
- Boca House;
- nearby ridges;
- the approaches across open ground.

## The battle

The fighting lasts more than a week.

British units repeatedly discover that Argentine troops are not the brittle conscripts anticipated by some newspapers.

The best Argentine battalions:

- hold under bombardment;
- conduct night counterattacks;
- use German-pattern night sights;
- relocate mortars rapidly;
- employ anti-tank missiles effectively;
- withdraw before being encircled.

Some Argentine units break. Others fight almost to destruction.

British combined-arms coordination is superior, particularly in integrating artillery, helicopters, engineers, and naval fire.

## The armored fighting

This is not yet the great tank battle.

Argentine Panzer 10 medium vehicles and British light armor engage around Darwin’s roads and hardened ground.

Several vehicles on both sides are destroyed, but tanks mainly act as:

- mobile guns;
- protected artillery observers;
- infantry-support vehicles;
- local counterattack reserves.

The surrounding peat prevents broad maneuver.

## The fall of Goose Green

The Argentine commander withdraws the surviving garrison rather than allow encirclement.

Britain captures Darwin and Goose Green, together with prisoners, artillery, stores, and a usable southern airstrip.

The Union flag is raised over the settlement and broadcast within hours.

This becomes the government’s first undeniable televised land victory.

## Cultural impact

The names Darwin and Goose Green enter songs, advertisements, recruitment films, and political speeches.

For a week, the country feels that Stanley is next.

Military planners know better.

The Argentine army has surrendered its forward bastion in order to concentrate around Mount Pleasant and the Stanley ridges.

# May 1985: Operación Cóndor del Sur

Argentina decides that it cannot allow Britain to consolidate a continuous route from San Carlos through Goose Green.

If the British connect those positions securely, they can build:

- roads;
- pipelines;
- airstrips;
- artillery bases;
- a sustained eastern offensive.

The Argentine command therefore launches its largest ground counteroffensive of the war.

## The Argentine plan

Operación Cóndor del Sur uses:

- two infantry brigades;
- heliborne commandos;
- Panzer 10 and several Panzer 11 tanks;
- massed artillery;
- deception raids north of San Carlos;
- attacks on British helicopter bases;
- mainland air strikes against the supply corridor.

Its purpose is to cut the British position near Bluff Cove and Sussex Mountain, isolate Goose Green, and force Britain to abandon the southern advance.

## Initial success

The attack begins in poor weather, reducing British air observation.

Argentine infantry penetrates between British formations and overruns several supply sites.

A British battalion is temporarily isolated.

Argentine tanks and mechanized troops advance farther than expected along improved roads, while commando units attack British artillery and communications positions.

For approximately forty-eight hours, the British front appears close to splitting.

## The Battle of Sussex Ridge

Britain commits:

- its air-mobile reserve;
- artillery firing almost continuously;
- naval gunfire from ships in Falkland Sound;
- light armor;
- available fighters and attack helicopters;
- troops pulled from the San Carlos perimeter.

The fighting becomes close and confused.

Several positions change hands repeatedly.

British forces ultimately hold Sussex Ridge and reopen the route to Goose Green, but cannot immediately pursue the withdrawing Argentines.

## Argentine achievement

Argentina fails to destroy the British lodgment.

It does demonstrate that:

- it retains offensive capacity;
- Mount Pleasant is not merely waiting to be captured;
- British lines can be penetrated;
- Stanley’s defenders are not demoralized.

The Argentine government broadcasts footage of British prisoners, destroyed vehicles, and captured supplies.

## British low point

May is the political nadir.

The government had allowed the public to believe that Goose Green meant imminent victory. Now television shows British troops fighting over ground supposedly secured weeks earlier.

The phrase **“map-board victory”** becomes common: ministers move flags eastward on television maps while soldiers repeatedly fight to hold the roads behind them.

The No Second Torch faction gains support.

It does not yet command a majority, because few Britons favor simple evacuation after so much blood has been spent.

# June 1985: Operation Sceptre

The military concludes that Stanley itself is still too difficult to assault.

The more useful objective is **Mount Pleasant airfield**.

Capturing it would:

- end regular Argentine fixed-wing operations from the islands;
- give Britain a major runway;
- split the Argentine defensive system;
- place British artillery and aircraft much closer to Stanley;
- provide a visible strategic victory before the election.

## Why the tanks matter here

Mount Pleasant is one of the few places where heavier armor can operate.

The area contains:

- runway surfaces;
- engineered roads;
- graded approaches;
- compacted building zones;
- Argentine trackway;
- frozen or temporarily hardened winter ground.

Argentina has concentrated a small company of Panzer 11 export tanks around the airfield.

Britain lands a comparable force of Challenger-class expeditionary tanks, accepting the immense logistical burden because the airfield battle justifies it.

## The first Panzer–Challenger battle

The iconic engagement occurs west or southwest of the airfield.

It involves perhaps:

- 10–12 Argentine Panzer 11s;
- 8–10 British Challenger-class tanks;
- reconnaissance vehicles;
- infantry anti-tank teams;
- artillery;
- helicopters;
- electronic warfare.

The tanks are technically comparable.

### Argentine advantages

- longer familiarity with the local ground;
- prepared firing positions;
- German-derived night optics;
- pre-registered artillery;
- proximity to workshops and fuel.

### British advantages

- better integration with infantry and artillery;
- more experienced recovery crews;
- stronger battlefield communications;
- superior naval and airborne reconnaissance;
- a clearer operational chain of command.

The engagement begins with Argentina damaging or destroying several British tanks from prepared positions.

British artillery and infantry then force the Argentines to move. Once mobile, the Panzer formation becomes exposed to British tanks and helicopters.

Several vehicles bog down when trying to leave the prepared corridor.

The battle ends with:

- four or five British tanks knocked out or disabled;
- six or seven Argentine tanks destroyed or abandoned;
- surviving Argentines withdrawing toward Stanley.

Neither vehicle is exposed as technologically inferior.

The British win because they combine arms more effectively at the decisive moment.

## Capture of Mount Pleasant

After approximately ten days of fighting, British infantry reaches the airfield.

The Argentines demolish:

- navigation equipment;
- fuel facilities;
- parts of the runway;
- hangars and communications systems.

They cannot destroy the entire complex before withdrawing.

Britain raises the flag over Mount Pleasant on camera.

Engineers begin repairing the runway almost immediately.

## Strategic result

This is Britain’s greatest victory of the war so far.

Argentina can still supply Stanley through:

- helicopters;
- small aircraft using emergency strips;
- submarines;
- fast vessels;
- occasional nighttime transport flights.

But the volume declines sharply.

Stanley is now under increasingly complete siege.

The war is not over because the principal Argentine army remains entrenched around:

- Mount Longdon;
- Two Sisters;
- Wireless Ridge;
- Tumbledown;
- Stanley itself.

An assault upon that system could still cost thousands of casualties.

# The election call

Assume Thatcher’s government was elected in autumn 1980.

Under the traditional British system, a general election must occur at least once every five years, while the prime minister can request an earlier dissolution from the monarch. citeturn848706search28turn848706search39

Thatcher has delayed because:

- a campaign after the failed 1984 landing would have been disastrous;
- a campaign after the May counteroffensive would have looked desperate;
- she wants a visible military achievement.

Mount Pleasant gives her the opportunity.

On approximately **June 24, 1985**, Thatcher announces that she has requested dissolution.

The election is scheduled for late July.

It quickly becomes known as:

- **the Runway Election**;
- **the Mount Pleasant Election**;
- or, among critics, **the Blood-and-Ballot Election**.

# Britain entering the election

The electorate has not divided simply into patriots and defeatists.

There are four major positions.

## 1. Complete liberation

This is the government’s official position.

Britain will:

- hold West Falkland;
- hold San Carlos, Goose Green, and Mount Pleasant;
- tighten the blockade;
- repair the airfield;
- advance methodically toward Stanley;
- accept negotiations only after Argentina agrees to withdraw.

The government insists that victory is now visible.

Its slogan might be:

> **Hold Fast. Finish the Task.**

## 2. Victory without another Torch

This is the strongest Labour position, particularly under a figure such as Denis Healey.

It does not advocate abandoning the British lodgments.

It argues:

- Mount Pleasant should be fortified;
- Stanley should be isolated;
- mainland attacks must remain forbidden;
- no frontal assault should occur merely to satisfy an election timetable;
- negotiations should seek Argentine withdrawal in exchange for future sovereignty talks and demilitarization.

Healey can make this argument without appearing ignorant of military affairs. In this timeline, he may personally remember the failed wartime Mediterranean expedition from which the “Second Torch” analogy comes.

His central line is:

> “The courage of the Army is not a substitute for judgment in the Cabinet.”

## 3. The No Second Torch settlement

The more antiwar opposition favors an immediate cease-fire.

Its proposed settlement includes:

- Britain retaining West Falkland temporarily;
- Argentina retaining Stanley temporarily;
- withdrawal of heavy weapons;
- international or Brazilian-Vatican administration;
- guaranteed islander rights;
- eventual sovereignty referendum or conference.

This faction has grown, but it remains a minority because many voters regard a divided-island settlement as surrender after Mount Pleasant.

## 4. The mainland war

The imperial hard right argues that the campaign cannot be won while Argentina’s mainland airfields, ports, missile stores, and factories remain untouched.

It demands strikes on:

- Río Grande;
- naval installations;
- submarine bases;
- military fuel;
- missile depots.

Thatcher does not openly embrace this position because Reagan has made clear that attacks upon Argentina proper risk American intervention.

The hard right accuses Washington of protecting Argentina.

# What the British public thinks

The most plausible mood is:

> **Continue—but do not waste the victory.**

The public is not prepared to order withdrawal while the Army holds Mount Pleasant and Stanley appears increasingly isolated.

At the same time, there is little appetite for a headlong assault against the final ridges.

Approximate working attitudes might be:

- 55–60% support continuing the campaign in some form;
- 25–30% support an immediate assault on Stanley;
- 30–40% favor blockade plus negotiations;
- fewer than 20% favor unilateral withdrawal.

These categories overlap depending upon wording.

The government’s problem is that “continue” does not automatically mean “endorse Thatcher.”

A voter may simultaneously believe:

- Argentina must not keep the islands;
- the soldiers have fought magnificently;
- Mount Pleasant proves victory is possible;
- the government badly underestimated the enemy;
- the July 1984 landing was reckless;
- the election is being timed cynically.

# The military position during the campaign

British commanders privately estimate that Stanley can probably be taken, but not immediately.

Their preferred sequence is:

1. Repair Mount Pleasant.
2. Establish land-based fighter operations.
3. Cut remaining Argentine resupply.
4. Move artillery and logistics east.
5. Conduct raids and limited attacks against the outer ridges.
6. Wait for isolation, hunger, and exhaustion to weaken Stanley.
7. Assault only after the defensive system has begun breaking.

That may require another four to eight months.

The Cabinet wants something faster.

This is where the election becomes dangerous. Even without an explicit political order, commanders know that a flag raised on one of the Stanley ridges before polling day would be politically valuable.

The Army’s senior leadership must prevent subordinate officers from interpreting political expectation as an operational command.

# The soldiers’ view

British troops do not generally believe they are losing by June 1985.

They believe:

- the campaign was initially mishandled;
- Argentina is a serious enemy;
- Britain now possesses the operational advantage;
- Stanley will eventually fall if the supply system holds;
- politicians may either force a premature attack or negotiate away the gains.

That creates the seed of a future betrayal narrative.

Should an incoming government trade Mount Pleasant or West Falkland for a cease-fire, many veterans will say:

> “We had broken the airfield, divided their army, and put Stanley under siege. Parliament surrendered what the Army had won.”

Whether that judgment is accurate would matter less than its emotional power.

# The electoral starting position

The Mount Pleasant victory gives Thatcher and the Conservatives a lead, but not an overwhelming one.

A plausible opening position is:

- Conservatives narrowly ahead;
- Labour competitive and gaining among families of servicemen, industrial cities, and voters concerned about operational competence;
- settlement-oriented parties stronger than before but unlikely to form a government alone;
- the hard imperial right capable of damaging Thatcher if it accuses her of accepting American restrictions.

The election is therefore not a referendum on whether Britain should remain British.

It is a referendum on:

> **Whether the government that brought Britain this far can be trusted to finish the war without sacrificing either the Army or the country’s remaining strategic freedom.**

And that is the proper cliffhanger.

On election day Britain will not be choosing between war and peace in the abstract.

It will be choosing among:

- a methodical siege;
- a politically accelerated assault;
- and an incomplete negotiated settlement

while Stanley remains Argentine and British guns are already within reach of it.
