# Computing Race I: 1944–1947  
## The five founding traditions

This period should not yet be treated as a contest among five mature national “computer architectures.” Between 1944 and 1947, the word *computer* still covers several only partially connected technological families:

| Family | Typical machinery | What is “programmed” |
|---|---|---|
| Scientific digital calculation | Relays, valves, mechanical memories | Sequences of arithmetic operations |
| Analog calculation and control | Amplifiers, integrators, servomechanisms | Physical equations embodied in circuits |
| Cryptanalytic machinery | Rotor machines, counters, Boolean valve circuits | Tests, correlations, key-search procedures |
| Administrative data processing | Punched cards, sorters, tabulators, printing calculators | Record formats, card flows, accounting procedures |
| Fire control and guidance | Mechanical predictors, analog electronics, radio control | Control laws, interception geometry, stabilization |

The stored-program electronic computer is only just becoming imaginable as the machine that might eventually absorb most of these functions. There is no operational FORTRAN, COBOL, BASIC, Rechenplan, or Japanese procedure language. Even Plankalkül exists principally as a body of notation and design thought rather than a language routinely compiled and executed.

“Software” in 1947 means:

- plugboard diagrams;
- switch-setting tables;
- punched-tape preparation;
- machine-code sheets;
- lists of numerical constants;
- hand-optimized operation sequences;
- test cases and expected answers;
- card-deck procedures;
- operator notebooks;
- physical rewiring.

This matters because the later national styles should grow from what each country is already doing—not appear retroactively, fully formed, in 1944.

You named five blocs rather than four, so I am treating Germany, Britain, the United States, Japan, and the emerging Latin system separately.

---

# I. Germany: the plan, the machine, and the control circuit

## 1. What Germany possesses in 1944

Germany begins this period with the most unusual combination of assets.

### The Zuse digital lineage

Konrad Zuse has already demonstrated a genuinely distinctive conception of digital calculation:

- binary arithmetic;
- floating-point representation;
- automatic program sequencing;
- punched-film or punched-tape program control;
- separation between the calculating mechanism and the program medium;
- a machine conceived by a civil and structural engineer to remove repetitive mathematical labor.

The Z3 was a working program-controlled electromechanical computer using binary floating-point arithmetic. Its program arrived from punched film rather than being stored internally, and the machine itself was destroyed in a 1943 air raid. Zuse’s Z4 was developed between 1942 and 1945 as a larger successor. citeturn148526search0turn379023search3

The critical point is that Zuse is **not merely building a faster adding machine**. He is already thinking in terms of a general calculating mechanism upon which different procedures can be imposed.

### Plankalkül

Zuse is also moving beyond the machine itself. His surviving papers include early concepts for what he later calls Plankalkül and a substantial 1942 manuscript on binary calculation. citeturn148526search1

Plankalkül should not yet be treated as an operational programming language. There is no practical compiler in 1945, and the Z4 is not natively executing Plankalkül source code. Its immediate importance is intellectual:

> Zuse has begun to distinguish the **description of a calculation** from the physical machine instructions used to perform it.

That is an extraordinary head start in software thinking.

### The analog-control lineage

Germany also has a separate and, for aerospace, equally important tradition. Helmut Hölzer develops electronic analog equipment for the A-4 rocket’s control system and for simulation of its behavior. The machine represents control equations through continuous electrical quantities and directly interfaces with guidance and actuator problems. citeturn148526search2turn148526search5

This is not a primitive digital computer. It is something different and, for 1944 rocketry, often more useful:

- it operates continuously;
- it naturally accepts voltages from sensors;
- it embodies differential equations directly;
- it produces real-time control outputs;
- it does not need a general-purpose instruction sequence.

The later German space program should descend from **both** Zuse and Hölzer. It is a mistake to imagine that the digital lineage simply swallows the analog lineage immediately.

### The administrative-machine lineage

Germany also possesses commercial punched-card and office-machine capacity, but it should not be imagined as a perfectly computerized state. Punched-card systems are powerful for statistics, sorting, accounting, and repeated record operations, while much day-to-day labor administration remains dependent upon paper files, forms, indexes, clerks, and ordinary registration technology. Research into German administrative machinery emphasizes precisely this coexistence of mechanization with an enormous paper bureaucracy. citeturn261528search0

Thus Germany in 1944 has at least four computational cultures:

1. **Zuse’s binary engineering calculator.**
2. **Hölzer’s analog control and simulation machines.**
3. **Punched-card statistical and commercial machinery.**
4. **Cryptographic and rotor-machine engineering.**

They do not yet form one computer industry.

---

## 2. German pressure points, 1944–1947

### Pressure one: finishing the eastern war

Germany is still fighting a vast continental campaign. Its numerical demands include:

- artillery tables;
- bridge and structural calculations;
- railway capacity;
- fuel distribution;
- aircraft performance;
- jet-engine development;
- rocket trajectories;
- optical and radar calculations;
- production scheduling;
- weather;
- survey and mapping;
- logistics across devastated territory.

The decisive difference from the historical German situation is not that Germany suddenly acquires unlimited resources. It is that the senior state eventually receives repeated proof that advanced calculation contributes to **victory**, rather than appearing as an esoteric project competing with an increasingly desperate war effort.

Zuse’s machines therefore acquire a stronger institutional sponsor.

### Pressure two: the naval cipher crisis

The setting already fixes the 1946–47 crisis in which British exploitation of German naval communications becomes operationally apparent and Germany replaces the compromised architecture with a more secure shore-designed system assisted by Zuse’s computational work. fileciteturn5file3 fileciteturn5file4

The computers do not sit aboard U-boats. They are used ashore for such work as:

- examining rotor arrangements;
- identifying weak key schedules;
- simulating operator mistakes;
- measuring cycle lengths;
- testing indicator procedures;
- checking whether different traffic classes accidentally reuse structure;
- generating and validating key material;
- comparing proposed machine designs;
- searching for correlations in captured or deliberately generated test traffic.

This gives German computing a second institutional parent besides aerospace:

> The rocket establishment wants machines to calculate nature.  
> The naval cryptographic establishment wants machines to calculate hostile intelligence.

The second demand is especially important because it rewards formal logic, symbolic structure, and exhaustive test methods rather than only numerical arithmetic.

### Pressure three: guidance and interception

The Second Battle of Britain gives Germany an immediate need for:

- jet interception calculations;
- bombing navigation;
- radar plotting;
- radio navigation;
- guided weapons;
- antiaircraft predictors;
- long-range weather estimation;
- reconnaissance-image analysis.

Most of this is not yet done by a single general-purpose computer. It strengthens specialized analog and electromechanical systems, especially where an answer must be produced in real time.

### Pressure four: organizing victory

Only in 1947 does the administrative future of the German empire begin to become visible.

The new Reich controls or supervises:

- continental railways;
- displaced populations;
- settlement regions;
- resource zones;
- military governments;
- captured factories;
- protectorate clearing accounts;
- labor pools;
- enormous stocks of rolling stock, machinery, weapons, and material.

The later Reichsgüterausgleich, eastern corridor system, and MOSAIK administration have not yet been built, but their central problem is already present: Berlin is trying to govern quantities of people and material that exceed the capacity of traditional filing systems. The later canon explicitly makes computing central to German accounting, commodity balances, railway scheduling, industrial control, and imperial administration. fileciteturn5file3

In 1947, this produces demand for **data processing**, but not yet a unified electronic imperial database.

---

## 3. Likely German development, year by year

### 1944

The Z3 is gone, but the Z4 project survives under military-industrial protection. Germany still treats it principally as an advanced engineering instrument rather than the prototype of an entirely new industry.

The state’s practical view is:

- Zuse has built useful automatic calculators;
- Hölzer has built useful control machines;
- commercial firms already possess tabulating equipment;
- therefore each office should continue funding the machinery relevant to its own work.

There is not yet a Reich computer ministry.

Plankalkül remains mostly Zuse’s private or semi-private theoretical project. Selected assistants may use elements of its notation when describing calculations, but ordinary machine preparation remains much closer to a sequence of low-level operations.

### 1945

As the Soviet system collapses, the Z4 receives more reliable resources than it did historically. The machine is moved to a protected southern or underground establishment, but Germany does not have to abandon it to an uncertain postwar exile.

I would establish that:

- the first operational Z4 configuration becomes available in late 1945;
- it remains relay-based;
- it uses binary floating-point arithmetic;
- the program is externally controlled;
- its working memory remains small and expensive;
- its reliability is acceptable only with trained attendants;
- it is used principally for aerospace, structures, optics, and difficult numerical work.

There should **not** yet be a fleet of dozens. A sensible 1945–47 outcome is:

- one principal Z4;
- one military or industrial derivative under construction;
- one component or experimental machine;
- several special-purpose calculators derived from related concepts.

That is enough to establish a living engineering tradition without granting Germany an implausible mature computer industry overnight.

### 1946

The cipher crisis transforms the status of automated calculation.

Zuse’s establishment, Siemens, Telefunken, naval cryptographers, mathematicians, and rotor-machine engineers are brought into a joint but heavily compartmentalized program. The result is not that a Z4 “cracks Enigma.” Rather, computational machines assist in the design and verification of a replacement system.

This has three lasting consequences.

First, the German state learns that a general calculating machine can be used for work that its original builder never anticipated.

Second, cryptographers become important early German programmers. They bring:

- combinatorics;
- Boolean tests;
- pattern matching;
- symbolic alphabets;
- state-transition thinking;
- adversarial testing;
- concern with information leakage.

Third, secrecy becomes embedded in the German computing industry. Machine designs, libraries, peripheral specifications, and even numerical methods are divided among offices according to clearance and political reliability.

### 1947

Victory brings recognition but also bureaucratic competition.

A working 1947 institutional arrangement would be a small **central machine-calculation coordinating office** under the armaments or technical administration, rather than a great ministry of computation. Its duties would be:

- registering major machines;
- allocating scarce relays and valves;
- preventing wholly redundant projects;
- maintaining numerical libraries;
- assigning priority calculations;
- evaluating whether new work needs analog, digital, punched-card, or human methods;
- collecting operating experience.

It does not own every machine. Peenemünde, the Navy, major firms, economic offices, and intelligence services retain their own establishments.

That institutional disorder is important. German computing benefits from state priority but suffers from the Reich’s characteristic plurality of overlapping authorities.

---

## 4. German architecture at the end of 1947

### The principal scientific machine

The German general scientific computer is still recognizably Zusean:

| Characteristic | German tendency, 1947 |
|---|---|
| Number system | Binary |
| Numerical representation | Floating point favored for engineering |
| Logic technology | Electromechanical relays |
| Main memory | Small electromechanical or mechanical store |
| Program storage | External punched film or tape |
| Execution style | Sequential |
| Primary users | Engineers, aerospace establishments, military research |
| Output | Printed or electromechanical display/output |
| Main strength | Complex numerical work with very little human arithmetic |
| Main weakness | Speed, memory, relay maintenance, difficult programming |

The absence of stored program is decisive. Changing a program is easier than rewiring an analog machine or ENIAC-like plugboard, but instructions do not yet occupy the same memory as data.

### The German analog machine

| Characteristic | German analog tendency |
|---|---|
| Representation | Continuous voltage, rotation, or physical displacement |
| Program | Wiring and component configuration |
| Strength | Real-time differential equations and control |
| Weakness | Accuracy, drift, reconfiguration, poor generality |
| Principal use | Rockets, aircraft, servos, guidance, simulation |

Analog engineers regard many digital-machine enthusiasts as people proposing a much slower answer to a problem analog equipment already solves continuously.

### The administrative machine

| Characteristic | German administrative tendency |
|---|---|
| Representation | Decimal fields and categorical codes |
| Storage | Punched cards and paper records |
| Program | Card routes, plugboards, sorter/tabulator setup |
| Strength | Large repeated record operations |
| Weakness | Poor flexibility, weak cross-file integration, input dependent on clerks |
| Principal use | Payroll, census, production, inventory, labor, accounts |

This line is initially much more relevant to administering the empire than the Z4.

---

## 5. German programming in 1947

There is no usable Rechenplan compiler yet.

German software exists at four levels:

### Level one: mathematical specification

A mathematician or engineer defines the equations, approximations, convergence criteria, and required precision.

### Level two: plan description

Zuse and his closest collaborators increasingly describe data and operations in a structured, Plankalkül-influenced notation.

This may include conceptual distinctions among:

- scalar values;
- vectors;
- tables;
- logical truth values;
- intermediate results;
- repeated operations;
- conditions;
- input and output structures.

### Level three: machine preparation

The plan is manually translated into the Z4’s available operations and punched onto film or tape.

### Level four: machine operation

Operators:

- load constants;
- verify tape;
- inspect relay states;
- run test cases;
- detect mechanical faults;
- compare results with known values;
- repeat calculations when relay errors are suspected.

This division creates a profession before it creates a language. Germany may already distinguish between:

- the scientist who owns the problem;
- the *Planer* who reformulates it;
- the machine coder;
- the operator;
- the maintenance engineer.

That professional hierarchy becomes one of the roots of the later German software culture.

---

## German position on 31 December 1947

Germany does **not** possess the world’s best electronic stored-program computer. It does possess:

- the strongest native binary floating-point engineering tradition;
- the most advanced body of high-level programming thought;
- a mature analog rocket-control tradition;
- a new cryptographic demand for formal computation;
- a victorious state prepared to fund machinery;
- immense impending administrative workloads.

Germany’s central weakness is that these are still separate islands.

Its central long-term advantage is that one man—Zuse—already sees hardware and programming as related but distinct disciplines.

---

# II. Britain: from codebreaking establishment to national computer system

Britain is probably the strongest overall computing power in 1947, though not in every category.

It has something no other bloc possesses: a large wartime community that has already operated electronic logical machinery under continuous operational pressure.

## 1. What Britain possesses in 1944

### The Bombe establishment

The British Bombe is electromechanical machinery for testing candidate Enigma settings. It is not a general-purpose computer. Its importance lies in organizational methods:

- jobs are prepared systematically;
- machine time is scheduled;
- intercepted traffic is triaged;
- candidate results are checked by humans;
- engineering and cryptanalysis are tightly integrated;
- large numbers of operators follow exact procedures.

The lasting inheritance is as much bureaucratic as technical.

### Colossus

Colossus is a much more consequential electronic achievement. It uses high-speed valve logic and reads intercepted material from punched paper tape. It performs configurable Boolean and statistical operations against teleprinter traffic, but it is not a stored-program general-purpose computer.

Historically, ten Colossi existed and eight were destroyed after the war, while their engineers and users were bound to secrecy for decades. citeturn187083search0

In this setting, neither the destruction nor the total historical silence makes sense.

### Radar and telecommunications

Britain also has:

- Post Office valve engineering;
- high-speed pulse and counting expertise;
- radar displays;
- servomechanisms;
- telecommunications switching;
- operational research;
- antiaircraft prediction;
- naval plotting;
- extensive experience maintaining delicate electronics in military use.

The people who built Colossus do not begin from the same intellectual place as Zuse.

Zuse asks:

> How can a machine execute a general mathematical plan?

Flowers and the Newmanry ask:

> How can a machine consume a rapid stream of symbols and continuously test it for useful relationships?

That difference eventually becomes the core of the British “flow” tradition.

---

## 2. The secrecy question

The user’s instinct is correct, with one qualification.

By 1946–47, Germany has inferred from convoy behavior, routing, repeated operational failures, and British reactions that its naval system has been compromised. The exact British method may remain uncertain, but the strategic secret—*Britain can read important German naval traffic*—has already been lost.

Britain therefore gains little by maintaining the fiction that Enigma was never broken.

But Britain still has reasons to conceal:

- the scale of its cryptanalytic establishment;
- attacks on other German systems;
- the details of the Lorenz/Tunny attack;
- the internal architecture and speed of Colossus;
- traffic-analysis techniques;
- which Italian and Japanese systems are readable;
- how much postwar commercial or diplomatic traffic it can exploit;
- machine-assisted statistical methods.

The most plausible settlement is **selective disclosure**.

### What becomes public after Lisbon

Britain acknowledges that:

- German naval and military ciphers were penetrated;
- captured material and mathematical analysis were both important;
- electromechanical machines assisted the attack;
- the Bombe establishment existed;
- British codebreakers materially prolonged national survival.

A Bombe can be displayed or photographed relatively early.

### What remains classified

Britain continues to conceal:

- full Colossus circuitry;
- operational tape speeds;
- detailed Lorenz methods;
- machine configurations;
- statistical algorithms;
- ongoing attacks on foreign teleprinter systems;
- postwar repurposing.

Colossus becomes an acknowledged category before it becomes an openly documented machine. Official language might refer to **electronic statistical analyzers** without revealing their complete capabilities.

This preserves national credit without handing every foreign intelligence service a technical manual.

---

## 3. Britain does not destroy the Colossi

The actual postwar destruction reflected the historical disappearance of the immediate continental enemy, a desire to conceal British signals-intelligence capabilities, and a political decision not to preserve a visible computer establishment. In the present setting, Britain remains surrounded by Germany, Italy, Japan, colonial wars, hostile clients, and uncertain American policy.

It has every reason to preserve the machinery.

I would set the 1947 outcome as follows:

| Colossus disposition | Number |
|---|---:|
| Active operational cryptanalytic machines | 6 |
| Research and conversion machines | 2 |
| Training, component, or ready-reserve machines | 2–4 |
| Deliberately destroyed | Damaged or obsolete subassemblies only |

Continued war through 1947 may raise total production slightly above the historical ten, but there is no need to invent twenty or thirty. Ten to twelve retained machines are sufficient.

Their roles broaden:

- foreign diplomatic traffic;
- Japanese teleprinter systems;
- Italian and German successor systems;
- high-speed tape comparison;
- statistical tests;
- communications routing experiments;
- radar-track correlation research;
- data conversion;
- training electronic technicians.

They do **not** become normal scientific computers. Their architecture is too specialized.

---

## 4. The four British architecture schools

Britain’s great strength—and immediate weakness—is that it has four credible paths toward the general-purpose computer.

## A. The Flowers–Newman stream processor

This is the Colossus inheritance.

| Characteristic | Tendency |
|---|---|
| Logic | Electronic valve logic |
| Input | High-speed paper tape |
| Data model | Streams of symbols |
| Program | Switches, plugboards, configured tests |
| Memory | Registers and short internal state, not general stored program |
| Natural tasks | Cryptanalysis, filtering, correlation, message processing |
| Intellectual style | Events and symbols flowing through logical stages |

This school is comfortable with:

- pipelines;
- counters;
- simultaneous tests;
- data arriving from an external source;
- fixed high-throughput tasks;
- machine-supported human analysis.

It is the seed of later communications and signal-processing computers.

## B. Turing’s ACE

Turing’s Automatic Computing Engine proposal is an aggressive stored-program design developed for the National Physical Laboratory. Work on ACE began in 1946, and Turing’s design emphasized a high-speed serial machine using mercury delay-line storage and carefully optimized instruction timing. citeturn187083search17turn187083search28

The ACE school values:

- stored instructions;
- binary arithmetic;
- very high logical efficiency;
- small but carefully designed instruction sets;
- subroutines;
- machine code organized around memory timing;
- a close relationship between mathematical method and instruction scheduling.

ACE is not simply “the British version of EDVAC.” Turing is willing to demand more intellectual work from programmers in exchange for extracting more performance from limited hardware.

## C. Manchester random-access storage

Freddie Williams begins CRT storage work in 1946. By the end of 1947, Williams and Tom Kilburn can retain roughly 2,048 bits on a CRT for extended periods and are ready to build a small computer around the store. citeturn187083search6turn187083search17turn187083search25

This line is architecturally revolutionary because it promises **random access**.

A mercury delay line gives access to words as they circulate past a read point. A CRT store allows the machine to select an address directly, although it requires refreshing and careful electronics.

The Manchester school is:

- experimental;
- hardware-driven;
- accumulator-oriented;
- interested in fast random-access memory;
- less initially concerned with elegant programming systems than with proving that electronic storage works.

## D. Cambridge service computing

Maurice Wilkes begins designing EDSAC in 1947. Its guiding principle is not maximum speed or a wholly new theory of information. It is to build a conservative stored-program computer that a university can actually use as a dependable scientific service. citeturn187083search7turn187083search18

The Cambridge school emphasizes:

- reliability;
- simplicity;
- regular service;
- reusable routines;
- understandable machine organization;
- a library of proven subprograms;
- access for scientists who are not computer engineers.

This is the seed of Britain’s software-library tradition.

---

## 5. British pressure points, 1944–1947

### Pressure one: surviving the air and submarine war

Britain needs machines for:

- radar coordination;
- antiaircraft defense;
- aircraft interception;
- convoy routing;
- weather;
- antisubmarine warfare;
- signals intelligence;
- fuel and food allocation;
- repair scheduling;
- merchant shipping.

The computer is not a prestige toy. It is part of the machinery preventing national death.

### Pressure two: German cipher replacement

Germany’s 1946–47 cipher change does not make Bletchley obsolete. It proves the danger of building machinery around only one target.

The British response is to demand more **reconfigurability**:

- switchable logic;
- faster preparation;
- reusable counting units;
- flexible tape readers;
- stored routines;
- machine-assisted testing of new attacks.

The failure to retain access to German naval traffic becomes one of the arguments for general-purpose computers.

### Pressure three: physical attack and dispersion

The Second Battle of Britain attacks communications centers, radar, operations rooms, factories, and laboratories. That should affect British architecture.

Britain learns that one magnificent centralized installation is vulnerable. It therefore values:

- duplicate facilities;
- machines that can be transported in sections;
- standardized peripheral interfaces;
- remote teleprinter access;
- dispersed calculation centers;
- interchangeable operators;
- the ability to send problems over communications lines.

This is the beginning of the British conception of computing as a **networked national service**, even before practical computer networking exists.

### Pressure four: post-defeat reconstruction

After Lisbon, Britain cannot afford to build every proposed machine. It must choose among ACE, Manchester, Cambridge, Bletchley, commercial tabulators, and military analog projects.

This scarcity does not drive Britain into the American system. It forces Britain to organize its own.

---

## 6. A British national computing program

I would establish a working 1946–47 institution—its final name can be fixed later—bringing together representatives from:

- National Physical Laboratory;
- Government Code and Cypher School;
- Post Office Research Station;
- Telecommunications Research Establishment;
- Admiralty;
- Air Ministry;
- universities;
- British Tabulating Machine Company;
- Ferranti;
- English Electric;
- major Commonwealth scientific establishments.

It should **coordinate**, not merge, all work.

Its first decisions are:

1. Preserve Colossus and its personnel.
2. Continue ACE as the high-performance national scientific design.
3. Continue Manchester CRT storage as a strategic memory project.
4. Permit Cambridge to build a conservative university service machine.
5. Fund at least one commercial manufacturer to learn production engineering.
6. Create common paper-tape, teleprinter, valve, test, and documentation practices where possible.
7. Retain a classified machine-computation establishment inside signals intelligence.

This avoids the historical danger of allowing each pioneering team to disappear into a separate institutional cul-de-sac.

---

## 7. Turing’s position

Keeping Turing alive should be adopted as a setting constraint, but that cannot be accomplished solely by declaring that he survives in 1954. The foundations must change now.

The 1944–47 divergence should give him:

- continuous senior government employment;
- a permanent research staff;
- direct access to the national computing board;
- recognized authorship of ACE;
- responsibility for compiler and programming research as well as hardware;
- continued classified importance;
- public honors once the Enigma story is selectively released;
- institutional colleagues rather than professional isolation.

I would make Turing, by late 1947, something like **Chief Scientific Officer for Automatic Computation at the NPL**, while remaining a high-level consultant to signals intelligence.

This does not automatically abolish the later legal danger to him. It does make him:

- harder to discard;
- less isolated;
- more publicly valuable;
- surrounded by colleagues with an institutional reason to intervene;
- less likely to enter the exact personal and professional circumstances that historically culminated in prosecution.

The later legal event still requires deliberate treatment when we reach 1951–54. But the first survival mechanism is to prevent the state from treating him as a brilliant wartime disposable.

---

## 8. British programming in 1947

Britain has the world’s richest variety of programming practice.

### Colossus programming

- switch settings;
- plugboard routes;
- counter selection;
- tape preparation;
- synchronization;
- statistical thresholds;
- operator checklists.

### ACE programming

- binary machine code;
- instruction sequences arranged around delay-line timing;
- manually scheduled data movement;
- reusable subroutines;
- tables of constants;
- explicit concern with how the program occupies memory.

### Manchester programming

At the end of 1947, Manchester is still principally building storage. Its emerging code culture is very low level:

- accumulator operations;
- binary words;
- direct addresses;
- test patterns;
- diagnostic programs intended to expose memory failure.

### Cambridge programming

EDSAC’s design encourages:

- standard routines;
- symbolic abbreviations;
- library discipline;
- machine access as a service;
- separation between machine maintainers and scientific users.

### The Bletchley social inheritance

Britain also possesses something more important than an instruction set: thousands of people who already understand that a machine process requires:

- preparation;
- disciplined operators;
- verification;
- logs;
- repeated runs;
- error classification;
- division of labor;
- secure handling;
- routine maintenance.

That institutional knowledge is exceptionally difficult for another country to imitate quickly.

---

## Does Britain remain independent?

**Yes—more decisively than in real history.**

Britain may learn from the American EDVAC discussions, and British scientists will continue exchanging papers with Americans. But by 1947 Britain has:

- Colossus;
- ACE;
- Manchester CRT storage;
- EDSAC;
- its own valve industry;
- its own teleprinter standards;
- its own punched-card companies;
- its own military requirements;
- an urgent sovereignty problem;
- no dependable American subsidy.

American aid ends in early 1947 in the setting, while British reconstruction explicitly preserves computing, radar, telecommunications, aerospace, and high-value technical industry. fileciteturn5file3 fileciteturn5file4

Britain is therefore not absorbed into an American architecture. Its danger is **internal fragmentation and underfunding**, not Americanization.

---

# III. United States: immense potential without wartime concentration

## 1. What America retains despite neutrality

The United States does not enter the general war, but that does not erase every American computer project.

Several lines predate or do not strictly require belligerency.

### Harvard–IBM Mark I

The Harvard Mark I project originates before American entry into the historical war. It is delivered to Harvard in 1944 and historically operated by the Navy Bureau of Ships. It is an electromechanical automatic sequence calculator whose instructions are read from tape. citeturn655578search1

In this setting, it still exists.

The Navy is expanding, America is watching a global war, and the United States possesses an enormous battleship and carrier program even without becoming a belligerent. The Bureau of Ships has ample reason to fund:

- naval architecture;
- gunnery;
- propeller calculations;
- armor;
- stability;
- ballistics;
- range tables.

The precise personnel structure changes, but the machine survives.

### Bell Laboratories relay calculators

Telephone switching gives Bell Laboratories a strong relay-logic tradition. The American telephone system creates demand for reliable switching, fault isolation, logic design, and long-lived electromechanical components.

This line is closer to communications engineering than to university mathematics.

### IBM punched-card processing

America possesses the world’s deepest commercial punched-card ecosystem:

- census;
- insurance;
- banking;
- railways;
- inventory;
- utilities;
- payroll;
- government records.

Punched-card tabulation is already a mature form of automatic data processing rather than a speculative science. The Hollerith system’s central idea is that each card carries a structured record that can be sorted, counted, and summarized electrically. citeturn261528search11turn261528search12

This becomes America’s most important early commercial advantage.

---

## 2. Does ENIAC still exist?

Yes, but its schedule and social environment should change.

Historically, ENIAC was an Army-financed wartime project for ballistic tables, constructed from 1943 and publicly announced in 1946. It proved that large-scale electronic calculation was practical, but programming required manual switches and plug connections rather than an internally stored instruction sequence. citeturn431178search6turn431178search10

The historical urgency is weaker here because:

- America is not firing millions of artillery rounds in Europe;
- there is no vast expeditionary Army;
- no Manhattan Project supplies a secret high-priority calculation customer;
- the military has fewer emergency appropriations;
- there is no comparable wartime shortage forcing every calculation bottleneck to receive money.

Nevertheless, the project remains plausible because America is:

- rearming;
- supplying Britain;
- maintaining major coastal and hemispheric defenses;
- studying German rockets and jets;
- building advanced ships and aircraft;
- increasingly alarmed by foreign military technology.

### Recommended alternate schedule

| Event | Historical | Setting recommendation |
|---|---:|---:|
| Formal project authorization | 1943 | Late 1943 or 1944 |
| Major construction | 1943–45 | 1944–46 |
| Initial operation | Late 1945 | Late 1946 |
| Public announcement | February 1946 | Spring or summer 1947 |
| Stored-program conversion discussion | 1945 onward | 1946–47 onward |

It remains ENIAC because the responsible institution, engineers, and general requirement still exist.

Its first serious setting workloads are:

- artillery and naval tables;
- supersonic and rocket trajectories;
- weather;
- aircraft performance;
- hydrodynamics;
- statistical sampling;
- perhaps cryptanalytic research.

It does **not** perform an initial thermonuclear calculation because there is no weapons program of that kind.

---

## 3. The EDVAC idea arrives later and more diffusely

The core conceptual leap is to store instructions in electronic memory alongside data.

Historically, ENIAC proved electronic arithmetic while EDVAC and related designs pursued stored-program operation. In 1947, the U.S. Bureau of the Census, Army, and Air Force were already contracting for a stored-program commercial machine. citeturn431178search6

In the setting, this process is slowed by roughly a year, not prevented.

The reason is that the intellectual argument remains compelling:

- rewiring ENIAC takes too long;
- external paper tape limits branching and self-modification;
- military and scientific users want to change problems rapidly;
- one machine should solve many tasks without a major physical reconstruction.

By the end of 1947, the United States has designs and reports for binary stored-program machines, but no mature operational American stored-program installation.

---

## 4. American pressure points, 1944–1947

### Pressure one: naval expansion

The United States has the world’s largest untouched capital-ship and naval-industrial base. Its computational problems include:

- hull design;
- fire-control tables;
- antiaircraft prediction;
- carrier operations;
- fleet logistics;
- radio and radar;
- submarine detection;
- weather routing;
- industrial procurement.

Unlike Britain, these are not existential daily problems. That reduces urgency but creates steady institutional demand.

### Pressure two: aviation and rocketry

German jets and long-range rockets demonstrate that future military technology will require more computation.

American engineers want:

- compressible-flow tables;
- high-speed aerodynamics;
- structural modes;
- engine analysis;
- missile trajectories;
- guidance simulation.

This is the strongest argument for completing ENIAC despite the Depression.

### Pressure three: business

The commercial market matters earlier in America than elsewhere.

Insurance companies, banks, railways, utilities, and the Census do not initially want a mysterious universal electronic brain. They want:

- faster sorting;
- billing;
- account reconciliation;
- actuarial calculations;
- payroll;
- inventory;
- printed reports.

IBM therefore has no reason to abandon cards for speculative electronic machines immediately. It develops electronic arithmetic as an attachment or accelerator to an existing card-centered workflow.

### Pressure four: limited federal funds

The setting’s United States remains economically weak through much of this period and receives none of the historical war-mobilization transformation. fileciteturn5file3

That produces a characteristic American pattern:

- the government funds prototypes;
- universities own the intellectual projects;
- large companies preserve commercially proven machinery;
- military branches sponsor different designs;
- no central authority imposes one system.

American fragmentation is not merely waste. It produces multiple competing architectural traditions.

---

## 5. American architecture at the end of 1947

## A. Harvard–IBM sequence architecture

| Characteristic | Mark I tendency |
|---|---|
| Number representation | Decimal-oriented |
| Technology | Electromechanical |
| Program | Punched tape |
| Data | Registers, switches, cards |
| Execution | Strict sequence |
| Strength | Reliability and long unattended calculations |
| Weakness | Very slow, inflexible branching, no stored program |

Its natural cultural descendant is the dependable large calculator.

## B. Bell relay architecture

| Characteristic | Bell tendency |
|---|---|
| Technology | Telephone relays |
| Logic | Switching-network logic |
| Input/output | Teletype and telecommunications equipment |
| Strength | Reliability, remote operation, logical switching |
| Weakness | Speed |
| Natural future | Communications and control systems |

## C. ENIAC architecture

| Characteristic | ENIAC tendency |
|---|---|
| Number representation | Decimal |
| Technology | Electronic valves |
| Program | Plugboards, cables, switches |
| Arithmetic | Parallel electronic accumulators |
| Strength | Extraordinary arithmetic speed |
| Weakness | Long setup time, huge size, no original stored program |

## D. EDVAC/IAS-type concept

| Characteristic | Emerging tendency |
|---|---|
| Number representation | Binary |
| Technology | Electronic |
| Program | Internally stored |
| Memory | Delay-line or electrostatic under consideration |
| Strength | Generality |
| Weakness | Not yet operational, memory technology immature |

## E. IBM administrative architecture

| Characteristic | Commercial tendency |
|---|---|
| Representation | Decimal fields and card codes |
| Storage | Punched cards |
| Program | Plugboards and card-deck flow |
| Output | Printed reports and punched summaries |
| Strength | Scale, business integration, service network |
| Weakness | Limited scientific flexibility |

There is no single American architecture in 1947.

---

## 6. American programming culture changes substantially

The absence of full mobilization alters who becomes a programmer.

Historically, ENIAC’s programming team emerged from a wartime pool of women employed as human computers, while Grace Hopper entered naval service and joined the Mark I establishment amid wartime personnel mobilization. ENIAC’s women programmers were recruited partly because wartime demand had drawn male engineers elsewhere. citeturn431178search18

In this setting:

- Grace Hopper does not automatically enter the Naval Reserve on the same timetable;
- fewer women are recruited into large military calculation pools;
- Aberdeen has fewer emergency firing-table requirements;
- programmers are more likely to be electrical engineers, physicists, and existing card-machine specialists;
- machine operation remains more tightly subordinate to hardware engineering.

Hopper can still enter the field. Aiken or IBM may recruit her as a civilian mathematician in 1945–47. But it should be a positive alternate event, not an unchanged historical carryover.

This has consequences.

Early American programming is probably:

- less extensively documented;
- less separated from hardware engineering;
- less conscious of programming as an independent profession;
- more dominated by men already holding engineering appointments;
- slower to develop systematic coding manuals.

America retains enormous talent, but its early software culture is thinner than Britain’s.

---

## 7. American position on 31 December 1947

America possesses:

- the widest industrial base;
- the largest commercial data-processing market;
- a functioning large electromechanical computer;
- a newly operating ENIAC;
- advanced relay research;
- stored-program designs;
- powerful telephone and office-machine companies.

But it lacks:

- a Bletchley-scale operational computing culture;
- Germany’s indigenous high-level algorithm notation;
- a unified national computer policy;
- wartime urgency;
- a large trained programmer corps;
- an operational stored-program electronic machine.

America is behind in concentration, not in potential.

Its later dominance will arise when its fragmented military, university, business, and consumer traditions finally converge.

---

# IV. Japan: computation as control over an overstretched empire

## 1. Japan’s real starting point

Japan is not computationally empty in 1944.

Japanese researchers have already produced important work in relay switching theory. Akira Nakashima and Masao Hanzawa published logical methods for relay-circuit design in the 1930s, developing an algebraic treatment of relay networks before recognizing its relationship to Boolean algebra. citeturn293301search2turn293301search4

Japan also possesses:

- a large mechanical differential analyzer built at Tokyo Imperial University’s Aeronautical Research Institute in 1942;
- a machine for solving nine simultaneous equations around 1944;
- wartime statistical-machine research;
- telecommunications and relay engineering;
- mechanical and electromechanical calculators;
- naval analog fire-control machinery. citeturn293301search0

Hideo Yamashita’s statistical machine, built around relays and counting registers, appears around 1947–48 historically. citeturn293301search4

Thus Japan’s weakness is not ignorance of logic. It is the absence of a mature general-purpose electronic-computer project.

---

## 2. Japanese pressure points

### Pressure one: the oceanic empire

Japan must coordinate shipping across:

- the home islands;
- Korea;
- Manchukuo;
- China;
- Indochina;
- Malaya and Singapore;
- the East Indies;
- Pacific islands;
- eastern Siberian clients;
- associated Siam.

The immediate problems are:

- tanker allocation;
- escort schedules;
- port congestion;
- repair;
- aviation fuel;
- food shipping;
- convoy routing;
- merchant tonnage;
- railway-to-port transfer;
- exchange and customs records.

This does not initially demand a scientific binary computer. It demands cards, counters, tabulators, teleprinters, and disciplined clerks.

### Pressure two: carrier and naval warfare

Japan’s fleet is the central military instrument of its empire. It needs:

- fire control;
- carrier-cycle planning;
- air-search plotting;
- radar;
- radio direction finding;
- torpedo calculations;
- antisubmarine analysis;
- meteorology;
- aircraft maintenance scheduling;
- long-range maritime reconnaissance;
- radio-command weapon development.

Japan’s initial computing style is consequently more closely connected to **operations and control** than to pure mathematical research.

### Pressure three: guided weapons

The setting’s Type 7 Ōka is a radio-command anti-ship weapon rather than a suicide craft. fileciteturn5file1

That requires:

- stabilization;
- command encoding;
- tracking;
- operator displays;
- range estimation;
- interference resistance;
- testing of control laws.

The most useful machines are analog simulators and specialized control calculators, not a room-sized general-purpose digital computer.

### Pressure four: skilled-labor scarcity

Japan has conquered an empire far larger than the supply of Japanese engineers and administrators capable of managing it.

This is the earliest form of the pressure that later makes Japan the great automation power:

> Every routine decision performed automatically frees a scarce trained Japanese technician for work only a trained Japanese technician can perform.

During 1944–47 this remains an emerging awareness. After victory, it becomes doctrine.

### Pressure five: Army–Navy and corporate duplication

Japan’s research is divided among:

- Army bureaus;
- Navy arsenals;
- universities;
- Electrotechnical Laboratory;
- NEC;
- Hitachi;
- Toshiba predecessors;
- Mitsubishi;
- other zaibatsu and communications firms.

Each institution has legitimate security reasons not to disclose its work.

The result is duplication:

- different relay symbols;
- different record codes;
- different tape widths;
- different electrical standards;
- different numerical conventions;
- different military reporting formats.

This is the principal reason Japan does not immediately turn strong switching theory into a unified computer.

---

## 3. Japanese development, 1944–1947

### 1944

The nine-equation solver and differential analyzer represent the scientific end of Japanese computation.

Their users are concerned with:

- aircraft structures;
- aerodynamic equations;
- ballistics;
- vibration;
- naval engineering.

At the same time, the Navy and telecommunications industry possess advanced relay and analog expertise.

No one institution yet proposes that one general-purpose machine should replace all these systems.

### 1945

Japan is not devastated by American bombing or blockade. Its laboratories, engineers, electrical factories, and technical schools survive.

This is a very large advantage over historical Japan.

However, the war still consumes:

- copper;
- high-quality electrical components;
- valves;
- skilled assembly labor;
- precision instruments.

Radar, radios, fire control, aircraft, and ships have priority over an experimental universal calculator.

A plausible 1945 result is the authorization of separate:

- Navy relay plotting calculators;
- Army statistical and logistics machines;
- university scientific calculators;
- zaibatsu punched-card installations.

### 1946

As Japan consolidates Southeast Asia and fights Britain around the remaining imperial frontiers, shipping administration becomes critical.

Singapore begins its transformation into the imperial counting house. It acquires:

- captured British tabulators;
- Dutch commercial equipment;
- insurance and port records;
- teleprinters;
- accounting machinery;
- customs systems.

Japanese administrators do not simply replace all of this. They impose Japanese codes on top of heterogeneous machinery.

This encourages a Japanese habit that will remain important:

> Standardize the transaction and procedure before standardizing every machine.

A Singapore manifest can be accepted into the imperial system even when prepared on a different firm’s equipment, provided its commodity codes, destination fields, and currency treatment follow Tokyo’s rules.

### 1947

Yamashita’s relay statistical machine becomes the most promising administrative-computing project.

I would make it the first machine to receive explicit postwar imperial backing.

Its likely characteristics are:

- decimal counters;
- relay logic;
- punched-card or prepared record input;
- strong statistical and summation functions;
- limited conditional operations;
- printed or tabulated results;
- no stored program;
- no general floating-point scientific architecture.

The machine is useful for:

- population totals;
- industrial reporting;
- food estimates;
- shipping;
- military personnel;
- provincial returns.

This is Japan’s first serious bridge between office machinery and automatic logic.

---

## 4. Japanese architecture at the end of 1947

## A. Analog scientific and control machines

| Characteristic | Japanese tendency |
|---|---|
| Representation | Continuous mechanical or electrical quantities |
| Natural tasks | Aerodynamics, guidance, fire control, simulation |
| Strength | Real-time control and equations |
| Weakness | Difficult to reconfigure, limited precision |

## B. Relay logic systems

| Characteristic | Japanese tendency |
|---|---|
| Representation | Binary switching states |
| Intellectual basis | Native relay-switching theory |
| Natural tasks | Telephone control, sequence logic, military systems |
| Strength | Reliability and formal circuit design |
| Weakness | Slow and institutionally fragmented |

## C. Statistical relay machines

| Characteristic | Japanese tendency |
|---|---|
| Representation | Decimal counters and coded fields |
| Natural tasks | Census, shipping, production, personnel |
| Strength | Direct administrative relevance |
| Weakness | Not general-purpose |

## D. Punched-card empire

| Characteristic | Japanese tendency |
|---|---|
| Machinery | Japanese, captured, imported, and licensed tabulators |
| Data | Commodity, personnel, port, finance, food |
| Strength | Immediate scale |
| Weakness | Incompatible formats and multilingual clerical input |

Japan has no operational equivalent to ACE, ENIAC, or Z4 as a broadly programmable national scientific computer.

---

## 5. Japanese programming in 1947

Japanese “programming” consists of:

- relay equations;
- switching diagrams;
- plugboard setup;
- punched-card field definitions;
- machine-cycle charts;
- analog circuit layouts;
- naval fire-control procedures;
- prepared sequences of operations.

There is no katakana high-level language yet.

Katakana begins to appear naturally in:

- panel labels;
- operator instructions;
- error indicators;
- teleprinter messages;
- punched-card field names;
- maintenance documents.

Latin letters and mathematical notation remain common for formulas and technical symbols.

The later Japanese language environment should emerge from these operator and procedural conventions, not from an implausible 1945 attempt to write ordinary Japanese prose as source code.

---

## Japanese position on 31 December 1947

Japan is last among the five systems in general-purpose electronic computing.

It nevertheless has:

- significant native switching theory;
- intact electrical industry;
- analog scientific machinery;
- relay statistical machinery;
- powerful commercial houses;
- an enormous administrative workload;
- a severe long-term incentive to automate;
- no occupation suppressing military electronics or breaking up its industrial groups.

Japan’s 1947 weakness is the absence of synthesis.

Its future strength is that the empire gives it the clearest reason to put computation **inside the process itself**.

---

# V. The emerging Latin system: Italy’s office machine and Occitania’s electronic laboratory

The “Latin Bloc” does not yet possess a common computing architecture in 1947. It is better understood as several traditions that will later be forced together.

## 1. Italy

### Adriano Olivetti and Natale Capellaro

A useful correction is necessary.

Adriano Olivetti is the industrial organizer, social thinker, company leader, and patron. The crucial mechanical-calculator designer is **Natale Capellaro**.

Capellaro leads the development of Olivetti’s postwar Series 14 calculating machines. The Elettrosumma 14 appears in 1946, followed by multiplication-capable machinery and, shortly afterward, a four-operation printing calculator. citeturn891385search1turn891385search8

Olivetti’s importance in 1947 is not that it already manufactures electronic computers. It does not.

Its importance is that it understands the **office machine as a complete human system**:

- keyboard;
- mechanism;
- operator;
- paper;
- printed audit trail;
- maintenance;
- sales;
- training;
- industrial design;
- mass production.

### The Italian computing style begins with the printed answer

The Z4 is an engineering instrument. Colossus is a cryptanalytic instrument. ENIAC is an electronic mathematical instrument.

The Olivetti calculator is a machine intended to sit in an ordinary office and become part of daily commercial work.

Its design priorities are:

- ten-key entry;
- decimal arithmetic;
- immediate printed proof;
- low operator training requirements;
- physical compactness;
- attractive enclosure;
- reliability;
- serviceability;
- mass production;
- understandable controls.

This is a major computing inheritance, even though it is not yet programmable.

### Italian military computation

Italy also has:

- mechanical naval fire-control computers;
- antiaircraft predictors;
- analog aircraft instruments;
- radio-navigation systems;
- artillery tables;
- punched-card accounting;
- IRI and military-industrial statistical offices.

Its 1944–47 pressures include:

- Mediterranean naval operations;
- convoy and port management;
- Suez planning;
- colonial customs;
- air and naval navigation;
- occupation administration;
- reconstruction of transport and industry.

But Italian research remains scattered among:

- armed services;
- universities;
- STET telecommunications;
- IRI enterprises;
- Olivetti;
- aerospace and naval firms.

There is no Italian general-purpose electronic computer in operation by 1947.

---

## 2. Occitania

Occitania does not exist as a consolidated state until the 1946–47 French collapse and Toulouse evacuation.

It cannot simply inherit “French computing” intact.

### What remains in northern France

Compagnie des Machines Bull has a strong prewar and wartime punched-card position. Historically, Bull emerged from the war with an important mechanographic business comparable in market function to IBM, while the Société d’électronique et d’automatisme was founded in 1947 and later developed a succession of French electronic and analog machines. citeturn542503search1

Much of Bull’s corporate center and manufacturing base is likely to remain in or near German-controlled northern France.

Germany will want:

- its card equipment;
- sales organization;
- skilled technicians;
- patents;
- French administrative customers.

Thus Occitania should **not** receive Bull whole.

### What can move south

The Toulouse–Bordeaux evacuation can preserve:

- aeronautical computing staff;
- radar specialists;
- guidance engineers;
- mathematical physicists;
- telephone and radio engineers;
- university groups;
- military research records;
- selected Bull or independent machine engineers;
- prototypes and components;
- technical libraries;
- men who do not wish to work under German supervision.

Toulouse, Bordeaux, Marseille, Lyon if included, and the Rhône industrial system give this group a credible base.

### Occitan pressure points

The new state needs machines for:

- aircraft development;
- air defense;
- artillery;
- radar;
- customs;
- railway reconstruction;
- port administration;
- military integration;
- establishing financial independence from both Paris and Rome.

Occitania’s computer establishment is therefore born in a peculiar condition:

> It has advanced engineers but no settled national computer industry.

That encourages prototypes rather than mass production.

### Occitan architecture in 1947

The most plausible initial Occitan work is:

- analog flight and guidance calculators;
- valve counters and pulse circuits;
- radar-track equipment;
- binary arithmetic test assemblies;
- punched-card installations purchased or salvaged from French firms;
- an experimental stored-program study based on British and American reports.

It does not yet have an operational large digital machine.

Occitania’s long-term contribution will be electronics, avionics, compactness, and system integration—not office-machine volume.

---

## 3. Spain

Spain remains poor, damaged by the Civil War, and technically behind the principal combatants.

Its 1944–47 computing assets are principally:

- mechanical calculators;
- imported tabulators;
- military analog instruments;
- telephone and telegraph equipment;
- naval navigation systems;
- census and customs machines;
- German and Italian technical missions.

Spain has genuine engineers, but not the spare capital or component industry required for an independent electronic computer program.

Its immediate strategy is rational:

- buy Italian office machines;
- buy or license German scientific machinery where permitted;
- acquire French/Occitan punched-card equipment;
- train operators;
- build peripheral and repair capacity;
- delay an indigenous central processor.

Spain is a customer with bargaining power, not yet an architectural leader.

---

## 4. Portugal

Portugal is even less likely to build a large computer in this period.

Its needs are:

- shipping;
- colonial records;
- customs;
- telegraph routing;
- insurance;
- naval navigation;
- port administration;
- banking;
- Lisbon Conference accounting and diplomatic communications.

Portugal’s strength is geographic and diplomatic. It can purchase from:

- Britain;
- Italy;
- Germany;
- later Occitania;
- possibly America.

Portuguese engineers become skilled at making unlike teleprinters, cards, office systems, and communications equipment work together. This is useful, but it is not yet an autonomous computer architecture.

---

## 5. Latin pressure points, 1944–1947

The prospective Latin system has three distinct demands.

### Administrative empire

Italy has acquired or will control territories around:

- North Africa;
- Egypt;
- Suez;
- Greece;
- Cyprus;
- Syria;
- the Adriatic.

It requires:

- customs;
- port records;
- currency conversion;
- military payroll;
- shipping;
- rationing;
- police records;
- railway movements.

This favors decimal record processing and printed documentation.

### Military modernization

German radar, jets, rockets, and submarines reveal the danger of technical dependency.

Italy and Occitania require:

- radar computation;
- fire control;
- aircraft design;
- signals analysis;
- guided-weapon calculation.

This favors analog and electronic scientific systems.

### Multinational coordination

The future bloc contains Italian, Occitan, Spanish, and Portuguese institutions that refuse to surrender national sovereignty.

A single Italian imperial computer standard will be politically unacceptable.

The later Latin system will therefore need interoperability among national systems rather than total uniformity.

---

## 6. Latin architecture on 31 December 1947

There is no single Latin computer. There are three layers.

## Italian office machinery

| Characteristic | Tendency |
|---|---|
| Arithmetic | Decimal |
| Technology | Mechanical and electromechanical |
| Input | Ten-key or full keyboard |
| Output | Printed paper record |
| Program | Fixed mechanism and operator procedure |
| Strength | Human interface, reliability, mass office use |
| Weakness | Not freely programmable |

## Occitan scientific electronics

| Characteristic | Tendency |
|---|---|
| Arithmetic | Mixed analog and experimental binary |
| Technology | Valves, relays, servos |
| Input/output | Laboratory and military equipment |
| Program | Wiring and prototype control |
| Strength | Avionics, radar, compact integration |
| Weakness | No industrial scale, politically displaced workforce |

## Iberian data processing

| Characteristic | Tendency |
|---|---|
| Machinery | Imported cards, calculators, teleprinters |
| Program | Administrative workflow |
| Strength | Practical adoption |
| Weakness | Dependence on foreign suppliers |

The future Latin architecture will emerge only when Italy’s manufacturing and office discipline is joined to Occitania’s electronic and aerospace expertise.

---

# The world balance at the end of 1947

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Operational general scientific digital machinery | Strong relay-based | Multiple electronic designs approaching operation | Mark I and ENIAC; stored-program work incomplete | Very limited | Very limited |

# The five national conceptions taking shape

By the end of 1947, the later computing philosophies are visible, but only as tendencies.

## Germany: **the computer as a plan**

The machine exists to execute a formally specified calculation. Its natural users are engineers, cryptographers, logisticians, and state planners.

## Britain: **the computer as an information service**

The machine receives signals, transforms them, passes results onward, supports a community of users, and belongs inside a communications system.

## America: **the computer as a replaceable general tool**

No one design has won. Relay, decimal electronic, binary stored-program, cards, and commercial machines compete. The eventual winner will be the architecture that can be sold, expanded, documented, and adapted.

## Japan: **the computer as a controlled procedure**

The first priority is not universal calculation but making a process—shipping, switching, fire control, statistics, production—operate reliably with fewer scarce experts.

## Latin bloc: **the computer as an intelligible instrument**

Italy begins with a machine the ordinary clerk can operate and audit. Occitania contributes compact military electronics. Their eventual synthesis favors usable, modular, human-facing machines rather than the largest possible mainframe.

---

# Working canon I would adopt from this phase

1. **The original Z3 remains destroyed**, but the Z4 is protected, completed, and operational by late 1945 or early 1946.

2. **Germany has only a tiny Z4-derived fleet by 1947**, not mass-produced computers.

3. **Plankalkül exists as advanced specification notation**, but no compiler or routine machine execution exists before 1948.

4. **The 1946–47 naval-cipher replacement becomes Germany’s first demonstration that a general calculator can serve cryptographic design as well as engineering.**

5. **Britain retains ten to twelve Colossus machines**, with approximately six operational, two research machines, and the remainder in training or reserve.

6. **Britain selectively discloses the Enigma/Bombe story after Lisbon**, while retaining the detailed Colossus and Lorenz methods under classification.

7. **A national British computing board or program is created by 1947**, coordinating NPL, signals intelligence, TRE, the Post Office, universities, and industry without imposing one design.

8. **Turing receives a senior permanent computing appointment and staff**, making his continued life and influence a setting objective rather than a last-minute rescue in 1954.

9. **Britain maintains four competing schools:** Colossus stream processing, ACE high-speed serial design, Manchester random-access storage, and Cambridge service computing.

10. **ENIAC survives in America but enters operation about a year later**, with public presentation in 1947 and no nuclear-weapons workload.

11. **America’s early programmer culture is altered by the absence of wartime personnel mobilization.** Grace Hopper and the historical ENIAC programmers may still enter computing, but through different civilian or limited-defense routes.

12. **Japan’s Yamashita-type statistical machine becomes its first explicitly imperial data-processing project in 1947**, while its scientific computing remains analog and relay based.

13. **There is no unified Latin architecture in 1947.** Italy supplies office-machine manufacturing and decimal workflow; Occitania begins as an evacuated electronic and aerospace research community; Spain and Portugal remain customers and integrators.

The next natural interval is **1948–1952**, when the decisive question ceases to be whether electronic stored-program computers can exist and becomes which of these wartime traditions can turn a prototype into a reproducible institution.

A few modifications, or flavor modifications. First, the white parachutes event that ends up causing the British surrender or negotiated surrender at the end of the Second World War is actually not Goering's design. Goering didn't come up with the idea. Perhaps Rommel comes up with it as like a, hey, we could try it. Or it could be someone lower than Goering, who perhaps thought of it at... The doctrinal idea of why the Germans do it that I had in my head when I wrote it was that the Germans are kind of in a position where by the end of the Second Battle of Britain, they are actually getting low on their strategic reserves for fuel. They're still trying to figure out how to handle the east. They're really operating with an exhausted military. And the hope initially with the Second Battle of Britain was that they were going to be able to exhaust the British enough to make them concede, and then voila, we can finally manage everything. That was the hope. And it works, but it didn't work because of the intention. Rather, the white parachutes event was basically a last chance kind of idea of, you know, this is going to be the last raid we do. We don't have a large bombing contingent we can really do, but we've got, you know, we have these bombers available. We're ordered to do a strike, but we don't really have the munitions to outfit them completely. What if we did something different? Like, for this last thing, we'll pile in together all the rations and stuff that we've got from the area. We're going to be heading out anyways. Pile them all into the planes and drop them. Maybe this could be a Goering suggestion of like, hey, maybe this is a great idea to end the war. But ultimately, it's not, or not Goering, Goebbels who proposes to do this as a great propaganda victory. But I think it is more flavorfully significant for having it be not somebody who is one of the head of the order at the end of 1947. It is actually somebody who is relatively low down on the totem pole. Not, I will note, somebody who gets elevated. Oh, no. The person does not get elevated for doing this.
