# Computing Race III: 1955–1960  
## The compiler revolution, Raumbote I, and the first imperial data systems

This is exactly the right period for proper high-level languages to appear. It is not aggressive.

By 1955, all five systems already have:

- stored-program computers;
- symbolic assembly systems;
- reusable routine libraries;
- enough installed machines to make recoding every program intolerably expensive;
- more potential users than expert machine coders;
- several incompatible processors inside each bloc.

That last problem creates the compiler revolution. High-level languages do not initially arise because executives dream of friendly computers. They arise because hardware proliferation threatens to trap every program inside the machine for which it was written.

The important distinctions are:

| Milestone | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Language specification | A published syntax and semantic model exists |
| Experimental translator | A restricted subset can be translated automatically |
| Production compiler | Ordinary customers can submit real work through it |
| Portable language system | Several machines can compile substantially the same source |
| Software ecosystem | Libraries, training, documentation and institutional expectations surround the language |

By 1960, every bloc can possess the first three. Germany, Britain and America can possess the fourth. None yet possesses a truly mature modern software ecosystem.

Germany’s apparent “single language” should be real, but carefully understood. **Rechenplan becomes one state-recognized language family with different profiles**, rather than one identical compiler somehow governing scientific computing, accounting and missile control.

---

# The common technological transition

Between 1955 and 1960, four changes affect every bloc.

## Transistors begin replacing valves—but unevenly

The transistor is no longer merely a laboratory curiosity. It begins entering:

- arithmetic units;
- peripheral controllers;
- communications equipment;
- small scientific machines;
- airborne and shipboard electronics;
- industrial logic.

Large, proven valve machines remain common because transistor manufacturing is initially inconsistent. Relay systems also continue to be sold where speed matters less than reliability and maintainability.

A 1960 computer room may contain:

- a transistorized processor;
- magnetic-core memory;
- valve-driven tape units;
- relay-controlled printers;
- electromechanical card readers;
- analog instruments;
- human operators carrying paper job sheets.

There is no clean “generation change” on one date.

## Magnetic core becomes the preferred working memory

Core memory is attractive because it is:

- random-access;
- nonvolatile when power is lost;
- faster than drums;
- more robust than electrostatic tubes;
- manufacturable as a standardized component.

The United States leads early mass production. Britain follows closely. Germany builds domestic alternatives and adopts core selectively. Japan and the Latin bloc begin through a mixture of domestic work, licenses and imported materials.

Magnetic drums remain essential as larger, cheaper backing storage.

## Batch monitors appear

These are not yet full modern operating systems.

A typical monitor:

1. reads a control card or tape;
2. loads a compiler or program;
3. assigns standard input and output devices;
4. detects the end of the job;
5. prints an account of machine time and errors;
6. automatically begins the next job.

This removes much operator labor and allows several users to share a machine without manually restarting it for every program.

## Languages divide by purpose

Every bloc discovers that one problem description does not naturally serve every field.

Three broad families emerge:

| Family | Designed around |
|---|---|
| Scientific language | Formulas, arrays, loops, floating-point calculations |
| Administrative language | Records, decimal money, sorting, files and reports |
| Control language | Time, events, interrupts, devices and predictable execution |

Germany tries to hold all three inside Rechenplan. Britain accepts several related but distinct traditions. America embraces separate commercial language markets. Japan standardizes procedures before languages. The Latin bloc adopts one common scientific language while tolerating national commercial systems.

---

# I. Germany  
## Rechenplan becomes the language of the Reich

Germany enters 1955 with three principal digital traditions:

- Zuse’s relay-based binary floating-point machines;
- the Göttingen/Billing stored-program scientific line;
- the Schreyer–Telefunken electronic and military line.

It also possesses sophisticated analog control equipment, punched-card administration, cryptographic establishments and an enormous demand for imperial accounting.

Its principal challenge is no longer whether it can build a computer. It is whether a program created for one German machine can survive the procurement of the next one.

---

## 1. The space program does not require a digital computer aboard Raumbote I

Germany’s 1957 satellite is entirely plausible with late-1950s computing.

The first satellite does **not** require:

- a powerful onboard digital computer;
- live global networking;
- automated mission planning;
- transistorized guidance throughout;
- a mature operating system.

Raumbote I’s computing burden is primarily on the ground.

### Before launch

Digital machines calculate:

- staging trajectories;
- velocity losses;
- structural loads;
- launch windows;
- expected dispersions;
- atmospheric corrections;
- tracking-station geometry;
- orbital lifetime;
- radio visibility;
- failure envelopes.

Analog machines simulate:

- guidance loops;
- accelerometer behavior;
- engine transients;
- steering commands;
- vibration and control interaction;
- electrical-system faults.

### During launch

The launcher uses:

- analog inertial guidance;
- electromechanical or electronic sequencing;
- fixed control schedules;
- radio and telemetry;
- redundant cutoff logic.

A small onboard sequence controller may contain valves, relays or early transistors, but it is not a general computer.

### After launch

Tracking stations send observations by teleprinter to a central calculation establishment. Electronic computers determine a revised orbit from:

- radar range;
- bearing;
- Doppler shift;
- timing;
- optical observations.

The first orbit solution may take tens of minutes rather than appearing instantly on every console.

Germany uses redundant calculation:

1. a primary electronic solution;
2. an independent secondary machine;
3. selected hand or desk-calculator checks;
4. comparison against predicted tables.

This is sufficient to support the canonical 1957 launch without making German 1957 computing fantastically advanced. Raumbote I is the public culmination of a calculation-heavy rocket program already centered on Peenemünde and von Braun’s heavy-launch architecture. fileciteturn9file0

---

## 2. The German hardware settlement

Germany increasingly stops treating Zuse, Billing and Telefunken as competitors for one winner-take-all contract. Each occupies a distinct layer.

### The Zuse office and engineering line

The Zuse line remains important because relay machinery is:

- reliable;
- comparatively easy to repair;
- suitable for provincial engineering bureaus;
- tolerant of imperfect electrical supply;
- adequate for surveying, structures and repeated industrial calculations.

By 1960, new relay computers are still being purchased.

Their principal users include:

- construction firms;
- railway engineering offices;
- optical companies;
- provincial universities;
- mining combines;
- cadastral and surveying services;
- military depots.

Later models receive:

- larger magnetic-drum storage;
- faster tape readers;
- standardized printers;
- limited transistor peripheral controls;
- Rechenplan translators.

The Zuse machine becomes the German equivalent of a dependable engineering office computer rather than the apex of national supercomputing.

### The Göttingen scientific line

Billing’s tradition becomes the normal university and advanced-science architecture.

Its machines favor:

- binary stored-program operation;
- magnetic drums and core memory;
- larger numerical libraries;
- easier program replacement;
- conventional scientific service;
- faster arithmetic than the relay line.

They handle:

- physics;
- reactor calculations;
- astronomy;
- weather;
- metallurgy;
- advanced aerodynamics;
- orbital work not requiring classified Peenemünde systems.

### The Telefunken military-industrial line

Telefunken develops Germany’s fastest and most expensive installations.

These systems receive:

- valve logic at first;
- partial transistorization after 1957;
- magnetic-core working memory;
- drum and tape storage;
- independent peripheral controllers;
- high-speed teleprinter and radar interfaces;
- hardened or duplicated power systems.

They are concentrated in:

- aerospace;
- cryptography;
- radar and air defense;
- guided weapons;
- railway control;
- large industrial combines;
- central imperial administration.

A fully transistorized production mainframe need not appear before 1960–61. By 1959, however, Germany can operate experimental transistor processors and transistorized peripheral or control equipment.

---

## 3. Rechenplan 56

**Rechenplan 52** established the first practical high-level specification. **Rechenplan 56** becomes the first genuine production language standard.

Its adoption is driven by a state procurement rule:

> Every major general-purpose German computer accepted after 1957 must supply either a certified Rechenplan compiler or a documented path to the standard Planform intermediate representation.

That rule creates a unified software world without imposing one instruction set.

## The common language core

A representative Rechenplan program contains concepts equivalent to:

- `GANZZAHL` — integer;
- `FESTZAHL` — fixed-point quantity;
- `GLEITZAHL` — floating-point quantity;
- `WAHRHEITSWERT` — Boolean value;
- `ZEICHEN` — character;
- `FELD` — array;
- `SATZ` — structured record;
- `WENN` / `SONST` — conditional;
- `FÜR` — counted loop;
- `SOLANGE` — while loop;
- `WIEDERHOLE` — repetition;
- `VERFAHREN` — procedure;
- `EINGABE` / `AUSGABE`;
- `ENDE`.

Exact spellings can be adjusted later, but the language should unmistakably use German technical vocabulary rather than translated English acronyms.

## Important features

Rechenplan is more strongly typed than contemporary American commercial languages.

The compiler checks:

- dimensions;
- declared units where the engineering library uses them;
- array bounds when statically knowable;
- incompatible record fields;
- decimal versus binary quantity conversions;
- procedure parameters;
- prohibited operations inside restricted control profiles.

It supports:

- multidimensional arrays;
- matrices;
- fixed-size records;
- subroutines and procedures;
- nested conditions;
- counted iteration;
- symbolic constants;
- formatted input and output;
- standard numerical libraries.

It does not yet normally support:

- dynamic memory allocation;
- general recursion;
- unrestricted pointers;
- sophisticated text manipulation;
- separate compilation on every machine;
- interactive debugging.

---

## 4. One language, three profiles

The language’s single-system appearance is preserved through formal **application profiles**.

| Profile | Common abbreviation | Principal uses |
|---|---|---|
| Wissenschaftlicher Rechenplan | RP-W | Science, engineering, orbital mechanics |
| Verwaltungs-Rechenplan | RP-V | Accounts, records, clearing and MOSAIK |
| Steuerungs-Rechenplan | RP-S | Industrial, radar and aerospace control |

All three share:

- lexical rules;
- declarations;
- conditions;
- procedures;
- arrays and records;
- compiler infrastructure;
- Planform representation.

They differ in permitted operations and libraries.

### RP-W

RP-W adds:

- floating-point mathematics;
- complex numbers on machines supporting them;
- vectors and matrices;
- interpolation;
- differential-equation libraries;
- orbital and ballistic libraries;
- numerical integration;
- table generation.

This is the language used for much of the Raumbote program’s offline calculation.

### RP-V

RP-V adds:

- decimal fixed-point arithmetic;
- records;
- keyed files;
- sorting and merging;
- report formatting;
- currency and commodity fields;
- date and district codes;
- card, tape and printer definitions.

It is not as natural or verbose as COBOL will become, but it is far more integrated with scientific Rechenplan.

### RP-S

RP-S is deliberately restrictive.

It permits:

- fixed memory allocation;
- bounded loops;
- device declarations;
- interrupt or event procedures;
- timing estimates;
- state tables;
- explicitly ordered input and output;
- fail-safe branches.

It prohibits or sharply restricts:

- recursion;
- dynamically sized data;
- unbounded loops;
- implicit conversions;
- unpredictable library calls.

The compiler can produce a timing and memory report. Military certification authorities can compare that report against the hardware’s schedule.

This becomes the root of German deterministic real-time programming.

---

## 5. The Planform

Germany’s most important software invention of the period is not a visible keyword. It is the standardized intermediate language called, provisionally, **Planform**.

The compilation path is:

> Rechenplan source → typed Planform → optimized machine plan → native instructions

Planform describes:

- operations;
- data types;
- procedure calls;
- control flow;
- memory requirements;
- input and output classes;
- required libraries.

Machine manufacturers write back ends for Planform rather than inventing a complete language from nothing.

The benefits are immense:

- Rechenplan programs can be moved between machine families;
- libraries can be distributed in source or Planform;
- the state can certify the high-level meaning separately from the native code;
- manufacturers compete in code generation;
- administrative applications outlive particular processors.

The limitations remain serious:

- peripheral operations are often machine-specific;
- floating-point precision differs;
- compilers generate inefficient code;
- complex programs still require hand optimization;
- classified libraries cannot circulate freely;
- self-hosting compilers remain mostly a 1960s objective.

---

## 6. German batch operating environments

By 1958–60, major German installations operate a simple **Planlauf** or comparable job monitor.

A job deck identifies:

- user and security class;
- Rechenplan profile;
- compiler version;
- libraries required;
- input tapes or card files;
- output destination;
- maximum machine time;
- accounting center.

The monitor sequences jobs and maintains a printed audit.

German computers remain less interactive than American real-time machines. Their normal social model is:

1. an engineer writes or approves a program;
2. a coding office prepares it;
3. operators schedule it;
4. the machine produces printed results;
5. the responsible office signs the result.

This reinforces hierarchy and certification.

---

# MOSAIK, 1955–1960

The fully linked MOSAIK system belongs to the late 1960s. The end of this period establishes its first machine-readable layer. Canon already fixes the progression from paper and punched cards to regional computer centers and then a linked system. fileciteturn9file0

A useful formal expansion of the name is:

> **Maschinelles Ordnungs-, Siedlungs-, Arbeits- und Informationskataster**  
> Machine Order, Settlement, Labor and Information Cadastre

This can be a later official backronym, but it captures the system’s functions.

## 1955–1957: data reform

The African Language and Mediation Service, Tribal Cadastre and regional administration agree upon standardized codes for:

- person;
- household;
- registered community;
- recognized chief or jurisdiction;
- place of residence;
- place of work;
- labor category;
- tax and delivery obligation;
- language and mediation requirement;
- movement authorization;
- wages and communal payments;
- mine, estate or concession;
- production and shipping totals.

German remains the official machine language of administration even when the source record is French or African-language testimony.

## 1957–1958: the Kongostadt pilot

A first electronic-registry center is established at the practical Mittelafrika headquarters around Kongostadt.

It does not contain every person’s live file.

It receives:

- card decks;
- punched tape;
- district summaries;
- mine payroll;
- railway consignments;
- tax and labor returns;
- corrections from the mediation service.

Its initial tasks are:

- detecting duplicate identities;
- reconciling district totals;
- matching labor allocation against payroll;
- identifying unregistered movement;
- summarizing production;
- generating administrative reports.

## 1959–1960: regional centers

Several regional machine centers begin exchanging standardized tapes and teleprinter summaries.

Likely early nodes include:

- Kongostadt;
- the Katanga industrial region;
- Cameroon/Buea–Douala–Kribi;
- one West African administrative center;
- a central Berlin or Hamburg imperial clearing center.

The precise node list can remain open.

There is no continuous online connection. Data moves on schedules:

- daily teleprinter totals for urgent matters;
- weekly punched-tape summaries;
- monthly card or tape reconciliations;
- periodic complete district copies.

MOSAIK’s first-generation output is accurate in a narrow mechanical sense but only as honest as the local registration system. Coerced, delayed or politically manipulated data enters the machine and returns with the prestige of exact calculation.

---

## German position in 1960

Germany leads in:

- unified high-level-language policy;
- typed scientific programming;
- source-level portability;
- hybrid analog-digital aerospace work;
- deterministic control software;
- centralized administrative data standards.

It does not lead in:

- total installed machines;
- commercial openness;
- character processing;
- interactive computing;
- independent software entrepreneurship.

Its first satellite proves competence in calculation and systems engineering, not universal computer superiority.

---

# II. Britain and the Commonwealth  
## Autocode, service computing and the Silent Overflight

Britain enters the period with the broadest software culture but a badly fragmented hardware market.

Its principal machines include descendants of:

- Manchester/Ferranti;
- EDSAC;
- ACE/DEUCE;
- LEO;
- Elliott;
- BTM punched-card systems;
- classified Colossus successors;
- Commonwealth local systems.

The British response is not to impose one processor. It is to make translation, libraries and communications increasingly independent of the processor.

---

## 1. Political turbulence does not destroy computing

Butler’s strengthened government after 1955 protects computing through:

- Commonwealth technical contracts;
- nuclear-power research;
- signals and guided weapons;
- shipping;
- commercial exports;
- technical colleges;
- defense procurement.

The short Bevan return in 1959 does not cancel these programs. It changes their public justification from imperial-security machinery toward civilian science, planning, medicine and industrial modernization.

British computing therefore experiences administrative friction but not strategic abandonment.

---

## 2. Hardware from 1955 to 1960

### Ferranti and Manchester

Ferranti moves toward:

- transistorized arithmetic;
- magnetic-core memory;
- faster drums;
- multiple peripheral channels;
- scientific and university markets;
- increasingly capable autocodes.

Manchester remains Britain’s most experimentally adventurous hardware center.

### ACE and DEUCE

ACE-derived machines become the high-performance national scientific and government line.

They retain a reputation for:

- compact instruction sets;
- carefully scheduled code;
- excellent numerical performance;
- demanding professional programmers.

Later machines reduce the programmer’s dependence on delay-line timing as core memory spreads.

### LEO

LEO expands from food and payroll applications into:

- shipping;
- railways;
- insurance;
- state industries;
- hospital administration;
- Commonwealth supply;
- government contracts.

LEO becomes the world’s strongest school of **business systems analysis**, even when American firms sell more machines.

### Elliott and classified stream systems

Elliott and Post Office-derived systems become increasingly important for:

- radar;
- naval command;
- guided weapons;
- communications;
- telemetry;
- compact industrial control.

The classified Colossus lineage continues to shape stream processing, character comparison and communications analysis without becoming a public commercial architecture.

---

# The Silent Overflight, 1957

The launch of Raumbote I is received in Britain less as a lunar challenge than as proof that Germany can place a machine over British and Commonwealth territory.

The canon already establishes that the shock produces the Commonwealth Space and Signals Board and the High Mast tracking network in 1958. fileciteturn9file0

Computing becomes central to:

- orbit prediction;
- radar correlation;
- Doppler tracking;
- telemetry interpretation;
- identification of launch and decay;
- communications among Woomera, Canada, Britain, South Africa and other stations;
- warning dissemination;
- analysis of whether an object is passive, photographic or radio-equipped.

This is quintessentially British computing.

A tracking station does not solve the complete orbit independently. It generates a stream of timed observations. Those observations are routed to one or more Commonwealth calculation centers. The centers return predictions to all stations.

The problem naturally favors:

- message formats;
- time stamps;
- peripheral channels;
- data queues;
- remote teleprinter access;
- standardized observation records;
- independent checking by geographically separated machines.

The British space-computing tradition begins as an information network before it begins as a launch program.

---

# British programming languages

Britain does not unify around one language. By 1960 it possesses three major families and several smaller ones.

## 1. Autocode

“Autocode” becomes a British generic term for a compiler-oriented scientific language.

Different machines have:

- Manchester Autocode;
- Mercury Autocode;
- ACE Automatic Orders;
- Elliott Autocode;
- Commonwealth local variants.

The Automatic Computation Council attempts to define **Common Autocode 58** or **Commonwealth Autocode**, but this is a source-level common subset rather than one perfect implementation.

Its typical features include:

- algebraic formulas;
- symbolic variable names;
- loops;
- conditions;
- arrays;
- subroutines;
- standard mathematical functions;
- limited formatted input and output.

It is less strongly typed than Rechenplan.

Its great advantage is usability. A physicist or engineer can write a program without belonging to the machine’s original design team.

Its weakness is dialect proliferation. A program moved from Ferranti to DEUCE may require:

- changed input/output statements;
- different array limits;
- revised numerical precision;
- replacement library routines;
- extensive retesting.

## 2. LEO commercial languages

LEO develops an English-oriented commercial language family.

The first versions remain closer to symbolic assembly and structured report description than mature COBOL. By 1959–60, a **CLEO-like** system is emerging with:

- named business records;
- decimal fields;
- payroll and currency formats;
- tape files;
- sorting and merging;
- report layouts;
- conditional processing;
- readable operation names.

British business language is more procedural and systems-oriented than American COBOL.

A LEO team ordinarily studies the entire organization before writing the program. The source language therefore includes concepts tied closely to:

- files;
- schedules;
- exception reports;
- audit totals;
- operator intervention.

## 3. Stream and control languages

Signals, radar and guided-weapons establishments develop small languages or macro systems describing:

- incoming character streams;
- counters;
- matches;
- timing windows;
- event conditions;
- device actions;
- message routing.

These remain partly classified and highly machine-specific.

They are not general-purpose competitors to Autocode. They are the ancestors of Britain’s later event-driven and communications languages.

---

## Turing’s influence

Turing does not try to impose “Turing” as the name of Britain’s standard programming language.

His influence appears through several principles:

- a language should describe an algorithm independently of a particular machine where possible;
- machine equivalence does not imply practical interchangeability;
- translators should be treated as programs worthy of mathematical analysis;
- subroutines and generated code must be testable;
- interactive use and machine intelligence deserve serious investigation;
- program behavior cannot always be settled by a universal automatic proof.

British academia commonly uses **Turing’s Hypothesis** for the claim that effective procedures can be represented by a universal machine. American academia tends toward Church’s Thesis; Germany uses the combined formulation.

Turing’s continuing position also helps prevent automatic coding from being dismissed as mere convenience for mediocre programmers.

---

## The Commonwealth Programme Library

By 1960, the library has become a distributed publication system.

It circulates:

- printed algorithms;
- Common Autocode versions;
- machine-specific tapes;
- test data;
- known limitations;
- correction sheets;
- numerical tables;
- peripheral routines;
- translation advice.

Programs are sent physically by mail, diplomatic bag, military courier or teleprinter when short enough.

This gives Britain and the Commonwealth an enormous stock of reusable software, though not binary compatibility.

---

## British operating systems

British systems develop monitors emphasizing:

- job queues;
- tape and printer scheduling;
- accounting;
- remote job submission;
- peripheral overlap;
- error messages understandable to operators.

LEO systems add restart and audit mechanisms. Scientific machines add library loading. Signals machines emphasize continuous operation.

Britain begins experimenting with shared or interactive access at the very end of the period, but routine time-sharing belongs in the 1960s.

---

## British position in 1960

Britain leads in:

- compiler variety;
- software libraries;
- systems analysis;
- cross-machine translation;
- character and stream processing;
- distributed Commonwealth scientific service;
- orbital tracking and signals integration.

It remains weaker than America in machine-production volume and weaker than Germany in formal language unity.

The British architecture is not absorbed into America. Raumbote I makes independent computing more politically necessary, not less.

---

# III. United States  
## FORTRAN, COBOL and the post-Raumbote mobilization

America enters 1955 with the greatest production potential and the most clearly divided computing market.

Its three principal architectural worlds are:

- binary scientific machines;
- decimal and character-oriented business machines;
- real-time military and communications computers.

The late-1950s language explosion makes those divisions permanent.

---

## 1. Installed-base expansion

IBM and its competitors supply increasing numbers of:

- scientific computers;
- drum-based commercial machines;
- card-to-tape systems;
- core-memory installations;
- high-speed printers;
- magnetic-tape units.

America probably possesses the world’s largest number of installed general-purpose computers by 1959–60, even though Britain retains deeper average programming experience and Germany retains tighter state integration.

The American advantage is not one superior processor. It is the ability to build:

- hundreds of midrange machines;
- thousands of peripherals;
- nationwide service organizations;
- standardized replacement components;
- customer training programs;
- commercial manuals.

---

## 2. The 1956 political transition

The disputed House-selected Warren presidency does not immediately produce a grand computing program.

Computing funding continues through:

- the armed services;
- IBM and commercial customers;
- Bell Laboratories;
- universities;
- aviation companies;
- Census and Treasury;
- Philippine logistics.

Warren’s weak mandate makes him cautious about large ideological programs. Raumbote I then gives him a politically irresistible technical emergency.

---

# Raumbote I and Aerospace Command

The 1957 satellite, combined with the Philippine experience, produces United States Aerospace Command in 1958. fileciteturn9file1

The new command does not simply buy larger IBM computers. It funds an entire computing stack:

- orbital mechanics;
- radar tracking;
- missile-warning displays;
- telemetry;
- guidance simulation;
- digital flight control;
- high-speed memory;
- reliable transistors;
- programming-language research;
- automatic diagnostics;
- command networks;
- human-machine consoles.

America deliberately chooses a pilot-centered reusable aerospace identity rather than copying Germany’s ballistic architecture. That means computing must ultimately manage a more complicated vehicle:

- atmospheric ascent;
- orbital operations;
- reentry;
- cross-range;
- landing;
- maintenance and reuse.

The late-1950s investment therefore begins laying the foundations of America’s later spaceplane advantage.

---

# American programming languages

America develops the clearest separation among scientific, business and military languages.

## 1. FORTRAN

FORTRAN should survive under its recognizable name.

The same basic circumstances remain:

- IBM wants to sell scientific machines;
- customers distrust the cost of hand coding;
- John Backus and comparable engineers exist;
- formulas are already written in a broadly international mathematical notation;
- faster compiler-generated code will expand the customer base.

Because American computing began somewhat later, the setting’s first production FORTRAN compiler appears around **1958**, approximately a year behind the familiar chronology.

### FORTRAN I

It supports:

- algebraic expressions;
- integer and floating-point variables;
- loops;
- conditional branches;
- arrays;
- subprograms;
- formatted input and output.

Its compiler is judged by one unforgiving standard:

> Can it produce code close enough to expert hand coding that scientists will actually use it?

The compiler includes aggressive optimization because IBM must overcome the belief that automatic coding necessarily wastes expensive machine time.

### FORTRAN II, 1959–60

The next version improves:

- separate subroutines;
- larger libraries;
- program organization;
- compatibility across related IBM machines;
- debugging output;
- links to assembly routines.

FORTRAN becomes the dominant American scientific language by 1960, although universities retain other systems.

Church’s circle regards FORTRAN as practical but intellectually crude. It lacks a clean formal foundation and mixes mathematical expressions with machine-oriented assumptions. That criticism becomes important later.

## 2. Hopper’s compiler line and COBOL

Grace Hopper’s compiler work produces a commercial-language tradition emphasizing named operations and reusable routines.

Her systems are oriented toward:

- payroll;
- inventory;
- insurance;
- billing;
- government records;
- magnetic tapes;
- high-speed reports.

The proliferation of incompatible business languages leads federal agencies, large firms and machine manufacturers to convene a standardization effort in 1959.

**COBOL can still emerge**, although the precise committee composition differs.

Its governing principles are:

- English-like statements;
- explicit record definitions;
- decimal arithmetic;
- separation of data description from procedure;
- machine-independent source;
- readable reports and files;
- commercial portability.

The first specification appears in **1960**.

Early COBOL is verbose and compilers are inconsistent, but it gives American business computing an enduring common language.

## 3. Real-time aerospace language

Whirlwind descendants, radar networks and Aerospace Command require something different.

The relevant language—whether it retains the historical name **JOVIAL** or receives a divergent designation—appears around 1959–60.

It supports:

- fixed-size records;
- arrays;
- bit fields;
- procedure calls;
- device interfaces;
- predictable memory allocation;
- real-time tasks;
- assembly-language insertion.

It is used for:

- radar;
- interception;
- guidance simulation;
- command displays;
- prototype aerospace systems.

It is less formally restrictive than German RP-S but better suited to large American contractor teams.

The final service name can remain open; **JOVIAL-class language** is enough for now.

---

## 4. ALGOL and Church’s school

A neutral academic effort develops an international algorithmic language around 1958–60.

The conferences are likely held in Switzerland rather than being dominated by one great power. Participants include:

- American academics;
- British computer scientists;
- German and Swiss mathematicians;
- Italian and Occitan language researchers;
- selected neutral observers.

The result can still be called **ALGOL 58** and **ALGOL 60**.

Its primary initial purpose is not commercial programming. It is to provide a machine-independent notation for publishing algorithms.

The United States treats it differently from FORTRAN:

- FORTRAN is the language of laboratories and industry.
- ALGOL is the language of computer-science departments and formal algorithm discussion.
- Church’s theoretical community finds ALGOL more intellectually respectable.
- IBM does not abandon FORTRAN.

ALGOL therefore strengthens American academic language research without becoming the dominant American production language.

---

## 5. American operating systems

Commercial batch monitors become increasingly sophisticated.

They manage:

- card job-control statements;
- compilers;
- tape mounting;
- printers;
- program libraries;
- machine accounting;
- error dumps;
- multiple queued jobs.

Manufacturers begin selling software as part of the machine package.

This is an important American development: software becomes a **customer-acquisition expense**.

A compiler may be supplied without a separate visible price because it helps sell the hardware. This encourages wide distribution but hides the true cost of software production.

---

## 6. Architecture by 1960

America remains divided.

| Sector | Typical architecture |
|---|---|
| Scientific | Binary, 36–40-bit words, floating point, FORTRAN |
| Business | Decimal or character-oriented, tape-heavy, COBOL predecessors |
| Real time | Shorter words, core memory, consoles, device interrupts |
| Telecommunications | Switching and coding systems influenced by Shannon and Bell |
| University theory | IAS descendants, ALGOL, Church’s formal school |

There is no American equivalent of Rechenplan unification.

The divisions are economically productive because each market supports specialized firms. They are technically expensive because programs and data do not move easily between sectors.

---

## American position in 1960

America leads in:

- installed machine count;
- mass production;
- compiler use by ordinary customers;
- magnetic-core and real-time systems;
- commercial software distribution;
- business data processing;
- transistor manufacturing.

It does not lead universally in:

- language elegance;
- software verification;
- cross-vendor portability;
- imperial-scale administrative integration;
- communications-oriented programming practice.

By 1960, America has fully joined Britain and Germany as a peer and may possess the greatest industrial momentum.

---

# IV. Japan  
## From promising laboratories to the fourth national system

Japan enters 1955 behind the leading three but already possesses:

- relay computers;
- FUJIC and TAC electronic projects;
- FACOM commercial development;
- parametron research;
- strong telecommunications engineering;
- an enormous administrative and industrial need.

The 1957 shock does not create the industry. It changes its rank in national priorities.

Canon establishes that Japan is still behind but closing in the late 1950s, while its long-term economy increasingly emphasizes automation, microelectronics and imperial production chains. fileciteturn9file1

---

## 1. Hardware, 1955–1957

### Relay systems

FACOM and ETL relay computers continue to receive orders because they are dependable and comprehensible to switching engineers.

They serve:

- government statistics;
- railways;
- shipping;
- universities;
- insurance;
- industrial planning.

### FUJIC

FUJIC proves the domestic vacuum-tube scientific computer.

Its successful optical applications attract support from:

- camera firms;
- rangefinder manufacturers;
- aerospace;
- naval optics;
- precision machinery.

### TAC

The Tokyo–Toshiba machine becomes a central university scientific installation around 1955–56 rather than suffering a prolonged historical delay.

### Parametron

Parametron logic receives strong interest because it is:

- domestically invented;
- comparatively reliable;
- suitable for modular construction;
- less dependent upon the most difficult early transistor production.

It is slower and consumes significant power, but those disadvantages are tolerable in stationary scientific systems.

---

# The Japanese Raumbote response

Japan interprets the German satellite in three ways.

First, it is a military warning. Orbital observation threatens fleets, ports and island defenses.

Second, it is an industrial warning. Germany has demonstrated that advanced materials, guidance, electronics, calculation and production can be combined into one national project.

Third, it is an imperial warning. Japan governs more territory and shipping than Germany but does not yet possess comparable central technical coordination.

In 1958, Tokyo creates an **Imperial Electronics and Automation Program**.

Its principal objectives are:

- transistor manufacture;
- magnetic core;
- parametron production;
- scientific mainframes;
- compact naval and airborne electronics;
- programming languages;
- factory automation;
- imperial transaction standards;
- telemetry and guidance;
- advanced technical education.

Funding flows through the ministries, development banks and corporate houses rather than one centralized state arsenal.

---

## 2. Japanese hardware, 1958–1960

Japan deliberately maintains three logic technologies.

## Parametron scientific machines

Parametron machines equip:

- universities;
- mathematical laboratories;
- aerospace institutes;
- naval research;
- reactor research.

Their virtues are reliability and domestic control. Their weakness is speed and power.

## Transistor commercial and industrial machines

NEC, Fujitsu, Hitachi and other firms accelerate transistor computers for:

- banks;
- trading houses;
- factories;
- shipping;
- inventory;
- communication control.

Japan’s intact industrial system permits it to reach practical transistor production quickly after the national priority shift.

## Relay controllers

Relays remain widespread in:

- factories;
- telephone systems;
- port machinery;
- railway signaling;
- shipyards;
- warehouse control.

Japan does not regard these as obsolete when they perform their assigned sequence reliably.

This produces a uniquely layered computing industry:

> mainframes calculate; transistor systems supervise; relays act.

---

# Japanese programming languages

Japan does not immediately choose one national language because Army, Navy, ministries and corporate houses resist surrendering their own systems.

Two broader language families nevertheless emerge.

## 1. KEISAN

**KEISAN**—literally calculation—is the working name for the scientific language family.

It appears around 1958–59.

Its visible form uses:

- Latin mathematical formulas;
- Latin or short kana identifiers;
- katakana control words;
- Arabic numerals;
- standard scientific function names;
- punched cards or paper tape.

A typical core includes equivalents of:

- `MOSHI` — if;
- `SONOTA` — otherwise;
- `KURIKAESHI` — repeat;
- `YOMIKOMI` — read;
- `KAKIDASHI` — write;
- `OWARI` — end.

The exact source spelling can later be standardized in kana rather than romanization.

KEISAN supports:

- floating-point arithmetic;
- arrays;
- loops;
- procedures;
- formulas;
- mathematical libraries;
- formatted numerical output.

FACOM, ETL, NEC and university compilers initially use incompatible dialects. A 1959 national standard defines a portable core.

KEISAN becomes Japan’s counterpart to FORTRAN and scientific Autocode, but its compilers generate less efficient code in 1960.

## 2. TEJUN

**TEJUN**—procedure—is the administrative and process language.

It descends from the standardized processing-procedure sheets already used to describe clerical and industrial work.

TEJUN emphasizes:

- records;
- decimal fields;
- tables;
- sorting;
- files;
- device operations;
- state transitions;
- error and exception paths;
- explicit human authorization points.

Its first translators appear around 1959–60.

TEJUN is used for:

- trading-house accounts;
- shipping manifests;
- warehouse control;
- production schedules;
- government records;
- port operations;
- industrial sequence supervision.

It is not yet one language across the empire. The common standard is a specification, while individual firms supply dialects.

Later, TEJUN will naturally grow into industrial-control and event-driven programming.

---

## 3. Character encoding

Japan adopts an imperial kana code around 1958.

It supports:

- katakana;
- numerals;
- Latin capitals;
- punctuation;
- control characters.

The exact bit width can remain open, but a 6-bit code is too cramped for comfortable multilingual use. A **7-bit Japanese code with shift conventions** is more plausible for the long term, while many devices retain reduced subsets.

Kanji is handled through:

- numeric dictionary codes;
- special printers;
- paper-file cross-reference;
- high-end photo or mechanical output systems.

Ordinary source code is not kanji-based.

Multilingual imperial records normally store:

- numeric identity;
- kana form;
- jurisdiction code;
- paper or microfilm image of the full local-script record.

---

## 4. Industrial automation

The funding surge produces practical projects before it produces a German-scale scientific mainframe fleet.

By 1960 Japan is installing automatic or semi-automatic control in:

- rolling mills;
- refineries;
- shipyards;
- machine-tool lines;
- warehouses;
- port cranes;
- telephone exchanges;
- electric-power dispatch;
- quality-control stations.

Most remain dedicated systems, not general computers.

Japan’s distinctive achievement is the rapid spread of **small controllers and procedural logic**, not a single giant machine.

---

## Japanese position in 1960

Japan is still modestly behind the leading three in:

- supercomputer performance;
- installed scientific capacity;
- compiler maturity;
- memory production;
- programmer population.

It has become a genuine fourth power through:

- transistor systems;
- parametron machines;
- domestic high-level languages;
- industrial automation;
- strong corporate electronics;
- imperial data standards.

The gap is now narrow enough that Japanese leaders can realistically intend to close it during the 1960s.

---

# V. The Latin bloc  
## ALGOL as neutral sovereignty and Olivetti’s business machine

The Latin system enters 1955 with two principal centers:

- Italy’s office-machine, telecommunications and state-industry complex;
- Occitania’s scientific, avionics and military-electronics complex.

Spain and Portugal remain junior partners, but the creation of common military standards in 1958 demonstrates the broader movement toward Latin technical coordination. fileciteturn9file1

The bloc’s central computing problem is scale. It can design excellent machines but cannot match American production volume or German state purchasing.

---

## 1. Italy, 1955–1960

### Olivetti

Mario Tchou’s enlarged team pushes Olivetti from prototype to production.

The decisive product is a transistorized ELEA-class machine entering service around 1959–60.

Its defining characteristics are:

- transistor logic;
- magnetic-core memory;
- modular cabinets;
- magnetic tape;
- high-speed printers;
- decimal and alphanumeric processing;
- strong diagnostics;
- a carefully designed operator console;
- commercial rather than purely military documentation.

Olivetti’s machine is not the world’s fastest scientific computer. It is one of the world’s most coherent **business computer products**.

The customer receives:

- processor;
- storage;
- peripherals;
- operator training;
- application analysis;
- maintenance;
- programming support;
- standardized forms.

### IRI and STET

Public-industry machines serve:

- electricity;
- railways;
- telecommunications;
- Suez;
- imperial shipping;
- government accounts;
- military command.

These are often less elegant but more rugged than Olivetti systems.

Italy’s software world therefore divides between:

- Olivetti commercial programmers;
- IRI administrative teams;
- military assembly and control specialists;
- university scientific programmers.

---

## 2. Occitania

Occitania’s second-generation machines shift toward transistors and magnetic core.

They emphasize:

- compact processors;
- buffered input/output;
- radar and telemetry interfaces;
- avionics;
- missile and artillery calculations;
- numerical analysis;
- military command systems.

Occitania cannot produce hundreds of large machines. It can produce small runs of technically advanced systems and export designs or subsystems to Italy and Spain.

This is the beginning of its later role as the Latin bloc’s electronics and integration spearhead.

---

# Latin programming languages

The bloc does not attempt to invent one language for all purposes.

## 1. ALGOL

The Latin bloc becomes the strongest governmental adopter of **ALGOL 58/60**.

This is strategically useful because ALGOL is:

- not German-owned;
- not tied to IBM;
- not controlled by Britain;
- designed for machine-independent algorithm description;
- suitable for Italian and Occitan scientific cooperation;
- internationally respectable.

Italian, Occitan, Swiss and selected German mathematicians participate in its design. German universities may publish ALGOL algorithms, but Reich production remains Rechenplan-based.

The Latin bloc develops production compilers for:

- Occitan scientific machines;
- Italian university computers;
- Olivetti scientific configurations;
- Spanish university installations.

ALGOL becomes the shared Latin scientific language.

Its strengths include:

- block structure;
- nested procedures;
- lexical scope;
- clear mathematical notation;
- machine-independent publication.

Its weakness is poor direct support for:

- business records;
- input/output;
- industrial devices;
- commercial file processing.

## 2. Italian administrative language

Olivetti develops a commercial language provisionally designated **LIA-59**, *Linguaggio Italiano Amministrativo*.

The final name can change.

It supports:

- named records;
- decimal money;
- tape files;
- sorting;
- report descriptions;
- payroll;
- inventory;
- error messages;
- printer formatting.

It is less English-like than COBOL and more compact.

Olivetti expects professional systems analysts to design the application; ordinary managers are not meant to read the source unaided.

## 3. Occitan control languages

Occitan military projects retain assembly, macro systems and small control languages.

These emphasize:

- device registers;
- radar tracks;
- timed events;
- data channels;
- state tables;
- telemetry.

They are not standardized bloc-wide before 1960.

---

## 3. A Latin character and interchange standard

The Latin bloc faces a text problem absent from Germany and less difficult in America.

It must handle:

- Italian;
- Spanish;
- Portuguese;
- French;
- Occitan;
- Latin;
- Arabic transliteration;
- colonial names.

A Latin technical commission therefore adopts a **7-bit interchange code** around 1959–60.

It contains:

- Latin capitals;
- digits;
- common punctuation;
- control characters;
- shift or overstrike conventions for accents and additional letters.

It is used for:

- teleprinters;
- punched tape;
- magnetic tape;
- programming source;
- naval and commercial messages.

This does not create full machine compatibility, but it gives the bloc an early advantage in multilingual data exchange.

---

## 4. Spain

By 1960, Spain operates:

- Italian commercial machines;
- Occitan scientific systems;
- one or more domestically assembled university computers;
- locally manufactured peripherals;
- punched-card installations;
- technical training schools.

García Santesmases’s school produces enough engineers that Spain is no longer merely an operator of foreign equipment.

It remains dependent upon Italy and Occitania for advanced processors and software tools.

---

## 5. Portugal

Portugal develops:

- a Lisbon government computing center;
- bank and shipping applications;
- customs and colonial data processing;
- British and Italian machine installations;
- tape and character conversion expertise.

Portugal’s role is partly that of an interface country. Its technicians encounter British, Latin and occasionally German formats and become skilled in conversion.

It does not build a competitive indigenous mainframe before 1960.

---

## Latin position in 1960

The bloc is second-rank in aggregate scale but first-rank in several niches.

It leads or competes strongly in:

- office-machine ergonomics;
- commercial interface design;
- multilingual data;
- compact avionics;
- radar and guided-weapon integration;
- ALGOL implementation;
- exportable mid-sized systems.

It trails in:

- large-machine volume;
- semiconductor production;
- total programmer numbers;
- advanced operating systems;
- imperial-scale data networks.

No serious Latin policymaker advocates abandoning the domestic tradition for German machines. German equipment remains useful as a benchmark and occasional purchase, not a civilizational platform.

---

# The language map in 1960

| Bloc | Scientific language | Administrative language | Control language |
|---|---|---|---|
| Germany | Rechenplan RP-W | Rechenplan RP-V | Rechenplan RP-S |
| Britain | Autocode families | LEO/CLEO precursor | Stream and control autocodes |
| United States | FORTRAN | COBOL | JOVIAL-class systems |
| Japan | KEISAN | TEJUN | TEJUN and machine-specific control dialects |
| Latin bloc | ALGOL | Italian LIA-type languages | Occitan and Italian control systems |

## Germany’s language unity is genuine

Germany has one:

- common syntax;
- common type system;
- common Planform;
- official library structure;
- certification regime.

Its profiles still produce different programming communities.

An RP-V payroll programmer and an RP-S missile-control programmer can read one another’s syntax, but they do not possess interchangeable professional expertise.

## Britain’s plurality is institutional

Britain assumes that good translators and common documentation are more realistic than forcing all machines and users into one language.

## America’s plurality is commercial

Separate markets produce separate languages. Competition and vendor adoption determine success.

## Japan’s plurality is corporate and procedural

The same procedure-sheet culture underlies the languages, but firms retain dialects and proprietary implementations.

## Latin plurality is confederal

ALGOL provides scientific unity; national systems remain in administration and military control.

---

# What high-level languages can and cannot do in 1960

By 1960, high-level languages are common enough to shape procurement, but they have not replaced low-level programming.

They are normally used for:

- scientific calculations;
- engineering models;
- accounting;
- payroll;
- inventory;
- report generation;
- noncritical simulation;
- statistical processing.

Assembly or direct machine code remains dominant in:

- operating monitors;
- compilers;
- radar;
- cryptography;
- onboard guidance;
- high-speed input/output;
- device drivers;
- real-time control;
- extremely expensive numerical kernels.

A normal large application mixes levels.

For example, a German orbital program might contain:

- RP-W trajectory code;
- hand-coded floating-point library;
- RP-V mission inventory;
- RP-S ground-equipment sequences;
- assembly telemetry routines;
- analog guidance simulation.

There is no contradiction in saying that Germany uses one high-level language while still maintaining a great deal of low-level and analog work.

---

# Balance of power in 1960

| Field | Leading position |
|---|---|
| Largest installed base | United States |
| Strongest compiler-driven scientific market | United States |
| Most unified language ecosystem | Germany |
| Best formal types and certification | Germany |
| Best software-service culture | Britain |
| Best routine and translation libraries | Britain |
| Strongest real-time production base | United States, with Britain close |
| Best analog-digital aerospace integration | Germany |
| Fastest-growing industrial automation | Japan |
| Strongest commercial interface design | Italy |
| Best compact military systems integration | Occitania |
| Most important neutral academic language | ALGOL, strongest in Latin/Swiss academia |
| First imperial computer registry | German MOSAIK pilot |
| Strongest multinational tracking network | Britain/Commonwealth after 1958 |

The late 1950s remain a period of three-power parity, with Japan entering as the fourth serious system and the Latin bloc maintaining complete technical sovereignty. This matches the established canon that Germany, Britain, America and Italy are major computing competitors by the end of the decade, with Japan behind but closing. fileciteturn9file1

---

# Working canon to carry forward

1. **Raumbote I relies principally on ground computing, analog guidance simulation and fixed onboard sequencing**, not a sophisticated satellite computer.

2. **Rechenplan 56 becomes Germany’s first production high-level-language standard.**

3. **Rechenplan 58 formalizes RP-W, RP-V and RP-S as profiles of one language family.**

4. **Planform becomes the standard German typed intermediate representation**, giving source-level portability across Zuse, Göttingen and Telefunken machines.

5. **Germany requires major new computers to support Rechenplan or Planform after 1957.**

6. **The first MOSAIK machine-readable standard appears around 1956–57**, followed by a Kongostadt pilot in 1958 and several batch-linked regional centers by 1960.

7. **MOSAIK in 1960 remains a card, tape and teleprinter system**, not a live online database. The fully linked network remains a late-1960s achievement.

8. **Britain’s Raumbote response produces the Commonwealth Space and Signals Board and High Mast in 1958**, strengthening its information-flow and distributed-computing tradition.

9. **Common Autocode 58 provides a partial Commonwealth scientific standard**, but Britain retains multiple language families.

10. **LEO develops a CLEO-like commercial language by 1959–60**, while classified stream and control languages remain separate.

11. **FORTRAN appears in American production around 1958**, followed by FORTRAN II around 1959–60.

12. **COBOL’s first common specification appears in 1960**, built from Hopper’s compiler tradition, federal procurement and commercial-machine rivalry.

13. **An American JOVIAL-class real-time language begins under Aerospace Command around 1959–60.**

14. **ALGOL 58/60 survives as a neutral international academic language**, but no major bloc abandons its national production languages for it.

15. **Japan creates an Imperial Electronics and Automation Program in 1958.**

16. **KEISAN becomes Japan’s scientific-language family around 1958–59; TEJUN becomes its administrative and process-language family around 1959–60.**

17. **Japan adopts a kana-oriented machine code standard around 1958**, with Latin mathematical notation and numeric handling of kanji records.

18. **Olivetti fields a transistorized ELEA-class commercial system around 1959–60**, while Occitania fields compact transistorized scientific and military systems.

19. **The Latin bloc adopts ALGOL as its shared scientific language and a 7-bit multilingual interchange code**, while retaining Italian administrative and Occitan control languages.

20. **By 1960, Japan has become a credible fourth computing power; the Latin bloc remains second-rank in scale but technologically independent.**
