Yes—this works, but the incident becomes much more technically convincing if we define it as a **temporary seizure of the communications payload**, not complete control of the spacecraft.

Japan does not steer the satellite, alter its orbit, or threaten to deorbit it. It:

1. reverse-engineers the German uplink and command framing;
2. overwhelms the legitimate German carrier during a favorable pass;
3. commands the communications payload into a different operating mode;
4. relays Japanese traffic through it and requests a buffered telemetry dump;
5. relinquishes control as the satellite passes beyond the Japanese station’s effective horizon.

The newspapers still report that Japan “stole a German satellite for thirteen minutes.”

Technically, Germany knows the distinction. Diplomatically, it hardly matters.

# First, two orbital corrections

## Not every early satellite follows an equatorial route

Low-inclination satellites remain near the equator, but reconnaissance, signals-intelligence, weather, and many military satellites benefit from higher-inclination or polar trajectories. A satellite can only pass directly over latitudes no greater than its orbital inclination. Japan therefore cannot interfere with Germany’s low-inclination Raumhafen traffic merely because it is in orbit.

The victim should be a **high-inclination German communications and telemetry satellite**, probably launched from the Lower Volga range rather than equatorial Kribi.

A good reference orbit would be:

- altitude: approximately 1,000–1,300 kilometres;
- inclination: approximately 55–65 degrees;
- orbital purpose: military store-and-forward communications, telemetry relay, and experimental fleet communications;
- coverage: Germany, the Urals, Siberia, East Asia, and portions of the Pacific.

That allows a pass over Manchuria, Korea, Hokkaido, or northern Japan while a German eastern ground station can still see the satellite low on its horizon.

## The Orbitaler Raumhafen should not move to geosynchronous orbit

The existing canon fixes the Raumhafen at **720 kilometres and 5 degrees inclination**. That remains the correct location for a crewed construction yard supplied from equatorial Kribi. fileciteturn12file1 fileciteturn12file7

Geosynchronous orbit is approximately **35,786 kilometres** above Earth—nearly fifty times the Raumhafen’s altitude. Moving a large crewed 1975 station there would radically increase launch energy, radiation exposure, rescue difficulty, communications delay, and logistical cost. citeturn428756search0turn428756search1

Germany can later connect the Raumhafen to:

- separate geosynchronous communications satellites;
- high-altitude relay satellites;
- low-orbit satellites in compatible planes;
- global ground stations at Kribi, Iceland, Norway, the Volga, and elsewhere.

The Raumhafen itself should remain a low-orbiting yard, not become the stationary communications relay.

# The target satellite

I would provisionally designate the German spacecraft:

## **Fernmeldesatellit 4 — FMS-4**

Public nickname: **Botenstern**, “Messenger Star.”

It enters service around 1967–68 as part of a German experimental military communications network.

FMS-4 has two substantially separate systems.

### Spacecraft bus

This controls:

- attitude;
- power;
- batteries;
- thermal regulation;
- telemetry;
- perhaps minor orbit-maintenance thrusters.

### Communications payload

This controls:

- transponder channels;
- receive and transmit frequencies;
- recording and playback;
- store-and-forward message buffers;
- switching between military ground stations;
- diagnostic telemetry.

Japan compromises the second system.

It never gains propulsion or attitude control.

That limitation is prudent German engineering and keeps the incident from becoming an act that could accidentally destroy the satellite.

# Why the takeover is technically plausible

Early spacecraft did not automatically possess modern cryptographic authentication. Simple command systems could use combinations of tones or comparatively short digital command words. A 1966 NASA technical report explicitly noted that tone-command systems were highly susceptible to false commands and were reasonable only when false commands could not seriously harm the spacecraft. citeturn795141search12

A later declassified American intelligence analysis observed that decisions not to encrypt satellite telemetry, uplink channels, and command systems left them vulnerable both to detailed foreign understanding and to active countermeasures. citeturn713193view1

Likewise, a transparent communications transponder accepts an uplink and retransmits it on the downlink. Such transponders are inherently susceptible to intentional or accidental uplink interference. A sufficiently strong interfering transmission within the satellite antenna footprint can displace or degrade the intended signal. citeturn955205search2turn955205search4

A 1965 NASA transponder study specifically examined the effect of strong competing signals and found that a stronger signal could reduce the gain available to the weaker one. citeturn669997search1

So the core mechanism is sound:

> The Japanese transmitter does not win because Japan is geographically “closer” in a simple sense. It wins because the satellite is nearly overhead, the German controlling station sees it at a poor low-elevation angle, and Japan concentrates substantially greater effective radiated power into the satellite’s receiver.

# The Japanese preparation

The operation should take more than a year.

## 1967: passive collection

Japanese stations begin recording:

- FMS-4’s beacon;
- telemetry framing;
- command-channel frequencies;
- transponder switching;
- German ground-station schedules;
- Doppler shifts;
- orbital timing;
- maintenance transmissions.

Japanese engineers discover that user traffic is often enciphered, but the **engineering protocol and payload commands are not cryptographically authenticated**.

This is believable. Germany has treated:

- frequency secrecy;
- narrow antennas;
- classified timing;
- short visibility windows;
- the obscurity of its command vocabulary;

as sufficient protection.

It has protected the contents of important messages more carefully than it has protected the satellite’s own control language.

## 1968: protocol reconstruction

Japanese computing centers correlate thousands of intercepted transmissions.

Computers help identify:

- repeated synchronization sequences;
- command lengths;
- error-checking patterns;
- which commands correspond to channel changes;
- when the German station requests playback;
- the acknowledgment returned after a valid command.

The decisive breakthrough is not breaking a sophisticated cipher.

It is discovering that there is no true authentication cipher to break.

## 1969: ground rehearsal

Japan constructs a duplicate receiver and command simulator.

Engineers transmit reconstructed German commands into the simulator and confirm that they can:

- switch transponder channels;
- request engineering telemetry;
- initiate playback of a communications buffer;
- alter beacon modes.

They deliberately avoid experimenting with any probable spacecraft-bus commands.

The operation is approved as a demonstration of Japanese electronic parity, but its advocates also have a military purpose: proving that foreign satellites do not possess unquestioned operational immunity merely because they are physically unreachable.

# The interception

I would place it in **September or October 1969**, after the American Pathfinder spaceplane flight but before the German lunar landing.

The incident becomes known by several names:

- **The Hokkaidō Interception**;
- **The Thirteen-Minute Satellite**;
- the German **Botenstern-Zwischenfall**;
- internally in Japan, **Operation Amaterasu**.

## The pass

FMS-4 approaches from the northwest, crossing the Soviet-successor interior, Manchuria, Korea, northern Japan, and the Pacific.

Germany is controlling it through a Ural or eastern Russian ground station.

A Japanese high-power tracking station—probably in Hokkaido, with supporting stations in Korea and Manchuria—locks onto it.

Japan first transmits a carrier on the German command frequency.

German ground controllers see:

- falling signal-to-noise ratio;
- command acknowledgment errors;
- then complete loss of their uplink.

The Japanese station increases power and establishes receiver capture.

## What Japan does

Japan transmits a valid payload-access sequence and orders FMS-4 to:

1. change its active communications channel;
2. switch to a diagnostic relay mode;
3. play back part of its engineering and stored communications buffer;
4. retransmit a Japanese test frame.

The test frame contains:

- the Japanese time;
- the satellite’s orbital elements as calculated by Japan;
- a brief bilingual technical message;
- perhaps the first line of the Imperial Rescript on Science and Construction.

Something restrained would be more intimidating than a taunt:

> **“Your apparatus is functioning normally under local direction.”**

Japanese stations receive the raw buffered data.

They do **not** automatically receive every German secret in plaintext. Enciphered military messages remain enciphered. What they acquire includes:

- engineering telemetry;
- station schedules;
- routing information;
- message lengths and traffic patterns;
- some unclassified or weakly protected traffic;
- proof that they can command the payload.

The unauthorized session lasts approximately **thirteen minutes**.

As the spacecraft descends toward the eastern horizon, Japan can no longer maintain sufficient power. The German network reacquires the command channel and restores normal configuration.

No orbit change occurs.

No equipment is damaged.

No data is erased.

Nevertheless, the German command counter proves that valid unauthorized commands were accepted.

# The German panic

The first German fear is not that Japan has stolen one satellite.

It is that Japan may have understood the entire German orbital command system.

Officials cannot immediately determine:

- how long Japan has been reading telemetry;
- whether other satellites share the same protocol;
- whether Japan has discovered bus commands;
- whether America or Britain possess the same capability;
- whether Japan has distributed the command format to its allies;
- whether the attack was a technical demonstration or a rehearsal for war.

Germany grounds or limits command access to several satellites and begins an emergency review.

## The cryptographic lesson

The German conclusion is not merely “encrypt the messages.”

It is:

> **A satellite must authenticate the person issuing commands, not merely understand the command language.**

Germany introduces:

- cryptographic command authentication;
- frequently changed command keys;
- challenge-and-response procedures where hardware permits;
- command counters to reject reused transmissions;
- narrow command windows;
- frequency agility;
- lockout after repeated invalid commands;
- separate payload and spacecraft-bus keys;
- physical interlocks around propulsion and destructive commands;
- geographically directional receive antennas;
- autonomous safe modes when competing carriers are detected.

Older satellites cannot all be repaired in orbit. Some remain vulnerable until retirement.

That creates years of German anxiety.

# The diplomatic confrontation

Germany submits a severe protest accusing Japan of:

- unlawful interference with German state property;
- interception of sovereign communications;
- unauthorized command of a military spacecraft;
- establishing a dangerous precedent for orbital conflict.

Japan does not deny the technical facts.

It disputes Germany’s legal interpretation.

The Japanese statement argues:

> A foreign state placed an unannounced military radio apparatus over territory protected by Japan. Japan temporarily prevented that apparatus from receiving foreign military direction while it was directly overhead. Japan caused no permanent damage and asserted no title to the spacecraft.

Tokyo distinguishes between:

- **ownership of the object**, which remains German;
- **freedom of orbital passage**, which Japan does not deny;
- **immunity of the radio link**, which Japan refuses to concede.

Japan’s position is therefore not:

> “The satellite became ours over Japan.”

It is:

> “Orbital passage does not create a right to conduct immune military transmissions through Japanese sovereign space and territory.”

That is radical, but internally coherent.

# Why Japan does not apologize

Japan expresses **regret that Germany interpreted the demonstration as hostile** and offers complete evidence that:

- no propulsion commands were sent;
- no permanent configuration was changed;
- no data was destroyed;
- the satellite was not endangered.

German diplomats interpret this as a carefully worded apology.

Japanese ministers insist domestically that no apology was made.

Tokyo will not concede that foreign military communications over Japan are inviolable.

At the same time, it recognizes that uncontrolled satellite seizure could make every communications system unusable.

That tension produces the settlement.

# The Kobe Notes on Orbital Radio Interference, 1970

Germany and Japan privately negotiate during late 1969 and publish a limited agreement in 1970.

I would call it the:

## **Kobe Notes on Orbital Radio Interference**

The Notes do not declare that all satellite jamming is lawful.

They establish a narrow and controversial category of **territorial orbital denial**.

## Permitted or tolerated conduct

A state may temporarily interfere with the uplink or payload operation of an **unannounced foreign military or intelligence spacecraft** while that spacecraft is within a defined overhead territorial cone, provided that the interference:

- is reversible;
- ends when the spacecraft leaves the relevant geometry;
- does not alter its orbit;
- does not compromise attitude, power, thermal control, or structural safety;
- does not create debris;
- does not endanger human life;
- does not permanently erase data or damage equipment.

## Prohibited conduct

The parties disclaim any right to:

- issue propulsion commands;
- disable power or thermal regulation;
- interfere with crewed spacecraft safety;
- jam distress or rescue signals;
- interfere with declared civilian weather or disaster-relief spacecraft;
- continue interference after the satellite has left the immediate territorial pass;
- claim ownership or salvage rights merely because command access was obtained.

## The legal ambiguity

Germany does not formally concede that Japan possessed a right to perform the 1969 seizure.

Japan does not formally concede that the act was wrongful.

They agree that a comparable future event, if contained within these limits, will **not automatically be treated as an armed attack**.

That is the real achievement.

The agreement converts a possible casus belli into a regulated form of electronic competition.

# Why this is a major divergence from our world

Under real international telecommunications rules, intentional harmful interference and the transmission of false or misleading signals are prohibited. citeturn669997search4

Therefore Britain, America, and many neutral states reject the Kobe doctrine.

They argue that it would:

- destroy reliable satellite communications;
- encourage every state to jam overhead spacecraft;
- endanger weather and navigation services;
- make attribution difficult;
- blur espionage, electronic warfare, and armed attack.

Japan replies that great powers already use satellites for military collection without consent and cannot demand perfect immunity for the links that make that collection possible.

The result is not universal acceptance.

It is a divided international custom:

- **Japan and several associated states** endorse territorial orbital denial.
- **Germany** accepts the Kobe limits as a reciprocal practical arrangement without endorsing Japan’s legal theory.
- **America and Britain** reject the claimed right but prepare to exercise similar capabilities in wartime.
- **Neutral and Latin states** demand protection for registered civilian, meteorological, and rescue satellites.
- Military planners everywhere quietly assume that vulnerable overhead links may be attacked during crisis.

# The practical effect on satellite architecture

The incident produces four major changes.

## 1. Command authentication becomes mandatory

New military satellites no longer accept a command merely because its tone or bit pattern is correct.

They require cryptographic proof of origin.

## 2. Communications payloads are isolated

Payload switching, stored messages, attitude control, power, and propulsion receive separate command paths and increasingly separate hardware.

Seizing a transponder must not mean seizing the spacecraft.

## 3. Satellites become more autonomous

Because a ground link may be lost or jammed, satellites receive stronger onboard logic for:

- maintaining attitude;
- avoiding unsafe commands;
- returning to a standard configuration;
- continuing scheduled operations;
- waiting for authenticated reacquisition.

Japan’s later supervised-autonomous orbital doctrine emerges partly from this lesson.

## 4. Relay networks become attractive

A satellite that communicates directly with ground stations over hostile territory is vulnerable to local interference.

Later systems increasingly use:

- intersatellite crosslinks;
- narrow directional beams;
- higher-altitude relays;
- protected central gateways;
- scheduled burst transmissions.

This does push some military communications functions toward higher orbits.

It does **not** push every satellite higher. Reconnaissance systems still need proximity to Earth, while communications, early warning, and relay functions can be distributed across different orbital layers.

# Japanese prestige

For Japan, the incident becomes its equivalent of a dramatic space milestone.

Germany has:

- the first satellite;
- heavy lift;
- the lunar program.

America has:

- the spaceplane;
- increasingly ambitious crewed operations.

Japan demonstrates something different:

> It understands the operating language of the space age well enough to enter another power’s system, use it briefly, and leave it intact.

The event reinforces Japan’s self-image as the power of:

- electronics;
- protocols;
- automation;
- signals intelligence;
- disciplined systems engineering;
- machine-to-machine control.

Japanese popular culture turns the event into a slightly mischievous technological myth:

> Germany built the messenger. Japan taught it Japanese.

# Moving the Japanese crewed mission forward

I agree that **1983 is now too late** for Japan’s first crewed orbital flight.

It made sense under the earlier ultra-conservative sketch. It no longer fits a Japan that:

- has independent satellites by the early 1960s;
- has a mature tracking network;
- operates Biak;
- has advanced computing and automation;
- can seize a German satellite payload in 1969;
- deliberately pursues reliable machine-first spaceflight.

Japan should still avoid a reckless prestige sprint, but once Germany and America have landed on the Moon, continued absence of any Japanese crew becomes politically difficult.

## Revised sequence

### 1971

Japan announces a limited crewed-orbital program after the German and American lunar missions.

The objective is not the Moon.

It is:

- automated ascent;
- automated orbital insertion;
- automated attitude control;
- automated reentry;
- compact life support;
- human supervision of an otherwise machine-operated vehicle.

### 1972

An uncrewed full-system qualification vehicle completes:

- orbit;
- multiple ground-station handoffs;
- controlled reentry;
- recovery.

A second flight carries biological experiments and a fully pressurized cabin.

### 1973

Japan launches its first crewed mission from Biak.

I would make it:

- crew: two;
- duration: approximately three to five days;
- spacecraft: highly automated capsule or lifting capsule;
- mission: systems qualification, Earth observation, medical study, communications experiments;
- recovery: Pacific splashdown with Japanese and Philippine naval participation.

The pilot is not expected to manually fly every phase.

Japanese publicity emphasizes that the machine performs routine operations while the crew supervises, diagnoses, and authorizes.

### 1975–1976

A later mission docks with a small automated laboratory or logistics target.

The crew may include the first non-Japanese Co-Prosperity astronaut—potentially Filipino, Korean, Chinese, or Siamese.

### What remains for 1983

The former 1983 milestone can become:

- the first continuously occupied Japanese-led orbital platform;
- the first fully multinational Co-Prosperity crew;
- the first long-duration automated orbital laboratory;
- or the first Japanese crewed mission integrated with the mature Biak relay and robotic system.

This preserves 1983 as an important expansion without requiring Japan to wait twenty years after its first satellites before flying anyone.

# Canon-ready sequence

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **1967** | Japan begins systematic passive collection against German FMS-4 command, telemetry, and transponder links |
| **1968** | Japanese computers reconstruct the payload command framing; laboratory simulations confirm false-command access |
| **Autumn 1969** | Operation Amaterasu temporarily seizes FMS-4’s communications payload during a thirteen-minute pass over Northeast Asia |
| **Late 1969** | Germany protests; emergency satellite-command cryptography and authentication programs begin |
| **1970** | Kobe Notes establish limits on reversible territorial orbital interference without resolving its ultimate legality |
| **1971** | Japan authorizes a compact, highly automated crewed-orbital program |
| **1972** | Uncrewed full-system qualification and recovery |
| **1973** | First two-person Japanese orbital mission from Biak |
| **1975–1976** | First Japanese docking with an automated laboratory; associated-state astronaut program begins |
| **1983** | Revised milestone: first continuously occupied or fully multinational Japanese-led orbital platform |

The incident’s defining line should be:

> **Japan did not take possession of a German satellite. It demonstrated that possession of a satellite and possession of its voice were no longer the same thing.**

## 1. The transistor was serendipitous, but not accidental in the strong sense

The first working transistor appeared at Bell Labs in **December 1947**, not the early 1950s. The early 1950s were when improved junction transistors became practical and began entering production. Bell’s research group was deliberately trying to create a solid-state amplifier or switch that could replace unreliable vacuum tubes and slow electromechanical relays in telephone equipment. citeturn842171view1turn842171view3

What was serendipitous was the particular route to success:

- Shockley’s intended field-effect device failed.
- Bardeen theorized that electrical charge trapped at the semiconductor surface was blocking the applied field.
- Bardeen and Brattain experimented with germanium surfaces and closely spaced contacts.
- Brattain eventually used two gold contacts pressed onto germanium with a small plastic wedge.
- That arrangement unexpectedly produced substantial amplification.

So they did not encounter a random faulty bridge and suddenly realize it was a switch. They were consciously looking for semiconductor amplification, but the **point-contact mechanism was discovered through exploratory experimentation rather than built directly from a complete prior theory**. The image you may be remembering is the thin gold foil divided into two very closely spaced contacts. citeturn842171view3

### Can its date move?

Yes, but probably only modestly.

There are competing effects in this setting:

**Reasons it might come earlier**

- Shockley and other Bell researchers are not drawn as deeply into American wartime assignments.
- AT&T’s civilian need for more reliable telephone amplifiers still exists.
- Bell Labs remains wealthy, concentrated and technically ambitious.
- There may be more uninterrupted basic research in a neutral America.

**Reasons it might come later**

- Wartime radar work historically accelerated germanium purification, crystal-diode manufacture and semiconductor knowledge.
- A neutral America has a smaller military microwave-electronics program.
- There is less emergency federal funding for materials research.
- The solid-state group may be assembled less urgently.

Those effects approximately cancel. My recommendation is therefore:

> **Keep the first Bell point-contact transistor in late 1947 or early 1948.**

A movement of six to eighteen months is entirely plausible. Moving it to 1950–51 would noticeably alter everything we have just developed:

- transistor computers shift several years later;
- vacuum-tube systems remain dominant longer;
- Japan’s parametron becomes much more strategically important;
- German relay and hybrid systems remain competitive longer;
- American real-time aerospace computing develops more slowly.

That could be made to work, but it would create substantial downstream rewriting without giving the setting an especially useful distinction. The important counterfactual variation should occur in **who industrializes and applies the transistor most effectively**, not necessarily in whether Bell discovers the effect.

# 2. Turing: cyanide, not arsenic

The substance involved in Turing’s death was **cyanide**, not arsenic.

The official inquest ruled suicide by cyanide poisoning. Turing’s mother never accepted that conclusion. An item preserved in the Turing archive is a teaspoon she found in his laboratory, labelled with her belief that he intended to gold-plate it using potassium cyanide that he had prepared himself. She believed his death could have resulted from scientific experiments conducted carelessly. citeturn842171view2

The apple beside his bed was apparently never chemically tested. Consequently, the popular account that he certainly ate a cyanide-laced apple is not established beyond dispute. The accidental-exposure hypothesis remains possible, but so does suicide; the surviving evidence does not let us settle the matter confidently.

## What was the cyanide for?

Potassium cyanide can be used in gold electroplating because cyanide compounds hold gold in solution while an electric current deposits a controlled gold layer onto another object.

Gold plating has legitimate electrical uses:

- it resists corrosion and oxidation;
- it produces dependable low-resistance contacts;
- it improves the reliability of connectors, switches and relay contacts.

But the direct archival evidence concerns **gold-plating teaspoons**, not an identified experimental transistor or new switching device. It is possible that Turing was also interested in plating electrical contacts, but I would not treat that as established history.

## Where arsenic actually enters electronics

Arsenic is relevant to semiconductor technology in a completely different way. Tiny quantities of arsenic can be introduced into silicon or germanium as a **donor dopant**, increasing the supply of mobile electrons and creating n-type semiconductor material. Modern work still uses arsenic as a controllable donor in silicon and germanium. citeturn242306academia29turn196503academia42

Elemental arsenic would not normally be used as an ordinary metallic conductor or relay contact. Its importance is that a very small concentration can alter a semiconductor crystal’s electrical behavior.

Thus there are three distinct materials that should not be conflated:

| Material | Relevant use |
|---|---|
| Potassium cyanide | Gold-electroplating chemistry; acutely poisonous |
| Gold | Corrosion-resistant electrical contacts and plating |
| Arsenic | Semiconductor dopant, especially for n-type material |

---

# 3. What should happen to Turing in this setting?

The cleanest outcome is that the historical home-laboratory danger simply never develops.

Our Turing has:

- a senior NPL position;
- laboratory staff;
- institutional funding;
- security oversight;
- dedicated experimental facilities;
- technicians responsible for chemical and materials work;
- proper ventilation and chemical-storage procedures.

He has no reason to prepare cyanide plating baths in a small spare room. If he wishes to test gold-plated contacts, NPL’s laboratory staff does it.

That prevents his death without requiring us to rule authoritatively on whether the historical death was suicide or accident.

## Turing’s plausible solid-state role

Turing should not personally become Britain’s Bardeen, Brattain or Shockley. His greatest value remains in:

- architecture;
- computability;
- programming;
- artificial intelligence;
- numerical methods;
- cryptography;
- machine organization;
- mathematical biology.

But he would be exceptionally quick to understand the transistor’s consequences.

I would give him an influential role in establishing an NPL **Solid-State Switching and Machine Components Section** around 1949–50. Its physical scientists and electrical engineers investigate:

- transistor logic;
- reliable switching circuits;
- gold-plated contacts;
- component failure;
- error propagation;
- redundant logic;
- transistorized ACE successors;
- the relationship between component reliability and program design.

Turing’s personal contribution is not discovering a new dopant. It is recognizing that a transistor permits machines with vastly larger numbers of switching elements—and that this changes what architectures and programs are practical.

A characteristically Turing line of research would ask:

> How unreliable may each switching element be before the complete machine becomes unusable, and how can logical organization compensate for imperfect components?

That connects naturally to his work on unorganized machines, learning systems and machine intelligence.

## Recommended canon

- The Bell transistor remains a late-1947 or early-1948 discovery.
- Its discovery is described as **goal-directed research with a serendipitous experimental breakthrough**, not a pure accident.
- Arsenic is a semiconductor dopant, but it is unrelated to Turing’s historical poisoning.
- Turing’s historical cyanide apparatus was associated with gold electroplating.
- The setting does not declare definitively whether historical Turing intended suicide.
- In the alternate timeline, his senior institutional position moves chemical experiments into proper laboratories.
- Turing becomes an early patron of British solid-state switching and transistorized computing, while specialist physicists and electrical engineers conduct the materials research.
- No fatal laboratory accident is necessary. A minor cyanide-plating incident or safety scare could occur if we want an institutional origin for stricter British computing-laboratory safety rules, but Turing himself should not be the victim.

Yes. I would lock this in as a major distinguishing feature of the Japanese computing civilization. It supersedes the earlier suggestion that Japanese source code initially mixes Latin identifiers and mathematical notation with katakana.

The internal machine may still use binary, bi-quinary, or binary-coded decimal. What is Japanese is the **source representation, operator vocabulary, documentation, terminals, and programmer’s mental environment**.

# The native Japanese programming system

## Positional Japanese digits

Numeric literals use the ten positional glyphs:

> **〇 一 二 三 四 五 六 七 八 九**

Thus:

- ten is `一〇`;
- 1957 is `一九五七`;
- 3.1416 is `三・一四一六`.

The compiler does not ordinarily accept classical multiplicative numerals such as `千九百五十七` as numeric literals. `十`, `百`, `千`, and `万` remain ordinary characters usable in prose, labels, and strings, while machine-readable numbers use fixed positional notation.

The choice of **〇 rather than 零** emerges from practical convergence among firms:

- it is one simple glyph;
- it is visually distinct from every other digit;
- it prints reliably on cards, tape, teleprinters, and crude displays;
- it fits naturally into positional columns;
- it requires far fewer strokes than `零`;
- operators can recognize it instantly in a table.

Fujitsu, NEC, Mitsubishi, and government laboratories independently drift toward `〇`; the later national standard merely ratifies what working programmers already do. `零` survives as the written word “zero” in prose and formal terminology, while `〇` is the digit.

## Japanese arithmetic operators

The ordinary Western `+` and `-` are disfavored because, in early typefaces and low-resolution displays:

- `+` is easily confused with `十`;
- `-` is easily confused with `一`.

Japanese programming therefore develops a compact technical ideograph set:

| Operation | Character |
|---|---|
| Addition | `加` |
| Subtraction | `減` |
| Multiplication | `乗` |
| Division | `除` |
| Unary negative | `負` |
| Equality | `等` |
| Greater than | `大` |
| Less than | `小` |
| Assignment or setting | `置` |
| Decimal point | `・` |
| Scientific exponent marker | `指` |

A scientific value comparable to \(1.5 \times 10^{-3}\) could be written:

> `一・五 指 負三`

The exact final grammar can evolve, but **加・減・乗・除・負** should become enduring Japanese programming symbols.

# Early character encoding

## Proprietary zaibatsu codes

The first Japanese machines do not begin with one national code.

Different organizations create proprietary character systems:

- FACOM systems;
- ETL government machines;
- Navy and Army codes;
- NEC telecommunications systems;
- Mitsubishi industrial systems;
- parametron research machines.

Most early systems use five- or six-bit codes with shift states. One state contains katakana; another contains digits, operators, punctuation, and control commands. Dakuten and handakuten may initially be separate modifier characters.

There is **no Latin alphabet in the ordinary core set**.

A Latin letter encountered in a foreign formula is:

- rewritten as a katakana identifier;
- assigned a Japanese technical name;
- represented by a numeric field code;
- or handled through a special foreign-data peripheral.

## The first national Japanese code

Around 1957–59, the electronics-and-automation expansion produces a common seven-bit Japanese core standard. A suitable working title is:

> **帝国仮名機械符号**  
> Imperial Kana Machine Code

Its central repertoire contains:

- full katakana;
- `〇一二三四五六七八九`;
- Japanese punctuation;
- arithmetic ideographs;
- brackets and separators;
- control codes;
- tape, card, printer, and communications functions.

This is the setting’s functional equivalent of early ASCII, but it begins from Japanese telegraphy and technical writing rather than from American typewriters.

# Japanese programming languages

The language names previously transliterated as KEISAN and TEJUN are written domestically as:

- **ケイサン**, later displayed as **計算**;
- **テジュン**, later displayed as **手順**.

Early source code is written primarily in katakana.

Representative keywords include:

| Early written form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `モシ` | If |
| `ソノタ` | Otherwise |
| `クリカエシ` | Repeat |
| `テイギ` | Define |
| `ヨミコミ` | Read |
| `カキダシ` | Write |
| `ヨビダシ` | Call |
| `モドリ` | Return |
| `オワリ` | End |

Identifiers are also katakana. Technical abbreviations are Japanese abbreviations, not Latin initials.

An illustrative early program—not yet fixed syntax—might resemble:

```text
ゴウケイ 置 〇
カズ 置 一
クリカエシ　カズ 以下 一〇
　ゴウケイ 置 ゴウケイ 加 カズ
　カズ 置 カズ 加 一
オワリ
カキダシ「ゴウケイ」ゴウケイ
```

A Japanese programmer in 1959 does not need to learn English words such as `IF`, `DO`, `READ`, or `WRITE`. Foreign programmers must instead learn Japanese technical vocabulary.

# The Philippine catalyst

The Philippines enters the Japanese-associated system after the Philippine War and American withdrawal, bringing with it:

- a large Latin-script bureaucracy;
- English-language higher education;
- Filipino languages normally written in Latin script;
- commercial law, banking, and accounting records using Latin names;
- technically educated personnel who are allies rather than simply colonial subjects. fileciteturn9file3 fileciteturn9file4

Japan has already dealt with Chinese and Korean writing, but principally by imposing Japanese administrative codes, machine-readable numbers, and paper cross-references. The Philippines is different because its associated-state status gives Manila more leverage to insist that its own names, commercial records, addresses, laws, and technical personnel remain usable.

That makes the Philippines the political catalyst for **native Latin-script support**.

## The Latin supplementary library

The first response is not to rewrite Japanese languages around Latin characters. It is to provide a Latin supplementary package containing:

- capital and lowercase Latin letters;
- Filipino and English punctuation;
- common diacritics;
- Latin-script printers;
- translation tables;
- string and record libraries;
- optional Latin identifiers.

Filipino programmers still write the control structure in Japanese:

- keywords remain katakana;
- numeric literals remain Japanese digits;
- compiler messages remain Japanese;
- systems documentation is principally Japanese;
- programming courses teach Japanese technical vocabulary.

They can, however, write customer-facing text, personal names, commercial fields, and eventually identifiers in Latin script.

A Filipino program may therefore contain Japanese operations acting upon Latin-script data. This is the inversion you described: instead of Japanese programmers learning English to access the computer, Filipino programmers learn Japanese to command it.

Some Filipino programmers also write Tagalog or English identifiers phonetically in katakana when using older machines. This produces a recognizable imperial technical pidgin: katakana approximations of Filipino words embedded inside Japanese source code.

# The imperial character registry

Latin support immediately raises wider questions:

- Chinese characters;
- Hangul;
- Thai;
- Burmese;
- Vietnamese diacritics;
- Malay and Indonesian Latin spelling;
- indigenous names;
- scientific symbols;
- commercial marks.

Japan therefore moves beyond a collection of vendor code pages toward a central **character registry**.

A plausible sequence is:

| Period | Development |
|---|---|
| 1950s | Proprietary kana codes |
| 1957–59 | Common Japanese core code |
| 1960–63 | Latin supplementary character set |
| Mid-1960s | Multibyte imperial common-character system |
| 1970s | Mixed-script terminal and printer standard |
| 1980s | Mature universal imperial character environment |

A working formal name could be:

> **共栄圏共通文字符号**  
> Co-Prosperity Sphere Common Character Code

Its mature architecture resembles an early Unicode concept more than ASCII:

- every registered character receives a stable identity;
- scripts occupy defined blocks or planes;
- Japanese core characters retain compact one-byte forms;
- other scripts use lead bytes or multibyte sequences;
- vendors must map their internal encodings to the common registry;
- the same person or place name can travel between banks, ports, government systems, and corporate machines without being assigned an entirely new proprietary code.

It is not initially as universal or elegant as modern Unicode. It still contains duplicate compatibility characters, vendor extensions, politically imposed “preferred” forms, and awkward normalization rules. But its governing idea is already present:

> **A character belongs to the imperial information system independently of the machine displaying it.**

That is an enormous conceptual advance.

# Katakana-to-kanji terminal conversion

Once programming shifts from punched cards and paper tape to CRT terminals, Japan develops a second distinctive technology.

The programmer continues to type katakana. The editor recognizes reserved sequences and converts them into compact keyword tokens.

For example:

| Typed sequence | Terminal display |
|---|---|
| `モシ` | `若` or `条件` |
| `ソノタ` | `他` |
| `クリカエシ` | `繰` |
| `テイギ` | `定` |
| `ヨミコミ` | `読` |
| `カキダシ` | `書` |
| `ヨビダシ` | `呼` |
| `モドリ` | `戻` |
| `オワリ` | `終` |

The precise displayed forms can differ by language family. The underlying file need not store the full kanji sequence. It can store one compact token, which the terminal displays as:

- kanji on advanced terminals;
- katakana on older printers;
- a local explanatory word on foreign-compatible systems.

Thus the terminal-era version of the earlier example might display:

```text
合計 置 〇
数 置 一
繰　数 以下 一〇
　合計 置 合計 加 数
　数 置 数 加 一
終
書「合計」合計
```

Initially this is only a fixed programming-keyword dictionary. It is far easier than general-purpose kanji input because the system recognizes perhaps a few dozen reserved sequences.

Over time it expands into:

- kanji identifiers;
- comments;
- technical dictionaries;
- name conversion;
- word processing;
- publishing;
- electronic mail.

Japanese programming therefore becomes one of the principal parents of the Japanese input-method editor.

# Industrial consequences

This authorial decision has major effects beyond language design.

Japan invests unusually early in:

- font ROMs;
- bitmap glyph generators;
- mixed-script printers;
- terminal character memories;
- high-resolution CRTs;
- compact character displays;
- optical character design;
- dictionary-based input;
- multilingual sorting;
- text normalization;
- electronic typesetting;
- word processors.

That fits Japan’s established trajectory toward automation, microelectronics, compact electronics, robotics, and networked imperial production. fileciteturn9file3

It also means Japanese consumer-electronics firms enter the 1970s with unusually deep expertise in putting complex text on inexpensive screens. That naturally benefits:

- home computers;
- game consoles;
- arcade machines;
- electronic dictionaries;
- office terminals;
- portable word processors;
- navigation and industrial displays.

# Political meaning

Programming becomes a major instrument of cultural Japanization.

Local peoples may retain their languages for:

- printed output;
- customer records;
- comments;
- strings;
- local databases;
- user interfaces.

But the machine is commanded in Japanese.

Technical advancement therefore rewards:

- Japanese literacy;
- Japanese higher education;
- familiarity with Japanese corporate procedure;
- command of Japanese programming terminology.

The hierarchy is subtle but powerful:

> Local languages describe the data.  
> Japanese describes what the machine is permitted to do with it.

By the 1970s, foreign-language front ends exist, especially in the Philippines and Singapore. They are generally understood as compatibility systems layered over a Japanese-centered compiler and operating environment—not as equal founding languages.

This should become firm canon. It gives Japan not merely translated programming keywords, but a genuinely independent textual computing tradition whose later multilingual expansion grows from imperial necessity rather than Western imitation.
