# VI. Tanaka and the first crewed flight

## The Imperial Network Reconstruction Plan

Tanaka takes office in 1972 with a broader program than space.

His vision is to rebuild the empire as an integrated network of:

- ports;
- railways;
- airports;
- telephone and data links;
- power systems;
- industrial corridors;
- universities;
- weather stations;
- tracking facilities.

Biak is one part of that system.

Tanaka argues that Japan’s empire cannot remain centered exclusively on the home islands. Associated and subordinate territories must become indispensable pieces of the common infrastructure.

His space spending therefore goes to:

- Biak;
- Philippine recovery facilities;
- tracking stations in Palau and Taiwan;
- computers in Singapore;
- launch manufacturing in Japan and Korea;
- electronics production in Taiwan;
- weather-data processing in Manila;
- tropical test facilities.

He is the perfect premier to get Hikari-1 launched.

He is also the perfect premier to create a sprawling patronage network around it.

## Why he falls

Tanaka’s downfall does not repudiate the space program.

The scandal concerns:

- contract steering;
- political contributions;
- compulsory or inadequately compensated land acquisition;
- concealed cost overruns;
- procurement waivers;
- pressure upon safety inspectors.

The public conclusion is not:

> “Crewed spaceflight was a mistake.”

It is:

> “The imperial construction machine has grown too powerful to audit.”

This gives Miki a real political purpose.

---

# VII. The Miki Cabinet, 1974–1976

Miki forms a **Cabinet of Rectification and Public Trust**.

His major reforms include:

- an independent launch-failure commission;
- parliamentary review of major civil space appropriations;
- separation of range safety from booster contractors;
- publication of civilian mission objectives;
- local representation on the Biak Range Authority;
- compensation and resettlement rules;
- restrictions on hidden corporate political funds;
- formal separation of civilian and classified military payload accounts.

Miki is not hostile to empire or space.

He believes that Japanese leadership cannot claim to serve Asia while treating imperial territory as merely available ground for Japanese projects.

Under him:

- Kōbō is assembled more slowly;
- crew safety receives priority;
- the Weather Commons expands;
- Japanese meteorological data become more open;
- the first laboratory mission is authorized only after extended automatic operation.

The Miki period gives the Japanese program a reputation for **reliability after scandal**.

---

# VIII. The Fukuda Cabinet, 1976–1979

Fukuda is the most important prime minister for translating the space program into the developing moral culture of the Co-Prosperity Sphere.

Historically, Fukuda’s 1977 Manila speech emphasized trust, “heart-to-heart” relations, and cooperation with Southeast Asia. citeturn650864view1 In this timeline, those themes become even more consequential because Japan actually leads a hierarchical multinational order.

## The Manila Principles of Association

In 1977 Fukuda delivers a major speech in Manila.

Its three principles are approximately:

1. Japan’s strength exists for the defense of the common Asian peace.
2. Association does not erase the religion, nationhood, law, or honor of its members.
3. The scientific and technical accomplishments of the sphere must be shared among its peoples.

This is not a promise of equality.

It is a promise of reciprocal dignity.

The space program becomes one of the clearest fields in which Japan can demonstrate that principle.

## Associated-state astronaut program

In 1977 Japan begins selecting astronaut candidates from:

- the Philippines;
- Siam;
- Nanjing China;
- Manchukuo;
- Korea and Taiwan, though their constitutional status makes their representation politically sensitive;
- Burma.

The first non-Japanese participant should be Filipino.

That follows naturally from:

- the Philippines’ status as the most visibly sovereign associated member;
- its role in Hikari recovery;
- its weather and communications stations;
- the political importance of proving that Japanese spaceflight is not reserved exclusively for ethnic Japanese.

## 1977 mission

Hikari-4 returns to Kōbō for approximately twenty-one days.

The crew installs:

- improved environmental controls;
- replacement computers;
- additional experiment racks;
- a second external antenna;
- equipment for automated satellite control.

## 1978 mission

Hikari-5 carries:

- one Japanese commander;
- one Japanese systems engineer;
- one Filipino meteorological or communications specialist, using an improved three-person Hikari Kai vehicle.

This becomes one of the great images of the postwar Japanese system.

The Filipino is not presented as a colonial subject honored by Japan. He is presented as an officer or scientist of an associated nation contributing to a common mission.

Kōbō’s experiments include:

- tropical-storm observation;
- western Pacific oceanography;
- long-range radio propagation;
- agricultural imaging;
- human adaptation to longer orbital stays.

Fukuda’s political formula is:

> **Japan opened the road, but the road belongs to the order that built it.**

---

# IX. The Ōhira Cabinet, 1979–1980

Ōhira shifts the program toward the **information empire**.

His government sees the Japanese sphere as a system whose security depends upon:

- energy;
- food;
- shipping;
- communications;
- weather;
- computing;
- technical education;
- reliable data.

Space is one layer of this wider architecture.

## Tsubame-1

In 1979 Japan launches its first serious automated cargo and station-support vehicle.

Tsubame-1:

- docks automatically with Kōbō;
- transfers propellant and sealed cargo;
- raises the station’s orbit;
- removes waste;
- conducts a destructive controlled reentry.

This is at least as important to Japan as the first crewed flight.

It proves that a station does not require a crew merely to receive supplies and maintain its orbit.

## Kōbō-C

A third module is added around 1979–80.

Its functions include:

- Earth observation;
- meteorological calibration;
- communications experiments;
- remote handling of external instruments;
- larger data-processing equipment;
- additional living space.

Kōbō is now a genuine small station, but it remains intermittently occupied.

A typical year may include:

- one crewed mission;
- one cargo mission;
- several months of automated experiments;
- long periods with no people aboard.

## Ōhira’s death

Ōhira dies in office around 1980, as in the broad historical personal trajectory, before he can complete the political reorganization he envisioned.

His death produces a consensus government rather than a crisis.

---

# X. The Suzuki Cabinet, 1980–1982

Suzuki is not a visionary space premier.

That is useful.

His Cabinet asks whether Japan has accumulated too many prestigious technical programs:

- carriers;
- nuclear submarines;
- reactors;
- orbital launchers;
- computers;
- automation;
- Kōbō;
- lunar probes;
- weather satellites;
- military reconnaissance.

He does not cancel them. He imposes fiscal and organizational discipline.

## The reliability interval

Under Suzuki, the space program emphasizes:

- repeat flights rather than new firsts;
- improved Hikari reliability;
- rescue procedures;
- standardized docking collars;
- station fire safety;
- long-life solar arrays;
- orbital-debris tracking;
- automated cargo;
- better ground communications;
- associated-state training.

The slower pace prevents the program from becoming a brittle prestige machine.

## 1980–1981 missions

Hikari-6 and Hikari-7 conduct progressively longer stays:

- approximately thirty days;
- then forty-five days.

At least one crew includes a Siamese or Nanjing Chinese specialist.

Japan also launches an emergency return vehicle or keeps a second Hikari attached during the longest mission.

## Kōbō power modernization

In 1981 a new power-and-control module replaces or supplements the aging Kōbō-A systems.

It provides:

- larger solar arrays;
- improved batteries;
- more capable computers;
- two docking ports;
- better attitude control;
- expanded life support;
- the ability to support four people for several months.

This is the hardware that permits the later transition to continuous occupation.

## The 1981–82 orbital crisis

The American close approach to a German military satellite produces new negotiations over:

- approach notification;
- station safety zones;
- rescue duties;
- transponders;
- docking compatibility;
- protection of life support.

Japan participates heavily because it already possesses:

- automated docking;
- a crewed station;
- unmanned cargo vehicles;
- the Weather Commons;
- experience with orbital electronic interference.

Japan’s delegation argues that life-support safety and rescue must be protected even when intelligence and military operations remain legal.

That helps produce the established 1982 Geneva orbital-incidents arrangement.

---

# XI. Nakasone and the 1983 transformation

Nakasone enters office in 1982 believing that Japan has become technologically powerful but politically too modest about what it has created.

His view is not simply nationalist boasting.

He argues that Japan cannot claim honorable leadership while leaving every spectacular symbol of the future to Germany and America.

At the same time, he accepts the machine-first tradition.

He does not order a Japanese lunar landing merely for a flag.

He turns the existing Kōbō system into a permanent multinational platform.

## The Hōrai conversion

The expanded Kōbō complex is formally renamed:

# **Hōrai Orbital Platform**

Hōrai evokes the legendary island beyond the ordinary world. It also fits a maritime empire: the first permanent Japanese orbital habitat is conceived as an island in the heavens.

Between late 1982 and 1983 Japan adds:

- a new habitation module;
- improved radiation shelter;
- additional docking port;
- larger power system;
- command and data-processing section;
- medical compartment;
- dedicated robotic-control consoles;
- attached emergency-return vehicle;
- accommodation for four to six people.

The complete platform remains much smaller than the German Orbitaler Raumhafen and less traffic-oriented than America’s Columbia.

A useful comparison in 1983 is:

| Platform | Approximate character |
|---|---|
| German Raumhafen | Large orbital shipyard, depot, construction and lunar-logistics harbor |
| American Columbia | Reusable-vehicle destination, growing traffic hub and general orbital port |
| Japanese Hōrai | Compact automated laboratory, satellite-control center, and robotic-operations platform |
| Commonwealth program | Intermittent crewed science leading toward Resolution |
| Latin program | Preparing first multinational independent crew |

## Continuous occupation

Continuous occupation begins in 1983.

The first resident crew could be:

- two Japanese;
- one Filipino;
- one Siamese or Nanjing Chinese specialist.

Later rotations add Korean, Taiwanese, Manchurian, Burmese, and other personnel, though the constitutional meaning of each seat becomes politically contentious.

This is the proper 1983 milestone:

> **Japan begins permanent human presence in orbit, and it does so with a multinational Co-Prosperity crew.**

The crew operates:

- weather satellites;
- communications experiments;
- Earth-observation systems;
- automated orbital tugs;
- materials laboratories;
- long-duration medical studies;
- prototype robotic spacecraft;
- deep-space communications experiments.

Hōrai is not merely inhabited.

It is the command center from which humans supervise machines.

That directly anticipates Japan’s mature orbital doctrine:

> **The machine flies the trajectory; the human commands the purpose.**

---

# XII. The unmanned exploration sequence

Crewed flight does not replace Japan’s unmanned priorities.

## Lunar program

Japan’s lunar sequence can run approximately as follows:

### 1973–1974

- lunar communications and navigation experiments;
- improved deep-space tracking from Biak, Palau, the Philippines, and associated stations.

### 1975

- first successful Japanese lunar orbiter;
- photography and radio-science work.

### 1977

- automated soft lander;
- soil-mechanics experiments;
- weathering and temperature measurements;
- television imaging.

### 1979–1980

- small mobile rover;
- remote manipulation;
- sample selection without return;
- long-duration survival experiments.

### 1981–1983

- multiple cooperating lunar machines;
- relay orbiter;
- fixed lander;
- rover;
- communications package;
- experimental resource survey.

Japan does not beat Germany or America to the Moon with people. It begins demonstrating the distributed robotic method that later defines its Mars program.

## Mars preparation

By 1980, Japanese engineers are developing:

- autonomous navigation;
- fault-tolerant computers;
- small standardized landers;
- relay orbiters;
- cooperative rover protocols;
- long-delay command systems;
- automatic safe modes.

Hōrai gives them a place to test human supervision of several autonomous vehicles at once.

By 1983, Japan is ready to launch the distributed Mars system already intended for the 1984 window. The mission consists not of one enormous rover but of:

- an orbiter;
- communications relay;
- several small landers;
- two or more mobile vehicles;
- fixed meteorological stations;
- a sample cache or geological package.

The setting’s established 1984 distributed Japanese Mars mission can therefore remain intact. The difference is that it now grows naturally from a decade of Hikari, Kōbō, Tsubame, and Hōrai operations rather than appearing after Japan’s supposed first crewed flight. fileciteturn16file0

---

# XIII. The political meaning of the program

The Japanese space program evolves under seven Cabinets, and every Cabinet leaves a different layer.

## Satō

Makes space a disciplined strategic institution.

## Tanaka

Builds the physical network and launches the first crew—but nearly discredits the program through patronage and haste.

## Miki

Establishes public trust, safety, audit, and the modular laboratory.

## Fukuda

Turns space into a multinational expression of association.

## Ōhira

Integrates orbit with information, weather, communications, and comprehensive security.

## Suzuki

Makes the system reliable enough to endure.

## Nakasone

Gives the mature system a confident political identity and establishes permanent presence.

This sequence is stronger than giving one premier credit for everything.

It shows institutional accumulation.

---

# XIV. Canon-ready mission chronology

| Year | Mission or development |
|---:|---|
| **1971** | Satō authorizes the limited Human Orbital Systems Program |
| **1972** | Hikari-0 completes uncrewed full-system qualification and Pacific recovery |
| **1973** | Hikari-1 carries two Japanese astronauts for approximately four days; first Japanese crewed orbital flight |
| **Early 1974** | Two Musubi vehicles accomplish automatic rendezvous and docking |
| **Mid-1974** | Hikari-2 docks with an unpressurized Musubi target |
| **Late 1974** | Heavy-booster failure and Biak procurement scandal delay the laboratory and bring down Tanaka |
| **1975** | Kōbō-A and Kōbō-B launch separately and dock automatically; laboratory operates uncrewed |
| **1976** | Hikari-3 conducts the first fourteen-day crewed occupation of Kōbō |
| **1977** | Hikari-4 conducts a twenty-one-day maintenance and science mission; associated-state astronaut program begins |
| **1978** | Hikari Kai carries the first Filipino astronaut to Kōbō |
| **1979** | Tsubame-1 performs Japan’s first automated orbital cargo and reboost mission |
| **1979–1980** | Kōbō-C expands Earth observation, meteorology, communications, and habitation |
| **1980–1981** | Thirty- and forty-five-day missions; new power-and-control module installed |
| **1982** | Hōrai expansion begins; Japan helps negotiate orbital approach, rescue, and life-support rules |
| **1983** | Hōrai begins continuous occupation with a multinational Co-Prosperity crew |
| **1984** | Japan launches its first major distributed cooperative Mars robotic system |

# Final correction

The clean Japanese sequence is now:

> **Japan flies people early enough to remain a first-rank space power, but it never allows human spectacle to displace the practical machine network.**

The 1973 astronaut proves Japan can carry people.

The 1976 laboratory proves people can maintain Japanese machines in orbit.

The 1983 platform proves those machines, people, and associated nations can form a permanent operating system.

# Germany, 1970–1975: The Rival, the Client, and the Harbor

The five years after the German Moon landing give Wolfgang a different education from Iceland.

Iceland taught him that an unused weapon may achieve more than a fired one. The years 1970–75 teach him four additional distinctions:

> An opponent is not necessarily dishonorable.  
> An ideological friend is not necessarily an ally.  
> A weapon is not an institution.  
> A first achievement is not the same thing as permanent infrastructure.

By 1975 Wolfgang is twenty-eight. He has lost several of the older men who formed him, survived a disastrous war begun by a German client against his explicit advice, watched American democracy reorganize itself twice without collapsing, and personally opened the first true orbital harbor.

---

## I. The American Moon landing, 20 July 1971

Germany does not treat the American landing as irrelevant merely because it arrived seven months after the German mission.

The American achievement is technically different. Germany’s 1970 mission used an austere direct-ascent system developed alongside von Braun’s preferred station architecture. The American system uses a reusable Earth-to-orbit spaceplane, an orbital tug, and a dedicated lunar lander. Germany wins the date; America demonstrates a more reusable transportation system. fileciteturn15file6 fileciteturn15file7

Wolfgang understands this immediately.

He watches the American landing with von Braun, Eberhard Rees, senior controllers, and a small household group. The German engineers are not sneering. They are evaluating:

- turnaround procedures;
- orbital assembly;
- tug operations;
- landing accuracy;
- crew workload;
- the condition of the returning spaceplane;
- how quickly America can fly the system again.

The German propaganda apparatus initially prepares the predictable message: America has honorably followed where Germany led.

Wolfgang rejects the dismissive tone.

## Wolfgang’s congratulation

His official message should be genuinely gracious:

> **“Germany was first to arrive; America has shown another road. One nation’s achievement does not diminish another’s. The Moon is greater today because two peoples have reached it.”**

He congratulates:

- President Rockefeller;
- the American crew;
- mission control;
- the engineers and workers who built the system;
- the families who accepted the risks.

The Americans initially search the statement for sarcasm.

There is very little.

Wolfgang’s tone resembles two competitors congratulating one another after a difficult race. Germany still wants to win the next event. But Wolfgang understands that the other man ran well.

## Why this matters

This establishes a peculiar culture between the two space establishments.

The strategic relationship remains hostile. German and American systems conduct reconnaissance, support military communications, and increasingly become involved in orbital-security planning.

At the professional level, however, astronauts, controllers, flight surgeons, tracking officers, and engineers recognize one another as participants in the same extraordinarily dangerous activity.

The resulting relationship contains:

- genuine admiration;
- careful exchange of public technical papers;
- emergency tracking cooperation;
- quiet discussion of distress frequencies;
- shared concern about debris and abandoned upper stages;
- fierce competition over every milestone.

Wolfgang does not view respect as weakness.

He sees it as evidence that Germany’s confidence no longer depends upon pretending everybody else is incompetent.

One of Goebbels’s last propaganda disputes—assuming his working 1971 death remains—can be precisely this issue. Goebbels instinctively wants Germany to own the whole emotional meaning of the Moon. Wolfgang insists that praising the Americans makes Germany look stronger, not weaker.

The younger Führer wins.

# II. Space after the first landings

Wolfgang’s congratulation does not mean the race has ended.

Germany now commits decisively to the architecture Wolfgang has preferred since childhood:

1. heavy cargo launch;
2. orbital assembly;
3. fuel transfer;
4. long-duration habitation;
5. lunar ferries;
6. permanent stations;
7. repeatable access to the Moon;
8. eventual Mars expeditions.

The successful direct-ascent booster is redirected into station construction. Habitation sections, docking nodes, tanks, structural members, reactor components, workshops, and rotating-habitation hardware begin moving into orbit. fileciteturn15file6

Wolfgang’s internal interpretation is:

> The German landing proved a mission could be completed.  
> The American landing proved a transportation method could be repeated.  
> Germany must now prove that an extraterrestrial settlement system can be maintained.

This is why the Orbitaler Raumhafen becomes more personally important to him than even the first lunar landing.

The landing was spectacular.

The harbor is his philosophy made physical.

# III. Germany’s thorium turn

The thorium question requires one scientific correction.

Thorium is not discovered as a potential nuclear fuel in the 1970s. Its potential is already known. The meaningful alternate-history event is that Germany decides to give the thorium fuel cycle **large, sustained institutional backing**.

Thorium is substantially more abundant in nature than uranium, but natural thorium is fertile rather than directly fissile. It must absorb neutrons and breed uranium-233, and the cycle requires an initial fissile inventory such as uranium-235, plutonium, or previously bred uranium-233. That makes thorium attractive as a long-term fuel-cycle extension, not a magical replacement that can immediately fuel any reactor. citeturn583181search0turn583181search7turn583181search39

Coal and coal ash do contain trace uranium and thorium, and combustion concentrates noncombustible minerals in the ash. But ordinary European coalfields should not be treated as Germany’s principal thorium mines. The most useful thorium resources are associated more strongly with monazite, rare-earth minerals, veins, carbonatites, placers, and other specialized deposits. Coal ash can become an interesting low-grade byproduct stream, particularly where rare-earth recovery is already occurring, but not the foundation of the German programme. citeturn177525search20turn583181search27turn583181search29

## Why Germany cares

Germany is not facing immediate uranium starvation. Its sphere provides access to several potential uranium and thorium sources.

Wolfgang nevertheless likes thorium for the same reason he likes orbital infrastructure:

- it broadens the resource base;
- it rewards long-term systems planning;
- it creates high-temperature industrial applications;
- it reduces reliance upon one fuel chain;
- it may eventually support a closed or semi-closed breeder cycle;
- it offers technical leadership distinct from weapons development.

Since nuclear weapons have not defined this world, Germany’s nuclear establishment is much more openly organized around:

- electrical generation;
- process heat;
- propulsion;
- isotope production;
- industrial chemistry;
- district heating;
- synthetic fuels;
- aerospace power systems.

## The German Thorium Programme

A strong working sequence is:

### 1971: strategic review

Wolfgang orders the nuclear establishment to assess whether the expanding reactor fleet is becoming too dependent upon one fuel and enrichment chain.

The resulting report recommends a long-term thorium programme.

### 1972: two-track authorization

Germany funds two distinct routes.

The practical route uses thorium-bearing fuel in high-temperature gas-cooled reactors. This is attractive for:

- electricity;
- industrial heat;
- chemical processing;
- hydrogen;
- synthetic-fuel production.

The speculative route investigates molten-fluoride systems, online chemistry, breeding, and uranium-233 separation.

### 1973–1974: experimental fuel cycle

Small experimental cores, test loops, fuel-fabrication facilities, and reprocessing laboratories begin operating.

This does not yet mean a commercial thorium economy.

The difficult problems include:

- fissile startup requirements;
- fuel fabrication;
- chemical separation;
- radiation handling;
- reactor materials;
- reprocessing losses;
- economic comparison with already-functioning uranium plants.

### 1975: demonstration decision

Germany authorizes one or two larger demonstration systems for the later 1970s.

The uranium fleet continues expanding. Thorium remains the strategic second road.

Wolfgang is not personally fascinated by reactor chemistry in the manner he is fascinated by space. He is interested in the architecture of the programme:

> Where does the fuel come from?  
> What must be imported?  
> Which waste streams become inputs?  
> Which industries can use the heat?  
> What happens if one region is cut off?

He treats nuclear power as logistics measured in decades.

# IV. National Socialist Iraq, 1971–1973

Iraq is Wolfgang’s first great failure in managing an ideologically sympathetic foreign regime.

The German-backed revolutionary movement wins the Iraqi civil conflict and establishes a regime commonly called National Socialist Iraq. It suppresses rivals, drives surviving Hashemites into Jordan, claims Kuwait as territory severed from Basra, and increasingly presents itself as the vanguard of Arab unification. fileciteturn13file10

Germany wants the new Iraq to survive.

Germany does not want Iraq to start a regional war.

These are not the same objective.

## Why Baghdad misunderstands Berlin

The Iraqis receive messages through several German channels.

The Foreign Office tells them:

- consolidate internally;
- rebuild the railway and fuel systems;
- avoid provoking Britain;
- do not threaten every neighboring monarchy simultaneously;
- Germany has not granted an automatic military guarantee.

German arms representatives tell them:

- German weapons have transformed their army;
- the new Iraq is the strongest Arab military state;
- further purchases will make it stronger still.

Party and SS-linked visitors tell them:

- revolutionary states must not become timid after victory;
- Baghdad carries a historic mission;
- the old monarchies are politically obsolete.

Military advisers say:

- Iraqi logistics are not ready;
- officer training is inadequate;
- maintenance rates are poor;
- combined-arms exercises are being staged rather than learned.

Baghdad hears the message it prefers.

## Wolfgang’s warning

In 1973, after Iraqi military exercises and escalating claims against Kuwait, Wolfgang gives the Iraqi leadership an unambiguous warning.

It may be delivered privately through the German ambassador and then repeated during an Iraqi visit to Berlin:

> **“Germany will not fight a war which Baghdad begins and Berlin has not approved.”**

He explains that:

- German arms deliveries are not a mutual-defense treaty;
- ideological affinity does not give Iraq command of German forces;
- Britain has rebuilt much more effectively than Baghdad assumes;
- Saudi Arabia and Iran will not tolerate Iraqi control of Kuwait;
- Jordan and the Latin bloc will support Iraq’s enemies;
- Germany cannot rescue an Iraqi army from every coalition its rhetoric creates.

The Iraqis affirm that they understand.

They do not believe him completely.

Their assumption is that once the war begins, Germany will be unable to permit a fellow National Socialist state to be defeated by Britain.

That assumption is wrong.

# V. Germany and the American election of 1972

The 1972 American election reinforces Wolfgang’s negative opinion of parliamentary democracy.

After the 1968 House selection denied Rockwell the presidency despite his electoral plurality, the Democrats and Republicans fuse into the Democratic-Republican Party. Rockefeller then defeats Rockwell narrowly in 1972 while National Renewal captures the House and approaches Senate parity. fileciteturn14file0

To Wolfgang, the sequence looks almost absurd:

- three competing parties;
- no stable presidential majority;
- a House-selected president;
- the sudden fusion of two historic rivals;
- an opposition party controlling part of Congress;
- constitutional amendments being used to settle cultural questions;
- the same state somehow maintaining fleets, orbital launches, and a lunar programme.

He interprets the fusion less as democratic stability than as the ruling establishment changing the rules of coalition to keep an outsider from executive power.

His private conclusion is:

> “They call our continuity hereditary. Theirs is hereditary among parties.”

But Wolfgang is forced to concede something important.

The American state does **not** collapse.

Its rival parties continue funding the space programme, modernizing the military, and honoring the Mid-Atlantic Ridge Accord. America’s political system is chaotic, but the state possesses institutional depth beneath the chaos.

This slightly complicates his contempt.

He continues believing democratic government is wasteful, unstable, and vulnerable to emotional mass movements.

He no longer assumes instability automatically means incapacity.

# VI. Wolfgang’s assessment of Rockwell

Wolfgang recognizes much of Rockwell’s vocabulary.

Rockwell speaks of:

- organic nationhood;
- race;
- mission;
- labor and capital subordinated to national purpose;
- youth formation;
- military renewal;
- national humiliation;
- an establishment denying the people’s will.

But Rockwell is not simply an American Himmler.

Himmler is an order-builder, genealogist, colonial aristocrat, security patriarch, and mystical institutionalist.

Rockwell is a mass electoral politician shaped by:

- television;
- rallies;
- American constitutional language;
- Protestant political culture;
- racial populism;
- frontier mythology;
- the need to win millions of votes.

Wolfgang’s private formulation might be:

> Rockwell uses some of Himmler’s words, but he must make them survive an election campaign.

This makes Rockwell comprehensible to Wolfgang, not trustworthy.

Some German officials assume National Renewal will naturally become pro-German if it enters office. Wolfgang is more cautious.

An American nationalist government would still oppose:

- German submarines near American waters;
- German power in Argentina;
- German influence in Cuba;
- Icelandic restrictions on American Atlantic movement;
- German technological superiority.

Ideological resemblance does not erase strategic rivalry.

Iraq is already teaching him that lesson.

# VII. The Argentine correction

The current timeline wording that Argentina “expands licensed German arms and armored production” during 1972–75 should be superseded. The same applies to any equipment entry that assumes Germany simply transfers complete factories for current frontline German designs. fileciteturn13file9 fileciteturn13file11

The corrected model is:

> **Argentina imports the German arsenal. It does not manufacture the German arsenal.**

## What Germany directly exports

During this period Germany manufactures and delivers:

- Panzer X export vehicles;
- armored carriers;
- German-pattern rifles and machine guns;
- radar;
- air-defense systems;
- anti-ship missiles;
- aircraft;
- fire-control systems;
- sonar;
- Type XXIV-derived submarines;
- specialist communications equipment.

The weapons can receive:

- Spanish-language markings;
- Argentine service designations;
- Argentine radios or fittings;
- tropical modifications;
- local camouflage;
- local acceptance testing.

They remain German-built.

## What Argentina may build

Argentina is still permitted—and encouraged—to build the less sensitive supporting structure:

- ordinary ammunition;
- tires;
- trucks;
- uniforms;
- field equipment;
- simple radios;
- trailers;
- engineering equipment;
- naval auxiliaries;
- patrol craft;
- nonstrategic spare parts;
- repair and overhaul facilities.

It may eventually create indigenous Argentine systems using imported German guns, engines, optics, or electronics.

What Germany does not give away in the early 1970s is an entire contemporary production ecosystem for:

- Panzers;
- guided missiles;
- advanced assault rifles;
- submarine pressure hulls and propulsion systems;
- modern radar;
- sonar arrays;
- top-grade fire control.

This preserves Germany’s leverage.

Argentina may own the tank.

Germany still controls the replacement engine, sight package, gun tube, specialized ammunition, and next modernization.

# VIII. ARA *Almirante Brown*

The Argentine cruiser is not a surplus German ship sold cheaply after Germany loses interest in it.

It is designed from the beginning as a German-built Argentine flagship.

A useful working schedule is:

- **1967–68:** Argentine order and design negotiations;
- **1969:** keel laid in Germany;
- **1972:** launch;
- **1974:** commission as ARA *Almirante Brown*.

The established registry gives it approximately 12,800 tonnes full load, four 150 mm guns, a 32-round area-defense missile battery, eight heavy anti-ship missiles, and two helicopters. fileciteturn14file2

## Why Germany builds it

The ship serves several German objectives:

- anchor Argentina’s navy around German doctrine;
- establish a major South Atlantic customer;
- create demand for German missiles, radar, sonar, helicopters, and training;
- provide a prestige alternative to American or British naval patronage;
- demonstrate that Germany supports sovereign clients rather than only protectorates.

Argentina does not receive it as charity.

It pays through a combination of:

- long-term credit;
- commodity-clearing arrangements;
- naval-service contracts;
- maintenance commitments;
- favorable access for German commercial and technical missions.

## The export ceiling

The ship is formidable but deliberately below Germany’s newest standard.

It receives:

- excellent radar;
- good missile guidance;
- effective command spaces;
- credible anti-ship weapons;
- export electronic warfare.

It does not receive:

- the Reich’s best missile seekers;
- full Type XXXI submarine combat-system integration;
- the newest sonar;
- the most sensitive data processing;
- the complete VLS architecture publicly revealed on the new German cruiser generation.

This becomes particularly visible in 1974.

Argentina receives a powerful custom flagship.

Germany unveils the future.

# IX. The 1974 German missile-cruiser reveal

Germany publicly presents the first Admiral Scheer-class missile cruiser in 1974.

Foreign observers focus on the visible ship:

- vertical launch;
- integrated missile guidance;
- large command spaces;
- radar coordination;
- anti-ship and area-defense capability;
- helicopter support.

The deeper revelation is that much of the launch and guidance technology has already existed at sea in less visible form aboard German guided-missile submarines. fileciteturn10file2 fileciteturn14file0

This produces a delayed version of the Iceland shock.

Foreign navies realize that German surface demonstrations are often announcements of capabilities the submarine service has possessed for several years.

Wolfgang approves the public reveal for three reasons:

1. Germany no longer needs complete secrecy to preserve deterrence.
2. The visible system supports arms exports.
3. It reminds America and Britain that the 1968 Atlantic balance did not freeze German technology.

The simultaneous appearance of *Almirante Brown* creates a useful hierarchy:

- German allies can buy modern capability.
- They cannot buy the technological summit.

In 1974 Germany begins converting two Type XXXI guided-missile submarines into unarmed submersible transports.

The weapons and launch spaces are replaced by room for approximately 800 tonnes of high-value cargo and specialists. fileciteturn10file2 fileciteturn14file0

These are not underwater merchant ships.

Their intended cargo is:

- missile components;
- radar assemblies;
- sonar;
- engines;
- guidance equipment;
- specialized ammunition;
- medical supplies;
- technicians;
- intelligence equipment.

The conversion is partly a response to the legal world created by the Mid-Atlantic Ridge Accord.

Germany cannot openly deploy state forces into the American hemisphere.

It can still develop methods of placing decisive material at a distant partner’s disposal without sending a visible convoy or uniformed expedition.

The boats are not yet being built specifically for a Falklands war nobody has scheduled.

They are being built because Wolfgang’s Germany has learned that treaties create loopholes, and great powers build institutions to exploit them.

Iraq attacks Kuwait despite Wolfgang’s warning.

The Iraqi leadership expects a short campaign:

- seize Kuwait City;
- present annexation as an accomplished fact;
- assume Britain will negotiate;
- count upon Germany to deter a British counteroffensive;
- use German equipment to overwhelm a small protectorate force.

Instead, Operation al-ʿAwda creates the coalition Wolfgang predicted.

Britain’s Operation Covenant brings Commonwealth naval, air, marine, airborne, and ground forces into the Gulf. Saudi armed neutrality quietly works against Iraq. Iran mobilizes and shares intelligence. Jordan and the Latin bloc favor Iraqi defeat. Britain clears Kuwait, crosses into southern Iraq, takes or isolates Faw and Umm Qasr, and threatens Basra. fileciteturn13file4 fileciteturn13file12

## Germany’s conduct

Germany does not enter the war.

Wolfgang orders:

- no German combat formations;
- no serving German crews;
- no emergency weapons surge after the invasion begins;
- recall or neutralization of advisers who might become direct participants;
- diplomatic efforts toward a ceasefire;
- warnings to Britain against marching on Baghdad or destroying the Iraqi state.

Germany does not help Britain militarily.

It also does not save Iraq from a war Iraq began after an explicit warning.

## The captured weapons problem

British forces capture German equipment in substantial quantities.

British newsreels show:

- abandoned vehicles;
- missile systems without maintenance;
- damaged radios;
- ammunition depots;
- German manuals;
- sophisticated equipment used badly.

The British propaganda line is devastating:

> Germany sold Baghdad the tools of modern war. It could not sell Baghdad an army.

Publicly, Berlin answers that Iraqi failures prove nothing about German weapons.

Privately, Wolfgang agrees with the British diagnosis.

The Iraqi Army has:

- good equipment;
- poor maintenance discipline;
- a weak NCO class;
- politicized commanders;
- inadequate staff work;
- brittle communications;
- insufficient recovery and logistics;
- little capacity to coordinate armor, air defense, artillery, engineers, and supply.

Wolfgang sees this not only as an Iraqi failure but as a German one.

Germany allowed arms sales and ideological enthusiasm to create the appearance of a strategic guarantee it had never issued.

# XII. Wolfgang’s personal response to Kuwait

Wolfgang is angry, but the dominant emotion is not rage.

It is disappointment mixed with guilt.

He had warned Iraq. That protects him politically.

It does not satisfy him personally.

His questions are:

- Why did Baghdad believe Germany would intervene?
- Which German officials encouraged that belief?
- Why were German arms contracts allowed to masquerade as alliance commitments?
- Why did nobody stop the weapons flow when Iraqi operational incompetence was obvious?
- Did Berlin value a friendly slogan more than a stable client?

Rommel’s earlier lesson becomes painfully relevant:

> A force may own the correct weapons and still be incapable of the war it intends to fight.

If Rommel dies around 1972–73 as previously proposed, the Kuwait War becomes one of the first crises in which Wolfgang wishes he could consult him and cannot.

## The foreign-client reform

After the war Wolfgang creates a more unified procedure for foreign military clients.

Every major client relationship must distinguish among:

1. commercial arms sale;
2. advisory relationship;
3. political association;
4. defense consultation;
5. actual military guarantee.

No official, firm, Party organization, or SS network may imply that one automatically creates the next.

This does not eliminate competing German channels.

It makes their promises auditable.

The internal shorthand becomes:

> **No guarantee by invoice.**

---

# XIII. The Muscat Articles and Iraq’s altered relationship with Germany

The late-December 1974 Muscat Articles preserve Iraq but impose:

- recognition of the existing Kuwait boundary for twenty-five years;
- a demilitarized strip;
- naval restrictions;
- inspection;
- oil or commercial reparations;
- restoration obligations;
- continued British protection of Kuwait.

Britain withdraws from occupied Iraqi territory rather than destroying the regime. fileciteturn14file0

Iraq emerges humiliated and isolated.

It has alienated:

- Britain;
- Kuwait;
- Saudi Arabia;
- Iran;
- Jordan;
- the Latin bloc;
- much of the Arab monarchical world.

Germany is the only major power still willing to rebuild it.

## The postwar bargain

Iraq remains outside the Einheitspakt.

It nevertheless accepts a much deeper German advisory and consultation structure.

Germany provides:

- reconstruction credit;
- spare parts;
- officer education;
- logistics reform;
- NCO schools;
- maintenance systems;
- communications;
- industrial rebuilding;
- limited renewed arms deliveries.

Iraq accepts:

- German review of operational readiness;
- advance consultation before major external military action;
- tighter control over militias;
- staff reform;
- less extravagant public threats;
- economic concessions.

This is not Iraqi submission.

It is recognition of dependence.

Before Kuwait, Baghdad believes ideological kinship makes Germany dependent upon Iraq.

After Kuwait, Baghdad understands the reverse is closer to the truth.

---

# XIV. Britain’s restored credibility

Wolfgang also has to revise his view of Britain.

The Commonwealth victory is not overwhelming, effortless, or proof that Britain has restored its prewar empire.

It is nevertheless real.

Britain demonstrates that:

- the Cape and Indian Ocean logistical system works;
- the Royal Navy can support a distant campaign;
- the RAF can concentrate force;
- Commonwealth formations can deploy and sustain themselves;
- the political system can fight a limited war without collapsing.

The 1975 Kuwait Election gives Wilson 344 seats and confirms that the war has strengthened rather than destroyed his government. fileciteturn14file0

Wolfgang dislikes British imperial claims in the Gulf.

He respects the execution.

The internal German assessment after Kuwait is:

> Britain is no longer the exhausted state of 1947. It remains strategically limited, but it must be treated as a functioning great-power system.

This is a quiet but significant correction.

---

# XV. Rockwell’s assassination, 1975

The political horror film *The Last Republic* appears shortly before Rockwell’s assassination.

Its premise is deliberately extreme:

- a presidential candidate or president is murdered;
- the United States fractures;
- states and regions mobilize;
- civil war begins;
- Germany and Japan exploit the collapse;
- America is partitioned or subordinated.

The film is intended as a warning. It instead helps radicalize the accelerationist who murders Rockwell. After the assassination, the public remembers the film as though it had predicted events. fileciteturn15file5 fileciteturn15file12

## Wolfgang’s official response

Wolfgang issues condolences without endorsing National Renewal.

A suitable statement is:

> **“The murder of a political leader is an assault upon a nation’s right to determine its future without the rifle.”**

The message is sent both to the American government and to Rockwell’s family.

Germany avoids the appearance that it is encouraging National Renewal supporters to reject American authority.

## Wolfgang’s private fear

Wolfgang considers American civil war plausible enough to require planning.

Not inevitable.

Plausible.

He knows that America contains:

- divided parties;
- an angry National Renewal movement;
- racial and regional conflict;
- rival military and state institutions;
- a recent film teaching the population to imagine collapse;
- widespread belief that the presidency was stolen in 1968.

He orders a contingency study.

## What the contingency study covers

It is not a German invasion plan.

The study examines:

- evacuation and protection of German nationals;
- security of Iceland and the Mid-Atlantic line;
- American naval fragmentation;
- Greenland;
- Canadian mobilization;
- control of the Panama Canal;
- competing federal claimants;
- Caribbean and Cuban opportunities;
- Argentine security;
- Japanese action in the Pacific;
- recognition of rival American governments;
- accidental clashes with local American commanders;
- protection of spaceflight and tracking systems.

The first recommendation is restraint.

If the American command structure fragments, German submarines must avoid ambiguous movements near American bases unless directly ordered. A nervous American regional commander might interpret routine German movement as preparation for intervention.

Wolfgang wants Germany ready for American collapse.

He does not want Germany to cause it accidentally.

## Buchanan’s effect on Wolfgang

The assassination does not produce the civil war the film predicted.

Buchanan restrains National Renewal, prevents reprisals, insists upon lawful political action, and turns Rockwell’s memorial into disciplined mobilization.

Wolfgang is impressed.

He had regarded Buchanan principally as Rockwell’s Catholic-nationalist speechwriter.

He now recognizes him as a potential statesman.

Buchanan’s refusal to exploit martyrdom through immediate violence makes future German–American relations more interesting. Wolfgang may find Buchanan more personally comprehensible than Rockefeller while ultimately discovering that a competent American nationalist can be a more formidable opponent than a divided establishment president.

---

# XVI. The Orbitaler Raumhafen, 1975

The Orbitaler Raumhafen is commissioned in a circular orbit approximately 720 kilometers above Earth at five degrees inclination.

It is supplied primarily from the Kribi equatorial launch complex and consists of:

- a nonrotating central docking hub;
- crew and cargo ports;
- fuel storage and transfer systems;
- external assembly trusses;
- workshops;
- manipulators and cranes;
- command and tracking facilities;
- a separated reactor-power installation;
- radiation shelters;
- rotating partial-gravity habitation.

A normal initial population of roughly twenty-four, expandable toward thirty-six during construction or major assembly operations, fits the established physical concept. fileciteturn15file4 fileciteturn15file6

It is not a floating city.

It is a working harbor.

The interior contains:

- noise;
- pumps;
- cables;
- exposed maintenance panels;
- crowded storage;
- narrow passageways;
- machinery smell;
- carefully labeled emergency equipment;
- areas still being fitted while other areas operate.

Its magnificence comes from function rather than luxury.

## Why intelligence underestimated it

American and British tracking systems saw the launches.

They knew Germany was assembling something large.

What they did not fully understand was how integrated it would be when publicly opened.

They expected:

- several linked station modules;
- research laboratories;
- perhaps a symbolic rotating section.

Germany reveals:

- a fuel depot;
- a construction yard;
- a habitation system;
- a docking nexus;
- a lunar-ferry base;
- a reactor-powered permanent facility.

The Moon flag showed that Germany could reach another world.

The Raumhafen shows that Germany intends to operate between worlds.

---

# XVII. Wolfgang’s visit

Wolfgang insists upon attending the commissioning in person.

Heydrich’s security establishment strongly dislikes the idea. The Führer will be:

- beyond immediate Earth rescue;
- dependent upon a launch vehicle;
- dependent upon station life support;
- visible to foreign tracking systems;
- aboard a facility whose systems are still relatively new.

Wolfgang has trained for the flight, understands the emergency procedures, and refuses to open his defining project from a studio in Berlin.

He spends perhaps two or three days aboard.

## *Der Hafen im Himmel*

The live broadcast and subsequent documentary are titled:

> **Der Hafen im Himmel**  
> *The Harbor in Heaven*

The signature sequence follows Wolfgang from the nonrotating hub into the spinning habitation section.

At first he moves in weightlessness.

He passes through the transition.

His feet settle onto the floor as apparent gravity slowly returns.

This image matters more internationally than another rocket launch.

It tells audiences that Germany has built architecture in space rather than merely sent a capsule through it. fileciteturn15file2

## Wolfgang’s address

His defining line should be:

> **“A flag proves that men can arrive. A harbor proves that they intend to return.”**

He then explicitly refers to the rival space architecture:

> Germany first demonstrated that men could stand upon the Moon. America demonstrated that the road from Earth could be traveled again. Here Germany begins building the place from which those roads will continue.

This is not an admission of American superiority.

It is a mature statement of the race as Wolfgang understands it.

Different states are solving different pieces of the same future.

Germany intends to assemble those pieces around a permanent German center.

---

# XVIII. What the Raumhafen means to Wolfgang

The Raumhafen is more personally Wolfgang’s achievement than the 1970 Moon landing.

He inherited the satellite programme.

He inherited von Braun.

He inherited the heavy-rocket establishment.

He did not inherit the completed station.

He protected:

- the station-first architecture;
- the heavy-launch budget;
- the reactor programme;
- docking and fuel-transfer work;
- the Kribi infrastructure;
- the project after Iceland;
- the project after America’s reusable-spaceplane success;
- the project through Iraq and budget pressure.

The public therefore begins associating the station with Wolfgang’s personal style:

- patient;
- infrastructural;
- systems-oriented;
- less theatrical than Hitler;
- less exuberant than Göring;
- more willing to credit a rival’s achievement;
- determined to make Germany’s successes permanent.

It gives the young dynasty a future-oriented mythology no longer dependent entirely upon the Second World War.

Hitler conquered the continent.

Wolfgang builds beyond it.

---

# XIX. The concealed cost beneath the harbor

The authorial contrast should remain visible.

The station is supplied from Kribi in German Mittelafrika. Its equatorial launch advantage rests upon a German-controlled corridor cleared and secured across an African colonial system. The same years see the War of the Chiefs spreading from labor and registration disputes toward broader conflict, while German counterinsurgency grows increasingly severe. fileciteturn15file7 fileciteturn15file12

The station’s components are real.

The engineering achievement is real.

The people whose land, labor, and political subordination support part of the launch system are also real.

Wolfgang does not consider the station fraudulent because of this connection. He thinks the correct answer is to make Mittelafrika governable and productive, not to abandon the programme.

That is precisely the setting’s tension.

He can be sincere in his congratulations to American astronauts, sincere in his concern for Iraq’s unnecessary dead, sincere in his love of engineering, and still preside over an imperial order whose costs are pushed out of the Altreich’s view.

The 1975 reveal is therefore simultaneously:

- Germany’s greatest positive technical image since the Moon;
- the culmination of Wolfgang’s childhood interest;
- a triumph of long-range planning;
- a product of imperial geography and coercive power.

---

# XX. The changing German leadership, 1970–1975

The period also completes much of the generational transition discussed previously.

| Year | Working transition |
|---|---|
| **1971** | Goebbels dies after helping shape the Moon-era narrative; Werner Naumann takes over the propaganda machinery |
| **1972–73** | Rommel dies or withdraws finally; Ferdinand von Senger und Etterlin becomes the principal mobile-war doctrinal heir, while Manfred Rommel preserves the civic and family legacy |
| **1973–74** | Bormann dies or permanently retires; his concentrated machinery is divided among Party legal administration, personnel management, the Reich Chancellery, and Wolfgang’s personal staff |
| **1972–75** | Dönitz remains an elder grand admiral while Erich Topp increasingly controls daily naval professionalism |
| **By 1975** | Himmler, Heydrich, Speer, von Braun, and Eva remain major elder figures, but their deputies and institutional heirs are now visible |

This matters during Kuwait and Rockwell’s assassination.

Wolfgang is no longer merely listening while the founder generation decides.

More and more often, he is the oldest authority in the room that actually possesses final responsibility.

---

# XXI. Year by year

## 1970 — First on the Moon

- Germany lands two men on the Moon on 20 December.
- The enlarged direct-ascent booster is redirected toward station cargo.
- Wolfgang’s marriage and household stabilize his private life if the prior Katharina settlement remains.
- Iraq’s National Socialist revolution approaches victory.
- Germany’s Moon triumph gives Wolfgang enormous political capital.

## 1971 — The honorable rival

- America lands on the Moon on 20 July.
- Wolfgang delivers sincere congratulations.
- Germany studies America’s reusable architecture rather than dismissing it.
- The Thorium Programme begins as a strategic fuel-cycle review.
- National Socialist Iraq consolidates and begins claiming wider Arab leadership.
- Goebbels dies later in the year under the working generational sequence.
- Station construction accelerates.

## 1972 — Systems under strain

- Democrats and Republicans fuse into the Democratic-Republican Party.
- Rockefeller defeats Rockwell narrowly.
- Wolfgang sees American democracy as chaotic but unexpectedly durable.
- Germany begins experimental thorium-fuel work.
- Iraq escalates threats against Kuwait and the monarchies.
- Argentina continues receiving complete German-built systems rather than licensed factories.
- Rommel’s final decline or death removes an important restraining mentor.

## 1973 — The warning year

- Wolfgang explicitly warns Iraq that Germany will not enter a war Baghdad begins.
- Iraqi leaders formally acknowledge the warning and privately discount it.
- German agencies continue sending mixed signals.
- Thorium test loops and fuel-cycle experiments expand.
- Work on the Raumhafen’s habitation, fuel, and assembly sections intensifies.
- Bormann’s departure or decline accelerates the division of his old office.
- *The Last Republic* enters production or early exhibition planning amid worsening American rhetoric.

## 1974 — The client’s war

- Germany unveils the Admiral Scheer missile-cruiser generation.
- ARA *Almirante Brown* commissions as a purpose-built German export flagship.
- Type XXXI/T submersible-transport conversions begin.
- Iraq invades Kuwait under Operation al-ʿAwda.
- Britain defeats Iraq under Operation Covenant.
- Wolfgang refuses direct intervention.
- The Muscat Articles preserve Iraq but impose a major humiliation.
- America conducts a fully automated orbital-spaceplane mission.
- Germany supports limited space-law rules without accepting general orbital demilitarization.

## 1975 — The harbor and the assassination

- Iraq becomes more dependent upon German reconstruction, training, and consultation.
- Wilson wins Britain’s Kuwait Election.
- *The Last Republic* becomes the American cultural image of impending civil war.
- Rockwell is assassinated.
- Wolfgang issues restrained condolences and orders American-disintegration contingency planning.
- Buchanan prevents mass retaliation.
- Germany commissions the Orbitaler Raumhafen.
- Wolfgang visits the station and delivers the “flag and harbor” address.
- German counterinsurgency in Africa becomes increasingly difficult to conceal.

---

# XXII. Wolfgang at twenty-eight

By the end of 1975, Wolfgang is no longer the boy placed into office by Göring.

He has developed a recognizable foreign and strategic philosophy.

## Rivals

A rival’s genuine achievement should be acknowledged.

Respect improves judgment.

## Clients

A client is not an extension of Germany.

Ideological similarity does not create obedience.

## Arms

Weapons create capability.

They do not create maintenance, discipline, command judgment, or political restraint.

## Democracy

Parliamentary systems appear chaotic and frequently dishonest to Wolfgang.

They are not necessarily fragile.

## Treaties

Legal distinctions matter because they determine what Germany can sell, move, deny, or conceal.

## Technology

Prestige events matter.

Infrastructure matters more.

## Responsibility

A ruler cannot absolve himself merely because he gave good advice that a client ignored.

Wolfgang did not order Iraq to invade Kuwait.

He still asks what Germany did to make Baghdad believe it would be rescued.

That is an important difference between him and the more self-exculpatory parts of the old generation.

---

# XXIII. Public history and authorial truth

| Public account | Authorial truth |
|---|---|
| Germany graciously welcomed America to the Moon | Wolfgang sincerely respected the American achievement and recognized the danger of its reusable architecture |
| Thorium promised unlimited German energy | It was a difficult, long-term secondary fuel cycle requiring fissile startup, breeding, chemistry, and expensive development |
| Iraq betrayed Germany’s wise counsel | Baghdad ignored explicit warnings, but contradictory German agencies had encouraged its confidence |
| German weapons failed in Kuwait because Iraqis were inferior | The weapons often worked; Iraqi institutions could not sustain or integrate them |
| Germany abandoned Iraq | Germany refused to fight an unapproved aggressive war and then preserved Iraq through postwar support |
| Argentina became a German arsenal state | It became a heavily dependent customer receiving German-built systems, not a sovereign manufacturer of current German designs |
| ARA *Almirante Brown* proved German generosity | It was a carefully tiered export that bound Argentina to German maintenance and ammunition |
| Rockwell’s murder proved democracy was collapsing | The assassination produced panic, but Buchanan’s response demonstrated considerable American political discipline |
| The Raumhafen was the inevitable continuation of the Moon landing | It survived repeated budget, technical, military, and political competition because Wolfgang personally protected the architecture |
| The harbor represented peaceful human progress | It was a real civilizational achievement supported partly by a coercive African imperial system |

The defining image of 1970–75 is Wolfgang aboard the rotating section of the Orbitaler Raumhafen.

Below him are Germany, America, Britain, Iraq, Argentina, and Africa: rivals, clients, former enemies, and subject territories bound into systems that none of them fully controls.

He places his feet on the artificial floor and says that a harbor proves men intend to return.

The line applies as much to his own government as to space.

By 1975, Wolfgang is no longer merely visiting the Reich his father built.

He intends to remain and govern it.

# Computing Race V: 1965–1970  
## Networks, software engineering, embedded computers, and the first functional-language rivalry

The Japanese presentation rule should now be treated as fixed:

> **Native Japanese source begins at the upper-right, proceeds downward within each statement column, and advances toward the left.**

Horizontal left-to-right panels remain available for graphs, matrices, Latin-script data, and foreign compatibility, but Japanese programming education and native terminals are vertically oriented. By the later 1960s, portrait CRTs show several descending columns simultaneously, with katakana sequences rendered as compact kanji tokens on better terminals.

The resulting Japanese screen genuinely has the visual character of falling columns of code rather than Western horizontal lines.

---

# I. What changes historically between 1965 and 1970?

This is the period when the computer industry discovers that **software, communications, and data organization are at least as important as arithmetic speed**.

## The major transitions

| Development | Significance |
|---|---|
| Compatible computer families | Programs become long-term institutional investments rather than disposable accessories to one machine |
| Integrated-circuit minicomputers | Computers begin moving into laboratories, factories, vehicles, radar sites, and instruments |
| Time-sharing | Programmers interact directly through terminals instead of waiting for card batches |
| Operating-system growth | Scheduling, storage, access control, files, devices, and communications become permanent system services |
| New language paradigms | Simulation, systems programming, symbolic work, structured programming, and applicative programming diverge |
| Online databases | Records are queried and updated during business operations rather than only processed in periodic batches |
| Packet networking | Computers at different institutions begin exchanging information over shared communications links |
| Software engineering | Large programs become difficult enough that design, testing, configuration, documentation, and management form a distinct discipline |
| Computer graphics | Displays become working interfaces for design, command, scientific visualization, and interactive editing |

IBM’s System/360 established the strategic value of a software-compatible family, while Control Data’s CDC 6600 and 7600 gave America a temporary and highly visible lead in peak scientific performance. Smaller computers proliferated around instruments and control systems rather than merely serving as cheap mainframes. citeturn193772search0turn193772search2turn767091search1

Programming-language research also broadened considerably. Simula 67 formalized its general-purpose simulation language around processes and classes; Peter Landin’s 1966 work proposed an applicative language framework closely related to lambda calculus; and the growing scale of software led to the 1968 conference that popularized the idea of treating program construction as an engineering discipline. citeturn820144search2turn427412search0turn427412search20

The first RFCs appeared in 1969 as working notes for the emerging American research network. At the other end of the period, Codd’s 1970 relational model proposed separating the logical structure of data from its physical machine representation. citeturn820144search3turn820144search27turn427412search2

The period’s governing transformation is:

> **In 1965, a programmer normally writes for a machine. By 1970, a programmer increasingly writes for a language, operating system, database, or network that happens to be implemented on a machine.**

---

# II. What the established timeline requires

Several canonical events place hard requirements upon the five computing systems.

| Canonical event | Computing requirement |
|---|---|
| British Prospero I, 1965 | Tracking, telemetry reduction, guidance testing, orbital determination, and reliable communications between Britain and Woomera |
| Maracaibo Shock, 1966 | German radar prediction and fire-control integration; American electronic-warfare analysis and rapid threat-model revision |
| X-20 trials, 1966 | Compact guidance, reentry calculation, simulation, telemetry, and pilot displays |
| German emergency lunar program authorized, 1967 | Configuration-managed flight software, onboard digital guidance, extensive simulation, mission-control computing, and a larger tracking network |
| German Type XXXI missile submarine, 1967 | Compact navigation, fire-control, missile alignment, and shore-based target planning |
| Iceland crisis, 1967–68 | Submarine-track correlation, signals analysis, naval communications, weather and route calculation |
| Atlantic Accord, 1968 | Secure diplomatic communications, deployment registries, intelligence assessment, and independent British–Canadian planning |
| Japanese unified air procurement, 1968 | Standard avionics interfaces, common telemetry, digital fire control, and software reuse across manufacturers |
| American constitutional crisis, 1968–69 | Rapid election tabulation, communications resilience, and later political concern about central information systems |
| American orbital spaceplane, 1969 | Integrated-circuit flight computers, reentry guidance, navigation, digital displays, mission simulation, and global tracking |
| MOSAIK linked system by the late 1960s | Regional machine centers, stable identifiers, telecommunications, file reconciliation, audit procedures, and controlled remote inquiry |
| War of the Chiefs begins, 1969 | Administrative dependence on MOSAIK becomes both a German advantage and a target for refusal, falsification, and sabotage |
| Orbital collision-cascade studies, 1968–70 | Persistent object catalogs, numerical propagation, conjunction calculation, and statistical debris modeling |
| German lunar landing, December 1970 | A mature aerospace-software establishment, though not a futuristic onboard supercomputer |

These events are fixed in the current chronology. fileciteturn11file0 The space and aerospace references further establish the direct-ascent German mission, the American X-20 and Pathfinder lineage, and Maracaibo’s influence on American doctrine. fileciteturn11file1 fileciteturn10file2
