# III. Computing becomes an international profession

## The International Federation

I would preserve an organization recognizably equivalent to the **International Federation for Information Processing**, but make it considerably more central to world computing culture.

It develops from the Zürich and Rome software meetings of 1968–69 and becomes the principal neutral forum in which the five systems can speak without implying strategic alignment.

Its world congress sequence should be:

| Year | Host | Character |
|---:|---|---|
| 1971 | Zürich | First genuinely five-system congress; languages, software engineering, and architecture |
| 1974 | Stockholm | Large congress emphasizing networks, social effects, databases, and orbital registration |
| 1977 | Toronto | Personal computing, microprocessors, programming education, and software markets |
| 1980 | Tokyo and Melbourne | Joint Japanese–Commonwealth congress; multilingual computing, robotics, home systems, and universal character standards |

Stockholm, Toronto, and the planned Tokyo–Melbourne congresses parallel real IFIP activity, including the roughly four thousand participants at Stockholm. citeturn952896search1turn952896search16

## The specialist conference circuit

By the late 1970s there are regular international meetings on:

- programming-language principles;
- compiler construction;
- formal verification;
- industrial control;
- databases;
- networking;
- computer education;
- character encoding;
- computer graphics;
- artificial intelligence;
- software history and preservation;
- human consequences of automation.

The first History of Programming Languages conference in 1978 has an especially important alternate-world character. It is not merely Americans documenting American languages. It includes:

- Rechenplan and Planform representatives;
- British Autocode, CPL, BCPL, and ML researchers;
- American FORTRAN, COBOL, C, LISP, Lambda, BASIC, and Smalltalk representatives;
- Japanese `計算` and `手順` teams;
- Latin ALGOL, LIA, Pascal, and Prolog researchers.

Historically, ACM’s first HOPL conference was held in Los Angeles in 1978. citeturn952896search5turn952896search23

## Cooperation without naïveté

This is not an apolitical utopia.

The professional culture is affected by:

- the Kuwait War;
- German support for Iraq and Argentina;
- American pressure in the hemisphere;
- Japanese imperial labor practices;
- British and Latin colonial systems;
- German African atrocities;
- the 1978–79 demographic scandal.

Delegations walk out. Visas are denied. Papers are withdrawn. Protesters appear outside congress halls. German researchers complain that they are being blamed for policies they do not control; foreign programmers reply that German administrative computing helps implement those policies.

But the culture survives.

A programmer in Munich may not know a programmer in Kyoto personally, but he recognizes:

- Japanese `手順` process concepts;
- American C and BASIC;
- British ML and packet systems;
- Occitan Prolog;
- Italian desktop machines.

By 1980, ignorance of all foreign programming traditions is a professional embarrassment.

The conference culture becomes more peaceable than the space race because programs, papers, compilers, and standards are easier to exchange than launch systems. Space engineers may admire a rival’s achievement from a distance. Programmers often sit at the same table arguing over syntax.

---

# IV. The universal character project

## Why Japan begins it but cannot own it

Japan brings the most developed proposal because it already possesses:

- abstract character identities;
- mappings from several vendor codes;
- vertical and horizontal forms;
- kana and kanji;
- Latin and Filipino supplements;
- Hangul, Chinese, and Southeast Asian extensions;
- font memories and glyph generators.

But Japan cannot insist that the international code begin with katakana.

The numerical and political weight of:

- the United States;
- Britain and the Commonwealth;
- Germany and its clients;
- Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Occitania;
- Latin America;
- international teleprinter and scientific systems

makes a Latin-compatible low range unavoidable.

Japan concedes that point in exchange for something much more important:

> Japanese, Chinese, Korean, vertical-text, and combining-character support must be foundational, not optional national extensions added years later.

## Development sequence

### 1975–76: Character Interchange Group

A permanent international working group forms after disputes involving Japanese, Filipino, British, Latin, and American records.

It separates five concepts:

1. abstract character identity;
2. numeric character number;
3. storage encoding;
4. visible glyph;
5. writing direction and presentation.

This distinction comes heavily from Japanese experience.

### 1977: Kyoto draft

The Kyoto draft proposes a universal registry with:

- common controls;
- Latin letters;
- digits and punctuation;
- Greek and Cyrillic;
- Japanese kana;
- a large ideograph area;
- Hangul;
- Arabic and Hebrew;
- major South and Southeast Asian scripts;
- mathematical and technical symbols;
- vertical and horizontal presentation properties.

### 1978–79: Geneva compromise

The standard receives a provisional English name:

> **Universal Character Code**, normally shortened to **UNICODE**.

The name is deliberately international and not attached to one national language.

### 1980: UNICODE 80

The Tokyo–Melbourne congress approves the first edition.

## Technical form

UNICODE 80 is **not** modern Unicode running everywhere.

Its architecture is:

- a sixteen-bit abstract character number;
- local seven- and eight-bit encodings for ordinary machines;
- shift and escape forms for transmission;
- sixteen-bit internal text on expensive Japanese, British, and American workstations;
- mapping tables for German twelve-bit and Japanese multibyte systems.

A sixteen-bit space provides 65,536 primary positions. That is sufficient for an ambitious first standard but leaves less room than its designers expect.

## The low range

The first block contains:

- control functions;
- common punctuation;
- Arabic digits;
- Latin capitals and lowercase;
- mathematical and programming symbols.

This reflects existing international communications rather than a declaration that Latin is the world’s superior script.

Japanese positional digits `〇一二三四五六七八九` receive their own proper identities rather than being treated as fonts for Arabic digits.

## Ideographs

The most difficult compromise concerns Chinese characters.

The first edition uses:

- a shared core identity for ideographs judged semantically equivalent;
- national glyph-form properties;
- separate compatibility characters where governments or publishers refuse unification;
- distinct simplified and traditional forms where equivalence is disputed.

The result works but creates decades of technical debt.

## Writing direction

UNICODE 80 includes from its first edition:

- left-to-right horizontal writing;
- right-to-left horizontal writing;
- top-to-bottom vertical writing;
- right-to-left progression of Japanese vertical columns;
- alternate vertical punctuation;
- combining marks;
- national presentation preferences.

This is where Japanese leadership permanently changes the international standard.

Real-world computing treated many of these issues as later complications. In this setting, they are first-edition requirements.

---

# V. United States  
## The uncontrolled language garden

America’s greatest advantage is not merely its microprocessors. It is that **nobody successfully creates an American software aviation authority**.

There are restrictions concerning:

- cryptography;
- military software;
- strategic exports;
- fraud;
- government contracts;
- communications licenses.

There is no general rule requiring a programmer to obtain government approval before publishing:

- a language;
- a compiler;
- a game;
- an operating system;
- an accounting program;
- a hobbyist magazine;
- a disk utility.

National Renewal sponsors hardware, schools, and productive industry, but the software world grows largely beyond the program’s administrative reach.

That freedom produces duplication, scams, incompatibility, piracy, unfinished products, and remarkable invention.

## 1. The personal-computer sequence

### 1975–76: kits and clubs

Early machines are sold as:

- circuit boards;
- chassis;
- front panels;
- memory cards;
- expansion buses;
- terminal interfaces.

The buyer may need to:

- solder components;
- toggle in a boot loader;
- attach a teletype;
- write or acquire an interpreter;
- repair the machine personally.

User clubs circulate:

- paper tapes;
- newsletters;
- schematics;
- BASIC interpreters;
- Tiny BASIC variants;
- games;
- device drivers.

### 1976–77: the complete computer

The decisive transition is from a computer **kit** to a computer **product**.

Several fictional American firms—founded by people born after the divergence—introduce machines containing:

- keyboard;
- case;
- power supply;
- television or monitor output;
- cassette interface;
- built-in beginner’s language;
- expansion connectors;
- optional floppy disk.

This corresponds broadly to the historical 1977 personal-computer breakthrough, but the dominant companies and founders should be original.

### 1978: the retail ecosystem

Computer stores sell:

- machines;
- memory;
- disk drives;
- printers;
- modems;
- joysticks;
- books;
- magazines;
- commercial software.

A purchaser no longer needs to know an electrical engineer personally.

### 1979: the business breakthrough

A fictional programmer and business-school student develop an **electronic worksheet** organized into rows and columns.

The user can:

- enter numbers and formulas;
- change one assumption;
- watch dependent values recalculate;
- save several models;
- ask financial “what happens if” questions.

Historically, VisiCalc demonstrated that a spreadsheet could make customers purchase the computer required to run it. citeturn191059search5turn210235search18

In this timeline, the product’s exact title and creators should be fictional, but the effect remains:

> The personal computer stops being a hobbyist’s machine and becomes a small-business instrument.

### 1980: visible minority adoption

Personal computers remain far from universal.

They are common enough to be visible in:

- schools;
- engineering households;
- small businesses;
- parish and civic offices;
- mail-order firms;
- farms with substantial accounts;
- home publishing;
- insurance and bookkeeping;
- university dormitories.

## 2. The language explosion

America’s late-1970s home-computing environment contains an extraordinary number of languages.

### BASIC

BASIC becomes the normal beginner’s language because it can be:

- interpreted;
- stored in ROM;
- used interactively;
- taught quickly;
- printed in magazines;
- modified by ordinary users.

There is no single BASIC.

Every manufacturer adds:

- graphics;
- sound;
- disk commands;
- game-controller support;
- machine-specific memory access;
- different string handling.

A program printed for one machine may require substantial alteration on another.

### Tiny BASIC

Tiny BASIC dialects are circulated through clubs and magazines for machines with very little memory.

This reinforces the idea that a language can be:

- shared;
- modified;
- reimplemented;
- given away rather than sold.

### C

C spreads on:

- minicomputers;
- UNIX systems;
- sixteen-bit micros;
- professional development systems.

It is too demanding for many early home machines but becomes increasingly important as memory expands.

### Pascal

Pascal is used in:

- colleges;
- schools;
- structured-programming courses;
- professional microcomputer systems.

### Forth

Forth becomes popular in:

- instrumentation;
- telescopes;
- embedded control;
- hobby robotics;
- small systems whose memory is extremely limited.

### LISP, Scheme, and Lambda

Symbolic and functional programming remains primarily academic.

**Lambda** continues as America’s compiled functional language.

A small LISP-derived academic language analogous to Scheme appears as a deliberately minimal experiment in:

- lexical scope;
- functions;
- recursion;
- interpreters;
- teaching language semantics.

### Smalltalk

Smalltalk remains expensive and workstation-centered but influences how the younger generation imagines:

- objects;
- windows;
- graphics;
- direct manipulation;
- children programming computers.

### SQL and data languages

Relational database work begins producing commercial and institutional query systems.

These do not normally run on home machines yet.

## 3. The fictional founder generation

Two major American firms should emerge during 1976–80:

### The language company

Founded by young fictional programmers, it:

- writes BASIC interpreters for several machines;
- licenses rather than exclusively bundles them;
- ports tools across processors;
- later sells assemblers, operating systems, and business languages.

This is the setting’s Microsoft-like role, but its founders should not simply be Gates and Allen under changed names.

### The integrated-computer company

Founded by a hardware engineer and a charismatic commercial organizer, it:

- turns a board into a finished household product;
- emphasizes appearance and ease of use;
- establishes a retail and developer network;
- markets computing as personal expression.

This is the Apple-like role, again with original people formed by the Rocket Awakening, the Philippine memory, National Renewal politics, and the American spaceplane culture.

The historical archetypes survive. The biographies do not.

## 4. Buchanan and the free software market

The 1977 act supports the field indirectly through:

- semiconductor investment;
- school purchases;
- accelerated depreciation;
- small-business deductions;
- National Production Institutes;
- technical education;
- federal procurement;
- postal and telecommunications infrastructure.

It does **not** establish one National Renewal computer.

Some party technocrats want:

- a common patriotic operating system;
- national software certification;
- controlled educational content;
- standardized data services.

Congress, manufacturers, universities, and hobbyists prevent this.

The result is an important irony:

> Buchanan’s industrial policy finances the hardware base of a software culture that the government cannot centrally direct.

## 5. Games and consoles

America develops three overlapping game cultures.

### Arcade games

Commercial arcades feature:

- space combat;
- driving;
- sports;
- shooting;
- maze games;
- abstract puzzles.

### Home consoles

Cartridge-based consoles appear around 1976–77.

They connect to the television and provide a simpler experience than a personal computer.

### Computer games

Home-computer users type or load:

- text adventures;
- space-trading games;
- war games;
- simulations;
- educational programs;
- role-playing systems;
- graphical arcade imitations.

Games teach children programming because they want to change:

- scores;
- maps;
- enemies;
- speed;
- rules;
- graphics.

## 6. The beginning of dial-up culture

By 1979–80, a small number of users operate dial-up boards.

They exchange:

- messages;
- programs;
- game scores;
- club notices;
- political arguments;
- software reviews.

This is not yet the American Data Network of the early 1980s. Most home computers remain offline.

But the cultural principle has appeared:

> A private citizen can publish electronically without owning a newspaper or broadcasting station.

That will become politically important later.

## America in 1980

America leads in:

- personal-computer ownership;
- independent software;
- language variety;
- hobbyist culture;
- small-business applications;
- graphical experimentation;
- open expansion hardware;
- home-computer magazines and clubs.

Its weakness is fragmentation. Almost nothing is reliably compatible.

---

# VI. Japan  
## The equally large but differently organized consumer revolution

Japan reaches consumer computing at approximately the same time as America.

The two are peers by 1980, but they are not doing the same thing.

America’s market asks:

> What can an individual build with this machine?

Japan’s market asks:

> How complete, useful, reliable, and enjoyable can this electronic system become?

## 1. Japanese consumer chronology

### 1975–76: training machines

Japanese electronics firms sell microprocessor trainers to:

- technical schools;
- company apprentices;
- radio clubs;
- industrial engineers;
- universities.

They normally include:

- keypad;
- lamps or small display;
- processor;
- memory;
- expansion connector;
- Japanese manual;
- simple machine monitor.

### 1976–77: television game machines

Japanese firms enter the home-game market through self-contained television systems.

Historically, Nintendo introduced its first home television-game machines in 1977. citeturn191059search2

In this setting, several large electronics houses and smaller entertainment firms compete.

### 1977–78: integrated home computers

The Japanese home computer contains:

- keyboard;
- television output;
- katakana glyph ROM;
- `〇一二三四五六七八九`;
- vertical source mode;
- cassette storage;
- cartridge or expansion slot;
- built-in educational language;
- game and sound support.

Unlike American machines, it usually arrives as a polished product with fewer exposed internal components.

### 1978–79: arcade and home software boom

Japan becomes particularly strong in:

- shooting games;
- fleet and space games;
- construction puzzles;
- sports;
- railway and logistics games;
- rhythm and timing games;
- educational systems.

### 1979–80: sixteen-bit and business-oriented systems

High-end Japanese personal systems begin moving toward:

- larger memory;
- disk drives;
- improved kanji display;
- business forms;
- networking with corporate systems;
- sixteen-bit processors.

## 2. `計算三六`

Introduced in 1976, **`計算三六`** is the mature professional scientific language.

It adds:

- improved modules;
- instrument control;
- numerical libraries;
- cross-compilation to small processors;
- mixed vertical and horizontal page areas;
- stronger graphics and plotting;
- standard universal-character mappings.

It remains too elaborate for the ordinary household learner.

## 3. `手順三七`

Introduced in 1977, **`手順三七`** strengthens:

- distributed transactions;
- factory-network messaging;
- safe process restart;
- local and remote authorization;
- maintenance-state tracking;
- terminal forms;
- corporate file exchange.

It is Japan’s normal professional language for industrial and transaction systems.

## 4. `学習三八`

The consumer revolution requires a simpler language.

**`学習三八`**, introduced in 1978, is Japan’s analogue to BASIC.

Its source is:

- vertical;
- top to bottom;
- column progression right to left;
- katakana-heavy;
- displayed with kanji keyword tokens on better machines;
- written with Japanese positional numerals;
- free of required Latin characters.

It supports:

- immediate commands;
- numbered or named program columns;
- integer and decimal arithmetic;
- conditions;
- loops;
- simple arrays;
- text;
- graphics;
- sound;
- controllers;
- cassette and cartridge access.

The major firms produce dialects but agree on a national educational core.

A simple home program begins at the upper-right corner and descends like a set of narrow falling columns.

## 5. Programming and games reinforce each other

Japanese children encounter programming through:

- school clubs;
- home-computer magazines;
- game modification;
- programming contests;
- electronics stores;
- company-sponsored technical clubs;
- television instruction.

A game cartridge remains closed and finished. A cassette or magazine program is alterable.

Japan therefore develops both:

- a polished console culture;
- a participatory home-computer culture.

## 6. Vertical television display

A normal landscape television can still display vertical Japanese source.

The screen contains several narrow columns:

- the rightmost column is earliest;
- characters descend;
- later statements appear to the left;
- a horizontal strip at the bottom may show status or numeric data.

This is visually distinct from American rows of green text.

More expensive portrait terminals remain common in professional programming offices, but the home market uses ordinary televisions.

## 7. Filipino and imperial variants

Machines sold in the Philippines include:

- horizontal Latin mode;
- Latin keyboard overlays;
- Filipino and English strings;
- optional Latin identifiers;
- Japanese control keywords;
- imperial character support.

Filipino programmers increasingly write mixed-source programs:

- Japanese grammar;
- Latin names;
- local-language comments;
- Japanese or Arabic digits depending on customer requirements.

This produces a large localization industry centered in Manila and Singapore.

## 8. The Japanese software market

Japan does have independent developers, but the market is more structured than America’s.

Software reaches users through:

- hardware manufacturers;
- trading companies;
- licensed publishers;
- magazines;
- school systems;
- corporate dealerships;
- arcade distributors.

A small programmer has more difficulty reaching national distribution without a corporate partner.

The advantage is:

- better testing;
- documentation;
- customer support;
- hardware integration.

The disadvantage is less radical experimentation.

## 9. Factory and consumer feedback

Japan’s consumer market improves its industrial systems.

Cheap graphics chips, sound controllers, memory, and processors flow back into:

- training simulators;
- operator consoles;
- machine tools;
- vehicle displays;
- portable test systems;
- communications equipment.

Industrial investment, in turn, makes consumer products cheaper.

## Japan in 1980

Japan leads or shares leadership in:

- polished home-computer hardware;
- consoles and arcade systems;
- embedded microprocessors;
- memory and display manufacturing;
- home-computer character systems;
- consumer graphics and sound;
- industrial–consumer component integration.

America leads software openness and Japan leads product integration. They are the two principal computing rivals.

---

# VII. Germany  
## Wolfgang’s controlled consumer opening

Wolfgang Friedrich Hitler’s modernization program gives Germany the political permission required for a home-computer market.

His argument is not liberal.

It is strategic:

- Germany cannot allow America and Japan to define electronic childhood.
- German industry needs citizens comfortable with computation.
- The Reich needs programmers, engineers, technicians, and numerical workers.
- Imported consoles and software create cultural and commercial dependency.
- A prosperous great power should offer modern consumer electronics to favored citizens.

The slogan is effectively:

> **The computer must enter the German home before the foreign computer does.**

## 1. The political compromise

The security establishment fears that home computers might support:

- unauthorized encryption;
- copied foreign media;
- anonymous publication;
- political games;
- underground records;
- unlicensed telecommunications.

Wolfgang and the modernizers answer that early home computers are mostly offline.

Programs move through:

- cassettes;
- cartridges;
- disks;
- magazines;
- user clubs.

The state can tolerate uncontrolled calculation more easily than uncontrolled communication.

The compromise is:

- home computers are legal;
- programming is encouraged;
- modems and public network adapters are regulated;
- cryptographic products require approval;
- foreign software is licensed and censored;
- political publishing remains controlled;
- ordinary games, educational programs, and household software are widely available.

## 2. The German home-computer program

A **Heimrechnerprogramm** begins around 1976–77.

It does not produce one government machine. It gives:

- semiconductor credit;
- school contracts;
- common television and cassette standards;
- German-language documentation requirements;
- domestic-content preferences;
- tax treatment for educational purchases;
- youth-club and technical-school programs.

Siemens, Telefunken, Zuse-associated firms, Grundig, Braun, and smaller electronics companies produce competing machines.

## 3. Hardware

German home computers generally use:

- domestic eight-bit processors for entry models;
- sixteen-bit systems for professional and engineering models;
- television output;
- cassette and later disk storage;
- high-quality keyboards;
- German character support;
- expansion connectors;
- carefully documented power and interface standards.

They are typically more expensive and better built than American hobby machines, but less inexpensive and less playful than Japanese mass-market systems.

## 4. Rechenplan is too large for the home

The state’s first instinct is to place Rechenplan on every machine.

That fails.

Full Rechenplan requires:

- too much memory;
- compiler storage;
- formal declarations;
- libraries;
- slow compilation;
- training beyond the ordinary beginner.

Germany therefore creates a new interpreted civilian language.

## 5. Kurzplan 77

**Kurzplan 77** becomes the German home and school language.

It retains German vocabulary and a recognizable relationship with Rechenplan but simplifies radically.

It supports:

- immediate commands;
- numbers and strings;
- arrays;
- procedures;
- loops;
- conditions;
- graphics;
- sound;
- cassette and disk operations;
- game controllers.

Representative keywords include:

- `WENN`;
- `SONST`;
- `FÜR`;
- `WIEDERHOLE`;
- `EINGABE`;
- `AUSGABE`;
- `ZEICHNE`;
- `TON`;
- `ENDE`.

Kurzplan is not formally a Rechenplan profile. It is a new civilian language designed to feel familiar to the German educational system.

## 6. Germany’s language monopoly softens

International conferences and the home market make it impossible to pretend that one language family is enough.

By 1980 German universities and civilian laboratories openly use:

- Pascal;
- Simula;
- Prolog;
- C;
- ML;
- Lambda;
- ALGOL descendants;
- specialized graphics languages.

The rule becomes:

- strategic administration and weapons remain Rechenplan-centered;
- consumer and educational systems use Kurzplan;
- universities may teach and implement foreign languages;
- imported source must pass through German compilers and character gateways.

Germany retains a dominant national language without maintaining a true monopoly.

## 7. Consumer software

German home software includes:

- household accounts;
- tax and ration calculations;
- engineering;
- school mathematics;
- family records;
- railway simulation;
- construction;
- astronomy;
- spaceflight;
- military history;
- sports;
- music;
- drawing;
- games.

Not every game is propaganda.

Wolfgang’s modernizers understand that a consumer market made entirely of ideological lectures will lose to Japanese and American imports.

Political satire, anti-regime adventures, and explicit depictions of colonial violence remain forbidden.

## 8. The German game with the impossible ownership history

A strong working seed for the setting’s Tetris-like story is a game provisionally titled:

> **Mauerwerk** — “Masonry.”

Around 1979, a young programmer at a German technical institute writes a falling geometric-block game as:

- a Kurzplan demonstration;
- a study of packing and spatial planning;
- an amusement for students;
- an educational exercise in screen control.

The game spreads through the German programme-library system.

Nobody agrees who owns it.

Possible claimants include:

1. the programmer;
2. the technical institute;
3. the equipment manufacturer whose computer was used;
4. the national programme library;
5. the Reich software-export office;
6. a German publisher that first sold a cassette version;
7. a Japanese company that translated and improved it after a conference demonstration;
8. an Italian broker who believes he purchased international rights;
9. an American game publisher who buys rights from the wrong intermediary.

The Japanese adaptation may be called **`積木`**, “building blocks,” and the American version something like **Stack**.

The dispute intensifies because each legal system defines authorship differently.

The final settlement occurs only in the early or mid-1980s after:

- diplomatic correspondence;
- secret contracts;
- translated licenses;
- copied source;
- multiple cartridge versions;
- competing copyright registrations;
- a personal appeal from the original programmer.

That is an excellent in-universe movie story.

It should be seeded in 1979 rather than fully resolved during this period.

## 9. Space and military computing

Consumer opening does not displace Germany’s strategic priorities.

Late-1970s German computing supports:

- lunar prospecting;
- Mars rover operations;
- Rj 1 rendezvous and targeting;
- Wotan’s digital combat system;
- Raumhafen traffic;
- automated Eastern railways;
- Second Mosaic Settlement accounting;
- advanced industrial control.

The German computer industry therefore has a split identity:

- formal, certified strategic systems;
- increasingly playful and commercial home systems.

## 10. International scandal

The 1978–79 demographic scandal affects the computing profession directly because evidence includes:

- demographic databases;
- pharmaceutical orders;
- medical-status fields;
- sterilization and contraception statistics;
- benefit records;
- district targets.

Foreign programmers organize:

- conference protests;
- petitions;
- selective boycotts of German administrative-computing papers;
- demands that technical societies address professional responsibility.

German delegates divide among:

- defenders of national policy;
- people claiming technical neutrality;
- quiet reformers;
- researchers furious that their work has been associated with coercion.

The scandal does not end cooperation, but it destroys the belief that computing is automatically morally cleaner than rockets or weapons.

## Germany in 1980

Germany remains first-rank in:

- industrial and engineering systems;
- strategic software certification;
- space infrastructure;
- administrative computing;
- distributed control.

It enters consumer computing seriously but does not match American openness or Japanese sales volume.

---

# VIII. Britain and the Commonwealth  
## Education, packet services, and a smaller home-computer revolution

Britain recognizes the importance of ordinary people learning to program, but its late-1970s economic crisis limits the speed of consumer adoption.

The Commonwealth response is heavily educational.

## 1. Commonwealth educational computing

A **Commonwealth School Computing Programme** begins around 1977–78.

Schools receive:

- terminals connected to regional systems;
- small standalone microcomputers;
- teacher training;
- programming broadcasts;
- printed course material;
- shared software libraries.

Britain uses computing to reinforce Commonwealth technical identity.

Canada and Australia build or assemble machines locally.

## 2. The language compromise

Britain’s educational world already contains:

- Conversational Autocode;
- Pascal;
- BCPL;
- ML;
- CLEO;
- Prolog;
- several BASIC implementations.

The home market chooses BASIC because American and Japanese machines have made it the closest thing to an international consumer language.

Britain creates a **Commonwealth BASIC profile** defining:

- minimum arithmetic;
- strings;
- loops;
- arrays;
- graphics;
- sound;
- file operations.

Manufacturers still add dialects.

Conversational Autocode survives in older schools and institutional systems.

## 3. British home machines

Small British and Commonwealth firms introduce:

- kits;
- inexpensive keyboard computers;
- educational systems;
- professional machines;
- television adapters.

They are often technically clever and badly capitalized.

Britain’s strengths are:

- compact design;
- software;
- documentation;
- networking;
- educational use.

Its weaknesses are:

- limited production runs;
- high component costs;
- unstable public corporations;
- fragmented procurement.

## 4. Packet and videotex integration

Britain develops a public teledata or videotex service around 1978–80.

Most users access it through dedicated terminals rather than home computers.

Services include:

- news;
- weather;
- shipping;
- prices;
- travel;
- government information;
- messages;
- educational pages.

Home-computer adapters appear, but telecommunications charges and regulation limit mass use.

## 5. Games

Britain becomes strong in:

- text adventures;
- strategy;
- historical games;
- naval simulations;
- economic simulations;
- educational software;
- puzzle games.

British games are more often software products than hardware showcases.

## 6. Functional and logic programming

ML grows rapidly in universities.

Prolog crosses from Occitania into British research through Edinburgh and other centers.

Britain becomes the principal place where programmers compare:

- ML;
- Lambda;
- Prolog;
- LISP;
- Pascal;
- BCPL.

This reinforces Britain’s role as the interpreter among paradigms.

## 7. The 1980 political transition

Thatcher’s National Liberal–Constitutional victory is well timed for a later expansion of:

- small firms;
- employee-owned technology companies;
- educational computing;
- telecommunications;
- home enterprise.

The major expansion belongs in 1981–84, but its hardware and programmer base already exists by 1980.

## Britain in 1980

Britain is behind America and Japan in household penetration but strong in:

- school computing;
- software;
- packet networks;
- text services;
- small innovative manufacturers;
- programming-language research.

---

# IX. The Latin bloc  
## Prolog, Pascal, and the designed home machine

The Latin bloc participates in consumer computing without making it the center of its economic strategy.

## 1. Olivetti’s position

Olivetti remains the bloc’s principal civilian-computing firm.

Its late-1970s products span:

- mainframes;
- office systems;
- bank terminals;
- professional desktops;
- school computers;
- increasingly affordable home-oriented systems.

The typical Olivetti machine is:

- attractive;
- complete;
- well documented;
- expensive;
- designed around a specific user rather than an open hobbyist bus.

## 2. Consumer machines

Around 1978–79, Olivetti and several Spanish and Italian electronics firms introduce home and school systems with:

- keyboard;
- television or monitor;
- cassette;
- cartridge;
- Pascal or BASIC-like interpreter;
- printer option;
- Latin multilingual character support.

Occitan firms supply:

- graphics;
- microprocessors;
- real-time interfaces;
- game and display electronics.

## 3. Languages

The late-1970s Latin environment contains:

- Pascal for education;
- ALGOL-Latin for advanced science;
- LIA for administration;
- Prolog for logic and language;
- BASIC dialects for consumer machines;
- Modula-like structured systems languages;
- Occitan real-time languages.

The bloc does not impose one consumer language.

## 4. Prolog’s international expansion

Prolog becomes the first Latin-developed programming language that every major computing power feels obliged to investigate.

Applications include:

- natural-language analysis;
- diagnostics;
- legal rules;
- planning;
- expert systems;
- military maintenance;
- translation.

Japanese researchers are especially interested because Prolog can operate over multilingual symbolic records.

German researchers attempt to integrate logic rules with Rechenplan data.

American AI laboratories debate Prolog against LISP and Lambda.

## 5. Games and media

Italy and Spain develop:

- arcade machines;
- driving games;
- football games;
- architectural and artistic programs;
- educational Catholic and historical material;
- licensed Japanese games.

The Latin bloc is not the largest game market, but its industrial-design culture produces visually distinctive cabinets and consoles.

## 6. Legal culture

Latin law strongly distinguishes:

- authorship;
- moral right;
- commercial publication;
- translation;
- machine adaptation.

That becomes relevant in the Mauerwerk dispute, where an Italian intermediary claims to possess adaptation and distribution rights without possessing the German author’s moral right or the Japanese publisher’s software rights.

## Latin position in 1980

The bloc remains strongest in:

- Prolog;
- professional desktop systems;
- office ergonomics;
- multilingual Latin software;
- compact avionics;
- designed consumer products.

It lacks American and Japanese volume.

---

# X. Software ownership becomes a diplomatic problem

The international exchange of software exposes incompatible legal assumptions.

| System | Default view |
|---|---|
| United States | Program as copyrightable product and contractual license, mixed with a strong copying and hobbyist culture |
| Britain | Program as literary and technical work, often distributed through service and institutional contracts |
| Germany | Program as technical plan, institutional product, certified component, and sometimes controlled export |
| Japan | Program as corporate work embedded in a product or process |
| Latin bloc | Author’s moral right separated from commercial exploitation and adaptation rights |

Common disputes include:

- Does translating keywords create a new program?
- Who owns software written by a university employee?
- Can a national programme library distribute foreign copies?
- Is object code the same work as source code?
- Does a cartridge manufacturer own the game or only its implementation?
- Can an employee sell foreign rights?
- Does a government export license imply ownership?
- Is a program printed in a magazine free to copy?

A nonbinding **Lucerne Principles on Program Exchange** appears around 1978–79, recommending that licenses distinguish:

- source;
- executable code;
- translation;
- adaptation;
- hardware implementation;
- national distribution;
- international distribution;
- authorship credit.

The principles help and do not prevent spectacular disputes.

---

# XI. The computing generation arrives

A person born in 1955 is twenty-five in 1980.

He or she may have:

- seen Raumbote I as a child;
- watched German and American lunar landings;
- used a terminal in school;
- joined a computer club;
- typed programs from a magazine;
- played arcade games;
- owned or desired a home machine;
- regarded programming as a possible ordinary career.

This is the first generation for whom computing is not an exotic profession invented by older mathematicians.

## America

The computer-native youth sees software as something that may be:

- written at home;
- sold by mail;
- shared at a club;
- turned into a company;
- used to make games or run a family business.

## Japan

The young programmer sees computing as:

- normal corporate technology;
- a school subject;
- a consumer-electronics medium;
- a route into technical status;
- a language written natively in Japanese.

## Germany

The young German sees:

- Rechenplan as the language of institutions;
- Kurzplan as the language of the home;
- computing as patriotic modernity;
- foreign languages as intellectually interesting but politically bounded.

## Britain

The young Briton sees:

- terminals;
- school micros;
- public networks;
- multiple languages;
- small technology firms;
- Commonwealth software culture.

## Latin bloc

The young Latin programmer may move among:

- Pascal;
- Prolog;
- office systems;
- design;
- avionics;
- small programmable machines.

This generation will produce the setting’s original 1980s entrepreneurs.

---

# XII. Leadership balance in 1980

| Field | Leading power |
|---|---|
| Personal-computer software freedom | United States |
| Household and small-business computer culture | United States |
| Polished home-computer hardware | Japan |
| Video-game hardware and arcade integration | Japan |
| Merchant software market | United States |
| Embedded and factory computing | Japan |
| Industrial certification | Germany |
| Space and engineering computing | Germany and United States |
| International packet and translation expertise | Britain |
| Functional-language research | Britain and United States |
| Logic programming | Occitania/Latin bloc |
| Professional desktop design | Italy |
| Universal character architecture | Japanese-led international project |
| Consumer language variety | United States |
| Native non-Latin home programming | Japan |
| Controlled national home-computing system | Germany |
| Educational and public-service computing | Britain |

The main computing rivalry is now clearly **Japanese–American**.

America forces Japan to open machines to more software and users.

Japan forces America to improve:

- reliability;
- miniaturization;
- graphics;
- sound;
- packaging;
- consumer-electronics quality.

Germany remains an independent first-rank power but no longer sets the pace of consumer computing. Britain and the Latin bloc remain highly influential through specialized strengths.

---

# XIII. Working canon for 1975–1980

1. Japanese programming-language revisions use imperial-year suffixes written in Japanese numerals; Gregorian suffixes are retroactively removed.

2. `計算三六` appears in 1976 and `手順三七` in 1977.

3. `学習三八` appears in 1978 as Japan’s native vertical home-and-school programming language.

4. International computing conferences become regular after 1970 and form one of the world’s first genuinely cross-bloc professional cultures.

5. The principal world congresses are Zürich 1971, Stockholm 1974, Toronto 1977, and a joint Tokyo–Melbourne congress in 1980.

6. Programming-language, education, database, networking, character, and social-impact conferences develop alongside the main congress.

7. Strategic conflicts cause boycotts and disputes without ending professional exchange.

8. Japan’s character-registry approach becomes the intellectual foundation for an international universal character project.

9. The Kyoto draft appears in 1977, the Geneva compromise in 1978–79, and **UNICODE 80** is adopted at the Tokyo–Melbourne congress.

10. UNICODE 80 defines sixteen-bit abstract character identities but permits compact local and transmission encodings.

11. Its low range is Latin-compatible, but Japanese kana, kanji, Chinese characters, Hangul, vertical text, right-to-left scripts, and combining marks are present from the first edition.

12. America’s software industry remains unusually lightly regulated. Government supports hardware, education, and procurement without requiring general software licensing.

13. American personal computing moves from kits in 1975–76 to finished household products in 1977, broad retail in 1978, and business applications in 1979.

14. The dominant American home-computer and language-company founders born after 1947 are original fictional characters.

15. BASIC dialects explode across American machines; C, Pascal, Forth, LISP, Lambda, Smalltalk, SQL, and other languages coexist.

16. A fictional electronic worksheet becomes the decisive American small-business application in 1979.

17. Cartridge consoles, arcades, home-computer games, magazines, and programming clubs become major American youth institutions.

18. Japan reaches the consumer-computer market at roughly the same time as America, with greater product integration and less software-market openness.

19. Japanese home systems retain vertical source, Japanese numerals, katakana/kanji keywords, and mixed-script imperial compatibility.

20. America and Japan become the principal global computing rivals by 1980.

21. Wolfgang Friedrich Hitler sponsors a German Heimrechner program as part of national modernization and protection against American and Japanese consumer imports.

22. Germany legalizes broad offline home programming while regulating modems, cryptography, foreign media, and network access.

23. **Kurzplan 77** becomes the German consumer and school language.

24. Foreign languages become normal in German universities even while Rechenplan remains dominant in strategic and administrative work.

25. Britain creates a Commonwealth school-computing program and adopts a Commonwealth BASIC profile while retaining Autocode, Pascal, BCPL, ML, and Prolog.

26. Britain trails America and Japan in home-machine volume but remains strong in software, education, packet systems, and games.

27. The Latin bloc introduces stylish but relatively expensive Olivetti-centered home and school systems around 1978–79.

28. Prolog becomes an internationally recognized Latin-bloc language and a major object of Japanese, British, German, and American research.

29. Software ownership becomes a significant international legal field, with incompatible American, British, German, Japanese, and Latin doctrines.

30. A German falling-block puzzle provisionally titled **Mauerwerk** is created around 1979 and begins the tangled international rights history that will become the setting’s Tetris-like cultural story.

31. By 1980 personal computers remain a minority possession but programming has become culturally normal among technically inclined youth.

32. The postwar computer-native generation is now entering adulthood and will increasingly replace historical post-divergence personalities with original setting characters.

These corrections improve the cultural map and supersede the previous treatment.

## Formosa

Formosa should be treated as part of the **Japanese domestic cultural core**, not as a Chinese-influenced associated production center comparable to Nanjing or Manila.

Because there is no Nationalist evacuation to Taiwan after 1947:

- the enormous mainland Chinese influx never occurs;
- Japanese settlement and military development continue uninterrupted;
- Japanese becomes the dominant language of administration, education, commerce, and urban family life;
- intermarriage and migration increasingly make the island demographically Japanese;
- by the 1970s it is commonly imagined as the southern continuation of the Ryukyu–home-island chain;
- by the 1980s its studios, broadcasters, actors, electronics firms, and animation workers are counted as Japanese domestic institutions.

Taipei’s Japanese administrative name is **Taihoku**. One terminology note: *Formosa* and *Taiwan* are not translations of one another—*Formosa* is Portuguese-derived, while *Taiwan* has a separate indigenous and Chinese toponymic history. In-setting, however, **Formosa** can dominate English-language Japanese imperial usage, while Japanese domestic documents continue using forms derived from *Taiwan*.

A preservation delegation visiting Taihoku in the 1980s does not discover a suppressed modern Taiwanese-Chinese nation waiting to reemerge. It encounters an overwhelmingly Japanese city where even most Chinese immigrants conduct public life in Japanese.

The endangered cultures are principally those of the island’s indigenous Austronesian peoples. Preservation programs concentrate upon:

- indigenous languages;
- ritual and oral tradition;
- songs and dances;
- village histories;
- land claims;
- surviving religious customs;
- protected cultural districts.

This gives Formosa a different tragedy from Korea. Korea retains the memory of a major national civilization being absorbed. Formosa becomes a settler-majority Japanese province in which the original peoples have been reduced to small, curated cultural minorities.

## The Manila route into the Latin bloc

The Philippines becomes the great **cultural adapter between Japan and Catholic Europe**.

Japanese animation normally follows this route:

> Japanese original → Filipino subtitled edition → English or Tagalog Manila dub → Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, or Occitan localization.

Filipino editors have already addressed many of the concerns likely to trouble Latin Catholic broadcasters:

- unfamiliar Shinto language;
- spirits presented as gods;
- religious syncretism;
- sexual humor;
- revealing imagery;
- extreme violence;
- family relationships;
- suicide and death;
- ambiguous supernatural morality.

Consequently, the Latin bloc receives substantially more Japanese animation than Britain, Germany, or America might expect. Spain can work directly from the English-language Filipino package, while Italy, Portugal, and Occitania translate the already adapted script into their own languages.

The result becomes known informally as the **Manila edition** or **Manila cut**.

## Telephone-game animation

The intermediary system produces a wonderful fan-culture phenomenon.

A line may pass through:

1. original Japanese;
2. Filipino subtitle;
3. Filipino English dialogue rewrite;
4. Spanish translation;
5. Italian or Portuguese adaptation based partly upon the Spanish or English version.

By the time the program reaches Rome or Lisbon, a stern Shinto invocation might have become a prayer to Providence, a joke about rice cakes may concern pastries, and an ambiguous romantic confession may have turned into a declaration of friendship.

Latin fans develop a standard joke:

> “That is what he said in Madrid. Nobody knows what he said in Tokyo.”

Home video makes the discrepancies visible. Collectors compare:

- the Japanese original;
- unofficial literal subtitles;
- the Manila cut;
- the Spanish dub;
- their own national dub.

Some famously altered programs acquire several incompatible plots. Fan magazines publish side-by-side translations, missing scenes, restored dialogue, and explanations of Japanese customs. Knowing “what they actually said” becomes a mark of serious fandom.

This makes Latin anime culture unusually sophisticated. It is more welcoming than the British or German market, but also more conscious that every imported work has passed through layers of interpretation.

The revised contrast is now:

> **Formosa produces Japanese media as part of Japan itself. Manila translates Japanese media into a form the Catholic world can receive—and occasionally transforms it almost beyond recognition.**

# Computing Race VIII: 1980–1985  
## Internetworking, the German language explosion, and the Japanese–American computer age

This period is when computing ceases to be a specialized industrial sector and becomes an independent cultural force. By 1985, the five systems still possess different hardware, languages, legal assumptions, and political structures, but their programmers increasingly inhabit the same international conversation.

The established timeline also makes these five years unusually demanding. Germany opens Mondhafen Süd and fields operational orbital interceptors; America expands Columbia, Kennedy Station, Project Pilgrim, and the American Data Network; Japan flies a highly automated crewed spacecraft; the Commonwealth launches Endeavour and Resolution; the Latin bloc flies Aquila I; and the Falklands war tests British and German-derived Argentine information systems under sustained combat conditions. fileciteturn16file0

---

# I. Corrections to the universal character registry

## UNICODE 80 block order

The first-edition registry should use the order you specified:

1. **Common control functions**
2. **Latin letters**
3. **Digits and punctuation**
4. **Japanese kana**
5. **Large ideograph area**
6. **Hangul**
7. **Greek and Cyrillic**
8. **Arabic and Hebrew**
9. **Major South and Southeast Asian scripts**
10. **Mathematical and technical symbols**
11. **Vertical and horizontal presentation properties**

This does not mean every section receives equal space. The ideograph area is overwhelmingly the largest.

The order communicates the politics of the standard:

- Latin remains first among scripts because most existing international computing and telecommunications equipment depends upon it.
- Japanese kana and ideographs immediately follow because Tokyo supplied the conceptual architecture and possesses enough industrial weight to prevent Japanese text from being treated as a later national extension.
- Hangul receives an early independent area because Korea is a major industrial component of the Japanese system.
- Greek and Cyrillic are recognized but are not central to the technical or geopolitical origin of the standard.
- Presentation properties are placed last because they describe how registered characters behave rather than the identity of the characters themselves.

## No simplified Chinese

UNICODE 80 contains **traditional Chinese characters only**. There has been no Communist Chinese script-reform program comparable to the one that historically produced simplified Chinese.

The ideographic problem is therefore easier in one respect and harder in another.

It is easier because the commission does not have to reconcile two state-mandated Chinese writing systems.

It remains difficult because it must distinguish among:

- traditional Chinese forms;
- Japanese kanji variants;
- Japanese simplified or variant glyph forms where Japanese usage differs;
- historical and specialist characters;
- characters that share an origin and meaning but are written differently;
- national preferences concerning which form is authoritative.

The first standard therefore defines:

- one abstract identity where the commission agrees that Chinese and Japanese forms represent the same character;
- national presentation forms;
- separate identities where semantic or historical distinctions are significant;
- a compatibility area for disputed cases.

Traditional Chinese’s stroke complexity makes early display expensive. Low-cost systems frequently use:

- limited common-character ROMs;
- 16×16 pixel glyphs of mediocre quality;
- font cartridges;
- printer-resident character sets;
- phonetic or numeric fallbacks for rare characters.

High-end Japanese and Chinese-language terminals move toward 24×24 or comparable glyph matrices.

## Core and extension spaces

A single 16-bit space remains the public **Basic Universal Registry**, but it is understood by 1980 that 65,536 positions will eventually be inadequate.

UNICODE 80 therefore includes an extension mechanism from its first edition:

- the basic registry uses sixteen-bit identities;
- rare, historical, and specialist characters use extension-plane escapes;
- ordinary machines can implement only the basic blocks they need;
- conformity requires preserving unknown characters rather than silently replacing them.

This is more complicated than a pure fixed-width design, but it prevents the first standard from exhausting itself immediately.

Real Unicode began only in late 1987 and 1988, drawing partly on earlier East Asian two-byte and multilingual workstation systems. The setting’s UNICODE 80 is an acceleration of almost a decade, made plausible by Japan’s much earlier imperial character registry and by sustained cross-bloc standards work. citeturn657643search3turn657643search7turn657643search19

# II. Japanese programming-language names

Japanese official and domestic references always include the Japanese-language title and imperial-year suffix. Romanization appears here for readability.

| Introduction | Canonical name | Romanization | Role |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1976 | `計算三六` | *Keisan 36* | Professional scientific and engineering language |
| 1977 | `手順三七` | *Tejun 37* | Professional transaction and process language |
| 1978 | `学習三八` | *Gakushū 38* | Home, school, and beginner’s language |
| 1981 | `学習四一` | *Gakushū 41* | Revised consumer and educational standard |
| 1982 | `計算四二` | *Keisan 42* | Sixteen- and thirty-two-bit scientific revision |
| 1983 | `手順四三` | *Tejun 43* | Distributed transaction, industrial, and network-process revision |

Foreign technical literature may write **KEISAN 42**, but Japanese programmers see `計算四二`.

---

# III. The real historical clock

The historical 1980–85 period provides the right technological framework:

- IBM introduced its mass-market personal computer in 1981, and its relatively open architecture rapidly encouraged compatible machines and clones.
- The ARPA community completed its transition toward TCP/IP in 1983, while the first domain-name specifications appeared that November.
- “C with Classes,” begun in 1979, developed into C++ and received its first commercial compiler in 1985.
- Ada became an American standard in 1983 for large, reliable, long-lived software systems.
- Smalltalk-80 spread object-oriented programming and the graphical development environment.
- NEC introduced the sixteen-bit PC-9801 in 1982, while Nintendo launched the Family Computer in 1983.
- Japanese personal computers increasingly combined sixteen-bit processing with kanji ROMs and compatibility across product generations. citeturn497303search0turn497303search3turn497303search5turn497303search6turn122116search0turn122116search5turn657643search1turn657643search2turn657643search10

The central shift is:

> **In 1980, personal computers are competing products. By 1985, they are competing platforms, software economies, network identities, and cultures.**

---

# IV. Three new central figures

## Dr. Matthias Falkenberg  
### Germany’s network visionary

**Born:** 1940, Königsberg  
**Raised:** Riga, Reichskommissariat Ostland, after 1948  
**Field:** distributed computing, satellite communications, operating systems, network architecture  
**Public project:** **Weltnetz**  
**Political role by 1983:** Wolfgang’s *Sonderbeauftragter für Rechnerverbund und Weltnetz*—Special Commissioner for Computer Federation and the World Network

Falkenberg’s father is a railway-signaling and telecommunications engineer assigned to Ostland during the quota crisis. The family belongs to the German colonial technical middle class rather than the SS estate nobility. Falkenberg grows up amid:

- teleprinters;
- automated railway dispatch;
- German-controlled communication corridors;
- isolated administrative settlements;
- the extraordinary contrast between modern infrastructure and archaic surrounding life.

His formative insight is that **a thin technical elite can govern great distances only when its machines behave as one system**.

He studies at Darmstadt and Munich, works on Planwerk remote services, and later participates in Raumhafen telemetry and traffic control. He is not the inventor of packet switching, satellite communications, or every German network protocol. Like von Braun, he is:

- a systems architect;
- an organizer;
- a gifted recruiter;
- a public advocate;
- a politically adroit interpreter between engineers and the ruler.

His 1979 lecture, **“Das Weltnetz: Rechnen ohne Entfernung”**—*The World Network: Computing Without Distance*—makes him famous. Its best-known line is:

> **“Entfernung ist nur ein Übertragungsfehler.”**  
> “Distance is only a transmission error.”

### Relationship with Wolfgang

Helmut Gröttrup and Eberhard Rees introduce Falkenberg to Wolfgang around 1980–81. Wolfgang recognizes the same quality he admired in von Braun: a man who can turn technical infrastructure into a civilizational image.

Falkenberg presents the network as three things simultaneously:

1. **A global German commercial system** linking firms, banks, universities, clients, and software markets.
2. **A strategic communications system** that cannot be cut merely by severing terrestrial cables.
3. **A continuation of the space program**, with communications and relay satellites making the globe into one technical space.

He dramatically emphasizes satellites. His engineers know that terrestrial cable, microwave, fiber, and local packet networks will carry most high-volume traffic. Wolfgang nevertheless loves the orbital imagery, and space funding helps finance the network.

### His ideology

Falkenberg sincerely favors international technical communication, but he is not a political liberal.

His ideal network is:

- global;
- multilingual;
- interoperable;
- commercially active;
- personally identified;
- logged;
- hierarchically administered.

He regards anonymity as a defect. His vision is not “everyone may speak without authority.” It is “every authorized person and machine may reach every other through a known path.”

His Ostland background also gives him an unsettling vocabulary of technological evolution. During the German language panic, he argues:

> **“Ohne Varianten keine Auslese; ohne Auslese keine Bewährung.”**  
> “Without variants there is no selection; without selection there is no proving.”

He treats languages as lineages that must be allowed to reproduce, compete, combine, and disappear.

That argument is decisive in preventing a German clampdown.

---

## Elias Rowan Mercer  
### The charismatic founder of Concord

**Born:** 1951, Pasadena, California  
**Company:** **Concord Computer Works**  
**Political affiliation:** open National Renewal voter and cultural sympathizer  
**Principal architecture:** **Concord**  
**Application language:** **Civic**  
**First mass system:** **Concord One**, 1978  
**Graphical successor:** **Concord Meridian**, 1983

Mercer grows up in the American aerospace culture. His father works in instrumentation and his mother in educational television. He is neither a countercultural mystic nor a detached engineer.

He is:

- sociable;
- theatrical;
- patriotic;
- moralizing;
- relentlessly confident;
- genuinely gifted at explaining technology to nonprogrammers.

He believes the personal computer should be a complete cultural object, not a box assembled from unrelated parts.

His doctrine is:

> **“A citizen should not have to build the republic before he can live in it.”**

The Concord machine therefore arrives with:

- its own processor architecture;
- its own operating environment;
- its own display conventions;
- its own development language;
- controlled peripheral standards;
- approved application publishers;
- consistent manuals and visual design.

Mercer’s National Renewal sympathies inform his product philosophy. He regards coherence, responsibility, and bounded participation as virtues. Concord software is difficult to develop without owning an authorized Concord development system.

The restrictions are technical and contractual rather than a government requirement:

- undocumented low-level interfaces;
- proprietary object format;
- serialized development systems;
- controlled cartridge and disk publication;
- publisher agreements;
- mandatory interface conventions.

The system is not literally impossible to reverse engineer. It is deliberately inconvenient.

Mercer publicly describes this as protecting users from unreliable and fraudulent software. Critics call it **the gated republic**.

He supports Buchanan in 1980 and Phillips in 1984. Concord itself remains formally nonpartisan, but Mercer’s endorsement of Phillips produces employee protests and consumer boycotts in some urban markets.

---

## Martin Avery Keene  
### The architect of the portable software market

**Born:** 1953, Seattle  
**Company:** **Interlink Software Corporation**  
**Principal products:** portable language systems and the **Bridge** operating environment  
**Major system:** **Bridge/16**, selected for IBM’s 1981 personal-computer family

Keene is the opposite of Mercer.

He is:

- reserved;
- dry;
- impatient with ceremony;
- obsessive about interfaces and compatibility;
- personally indifferent to grand political narratives;
- much more comfortable examining a linker than addressing an audience.

He believes hardware is temporary and software interfaces are enduring.

Interlink initially sells:

- BASIC interpreters;
- Pascal;
- C;
- cross-assemblers;
- disk systems;
- terminal software;
- device abstractions.

Its decisive product is **Bridge**, an operating environment licensed to several hardware manufacturers. IBM selects Bridge/16 for its new mass-market machine in 1981, giving Keene’s company access to a vast compatible market.

Unlike Mercer, Keene does not care what the finished computer looks like. He wants the same source code to run on:

- IBM;
- domestic clones;
- laboratory machines;
- business systems;
- foreign licensed processors.

### Mercer and Keene

They first meet at the Toronto computing congress in 1977 and dislike one another almost immediately.

Mercer regards Keene as:

- rootless;
- culturally indifferent;
- willing to subordinate American industry to portability;
- incapable of understanding that design expresses moral responsibility.

Keene regards Mercer as:

- pompous;
- politically dangerous;
- wasteful;
- obsessed with controlling users;
- the builder of an elegant prison.

Their professional rivalry is real, but their personal dislike would exist even without market competition.

### The Munich Licensing Affair

In 1982–83, Interlink licenses Bridge translators, C tools, and network software to a nominally civilian German electronics consortium through a neutral commercial arrangement.

The technology then appears in:

- German civilian machines;
- Weltnetz gateway computers;
- Argentine business installations;
- military-adjacent logistics systems.

Keene’s defense is blunt: these are general tools, the sale was legal, and operating systems have no foreign policy.

The affair becomes explosive after Argentina seizes the Falklands. American critics accuse him of helping create the German–Argentine technical ecosystem. Keene’s refusal to perform remorse makes the scandal worse.

He is not secretly pro-German. He is genuinely irritated that politicians imagine a compiler can be assigned a nationality after it has been distributed.
