# 1970–1975: the microelectronic household and the networked marketplace

The central change in these five years is not that the computer enters every home. It is that **microelectronics begin entering products whose owners do not think of them as computers**.

A calculator calculates because it contains a processor. A camera sets exposure electronically. A car replaces breaker points with electronic ignition. A bank terminal checks an account against a distant file. A washing machine runs a more elaborate sequence through solid-state controls. An airline can confirm a seat while the passenger is still standing at the counter.

The general-purpose household computer appears only at the edge of the period. The established computing chronology places the true consumer break after 1975, when kits and clubs grow into complete machines, games, retail software, electronic worksheets and dial-up culture. fileciteturn20file15

Meanwhile, the space race remains unusually active. Germany lands on the Moon in December 1970, America follows through its reusable transportation architecture in July 1971, Japan flies Hikari-1 in 1973, America demonstrates a fully automated orbital-spaceplane mission in 1974, and Germany publicly opens the Orbitaler Raumhafen in 1975. The Weather Commons also begins operating in 1972. fileciteturn22file0

So the period’s consumer movement is:

> The 1960s put electronics inside the institution.  
> The early 1970s put electronics inside the product.  
> The later 1970s will put the programmable machine in front of the customer.

---

# I. What the microprocessor changes first

The microprocessor does not begin with the family computer. It begins where manufacturers need the same limited decision repeated cheaply.

The first major fields are:

1. calculators and office equipment;
2. industrial controllers and test instruments;
3. traffic, vending and ticketing systems;
4. vehicle and appliance controls;
5. educational and hobbyist machines.

The important distinction is between **programmable** and **user-programmable**.

An electronic sewing machine may contain a control device. The buyer cannot normally write software for it. A calculator follows stored internal logic, but it is not a general-purpose computer. A traffic-light controller can be reconfigured by a technician, but not by the driver waiting at the intersection.

That still matters because it creates a mass market for:

- memory chips;
- display drivers;
- keyboards;
- switches;
- small printers;
- power supplies;
- circuit boards;
- low-cost sensors;
- service technicians.

The consumer-computer industry grows out of this supporting ecology rather than appearing from nothing in 1975.

## The product hierarchy by 1975

| Category | Typical 1970 position | Typical 1975 position |
|---|---|---|
| Electronic calculator | Shared office machine | Affordable professional or upper-middle-class personal instrument |
| Quartz watch | Technical luxury | Expensive but recognizable consumer category |
| Digital clock | Laboratory or prestige object | Common in offices, hotels and affluent homes |
| Microprocessor control | Industrial and military | Entering cameras, business machines, vehicles and premium appliances |
| Video game | Laboratory or amusement experiment | Arcade product and primitive dedicated home system |
| Home computer | Technical demonstration | Hobby kit for enthusiasts |
| Video recorder | Broadcast and institutional equipment | Expensive institutional and affluent-home product |
| Automatic camera | Premium specialist item | Large middle-market category |
| Bank terminal | Major bank experiment | Growing urban service network |

---

# II. Calculators replace the slide rule from below

The electronic calculator is probably the defining small technology of 1970–75.

It becomes affordable before the home computer because its task is narrow. It needs:

- numeric input;
- arithmetic logic;
- a small display;
- a compact power supply;
- limited memory.

Japan is particularly well placed. Sharp, Casio-type firms, Seiko and specialist component houses combine displays, miniaturization, battery production and high-volume manufacturing. America remains strong in semiconductor design. Italy contributes Olivetti’s interface and office-machine design culture. Germany produces precise, durable professional instruments but may struggle to match Japanese prices.

By 1975, the market divides into four levels:

- desktop accounting machines with printers;
- scientific calculators for engineers and universities;
- pocket arithmetic calculators;
- specialized financial, surveying and industrial instruments.

The slide rule does not disappear immediately. It remains:

- cheaper;
- durable;
- independent of batteries;
- familiar to older engineers;
- allowed in places where electronic equipment is restricted.

But younger engineers begin treating it as an inherited manual skill rather than the natural center of technical work.

## Social consequences

The calculator changes more than speed.

It weakens the occupational status of people whose value rested partly on rapid manual arithmetic. At the same time, it raises the value of people who understand:

- what calculation to perform;
- whether the entered data are correct;
- whether the answer is physically plausible.

The machine removes some arithmetic labor. It does not remove judgment.

A bad engineer can now reach the wrong answer much faster.

---

# III. Watches, clocks and electronic time

The quartz watch becomes the most visible symbol of Japanese precision.

A 1970 quartz wristwatch is expensive and prestigious. By 1975, quartz clocks and less expensive wristwatches are beginning to spread through:

- airlines;
- broadcasters;
- offices;
- laboratories;
- railway systems;
- wealthy consumers.

The first digital wristwatches use glowing numerical displays. They are striking but limited by:

- battery consumption;
- poor visibility in sunlight;
- the need to press a button to display the time;
- high price;
- bulky cases.

Liquid-crystal displays offer better battery life and continuous visibility, but the early versions are less bright and have narrower viewing angles. The result is a brief, visible competition between glowing displays and reflective displays.

Japan’s advantage is mass electronics and precision assembly. Switzerland responds by repositioning mechanical watches around:

- craftsmanship;
- permanence;
- jewelry;
- inheritance;
- prestige independent of technical novelty.

Germany produces highly accurate professional and industrial timepieces. Britain remains strong in marine, aviation and institutional timing. America turns the digital watch into a consumer-fashion object more quickly.

By 1975, owning a quartz watch still says something about the owner. It suggests technical employment, wealth or deliberate modernity.

---

# IV. Television reaches maturity, but video does not

## Color television becomes normal aspiration

Color television moves from upper-class novelty into a broad middle-class aspiration.

It remains expensive because a color receiver requires:

- a more complex tube;
- precise convergence;
- more circuitry;
- better service skills;
- a reliable broadcast signal.

Most households still own monochrome sets in 1975, particularly outside America and metropolitan Germany or Japan. But major events are increasingly designed for color.

The German Moon landing, American landing, Japanese crewed flight and the live Raumhafen tour all become television sales events. The station’s docks, rotating section, colored warning markings and Earth views are much more convincing in color than on a monochrome set.

Germany’s 1975 broadcast has a special cultural effect. The Moon landing was a mission. The Raumhafen appears as a place with rooms, workshops, signs, machinery and people moving through daily tasks. That makes space feel less like an expedition and more like an extension of industrial civilization.

## The television cabinet changes

The set remains deep and heavy. But it begins to lose its identity as imitation furniture.

Three forms coexist:

- traditional wood cabinet for the family room;
- compact plastic tabletop receiver;
- modern modular component set.

Portable televisions become plausible but remain heavy by later standards. Battery television is possible for specialized or expensive models, not routine all-day use.

Remote controls remain luxury features. Most people still stand up to change the channel.

## Home video is only beginning

Video recording reaches institutions before ordinary households.

The first major customers are:

- broadcasters;
- schools;
- police;
- hospitals;
- corporations;
- sports organizations;
- military training establishments.

An institutional video cassette or cartridge system can record:

- lectures;
- medical procedures;
- interviews;
- technical instruction;
- television programs;
- sporting events.

But the machines are expensive, the tapes are bulky, and incompatible formats are emerging.

An affluent household might own one by 1975. A normal household does not.

Japan’s Totsuko and Matsushita are natural competitors in this field. Totsuko emphasizes compact professional and high-quality consumer recording. Matsushita emphasizes manufacture, distribution and compatibility. Japanese firms may also create separate character-marked and Roman-letter export versions for the Co-Prosperity market rather than building the system around American buyers.

The home-video standards conflict will become much more important after 1975.

---

# V. Audio becomes the first copyable consumer culture

The compact cassette or an equivalent broadly licensed small-tape format becomes one of the era’s most important products.

By the early 1970s, the cassette has three advantages:

- small enough to carry;
- easy enough for a child or office worker to operate;
- cheap enough to duplicate informally.

Its uses include:

- commercial music;
- family recordings;
- language lessons;
- sermons;
- political speeches;
- dictation;
- correspondence sent by post;
- copied radio broadcasts.

The automobile cassette player expands rapidly, particularly in Europe and Japan. America retains more competition from continuous-loop cartridges for part of the decade, especially in cars.

## The political problem of copying

Every regime discovers that magnetic tape is harder to supervise than radio.

A prohibited speech can be copied from one cassette to ten. A foreign song can circulate without official release. A priest can record a sermon. A political organizer can distribute instructions in his own voice.

The copies lose quality with each generation, but they remain intelligible.

Responses differ:

- Germany licenses commercial duplication and monitors large-scale production while tolerating ordinary private recording.
- Japan focuses on manufacturer and distributor control but has difficulty supervising the enormous sphere market.
- Britain relies more heavily on ordinary copyright and security law.
- America develops a legal dispute over private copying rather than one national censorship policy.
- The Latin bloc treats political and sexual content more restrictively but often permits family, religious and educational recording.

The cassette is not inherently revolutionary. It is simply difficult to centralize.

---

# VI. Games arrive before personal computers

Electronic games should begin becoming commercially recognizable between 1971 and 1975.

They appear in two forms.

## Arcade and public amusement

The first successful electronic cabinets use dedicated logic rather than general-purpose computer systems.

They offer simple games based on:

- moving points;
- paddles;
- shooting;
- racing;
- aircraft or space themes.

Arcades, bowling alleys, railway stations, holiday resorts, military canteens and youth clubs become the normal early locations.

The cabinet matters as much as the program:

- coin mechanism;
- durable controls;
- bright display;
- recognizable artwork;
- resistance to rough use.

## Dedicated home television games

The first home machines connect to the family television and play a small set of built-in games. They have no operating system, no software store and usually no proper programmable processor.

They are closer to electronic toys than computers.

America is likely to commercialize this field first because of its television market, component startups and lightly regulated entertainment culture. Japan follows quickly through toy, amusement and electronics firms.

Possible Japanese roots include:

- established card-and-toy houses such as Nintendo;
- Nakamura-type amusement operators;
- television manufacturers;
- calculator-component suppliers.

Japan’s first major games are likely to emphasize:

- simple family play;
- sports;
- shooting galleries;
- racing;
- space themes;
- mechanical-electronic hybrids.

Germany develops amusement machines, but political authorities are more suspicious of unsupervised youth arcades. The market is more likely to grow through clubs, resorts and officially inspected entertainment venues.

## The hobbyist threshold

At the end of 1975, the first genuinely general-purpose hobbyist kits appear in America and possibly Japan.

They are not convenient family products. A typical kit may require the owner to:

- assemble boards;
- provide a power supply;
- operate switches;
- interpret lights;
- obtain or build a terminal;
- write very small programs.

The founders and final names of the canonical American 1975 hobbyist machine remain deliberately open. fileciteturn20file10

The importance is cultural rather than numerical:

> For the first time, a private person can buy a computer because he wants one, not because his employer assigned him to it.

---

# VII. Cameras become electronically helpful

The camera is one of the first products in which consumers trust automatic electronics.

By 1975, middle- and upper-market cameras increasingly offer:

- automatic exposure;
- electronic shutters;
- through-the-lens metering;
- battery checks;
- exposure-warning lights;
- motorized film advance on premium models;
- compact electronic flash.

True mass-market autofocus remains a later development, but rangefinding and focus-assistance experiments are underway.

Japan’s camera industry benefits enormously:

- Canon;
- Nikon;
- Minolta;
- Seiko-linked shutter and timing suppliers;
- specialized optical and electronic firms.

These companies sell first through the Japanese sphere. Instructions and display markings are adapted for Japanese, Chinese and Roman-letter markets. Model numbers become especially important because one product may carry several locally read names.

America remains exceptionally strong in instant photography and casual family imaging. Germany retains prestige in optics and precision but finds Japanese electronic integration increasingly difficult to match on price.

## Space changes photographic demand

Space photography drives public interest in:

- telephoto lenses;
- fine-grain film;
- low-light photography;
- color accuracy;
- compact movie cameras;
- amateur astronomy equipment.

A large share of “space camera” advertising is exaggerated. The real connection is often a lens supplier, film chemistry, test method or corporate laboratory rather than the consumer camera literally sharing spacecraft hardware.

---

# VIII. The appliance becomes automatic—but not intelligent

The 1970–75 household appliance gains more controls without becoming a general programmable device.

## Washing machines

Premium machines offer:

- multiple wash programs;
- temperature selection;
- automatic water-level sensing;
- improved spin control;
- better safety interlocks.

Most sequencing remains electromechanical. Solid-state controls begin entering premium machines by 1975.

## Refrigerators and freezers

The important improvements are:

- automatic defrosting;
- better insulation;
- separate freezer compartments;
- improved thermostats;
- quieter compressors.

America favors large refrigerator-freezers. Japan develops compact appliances suited to urban homes. Germany emphasizes durability and repairability. Britain’s market still includes significant rental and service arrangements.

## Microwave ovens

Microwave cooking begins moving from restaurants and wealthy households toward the upper-middle consumer market.

Japan has strong reasons to miniaturize the oven:

- compact kitchens;
- magnetron production;
- high urban electricity availability;
- convenience-food markets.

America favors larger units and aggressively markets speed. Germany treats them more cautiously as supplementary kitchen equipment rather than a replacement for conventional cooking.

## Sewing and domestic work

Electronic and electromechanical sewing machines add:

- variable speed;
- automated stitch selection;
- buttonhole sequences;
- safety controls.

Japan, Germany and Italy all possess strong sewing-machine and garment-equipment traditions. These products matter particularly in societies where domestic clothing repair and home production remain more common than in affluent America.

## Air conditioning and building control

America continues spreading residential air conditioning.

Japan expands compact room units because of dense humid cities.

Germany and Britain use much less residential air conditioning but increasingly install:

- central heating control;
- district-heating meters;
- office ventilation management;
- automatic boiler control;
- large-building security and fire systems.

The “smart building” does not exist. The centrally controlled office or hotel does.

---

# IX. Medicine becomes visibly electronic

Medical technology is one of the period’s most important but unequal consumer benefits.

Advanced hospitals begin receiving:

- computerized X-ray reconstruction and early CT-type scanning;
- improved ultrasound;
- electronic fetal monitoring;
- intensive-care monitors;
- smaller pacemakers;
- automated laboratory analyzers;
- dialysis systems;
- improved prosthetics and rehabilitation devices.

These systems are expensive and concentrated in major urban hospitals.

## National patterns

**Britain** can spread expensive equipment through regional hospital planning, although queues and capital rationing remain.

**Germany** builds prestige maternal, pediatric and rehabilitation institutions, particularly as Katharina’s public medical work expands. Her interest gives political visibility to neonatal monitoring, childhood disability, rehabilitation and safer family products. The ruling household’s children are born in 1971, 1973 and 1975 during this interval, which makes maternal and pediatric medicine unusually prominent in public imagery. fileciteturn19file14

**Japan** connects hospital equipment to corporate electronics and precision manufacturing.

**America** produces advanced equipment rapidly but distributes it unevenly through private insurance, large hospitals, federal programs and wealthy regions.

The electronic hospital creates a new problem: machines produce more measurements than the staff know how to interpret. Training becomes as important as acquisition.

---

# X. Retail becomes machine-readable

Large retailers begin experimenting with machine-readable product and inventory codes.

The first applications are more likely in:

- warehouses;
- military supply;
- mail-order operations;
- wholesale food distribution;
- large supermarkets.

Checkout scanning spreads more slowly because every product must carry a reliable code and every store must invest in readers, computers and network connections.

There is unlikely to be one universal global code by 1975. Instead, the blocs develop partially incompatible systems.

## Probable standards pattern

| Bloc | Likely priority |
|---|---|
| America | Fast supermarket checkout and national consumer distribution |
| Germany | Manufacturing, warehouse and regulated product identification |
| Japan | Factory-to-retail traceability and dense distribution networks |
| Britain | Commonwealth freight and large-chain inventory compatibility |
| Latin bloc | National systems linked through agreed gateways |

The Japanese problem is particularly interesting. Product identity may need to accommodate:

- Japanese names;
- traditional Chinese characters;
- Roman model numbers;
- regional distributor codes.

That pushes Japan toward separating the machine-readable product number from the human-readable brand.

## Local shops remain viable

Optical checkout does not immediately kill the local merchant.

Large chains gain:

- inventory knowledge;
- faster replenishment;
- lower clerical costs.

The local shop retains:

- convenience;
- repair;
- personal credit;
- delivery;
- knowledge of the customer;
- specialized goods.

The technology strengthens national and regional chains without instantly erasing neighborhood commerce.

---

# XI. Banking and identification

The consumer increasingly encounters electronic records through money.

By 1975, advanced urban banking may include:

- automated cash dispensers;
- magnetic-stripe or machine-readable bank cards;
- direct wage deposits;
- computerized account ledgers;
- electronic transfers between major banks;
- centralized credit checks;
- remote teller terminals.

Cash and checks remain dominant. The electronic system is an additional layer, not a replacement.

## The experience of error

Computerization makes some services much faster and some errors much harder to correct.

A customer may be told:

> “The account does not exist in the central file.”

The local teller may know the customer personally but lack the authority to override the machine.

This creates different political reactions.

America develops a consumer-rights and privacy argument.

Britain develops administrative review procedures.

Germany treats accurate identification as a state and institutional responsibility but gives individuals fewer rights against the record.

Japan emphasizes reconciliation through the responsible company or bank, with less distinction between service failure and corporate dishonor.

The Eastern Reichskommissariats and Mittelafrika use identification systems principally for status, labor, movement and benefits. There, the inability to correct a record can alter where a family is permitted to live or work.

---

# XII. Telephones, satellites and daily communications

The telephone network becomes denser and more automatic.

Common improvements include:

- direct long-distance dialing;
- push-button phones;
- automatic exchanges;
- pagers for doctors and technical staff;
- business facsimile equipment;
- answering machines;
- car and train radiotelephones for wealthy or institutional users.

The ordinary home telephone remains fixed to the wall or table. Cordless telephones and pocket cellular systems remain later technologies.

## What satellites actually change

Communications satellites improve:

- intercontinental broadcasting;
- long-distance telephone capacity;
- maritime communications;
- disaster reporting;
- diplomatic links;
- television coverage of global events.

They do not make international telephone calls cheap for everyone by 1975.

The public sees the benefit most clearly through live television and reduced communication delay. The industrial customer sees it through reliable circuits between distant offices, ships, associated states and project sites.

## Weather Commons

The Weather Commons reaches initial operation in 1972. Its direct consumer product is the weather map, not a private satellite terminal. fileciteturn21file0

By 1975, viewers increasingly expect to see:

- photographed storm systems;
- typhoon and hurricane tracks;
- regional cloud cover;
- improved shipping forecasts;
- more accurate aviation weather.

Forecasts remain imperfect. Satellite imagery tells meteorologists where clouds are. It does not automatically tell them exactly what the atmosphere will do three days later.

Japan, Britain and the Philippines gain particularly visible benefits from storm warning. Germany gains continental agricultural and transport forecasting. America uses weather images as another public argument for its space program.

---

# XIII. Travel becomes a service system

Jet travel becomes a middle-class aspiration and a routine business practice.

The airliner itself matters, but the larger change is the system surrounding it:

- computerized reservations;
- ticketing terminals;
- automatic baggage sorting;
- jet bridges;
- moving walkways;
- airport hotels;
- rental-car desks;
- duty-free shops;
- package tours;
- standardized credit arrangements.

By 1975, a family of moderate means can plausibly save for a foreign or long-distance holiday. It cannot necessarily fly frequently.

## Bloc travel patterns

Germany promotes organized tourism throughout the Altreich, Scandinavia, northern France, the Balkans and selected model imperial districts.

Britain’s travel networks emphasize the Commonwealth, Atlantic islands, the Cape route and package holidays to friendly territories.

Japan develops dense imperial and associated-state air travel connecting Tokyo, Keijō, Taihoku, Shanghai, Singapore, Bangkok, Manila and major Indonesian centers.

The Latin bloc has the strongest Mediterranean package-tour potential:

- Italy;
- Spain;
- Portugal;
- Occitania;
- Greece;
- North Africa;
- the islands.

This is worth carrying into the Latin chat. The Latin bloc’s tourism industry becomes a major buyer of hotels, buses, airliners, reservation equipment, kitchen machinery, air conditioning, elevators and multilingual office systems.

## Supersonic travel

Supersonic passenger aircraft may enter limited prestige service or extended trials during this interval.

The absence of a strong anti-growth environmental movement removes some political obstacles. It does not remove:

- noise;
- fuel consumption;
- maintenance costs;
- limited routes;
- expensive tickets.

Supersonic travel remains a service for officials, wealthy passengers and strategically important routes rather than the future of all commercial aviation.

---

# XIV. Automobiles without the historical oil shock

The established setting does not reproduce the historical 1973 Arab oil embargo automatically. The Middle Eastern balance, oil ownership and great-power alignments are radically different.

The 1974 Kuwait War can still cause:

- temporary production disruption;
- shipping-insurance increases;
- British fuel controls;
- emergency stock releases;
- speculation;
- concern about Gulf vulnerability.

But Britain defeats Iraq, preserves Kuwait and imposes oil or commercial reparations through the Muscat Articles. fileciteturn21file15

I would therefore avoid a simultaneous worldwide automotive downsizing in 1973–74.

The national paths remain different.

## America

Large cars, V8 engines and performance models survive longer.

They are pressured by:

- insurance costs;
- urban smog;
- traffic congestion;
- safety regulation;
- compact-car competition;
- household debt;
- periodic recession.

They are not abruptly destroyed by a universal fuel panic.

American Motors retains a meaningful practical compact identity. Kaiser-Willys dominates utility and four-wheel-drive vehicles. The Big Three continue intermediate and large models while increasing compact lines.

## Germany

Germany continues toward:

- water-cooled front-wheel-drive mass cars;
- passenger diesels;
- electronic fuel injection;
- high-speed safety;
- radial tires;
- anti-lock braking experiments;
- turbocharged performance and diesel engines.

Volkswagen’s next-generation front-drive family should appear between roughly 1973 and 1975. The precise names can remain open, but this is the point at which Volkswagen stops being principally the company of one rear-engined design.

Auto Union uses Audi or DKW to test front-wheel drive, rotary engines and compact technical products. NSU’s rotary engine receives a longer commercial trial than it did historically because there is no sudden global fuel crisis to make its consumption politically intolerable. Its sealing, wear and service problems still prevent universal adoption.

Mercedes-Benz emphasizes diesel, safety and long-distance reliability. BMW and Porsche make turbocharging and sporting performance culturally prestigious.

## Japan

Japan’s vehicle market grows through:

- compact cars;
- motorcycles;
- delivery vans;
- small trucks;
- taxis;
- family sedans.

Honda’s car division is shaped by motorcycles, high-revving engines, compact packaging and Asian urban conditions.

Toyota and Nissan remain the mass leaders. Prince retains a plausible prestige and performance identity. Toyo Kogyo develops rotary vehicles for sporting and technical buyers.

Because America is not Japan’s formative market, Japanese cars are not primarily designed around American emission rules, bumper rules or advertising. They receive:

- Japanese domestic forms;
- Chinese-character sphere forms;
- tropical Southeast Asian packages;
- Philippine Roman-letter documentation;
- later extra-sphere variants.

## Britain

Britain continues consolidating automobile groups.

Its strengths remain:

- compact front-wheel-drive packaging;
- Land-Rover systems;
- sports cars;
- luxury vehicles;
- trucks and buses.

Its weaknesses remain:

- uneven quality;
- duplicated marques;
- labor conflict;
- undercapitalized factories.

The Kuwait victory helps British confidence and may protect strategic vehicle production, but it does not make every domestic car competitive.

## Latin handoff

Italy’s small and medium family cars, scooters, diesel trucks and sporting marques remain highly competitive.

Pirelli gains from radial tires and motorsport. Olivetti and Occitan suppliers contribute electronic instrumentation and manufacturing control. Spain’s SEAT network becomes more independent of direct Fiat assembly, while Pegaso remains important in trucks and buses.

---

# XV. Automotive electronics in 1975

The automobile is not yet a computer on wheels.

Common or emerging electronic features include:

- transistorized radios;
- electronic ignition;
- alternator regulation;
- electric fuel pumps;
- automatic climate control in luxury cars;
- intermittent wipers;
- warning-light test systems;
- cruise control in American cars;
- electronic tachometers;
- fuel-injection control on premium models;
- anti-lock brake trials;
- simple diagnostic connectors in experimental fleet vehicles.

Rare or experimental features include:

- digital speed display;
- computerized trip calculation;
- automatic route guidance;
- voice warnings;
- general-purpose engine computers.

Mechanical fuel injection remains important. Fully digital engine management belongs principally to later 1970s and 1980s production.

## Safety becomes normal engineering

By 1975, a modern car increasingly includes:

- three-point belts;
- head restraints;
- dual-circuit brakes;
- collapsible steering columns;
- laminated glass;
- controlled deformation;
- better door latches;
- padded interiors;
- child-restraint mounting guidance.

Germany, Sweden and Britain frame these as engineering duty. America frames them through a more contentious mixture of federal rules, insurance, medicine and consumer activism. Japan frames them around dense traffic, manufacturing discipline and export reputation.

Katharina’s German public-health role could also make child seats, rear-door locks and family-car safety more politically visible than they otherwise would be.

---

# XVI. Pollution without a general environmental revolution

The early 1970s still do not produce a single global environmental movement equivalent to ours.

But local pollution problems become impossible to ignore:

- lead exposure;
- urban smog;
- industrial mercury and chemical poisoning;
- dead rivers;
- sewage;
- oil spills;
- factory smoke;
- noise;
- roadside litter.

The response remains divided among four administrative languages:

- public health;
- industrial efficiency;
- resource protection;
- urban beauty and cleanliness.

## Automotive consequences

Catalytic converters are not necessarily mandated across entire national fleets on the historical American schedule.

Instead, different systems compete:

- lean-burn engines;
- improved carburetion;
- fuel injection;
- exhaust-gas control;
- lower-lead fuel in major cities;
- fleet inspection;
- cleaner buses and taxis.

This means leaded fuel and high emissions probably persist longer in several blocs. The health consequences also persist longer.

## Packaging and disposability

The weaker ecological movement permits faster expansion of:

- disposable bottles;
- synthetic packaging;
- plastic bags;
- aerosol products;
- disposable household and medical goods.

Germany and parts of Europe retain bottle deposits and reusable containers because of resource discipline and established distribution systems, not environmental activism.

Japan uses enormous quantities of packaging in its urban distribution system but also standardizes returnable commercial crates and containers.

America develops the strongest throwaway consumer culture.

---

# XVII. Design and the look of 1975

The exuberant “rocket fin” aesthetic is fading.

The defining visual language of 1975 is the **control panel**.

Typical features include:

- dark glass or plastic display windows;
- red, orange or green numerical lights;
- brushed metal;
- wood veneer;
- rectangular push buttons;
- labeled function groups;
- modular components;
- prominent model numbers;
- geometric sans-serif lettering.

National variations remain recognizable.

## Germany

Restrained controls, legible typography, muted surfaces and visible functional order. A product is meant to look engineered and serviceable.

## Japan

Compactness, dense but organized controls, small displays, folding or multifunction components and careful packaging.

## America

Larger objects, prominent styling, woodgrain, colored plastics, chrome details, more convenience controls and stronger annual product differentiation.

## Britain

Practical cases, modular repair, restrained styling and a continuing mixture of older domestic furniture with modern equipment.

## Latin bloc

Cleaner sculptural forms, bright materials, elegant controls and stronger integration between furniture, office machine and appliance design.

The early 1970s household therefore does not look like a spaceship. It contains several objects designed to look as though they belong in a control room.

---

# XVIII. Germany, 1970–1975

Germany’s consumer world is shaped by the difference between the Moon landing and the Raumhafen.

The 1970 landing creates celebration, souvenir production and color-television sales.

The 1975 station creates continuing product lines:

- educational models;
- tracking equipment;
- technical magazines;
- station-themed toys;
- household designs borrowing docking and modular imagery;
- public exhibitions;
- training simulators;
- engineering scholarships.

The station requires continuous support, software, certification and supply rather than a single burst of production. That reinforces Wolfgang’s preference for infrastructure over one-off spectacle. fileciteturn20file4

## German consumer position by 1975

A prosperous household can plausibly possess:

- color television;
- cassette or reel-to-reel equipment;
- refrigerator-freezer;
- automatic washing machine;
- telephone;
- one family car;
- several radios;
- camera;
- electric kitchen appliances.

A working-class family is more likely to possess the same categories in older, rented, smaller or monochrome forms.

Germany’s first hobbyist computers remain confined to engineers, radio clubs, universities and technically approved youth groups. The ordinary civilian home-computer market does not open fully until Kurzplan 77.

## Thorium’s limited consumer impact

Germany begins its Thorium Programme in 1971, with experimental fuel-cycle work in 1973–74 and a demonstration decision in 1975. It remains a strategic second road beside the expanding uranium fleet, not a source of miraculous household energy. fileciteturn21file4

Its near-term civilian effects are:

- reactor engineering jobs;
- materials and chemical research;
- district-heating demonstrations;
- industrial-process heat studies;
- state advertising about long-term energy security.

The electricity coming from the wall is not meaningfully “thorium-powered” for the normal German family yet.

---

# XIX. Japan, 1970–1975

This is probably Japan’s most important pre-home-computer consumer interval.

The combination of calculators, quartz timekeeping, cameras, compact televisions, cassette equipment, vending, motorcycles and small cars gives Japan an identifiable material culture of **portable precision**.

## Principal firms

- **Totsuko:** recording, compact televisions, professional video and portable electronics.
- **Matsushita/National:** mass appliances, televisions, radios, batteries and dealer networks.
- **Sharp and Casio-type firms:** calculators, numerical displays and office electronics.
- **Seiko:** quartz timing.
- **Canon, Nikon and Minolta:** increasingly electronic cameras.
- **Toyota and Nissan/Datsun:** mass vehicles and institutional fleets.
- **Prince:** prestige and technical vehicles.
- **Honda:** motorcycles, small engines and compact automobiles.
- **Toyo Kogyo:** rotary-engine niche.
- **Nintendo and domestic amusement firms:** toys and early electronic games, as a plausible working direction rather than fully locked company canon.

## Product localization

Japan’s primary market remains its sphere.

A calculator sold in Nanjing may use Chinese-character labeling and the same numeric model code as the Japanese version. A Philippine unit uses Roman letters and English or Filipino instructions. Korea and Formosa receive more directly Japanized models.

This creates extra engineering work in:

- keyboards;
- printed legends;
- manuals;
- character displays;
- packaging;
- service training.

The Imperial Network Reconstruction Plan beginning in 1972 also strengthens the transaction and distribution systems beneath this market. fileciteturn20file1

## The Biak failure and quality policy

The 1974 heavy-booster failure and procurement scandal remove Tanaka and bring Miki’s rectification government. fileciteturn21file13

Its consumer consequence should be indirect but real.

The resulting reviews emphasize:

- supplier traceability;
- conflict-of-interest controls;
- independent testing;
- clearer responsibility for subcontractors;
- certification records.

Japanese firms can use the scandal to strengthen an already developing public reputation for reliability. The state’s argument is not that failure is shameful enough to conceal forever. It is that every failure must produce a responsible procedural correction.

---

# XX. Britain, 1970–1975

By 1975 Britain declares physical reconstruction essentially complete. Its Sterling Commonwealth system is prosperous and technically formidable, while remaining dependent on shipping, Dominion cooperation and strategic public corporations. fileciteturn21file16

The 1974 Kuwait victory gives the period a distinct ending. Britain’s computing, communications, logistics and Commonwealth transport systems have proved useful in war rather than existing only as peacetime administrative projects.

## Consumer consequences

- Color television sales rise around the Kuwait coverage and victory.
- Television rental remains important.
- Packet and data systems improve banking, shipping and government service without becoming home internet.
- Containerization and computerized manifests lower some imported-goods costs.
- Commonwealth package tourism expands.
- British medical technology reaches regional hospitals through the public system.
- The vehicle industry remains troubled despite the national strategic recovery.

Temporary fuel controls during Operation Covenant are plausible, but a long global oil crisis is not necessary. The lasting political lesson is British dependence on the Gulf, not a universal rejection of large cars or petroleum.

Britain’s strongest consumer brands remain those supported by reliable service:

- Land-Rover;
- British radio and television firms;
- pharmaceutical and medical suppliers;
- household-appliance rental networks;
- department and cooperative retail systems.

---

# XXI. The United States, 1970–1975

America remains the world’s broadest private consumer market.

Its distinctive early-1970s developments include:

- bank cards and automated tellers;
- electronic calculators;
- arcade and home television games;
- microwave ovens;
- air conditioning;
- large and compact automobile markets;
- instant photography;
- expanding color television;
- suburban and regional shopping centers;
- hobbyist electronics.

The 1974 automated orbital-spaceplane mission accelerates automatic landing, digital flight control, navigation and later civilian avionics. fileciteturn21file15

Those benefits reach airlines first through:

- improved inertial navigation;
- automated approach and landing;
- fault monitoring;
- cockpit displays;
- more sophisticated flight simulators.

They do not create self-driving family automobiles.

## Political effects on media technology

The fusion of Democrats and Republicans, the 1972 election, *The Last Republic*, Rockwell’s assassination and Buchanan’s response make television, film and tape central political media.

The censorship panic around *The Last Republic* also teaches filmmakers that fictional media can produce consequences beyond entertainment. fileciteturn21file15

Cassette speeches, television addresses, recorded sermons and political films become part of the 1976 campaign environment. Buchanan’s rise is not merely a product of rallies. It is a product of a mature national audiovisual system.

---

# XXII. The imperial and colonial gap

The same technologies reach colonial territories very unevenly.

## Eastern Reichskommissariats

The German-controlled logistical spine gains:

- electronic rail scheduling;
- pipeline telemetry;
- computerized commodity records;
- improved German settler television;
- automated plant controls;
- standardized identification.

Native rural households do not receive equivalent access.

An industrial service-estate family may gain:

- a television in the plant club;
- refrigerator access through a cooperative;
- better clinic equipment;
- a motorcycle;
- technical schooling.

A remote peasant household may still possess only a radio, bicycle and hand tools.

## Mittelafrika

The technology contrast is more extreme.

Kongostadt, Katanga, Kribi and strategic corridors possess:

- MOSAIK administration;
- modern radio;
- jet transport;
- computer centers;
- medical facilities;
- launch tracking;
- imported German vehicles.

Large rural regions remain dependent on:

- river transport;
- manual agriculture;
- local intermediaries;
- limited electrification.

The Raumhafen is partly supported through this unequal imperial geography. Its positive technical achievement and coercive material foundation coexist. fileciteturn21file2

## Japanese sphere

Urban China, Korea, Formosa, Singapore, the Philippines and major Southeast Asian cities receive Japanese:

- radios;
- televisions;
- motorcycles;
- calculators;
- cameras;
- appliances;
- vending equipment;
- office systems.

Advanced design and component manufacture remain concentrated in Japan and favored industrial regions. Local assembly spreads more widely than local technological sovereignty.

---

# XXIII. Latin-bloc handoff

The parallel Latin chat should keep six developments in view.

1. **Olivetti becomes the bridge between office computing and consumer design.** Its calculators and desktop systems make electronics look intelligible rather than military.

2. **Fiat and SEAT expand mass family motorization**, while Alfa Romeo, Ferrari, Maserati and Lancia preserve technical prestige.

3. **Pirelli becomes strategically important** through radials, motorsport and high-speed tires.

4. **Italian and Occitan television and video systems compete in the standards market**, particularly in Latin America, North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean.

5. **Mediterranean package tourism becomes a major systems industry**, requiring reservation computing, air conditioning, hotel equipment, buses, ferries, payment systems and multilingual broadcasting.

6. **Occitania’s Prolog and control-electronics culture has little direct household effect before 1975**, but it strengthens industrial automation, aerospace systems and intelligent office-machine research.

---

# Working 1975 baseline

I would establish the following as the material-culture snapshot at the end of 1975:

1. **Color television is established but not universal.**

2. **The cassette is the dominant portable recording technology in much of Europe and Asia**, with America retaining greater format competition.

3. **Institutional video recording is normal; household video is rare and expensive.**

4. **Pocket calculators are a real consumer category.** Scientific and programmable models remain expensive.

5. **Quartz watches are spreading downward from luxury**, while digital watches remain conspicuous modern objects.

6. **Automatic-exposure cameras are mainstream.** Autofocus is still experimental or exceptional.

7. **Arcade games and dedicated television games exist before the personal-computer market.**

8. **The first hobby computers appear in 1975**, but they are kits for enthusiasts rather than family appliances.

9. **Barcodes or comparable machine-readable product systems enter warehouses and large retailers under competing bloc standards.**

10. **Automated banking, cards and terminals are spreading**, while cash and checks remain dominant.

11. **Satellites improve television, long-distance communications and weather forecasting**, not private mobile communication.

12. **Household appliances contain more automatic sequencing**, but most are electromechanical or narrowly electronic rather than generally programmable.

13. **Medical imaging, monitoring and laboratory automation become visible marks of an advanced hospital.**

14. **No common global oil shock forces universal automotive convergence.** American large cars survive longer; European and Japanese efficiency follows separate structural pressures.

15. **The rotary engine remains a respected niche contender**, especially in Germany and Japan, rather than collapsing immediately.

16. **Passenger diesel, turbocharging, fuel injection, radial tires, disc brakes and safety engineering matter more than exotic turbine cars.**

17. **Automotive electronics remain limited to specific functions.** Digital dashboards and computerized navigation remain demonstrations.

18. **Pollution is regulated as health, sanitation and industrial discipline**, not yet as a comprehensive anti-growth environmental philosophy.

19. **Disposable plastics and packaging grow more rapidly than in a strongly ecological 1970s**, though returnable containers survive where they are economically efficient.

20. **The visual future has shifted from rocket fins to control panels:** dark display windows, glowing numbers, modular units and function-labeled buttons.

21. **Germany’s defining consumer-space event is the Raumhafen, not the Moon landing.** The harbor makes aerospace a continuing industrial service.

22. **Japan’s defining consumer identity is portable precision:** calculator, quartz watch, compact recorder, camera, motorcycle and small automobile.

23. **America stands at the threshold of the private programmable market.**

24. **Britain has turned reconstruction technology into a functioning high-value Commonwealth economy.**

The defining household object of 1975 is probably not the computer.

It is the device that contains a small computer without telling its owner that the age of personal computing has already begun.

---
