Yes. This means that by 2000, Japanese politics does **not** interpret corporate domination as an unresolved constitutional crisis.

The conflict of the 1970s and 1980s has been retrospectively rewritten as a successful adjustment period. The national governments tested their jurisdiction, the zaibatsu defended the economic system, Tokyo prevented either side from becoming reckless, and the eventual result appears stable, prosperous, and broadly accepted.

> **What an outside critic describes as corporate capture, the Japanese political establishment describes as mature coordination.**

This supersedes the implication that a substantial anti-zaibatsu political counter develops inside Japan. Individual politicians may oppose a particular company, condemn a particular scandal, or demand a particular reform. But by the end of the century, almost no serious Japanese governing faction concludes that the corporate organization of the Sphere is itself the problem.

## Tokyo sees the results, not the machinery

From the perspective of a Japanese minister in 2000, the Co-Prosperity Sphere appears to have achieved most of its stated objectives.

There has been:

- no general rebellion against Japanese leadership;
- no successful foreign penetration of the associated states;
- no return to the major wars of the 1940s and 1950s;
- continued economic growth;
- expanding consumer access;
- functioning rail, shipping, energy, banking, and communications systems;
- greater use of national languages;
- visibly local governments and political parties;
- increasing numbers of local engineers, managers, and professionals.

Japanese companies remain dominant, but the associated populations are not standing outside their factories with rifles. Local governments continue signing contracts. Local politicians campaign on development projects negotiated with Japanese houses. National elites send their children to Japanese technical universities and then return to manage corporate subsidiaries.

To Tokyo, that looks like cooperation.

The machinery behind it is harder to see:

- opposition parties denied favorable credit;
- broadcasters quietly dependent upon corporate advertising;
- ministers selected through patronage networks;
- national companies prevented from reaching strategic scale;
- laws softened before they are introduced;
- technically legal campaign assistance;
- investment directed toward politically cooperative provinces;
- local elites whose careers depend upon Japanese corporate approval.

Japanese politicians normally encounter the finished agreement, not the months of pressure that produced it.

A port opens. A railway is modernized. A hostile minister resigns. A more cooperative cabinet takes office. Trade rises the following year.

The political conclusion is obvious from Tokyo:

> The system resolved another dispute.

## The invisible cost is the alternative that never develops

The corporate system’s greatest political advantage is that much of its cost is counterfactual.

A Japanese minister can see:

- the factory that Mitsubishi built;
- the jobs that Mantetsu supports;
- the power station financed by a Japanese bank;
- the software network maintained from Tokyo;
- the politician who successfully delivered these projects.

He cannot easily see:

- the Manchukuoan corporation that never became large enough to compete;
- the Filipino technology company denied the credit needed to expand;
- the Vietnamese program abandoned because Japanese licensing was cheaper;
- the policy a minister never proposed because his advisers warned that investment would flee;
- the political candidate who never became viable because no major sponsor supported him.

The companies can always point to something real that they created.

Their critics must point to something that might have existed under a different arrangement.

That is a much harder political argument.

## Scandals are treated as breaches of method

When a corporate scandal breaks, the dominant Japanese interpretation is not:

> “The zaibatsu should not be influencing associated-state politics.”

It is:

> “This company influenced politics carelessly, illegally, or too visibly.”

The offense is usually one of method:

- undisclosed payments;
- an embarrassingly direct instruction to a minister;
- falsified accounts;
- coercion that became publicly obvious;
- manipulation of a public investigation;
- excessive pressure causing unrest;
- conduct that damages Japan’s reputation;
- a local executive who failed to maintain plausible separation between company and government.

Japanese politicians condemn the scandal because the company has embarrassed the system.

They may require:

- resignations;
- repayment;
- new disclosure rules;
- a temporary suspension from public contracts;
- prosecution of a few executives;
- restructuring of a subsidiary;
- compensation to the affected government.

But the underlying development project normally survives. Another executive takes over. The corporate group remains. The associated government signs a revised agreement.

The lesson is not that the direction was wrong.

The lesson is that the company should have been more careful.

> **A scandal is a rotten branch, not evidence of a rotten tree.**

In some cases, Japanese officials may privately admire what the company achieved while condemning how it achieved it.

## Corporate sponsorship becomes a normal public institution

By the 1990s, corporate political support is no longer understood solely as bribery.

It has been converted into respectable categories:

- development sponsorship;
- civic partnership;
- technical education;
- policy research;
- electoral information;
- national modernization;
- public-private coordination;
- commercial consultation;
- leadership training.

A Mitsubishi foundation funds an institute studying Philippine port policy. Mitsui sponsors a conference on Mekong agricultural markets. Mantetsu provides transport data to Manchukuoan parliamentary committees. A Japanese bank finances a nonpartisan school for municipal officials.

These institutions do real work. Their research can be excellent. Their scholarships produce competent people. Their development programs improve communities.

They also establish the boundaries within which respectable policy is discussed.

A politician does not need to receive secret instructions. He has spent twenty years moving through institutions where everyone agrees that:

- Japanese capital is indispensable;
- ownership stability is necessary;
- nationalization would endanger growth;
- corporate confidence must be protected;
- reform must proceed gradually;
- economic nationalism is acceptable only when it remains interoperable with the Japanese system.

By the time he becomes a minister, the corporate position feels less like an external demand than professional common sense.

## The bureaucracy and corporate world merge socially

Japan’s ministries and great companies remain legally distinct. Socially and professionally, the distinction becomes increasingly difficult to maintain.

Officials rotate through:

- ministries;
- economic boards;
- corporate advisory positions;
- Japanese banks;
- associated-state development missions;
- policy institutes;
- imperial standards councils;
- university posts;
- retirement appointments.

Corporate experts are seconded into government commissions. Retired officials join company boards. Younger civil servants depend upon corporate statistics and technical reports. Politicians employ advisers trained by corporate foundations.

The result is not that the zaibatsu command every ministry.

Rather, the state and corporations develop the same assumptions, professional vocabulary, and definition of competent policy.

Tokyo can still punish a company. But the officials designing the punishment may have spent their careers working alongside that company, may depend upon it to implement the next development plan, and may expect to serve on an industrial board after retirement.

This creates a strong presumption in favor of correction rather than confrontation.

## Why there is no major Japanese political counter

A durable anti-corporate movement would need to persuade Japanese voters and institutions that the zaibatsu are damaging Japan.

By 2000, that argument is difficult to sustain.

The corporations provide Japan with:

- high employment;
- technological prestige;
- export markets;
- secure resource access;
- shipping and industrial capacity;
- influence throughout the Sphere;
- political stability abroad;
- consumer goods at home;
- pensions, insurance, housing, and education for millions of Japanese families.

Their overseas political machinery appears to reduce the need for direct Japanese coercion. Associated states remain aligned without frequent military intervention. Local politicians publicly defend cooperation. The Sphere functions with less visible Japanese command than it did in the 1950s.

From the Japanese perspective, the companies have solved a difficult imperial problem:

> They have made Japanese predominance operate through apparently voluntary local politics.

A domestic politician who attacks that arrangement risks being accused of endangering:

- Japanese jobs;
- retirement savings;
- national security;
- access to oil and minerals;
- associated-state stability;
- the wider peace of Asia.

So reformist Japanese politicians normally demand **better corporate conduct**, not weaker corporate power.

They want:

- cleaner accounts;
- less embarrassing patronage;
- stricter internal discipline;
- more cultural sensitivity;
- better treatment of local workers;
- clearer separation between public and private funds;
- greater consultation with associated governments.

They do not demand the surrender of Japanese ownership or the creation of nationally independent economies.

The consensus becomes:

> **The zaibatsu must exercise their authority responsibly because their authority is necessary.**

## Complaints from associated states reinforce the Japanese interpretation

The associated states continue to complain, but those complaints are absorbed into ordinary Sphere politics.

Manchukuo demands greater jurisdiction over Mantetsu. The Philippines asks for more local management. Vietnam asks for technology transfer. Siam objects to a Japanese banking practice. An Indonesian government demands a larger share of petroleum revenue.

Negotiations follow. Some concessions are made. The governments remain in the system.

Japanese politicians take this as evidence that the arrangement is functioning.

They do not necessarily recognize that the associated states are often negotiating over the terms of a dependency they cannot escape.

To Tokyo, the fact that Manchukuo can protest Mantetsu demonstrates Manchukuoan sovereignty.

To Manchukuoan nationalists, the fact that the protest never alters Mantetsu’s controlling ownership demonstrates the limit of that sovereignty.

Both observations are true. Japanese politics emphasizes the first.

## The local corporate political machine looks like consent

By 2000, corporate sponsorship has been operating long enough that the politicians supported by Japanese firms are no longer obviously foreign clients.

They are:

- Manchukuoan nationalists;
- Filipino Catholics;
- Siamese royalists;
- Vietnamese developmentalists;
- Cambodian monarchists;
- Chinese provincial conservatives;
- Indonesian commercial politicians.

They speak their own languages and represent genuine domestic constituencies. Many sincerely believe that Japanese corporate partnership is the best available path for their country.

When such a politician wins an election or enters a cabinet, Tokyo does not perceive Japan as having appointed him.

Japan sees a local political leader who independently understands the value of cooperation.

The patronage system becomes especially difficult to identify because it rarely manufactures a politician from nothing. It selects, strengthens, and connects people who were already compatible with corporate interests.

The result is real local politics within a narrow economic boundary.

## The emperor and court have little reason to oppose it

The zaibatsu remain careful not to challenge the emperor, the imperial household, or Japan’s ultimate military authority.

They sponsor:

- imperial charities;
- cultural preservation;
- disaster relief;
- national commemorations;
- religious and historical restoration;
- visits throughout the Sphere;
- development projects announced beneath imperial patronage.

This allows the court to interpret corporate power as an instrument through which Japan discharges its duties.

The companies may privately understand the Sphere as serving Japanese interests. Publicly, they build the schools, ports, hospitals, railways, and communications systems through which guardianship becomes visible.

As long as they remain outwardly loyal and do not undermine the emperor’s symbolic headship, there is no natural court-versus-corporation confrontation.

## Cyberpunk remains cultural criticism, not governing analysis

This also clarifies the status of Japanese cyberpunk.

Writers, filmmakers, animators, and critics can depict corporations as states within the state. They can show a ministry unable to control the computer network it nominally owns, or a worker whose housing, body, identity, and memories all belong to his employer.

Some of these stories are closer to reality than Japanese politicians admit.

But the mainstream political response is similar to the way people respond to any exaggerated speculative fiction:

- the story identifies a genuine danger;
- the artist has intensified it for dramatic effect;
- stronger ethics and oversight are needed;
- the actual system remains fundamentally sound.

Dissident commercial cyberpunk is therefore tolerated, debated, and occasionally condemned, but it does not define mainstream Japanese understanding. Existing Japanese cultural material already places this branch at the edge of respectability: its fear is that a rational, efficient system may become morally complete in its own estimation, while the political mainstream continues to regard the system as successful. fileciteturn30file0

A politician might praise a corporate dystopian film and still vote for the next Mantetsu development package.

He sees the film as a warning against excess, not an argument against the corporate order.

# The Japanese retrospective by 2000

The official or semi-official history of the corporate conflicts would divide them into three stages.

## The difficult adjustment, 1970–1985

Associated governments asserted greater jurisdiction. Japanese companies defended investment and technical continuity. Several disputes became unnecessarily bitter.

The lesson taught in Tokyo is that both sides had legitimate concerns and lacked mature procedures.

## The partnership settlement, 1985–1992

Taxation, labor law, cultural protection, local management, and public jurisdiction were clarified. Japanese ownership remained secure. Corporate sponsorship became more transparent and institutionalized.

The political interpretation is that the Sphere moved from postwar dependency into mature association.

## The stable system, 1992–2000

Governments, corporations, courts, and common institutions learned how to cooperate. Economic disruption declined. Political turnover no longer threatened essential investment. Associated-state elites participated more fully in management.

The Japanese conclusion is that the original promise of Co-Prosperity has finally been fulfilled.

An outside observer might describe the same sequence as:

> national resistance → selective concessions → corporate capture.

Tokyo describes it as:

> conflict → accommodation → partnership.

## What a Japanese politician believes in 2000

A mainstream Japanese politician does not normally think:

> “The zaibatsu secretly rule Asia.”

He thinks:

> “Japanese enterprise gives the Sphere the continuity that politics alone cannot provide.”

He knows companies influence elections. He knows they cultivate ministers. He knows associated governments have limited room to move against them.

But he also sees functioning trains, expanding trade, stable governments, Japanese security, and local politicians voluntarily defending the arrangement.

His objection arises only when the method becomes crude enough to damage those results.

A company may be greedy. An executive may be corrupt. A subsidiary may mistreat workers. A political payment may be illegal.

But none of these proves that corporate predominance is mistaken.

They prove that powerful institutions require proper discipline.

# Revised canon

> **By 2000, the Japanese political establishment broadly regards the zaibatsu-centered organization of the Co-Prosperity Sphere as the successful mature form of Japanese leadership. Japanese firms dominate finance, transport, technology, trade, and strategic industry, but associated governments continue to function, local politicians cooperate with the system, and the Sphere remains peaceful and economically productive. These results are treated as evidence that corporate predominance has become mutually beneficial rather than evidence that national economic sovereignty has been lost.**

> **Corporate scandals are condemned as failures of discretion, legality, or responsible administration. They do not normally produce demands to dismantle the underlying patronage and ownership system. Reform seeks cleaner sponsorship, better cultural conduct, more effective oversight, and less public embarrassment rather than a reduction in Japanese corporate power.**

> **The zaibatsu’s political influence becomes normalized through development foundations, policy institutes, technical education, media sponsorship, campaign services, commercial associations, and personal networks linking companies, ministries, and associated-state elites. By the end of the century, these institutions are treated as the ordinary infrastructure of competent politics.**

> **Japanese cyberpunk and other cultural criticism may depict the companies as quasi-sovereign powers, but mainstream politicians interpret such works as warnings against excess within a fundamentally sound order. The political consensus is not that the zaibatsu have captured the Sphere. It is that the zaibatsu have made the Sphere work.**

The final irony is that Tokyo’s belief is not wholly false.

The system does work. It keeps the peace, moves goods, builds infrastructure, and gives associated populations a higher material standard than many plausible alternatives.

The distinction is that by 2000, the system works so thoroughly **through** the zaibatsu that Japanese politics has lost the ability to imagine the Co-Prosperity Sphere working without them.

This is one of the strongest places to combine Japan’s cultural particularism with the older imperial objective of preventing a dangerous continental or maritime rival.

The first point is that “hundreds of ethnic groups” is not an exaggeration. The region contains hundreds of named communities and more than seven hundred languages, depending upon how languages and dialects are classified. But Japan cannot create a sovereign state for every island, language, clan, or religious community. That would produce governments too small to collect taxes, operate ports, or maintain police. citeturn997325view0turn579130academia75

So Japan needs a stable organizing rule:

> **A community receives statehood when cultural distinction, geographic separation, inherited political institutions, and economic viability overlap.**

Ethnicity matters. Religion matters. Island geography matters most. But each state still needs a port, an administrative center, and some plausible revenue base.

## The appropriate number

I think the cleanest settlement produces **fifteen Indonesian states**.

Twelve is slightly too few. It forces Japan to construct several large composite countries that could eventually recreate Indonesia under another name. More than sixteen or seventeen begins creating dependent microstates with no administrative reason to exist.

The fifteen-state model does not include:

- Singapore, which remains its own city-state;
- western New Guinea, whose Papuan settlement should be handled separately;
- eastern New Guinea, which is a direct Japanese acquisition from Australia;
- Fiji, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, and the other Japanese Pacific acquisitions.

Those belong to the Papuan and South Pacific system rather than the Indonesian states proper.

“Indonesian states” is also probably not their preferred collective name. Inside the setting, **Indonesia** retains the implication that these territories ought to constitute one nation. Japanese and official language would favor something like **the Southern Archipelago States**. Foreigners, dissidents, and pan-archipelagic nationalists continue using “Indonesia.”

# The fifteen-state arrangement

The states can be organized geographically, from west to east.

## Java: three states

Java has to be divided more severely than any other island. It contains the population, administrative traditions, ports, educated elite, and political networks most capable of recreating a united Indonesia.

### 1. Sunda

**Territory:** western Java and Banten  
**Administrative capital:** Bandung  
**Principal port:** Batavia or Jakarta

Sunda becomes the state of the Sundanese-speaking west. Batavia remains inside Sundanese sovereignty but receives a special commercial charter. Japanese banks, shipping firms, insurers, and trading houses dominate the port district, making Batavia economically more international and Japanese-connected than the Sundanese interior.

That arrangement gives Sunda a valuable port without allowing the Sundanese government complete control over it.

Sunda’s economy emphasizes:

- tea and plantation crops;
- textiles;
- food production;
- light manufacturing;
- Batavian commerce;
- later consumer-goods assembly.

Its political weakness is the difference between Bandung’s national administration and Batavia’s corporate-commercial establishment.

### 2. Mataram

**Territory:** central Java  
**Political centers:** Yogyakarta and Surakarta

Mataram is a court federation built around the surviving Javanese royal houses. Yogyakarta probably becomes the principal administrative capital, while Surakarta retains a second royal and ceremonial position.

This is the most obviously traditional of the Javanese states. It possesses:

- the courts;
- classical Javanese culture;
- universities and learned institutions;
- rice and sugar districts;
- a large rural population;
- major religious and cultural authority.

But it does not control either Batavia or Surabaya. Japan deliberately denies the court federation the ports and heavy commercial system that might allow it to claim leadership over all Java.

### 3. East Java and Madura

**Territory:** eastern Java and Madura  
**Capital:** Surabaya

This is the maritime and industrial Javanese state.

Surabaya gives it:

- ship repair;
- naval facilities;
- rail workshops;
- sugar and tobacco exports;
- manufacturing;
- access to the eastern islands.

Madura retains substantial internal autonomy rather than being treated as merely another Javanese province. The state is less court-centered than Mataram and more commercial, military, and municipal.

Japan benefits from a three-way Javanese balance:

> Sunda controls the western population and Batavian hinterland. Mataram controls the cultural center. East Java controls the principal eastern port. None controls Java as a whole.

## Sumatra: four states

Sumatra is geographically too large and internally too divided to become one country. Historical Dutch administration already distinguished Aceh, Tapanuli, the west coast, east coast, Riau, Jambi, Palembang, Lampung, and other regions. Japan can consolidate these into four viable states without inventing entirely new borders. citeturn516438search7

### 4. Aceh

**Territory:** northern Sumatra  
**Capital:** Kutaraja  
**Government:** restored or reconstituted sultanate

Aceh is the strongest Islamic state in the archipelago.

It possesses:

- an old tradition of sovereignty;
- Islamic scholarly and military institutions;
- a history of resistance to Dutch rule;
- oil and plantation interests;
- control of the western approach to the Strait of Malacca.

Acehnese elites accept Japanese security and investment but resist cultural and administrative direction more strongly than most Indonesian states. Japan handles Aceh through the sultanate, ulema, military patronage, and carefully negotiated corporate concessions.

### 5. Tapanuli

**Territory:** the Batak highlands and western north-Sumatran coast  
**Capital:** probably Pematangsiantar, Tarutung, or a newly enlarged administrative city  
**Government:** federal state based upon Batak regional councils

Tapanuli prevents the Batak peoples from being placed inside either Aceh or a Malay-led Sumatran state.

It is internally diverse, but its distinctions are local rather than archipelagic. The state balances:

- Christian Batak communities;
- Muslim Batak communities;
- traditional clan and customary institutions;
- plantation and commercial districts;
- Japanese technical and missionary-era educational networks.

Medan probably does not belong to Tapanuli. It remains attached to the Malay federation and its plantation-commercial economy.

### 6. Minangkabau

**Territory:** western Sumatra  
**Capital:** Bukittinggi  
**Principal port:** Padang  
**Government:** a revived Pagaruyung monarchy or constitutional customary state

Minangkabau possesses enough cultural and institutional distinction to stand independently.

Its political order would have to reconcile:

- Islam;
- matrilineal customary law;
- merchants and overseas communities;
- traditional territorial councils;
- a revived royal institution;
- Japanese-backed modern administration.

Minangkabau becomes an important source of teachers, merchants, civil servants, and religious thinkers. It does not possess the resources to direct the southern system, but its educated elite gives it more cultural influence than its physical size suggests.

### 7. The Sumatran Malay Federation

**Territory:** the eastern and southern Sumatran lowlands, including Deli, Siak, Riau, Jambi, Palembang, Lampung, and associated islands  
**Political form:** loose federation of sultanates and provincial administrations  
**Economic centers:** Medan and Palembang

This is the least nationally coherent of the four Sumatran states, but it is economically the most valuable.

It contains:

- oil;
- rubber;
- plantations;
- tin and associated mining;
- major ports;
- the approaches to Singapore;
- dense Japanese corporate investment.

The federation survives precisely because it is weak. The sultanates, plantation districts, ports, and provinces possess enough autonomy that no single ruler can turn the oil and plantation economy into an independent regional power.

Japanese companies dominate this state more thoroughly than Aceh, Tapanuli, or Minangkabau. Medan and Palembang develop as corporate cities linked more closely to Japanese banks and Singaporean shipping than to one another.

## Borneo: two states

Borneo cannot be one state, but dividing every Dayak, Malay, coastal, and highland community separately would create unworkable microstates. “Dayak” itself covers numerous distinct inland peoples, while coastal Malay, Banjar, Bruneian, Iban, Kadazan-Dusun, Chinese, and other communities complicate any simple national border. citeturn772095search20turn772095search11

Japan therefore creates two large but deliberately federal states.

### 8. Bornean Malaya

**Territory:** Brunei, Sarawak, North Borneo, Labuan, and associated islands  
**Ceremonial capital:** Brunei  
**Administrative-commercial center:** probably Kuching  
**Secondary port:** Jesselton

This is the surviving island component of Malaya after Thailand absorbs the peninsula.

The Brunei sultan becomes the natural ceremonial head, but the state must contain extensive autonomies for:

- Sarawak;
- North Borneo;
- Iban and other Dayak regions;
- Kadazan-Dusun districts;
- Chinese commercial communities;
- coastal sultanates and chiefs.

Under the definition you established, Bornean Malaya is plainly an **empire**. It is a Malay-headed state ruling several nations rather than a homogeneous Malay kingdom.

It also carries a major national grievance. The Malay peninsula is under Thailand, Singapore is independent, and Bornean Malaya cannot plausibly recover either. It becomes the institutional refuge of Malay royal and national identity without controlling most of the traditional Malay commercial center.

Japan does not resolve that contradiction because Thailand is one of the principal powers of the Sphere.

### 9. The Kalimantan Federation

**Territory:** the former Dutch portion of Borneo  
**Administrative capital:** probably Banjarmasin  
**Principal corporate centers:** Balikpapan, Samarinda, Tarakan, and Pontianak

Kalimantan is a federation of:

- Banjar institutions;
- Kutai and other eastern rulers;
- western Malay sultanates;
- Dayak autonomous territories;
- oil and mining districts;
- Japanese corporate municipalities.

The interior possesses substantial local autonomy because no central government can administer it cheaply. The coastal and river cities contain the real state machinery.

Kalimantan is one of the most zaibatsu-dominated states because its economy depends upon:

- petroleum;
- timber;
- coal;
- mining;
- river transport;
- Japanese shipping;
- corporate port and settlement towns.

Its government is sovereign in law but dependent upon Japanese companies for almost every revenue-producing sector.

## Sulawesi: two states

Historical colonial and postcolonial schemes already treated southern Celebes, Minahasa, northern Celebes, and central regions as distinct political spaces rather than one natural unit. citeturn516438search14turn440758search22

### 10. South Sulawesi

**Territory:** the southern and southeastern peninsulas, with internal autonomy for Toraja and other highland regions  
**Capital:** Makassar

This is the Bugis-Makassar maritime state.

It possesses:

- a substantial seafaring population;
- commercial networks throughout the archipelago;
- rice and agricultural production;
- copra and fisheries;
- shipbuilding and coastal transport;
- older courts such as Bone and Gowa.

Japan treats South Sulawesi as the principal locally rooted maritime partner among the Indonesian states. Bugis merchants and sailors can work throughout the southern Sphere without the state itself controlling a unified Indonesian merchant marine.

Its greatest potential threat is not industrial. It is that South Sulawesi might become the human and commercial network through which the fragmented states reconnect.

### 11. North Sulawesi

**Territory:** Minahasa, Gorontalo, the northern peninsula, and nearby island chains  
**Capital:** Manado, with Gorontalo as an important secondary center

North Sulawesi is a more fragile federation.

It balances:

- heavily Christian Minahasa;
- Muslim Gorontalo;
- island communities;
- Japanese naval and aviation bases;
- plantation and fishing interests.

Its educational and Christian institutions give it unusually high literacy and administrative capacity for its size. Japan values it as a reliable naval frontier, but the division between Manado and Gorontalo prevents one community from defining the whole state.

## Bali and the eastern islands: four states

The Dutch grouped much of this region inside the “Great East,” but even that administration distinguished Bali and Lombok, Celebes, Menado, the Moluccas, and Timor and the surrounding islands. Japan can convert these existing regional divisions into separate protected states. citeturn516438search12turn516438search14

### 12. Bali

**Territory:** Bali and immediately associated islands  
**Capital:** Denpasar  
**Government:** federation of restored or retained royal houses

Bali is the clearest religious-cultural state.

It is:

- overwhelmingly Hindu in public identity;
- centered on court, temple, village, and irrigation institutions;
- economically dependent upon agriculture, crafts, tourism, and Japanese transport;
- culturally useful to Japan as evidence that the Sphere preserves rather than homogenizes Asian civilizations.

Bali receives more cultural protection than strategic industry. By the later twentieth century, tourism and heritage become major corporate sectors, creating disputes over whether Japanese companies are preserving Balinese culture or packaging it for sale.

### 13. Lombok–Sumbawa

**Territory:** Lombok, Sumbawa, and nearby western Lesser Sunda islands  
**Capital:** probably Cakranegara or another Lombok administrative center  
**Government:** federation of Muslim island administrations and royal houses

Japan separates Lombok and Sumbawa from Bali because island geography and religion reinforce each other.

The state depends on:

- livestock;
- rice;
- fisheries;
- local mining;
- inter-island shipping;
- Japanese development concessions.

It remains small, but it is more coherent than a single Bali-to-Timor state would be.

### 14. The Eastern Lesser Sunda Federation

**Territory:** Flores, Sumba, Dutch West Timor, Rote, Savu, Alor, and related islands  
**Capital:** Kupang

This state is Christian and customary rather than uniformly ethnic.

Its structure is necessarily federal because the islands have distinct societies and languages. Japan uses:

- Catholic and Protestant institutions;
- local rulers;
- customary councils;
- military airfields;
- shipping concessions;
- livestock and agricultural projects.

Portuguese Timor remains a separate open question. Unless later canon changes it, I would leave it outside this federation because its diplomatic settlement depends upon Japan’s relationship with Portugal and the Latin Bloc.

### 15. The Moluccan Federation

**Territory:** the northern and southern Moluccas, including Ternate, Tidore, Ambon, Banda, and neighboring islands  
**Political centers:** Ternate and Ambon

The Moluccas are too small to divide into several fully sovereign states, but too divided to function as a unitary country.

The federation therefore contains a deliberate dual structure:

- Ternate or Tidore represents the Muslim north;
- Ambon represents the heavily Christian south;
- smaller islands retain local councils and rulers;
- Japan controls the major naval and inter-island security system.

The state’s economy includes:

- spices;
- fisheries;
- shipping;
- naval supply;
- forestry and smaller plantation sectors.

Its politics repeatedly revolve around whether the northern sultanates or the Ambonese administrative class possess too much influence.

# Why western New Guinea should remain separate

I would not include western New Guinea among the fifteen Indonesian states.

Japan’s particularist argument works against attaching Papuan peoples to a Moluccan, Malay, or Indonesian political identity. Western New Guinea should instead become a separate **Papuan protected territory or confederation**, probably only gradually receiving national institutions.

Eastern New Guinea remains a direct Japanese acquisition from Australia. That creates an important future question:

> Does Japan eventually encourage one Papuan political identity across the island, or does it preserve the western associated state and eastern imperial territory as separate systems?

For the immediate postwar order, separation is more consistent. The western half comes from the Dutch East Indies settlement. The eastern half is a Japanese imperial acquisition.

Fiji, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, and the other British and French Pacific possessions belong to the same broader maritime empire but not to the Indonesian states. New Caledonia in particular becomes a major Japanese corporate mining territory rather than another Indonesian member state.

# How Japan creates the states

The important point is that the states do not receive sovereignty first and then invite Japanese investment.

The order is reversed.

## 1942–1947: the Japanese East Indies

The initial Japanese administration treats the region as a resource and logistical system.

Historically, Japan already divided the occupied archipelago into three major military spheres: Sumatra under one army administration, Java and Madura under another, and Borneo and the eastern islands under naval authority. It did not inherit or preserve one seamless Indonesian government. citeturn440758search1turn440758search7

In this setting, that temporary military division becomes the foundation for permanent fragmentation.

Japanese authorities seize or take custodianship of:

- Dutch plantations;
- oil companies;
- mines;
- banks;
- shipping lines;
- ports;
- warehouses;
- railways;
- utility systems;
- European commercial property.

The zaibatsu enter immediately because Japan’s military administration needs someone capable of keeping oil, rubber, tin, food, and shipping moving.

This is the crucial difference from the Mekong states. Japanese corporations do not arrive after independent governments have been formed. They are already operating the essential economy before those governments exist.

## 1947–1952: sovereignty after concession

Japan then forms the states in stages.

Before recognition, each state receives:

- a territorial administration;
- a court, sultan, council, or ministry;
- police and a small army;
- local citizenship law;
- a development currency;
- a treaty with Japan.

But the Japanese corporate rights are already embedded.

The new governments inherit:

- long-term concession contracts;
- Japanese-controlled banks;
- port authorities under Japanese management;
- oil and plantation companies;
- Japanese shipping monopolies;
- fixed railway and industrial standards;
- debts owed to Japanese development institutions.

The state owns the ground in principle. The company owns or operates the economic system on it.

Japan can therefore say, accurately, that the people have received independence. The zaibatsu can say, also accurately, that independence does not invalidate lawful property and contracts established before recognition.

> **The states are born sovereign after the commanding assets have already left their hands.**

# The suppression of Indonesia as a political project

This settlement cannot occur without opposition.

Indonesian national identity and political centralization were already developing before the war, and Japanese occupation historically strengthened some of the political networks that later attempted to create one republic. citeturn997325view3turn440758search21

Sukarno and Hatta therefore become major problems.

Japan can use them initially to:

- mobilize labor;
- denounce Dutch rule;
- build local institutions;
- encourage anti-European nationalism.

But their idea of Indonesia contradicts the final Japanese settlement.

Tokyo can offer them prominent positions:

- Sukarno might be offered leadership in East Java, Sunda, or a common cultural council;
- Hatta might be offered a role in Minangkabau or a Sumatran economic institution.

If they continue demanding one sovereign Indonesia, Japan cannot allow them to retain an unrestricted mass organization.

The likely options are:

- ceremonial isolation;
- house arrest;
- exile within the Sphere;
- controlled academic or cultural roles;
- detention after an attempted unity declaration.

The exact personal outcomes can remain open. The structural conclusion should be fixed:

> **No pan-Indonesian government survives the Japanese victory settlement.**

“Indonesia” becomes an opposition idea. Some people hear it as colonial centralism imposed from Java. Others hear it as the country Japan prevented from being born.

## Language

Malay remains useful as a commercial and inter-island lingua franca. A form resembling Bahasa Indonesia survives in trade, popular media, ports, and opposition politics.

But it does not become the compulsory national language of the archipelago.

Each state emphasizes its own language:

- Sundanese;
- Javanese;
- Acehnese;
- Batak languages;
- Minangkabau;
- Malay;
- Bugis and Makassarese;
- Balinese;
- local eastern languages.

Japanese becomes the language of:

- corporate management;
- advanced technology;
- inter-state technical standards;
- military liaison;
- high finance;
- major shipping.

This weakens political unity. A Bugis merchant and a Minangkabau official may converse in Malay, but the railway contract and banking software are Japanese.

# The first corporate laboratory

The Indonesian states are where the zaibatsu first learn to dominate politics without formally governing.

By the time Manchukuo, Siam, or the Philippines begin serious fights over corporate control, the southern firms have already spent two decades working through:

- sultans;
- royal households;
- port administrations;
- plantation associations;
- military governors;
- local merchant families;
- religious foundations;
- newspapers;
- banks;
- labor contractors.

The corporations do not need to invent political sponsorship in the 1980s. They refine in the Indonesian states methods they have used since the late 1940s.

## Fragmentation gives the companies leverage

A single Indonesian government might bargain with Japan over oil, rubber, shipping, and plantations as one large bloc.

Fifteen governments cannot.

If Kalimantan raises oil royalties, a Japanese company emphasizes investment in the Sumatran Malay Federation.

If South Sulawesi imposes unfavorable shipping regulations, traffic can be redirected through Surabaya, Singapore, or Bornean Malaya.

If one state insists upon creating a national plantation company, Japanese banks can favor producers across the border.

The governments are sovereign, but they compete for the same Japanese:

- capital;
- shipping;
- technical personnel;
- market access;
- insurance;
- development loans.

This creates a permanent race to avoid being classified as the difficult state.

## The different levels of dependence

Corporate control is strongest in:

- the Sumatran Malay Federation;
- Kalimantan;
- Bornean Malaya;
- the Moluccas;
- the Eastern Lesser Sundas.

These states rely upon a small number of extractive or logistical sectors.

It is weaker, though still substantial, in:

- Sunda;
- Mataram;
- East Java;
- Aceh;
- Minangkabau;
- South Sulawesi.

Those states possess larger populations, deeper local institutions, or more diversified economies.

Java can resist a company more effectively than the Moluccas. But the three-way division of Java ensures that no Javanese government can mobilize the island’s entire market against the Japanese system.

# Common machinery without federation

The Indonesian states still require technical coordination.

Japan probably creates a **Southern Archipelago Council** dealing with:

- shipping lanes;
- customs documentation;
- disease control;
- weather and disaster warning;
- fisheries;
- postal and radio standards;
- inter-island labor;
- piracy;
- search and rescue;
- shared corporate disputes.

The council is deliberately not a parliament.

It has:

- no common citizenship;
- no common army;
- no power to tax;
- no independent foreign policy;
- no authority to override national governments.

Japan chairs the strategic committees. Singapore supplies much of the finance and administrative support. The individual states implement agreements through national law.

This allows the islands to function as one economic area without becoming one political country.

# The Malayan contradiction

Bornean Malaya deserves particular attention because it carries two opposing claims.

It says that Japan liberated the Malay peoples from Britain.

But:

- the peninsula is under Thailand;
- Singapore is separate;
- Bornean Malaya itself governs large non-Malay populations;
- Japanese companies dominate much of its oil, timber, and shipping.

It is simultaneously:

- the surviving Malay national state;
- a small multiethnic empire;
- a Japanese resource client;
- a state with a permanent grievance against another principal member of the Sphere.

Japan permits commemorations of the lost peninsula but does not permit serious irredentism against Thailand.

This mirrors Cambodia’s Battambang grievance on a much larger scale.

# Development through 2000

## 1942–1947: extraction

The Japanese military and zaibatsu replace Dutch and British authority. Oil, rubber, tin, food, shipping, and military logistics dominate policy.

## 1947–1955: fragmentation and state formation

Fifteen governments receive recognition. Old courts and sultanates return where useful. Pan-Indonesian organizations are suppressed, divided, or absorbed into regional politics.

Corporate concessions are grandfathered into every independence treaty.

## 1955–1970: local consolidation

The states build schools, police, ministries, and national media. Japanese companies build ports, plantations, refineries, roads, and corporate settlements.

The contradiction between political independence and economic dependence becomes visible but remains manageable.

## 1970–1985: the first sovereignty contests

Governments attempt:

- higher royalties;
- taxation;
- local hiring;
- national development banks;
- limits on plantation and mineral concessions;
- local participation in ports and utilities.

The zaibatsu respond by playing states against one another. Their success makes the Indonesian states the model for later corporate political strategy elsewhere in the Sphere.

## 1985–2000: patronage becomes government

Japanese companies finance:

- royal development foundations;
- parties;
- newspapers;
- religious charities;
- technical schools;
- campaign logistics;
- local banks;
- political careers.

By 2000, the Indonesian states possess genuine rulers and governments, but almost no government can remain economically successful while opposing the corporate groups controlling its principal export sector.

# Working canon

> **The former Dutch East Indies do not become a unified Indonesia. After a transitional Japanese military and resource administration, Japan establishes fifteen separate associated states: Sunda, Mataram, East Java and Madura, Aceh, Tapanuli, Minangkabau, the Sumatran Malay Federation, Bornean Malaya, Kalimantan, South Sulawesi, North Sulawesi, Bali, Lombok–Sumbawa, the Eastern Lesser Sunda Federation, and the Moluccan Federation.**

> **The division is particularist but not microscopic. Japan recognizes communities as states when inherited political institutions, island geography, cultural distinction, and a viable administrative economy overlap. Smaller peoples receive autonomy inside federal states rather than separate sovereignty.**

> **Bornean Malaya is the surviving Malay state after Thailand annexes the peninsula and Singapore becomes independent. It is headed by Malay institutions but governs numerous non-Malay peoples, making it an empire in function despite its national title.**

> **Western New Guinea is treated separately as a Papuan protectorate or confederation. Eastern New Guinea and the acquired British and French Pacific islands remain Japanese imperial possessions rather than Indonesian associated states.**

> **The zaibatsu enter the region before the associated governments are created. They assume control of former European oil, plantation, mining, shipping, banking, railway, and utility assets during the Japanese East Indies administration. The later states inherit sovereignty over territories whose commanding economic institutions are already Japanese-owned.**

> **The Indonesian states become the earliest and most complete laboratory for Japanese corporate political influence. Their fragmentation allows the zaibatsu to redirect capital and shipping among competing governments, making resistance by any one state economically dangerous. The methods developed there—royal patronage, development foundations, media sponsorship, banking pressure, and political career support—are later exported throughout the Co-Prosperity Sphere.**

The basic Japanese achievement is therefore more sophisticated than simply dividing Indonesia into weak countries.

Japan creates **fifteen real national states**, gives each enough sovereignty to defend its identity, and ensures that none possesses enough economic independence to escape the Japanese companies that made that sovereignty possible.

iturn548790image0turn548790image1turn548790image4turn548790image3

Bornean Malaya is probably the **first southern-archipelago state that genuinely fails**.

The reason is not simply that its government is incompetent. The state embodies a contradiction in the Japanese settlement. Japan breaks apart the old Indonesian and Malayan world in the name of cultural particularism, but then places Sarawak, North Borneo, Brunei, and their many peoples beneath a Malay-headed national government.

That arrangement may function during the reconstruction years. It becomes harder to defend once a locally educated Bornean political class develops.

> **Japan has taught the peoples of Borneo that distinct nations deserve their own states. Eventually, they apply that argument to themselves.**

Historically, Sarawak, North Borneo, and Brunei already possessed separate administrative and political trajectories, while later Bornean politics developed durable grievances against control from the Malay peninsula. That does not dictate the alternate result, but it provides a strong foundation for a regional movement rejecting a distant Malay-centered state. citeturn520038search1turn520038search4turn520038search6

# The original Bornean Malayan settlement

Bornean Malaya is established after 1947 because Japan needs somewhere to place the surviving Malay national institutions.

The Malay peninsula has been incorporated into Thailand. Singapore has become a separate commercial city-state. Sumatra contains Malay sultanates and populations, but Japan does not want a Sumatran Malay federation claiming authority over both sides of the Strait of Malacca.

Northern Borneo therefore becomes the surviving recognized Malay state.

The arrangement probably combines:

- the Sultan of Brunei as the ceremonial monarch;
- a Malay-dominated central ministry;
- Sarawak and North Borneo as large constituent territories;
- local rulers and native councils beneath the federal government;
- Japanese defense and corporate concessions;
- Kuching as the main administrative center;
- Brunei as the court and ceremonial center;
- Jesselton or Sandakan as the northern commercial center.

The state is Malay-headed rather than demographically Malay.

Its Malay establishment controls:

- the court;
- the diplomatic service;
- much of the senior civil service;
- the federal police;
- the officer corps;
- Islamic institutions;
- the national historical narrative.

The Bornean peoples receive local councils, customary-law courts, provincial administration, and cultural guarantees. But the federal state treats these as autonomies granted by the Malay crown rather than as coequal nations possessing the state together.

That distinction produces the eventual revolt.

# A Bornean nation emerges from opposition

The revolt should not begin with one ethnic group claiming to represent the entire territory.

There is no single homogeneous Bornean people waiting to take power. The opposition contains several major components:

- Iban and other Dayak communities in Sarawak;
- Bidayuh and Melanau political organizations;
- Kadazan-Dusun and Murut groups in North Borneo;
- Chinese commercial and municipal communities;
- Christian schools and associations;
- local Muslim communities that do not identify politically with the imported Malay establishment;
- provincial officials who resent federal appointments;
- younger military officers born in Borneo.

At first, these groups do not agree on a national constitution. They agree on one negative proposition:

> **Borneo should not be governed as the remaining possession of a displaced Malay national state.**

“Bornean” therefore begins as a political identity rather than a single ethnic identity.

The older generation still says:

- Iban;
- Kadazan;
- Dusun;
- Murut;
- Melanau;
- Chinese;
- Bruneian;
- Sarawakian;
- North Bornean.

The younger political generation increasingly adds:

- Bornean.

The common identity is created by the state’s failure to distinguish between legitimate Malay cultural leadership and permanent Malay political supremacy.

## The Japanese contribution to the revolt

Japanese policy unintentionally accelerates the process.

By the 1960s, Tokyo is encouraging:

- indigenous-language education;
- local histories;
- cultural preservation;
- native administrative recruitment;
- regional broadcasting;
- ethnographic and archaeological work;
- the idea that every people has a proper national home.

A Japanese-sponsored school may teach an Iban child that Japanese leadership protects the unique cultures of Asia. The same child then asks why his country is officially Malay.

The government cannot answer merely that Malay rule is efficient. Efficiency is the language of the older imperial order. The newer Japanese doctrine claims that political order should reflect national reality.

Bornean nationalists therefore use Japanese political language against a Japanese-created settlement.

# The road to war

The crisis likely develops across most of the 1970s rather than erupting in one sudden rebellion.

## The constitutional phase

The first demands are moderate.

Bornean politicians ask for:

- an elected or corporative federal chamber;
- equal status for Sarawak and North Borneo;
- limits on Malay civil-service appointments;
- provincial control over education;
- a greater share of oil, timber, and port revenue;
- local command of police units;
- recognition of a common Bornean citizenship;
- removal of the doctrine that Bornean Malaya is principally the homeland of the Malay nation.

The Malay establishment can concede money and offices. It cannot easily concede the last point.

Without Malay primacy, the state no longer performs the purpose for which it was created.

## The charter crisis

A plausible immediate trigger is a proposed new federal charter.

The Malay government attempts to strengthen the center because it believes the state is becoming ungovernable. The revised charter might:

- place provincial police under federal command;
- standardize Malay-language education;
- restrict provincial resource taxation;
- strengthen the Brunei-centered monarchy;
- reduce the authority of native councils;
- place Japanese corporate negotiations under the federal government.

Bornean leaders interpret this as an attempt to turn an already unequal federation into a centralized Malay kingdom.

Sarawak and North Borneo assemblies reject the charter. The government dissolves one or both assemblies, arrests several leaders, and places local security forces under federal command.

This transforms a constitutional dispute into a question of national survival.

## The armed revolt

The first violence probably occurs through mutiny and provincial seizure rather than a mass rural uprising.

Local police, border units, and parts of the federal army defect. Bornean officials seize:

- provincial radio stations;
- airfields;
- government compounds;
- river crossings;
- arms depots;
- port facilities.

The movement is strongest where local institutions already exist. The interior provides sanctuary, but the decisive struggle concerns the towns, rivers, airfields, and coastal roads.

The rebel coalition establishes a provisional **Bornean National Council**. It does not immediately proclaim one centralized republic. Its initial program is federal and deliberately broad:

- dissolution of Malay supremacy;
- recognition of Bornean national sovereignty;
- protection of all resident communities;
- constituent autonomy;
- continued membership in the Co-Prosperity Sphere;
- continued Japanese bases and commercial access.

That last point is essential. The Borneans do not initially revolt against Japan. They appeal to Japan’s own stated doctrine.

# Why the Malay response becomes extreme

For the Malay establishment, this is not an ordinary provincial rebellion.

It has already lost:

- the peninsula to Thailand;
- Singapore to its separate civic system;
- political leadership of Sumatra;
- any prospect of a united Malay archipelago.

Bornean Malaya is the last state internationally recognized as the political homeland of the Malay people.

If Borneo leaves, the Malay state does not merely lose territory. It ceases to possess a homeland.

That produces a much more desperate response than the government’s material position might otherwise justify.

Malay leaders describe the revolt as:

- the destruction of the Malay nation;
- treason against the sultan;
- an attack on Islam;
- a conspiracy by Chinese merchants and Christian missions;
- a Japanese betrayal of wartime promises;
- an attempt to eliminate the only remaining Malay sovereign state.

The government mobilizes federal forces, Malay militias, royal guards, and refugee organizations. It receives volunteers and money from Malay communities in Sumatra, Singapore, and the Thai-held peninsula.

The war becomes total in political intention even though the armies remain modest by European standards.

Its characteristic features are likely:

- communal massacres;
- forced village relocation;
- attacks on river and coastal settlements;
- seizure of food and boats;
- urban expulsions;
- assassination of teachers, clerics, chiefs, and administrators;
- rival claims over mixed Malay-Bornean districts;
- large refugee movements through Singapore and Sumatra.

The objective on both sides becomes control of the population, not merely defeat of the opposing army.

# Japan’s initial hesitation

Tokyo does not immediately support the Bornean rebels.

Japan has several reasons to defend the existing government:

- Bornean Malaya is a recognized member state;
- Japan helped create it;
- the Brunei monarchy has treaty legitimacy;
- Japanese corporations hold concessions negotiated with the federal government;
- supporting secession could alarm every multinational member of the Sphere;
- Manchukuo would immediately worry about Han, Russian, Mongol, and Japanese districts;
- Thailand would suspect that Japan might later support Malay separatism on the peninsula.

But enforcing Malay victory creates a different problem.

If Japan suppresses the Bornean movement solely to preserve contracts and an inherited border, then its particularist doctrine becomes visibly conditional:

> A nation may have its own state unless doing so inconveniences Japan or one of Japan’s principal partners.

That would matter far beyond Borneo.

Tibet, Xinjiang, Mongolia, the Mekong states, the Philippines, and Far Eastern Russia would all watch the result. The crisis would indeed appear in newspapers from Vladivostok to Manila because it asks whether Japanese guardianship contains any principle beyond stability.

## The limiting doctrine

Japan eventually needs to distinguish this crisis from ordinary separatism.

The likely Japanese position becomes:

> Bornean Malaya was a postwar association created for administrative necessity. It never developed one common national people. Correcting a failed founding settlement does not establish a general right for every province or minority to secede from an established national state.

That is legally convenient, but it is not empty.

Japan can point to differences between Bornean Malaya and Manchukuo:

- Manchukuo has developed a common citizenship and established imperial state;
- Bornean Malaya continues to define itself as a Malay state governing several other nations;
- its constituent territories possessed recognized political identities before the federation;
- the Malay government has rejected a genuinely federal reconstruction.

This gives Tokyo a way to support Bornean statehood without declaring every composite state provisional.

# The three available settlements

## Enforce Malay rule

Japan could deploy forces, disarm the Bornean movement, and preserve Bornean Malaya.

This is the simplest legal answer and the worst long-term political answer.

It would require:

- permanent Japanese internal-security deployments;
- extensive repression;
- a stronger Malay federal army;
- control of Bornean schools and media;
- abandonment of the newer cultural doctrine;
- acceptance of a continuing insurgency.

The restored state would survive only because Japan had decided that Malay political need outweighed Bornean national claims.

It might preserve short-term order. It would make Japanese guardianship substantially less credible.

## Independent Borneo and Malay exile to Sumatra

Japan could recognize Borneo and direct the Malay establishment toward the Sumatran Malay Federation.

This resolves the immediate sovereignty question but creates a dangerous dispossessed population.

The Sumatran Malay Federation already contains its own sultanates, cities, and political arrangements. It would not necessarily welcome an exiled Brunei court claiming leadership over all Malays.

More importantly, the settlement would confirm the Malay fear that they have been driven from one homeland after another.

It would produce:

- permanent revanchism;
- pressure upon Singapore;
- conflict inside Sumatra;
- radical Malay politics;
- a large refugee and military-exile community;
- continuing claims upon Borneo and the Thai peninsula.

Japan would have solved one national problem by creating another.

## Borneo and a restored Peninsular Malaya

The strongest settlement is the triangular one you proposed.

It contains three linked acts:

1. Bornean Malaya is dissolved and replaced by a Bornean state.
2. A Malay state is restored on most of the peninsula.
3. Thailand receives enough authority and compensation that the change is presented as reorganization rather than defeat.

This allows every principal party to claim that it preserved something essential.

# The Bornean settlement

The new state should probably be called the **Bornean Federation**, commonly shortened to Borneo.

Because Kalimantan already exists separately, its constitution explicitly renounces claims to the rest of the island. “Bornean” describes its national origin rather than a claim to every Bornean territory.

The federation contains:

- Sarawak;
- North Borneo;
- Brunei;
- Labuan;
- recognized interior and native territories.

It is not a unitary ethnic state. It is a particularist federation created from peoples whose common national conclusion is that they belong to Borneo rather than Malaya.

## Brunei’s position

The Sultan of Brunei should not be expelled or abolished outright.

That would transform the settlement into an anti-Malay revolution and ensure permanent resistance in Brunei and the coastal districts.

Instead, the sultan loses the federal crown but remains:

- ruler of Brunei;
- protector of Bruneian Malay religious and customary institutions;
- a member of the federal council of rulers and peoples;
- a ceremonial figure with guaranteed autonomy inside the new federation.

Brunei becomes one constituent state rather than the ruling dynasty of the whole territory.

This is a serious defeat for the dynasty, but it preserves the old sultanate and avoids forcing indigenous Bruneian Malays to become exiles.

## Bornean nationality

The federation creates one Bornean citizenship while recognizing several paternal national or ethnic affiliations.

A citizen may be:

- Bornean-Iban;
- Bornean-Kadazan;
- Bornean-Dusun;
- Bornean-Murut;
- Bornean-Melanau;
- Bornean-Malay;
- Bornean-Chinese;
- or a member of another recognized community.

The state is therefore multinational in composition but national in political loyalty.

This also prevents the settlement from treating every Malay resident as a foreign colonist.

The people most likely to leave are not all Malays. They are:

- federal civil servants imported from the peninsula;
- military families attached to the old regime;
- officials and courtiers dependent upon the federal Malay state;
- recent Malay settlers who regard Malaya rather than Borneo as home;
- refugees who no longer trust the new government.

Long-established coastal Malay families remain part of Borneo.

# The restored Malayan state

The Malay state created on the peninsula should be the **Federated Kingdom of Malaya**.

It is not fully independent of Thailand.

Its domestic institutions include:

- a council of Malay sultans;
- a Malay federal ministry;
- national schools and religious institutions;
- local police;
- courts;
- taxation;
- citizenship;
- control over ordinary economic and social policy.

Thailand retains or supervises:

- foreign policy;
- strategic defense;
- major bases;
- transit rights;
- the principal north-south railway;
- restrictions on foreign military access;
- perhaps customs coordination and currency guarantees.

Malaya is therefore an associated state of Thailand, while Thailand remains one of the principal powers of the Co-Prosperity Sphere.

The arrangement resembles Vladivostok’s relationship with Japan more than an equal alliance.

Malaya exists as a country. Bangkok determines the strategic limits within which it operates.

## Thailand does not return everything

Thailand probably retains:

- the northern frontier belt;
- the Kra Isthmus and its military infrastructure;
- permanent basing and transit rights;
- some districts already heavily incorporated into Thai administration.

The new Malayan state receives enough of the central and southern peninsula to possess:

- a real territorial homeland;
- important cities and ports;
- an agricultural and commercial economy;
- room to receive returning Malay institutions and refugees.

Singapore remains completely separate.

Neither Thailand nor Japan is willing to place the imperial counting house under a newly created and politically aggrieved Malay government.

# What Thailand receives

Japan should avoid describing the settlement as purchasing territory. That would allow Thai critics to say Bangkok sold national land and Malay critics to say Japan bought their homeland.

Formally, the agreement is a **reconstruction of protected sovereignty**.

In practice, Japan compensates Thailand heavily through:

- debt cancellation;
- industrial credits;
- railway and port modernization;
- naval and aviation equipment;
- preferred access to Malayan markets;
- guaranteed Thai participation in Malayan customs and infrastructure;
- Japanese financing for refugee resettlement;
- recognition of Thailand as Malaya’s defense guarantor;
- perhaps territorial concessions elsewhere along the Thai-Burmese or Mekong frontier.

Thailand changes from direct ruler to paramount protector.

That is still a reduction in practical authority, but Bangkok can present it as a more sophisticated and durable imperial arrangement.

> Thailand has not abandoned Malaya. It has given the Malay nation domestic government beneath Thai protection.

# Who must govern Thailand for this to work?

The exact Thai prime minister remains open, but the institutional answer is clearer.

A hardline military-nationalist cabinet is unlikely to accept the settlement. It would regard the peninsula as a reward of victory and fear that surrendering direct rule would encourage Lao, Khmer, Shan, and Malay minorities elsewhere to demand similar treatment.

The compromise requires a Thai ruler or government that values:

- the monarchy;
- long-term strategic influence;
- stable relations with Japan;
- indirect rule over direct annexation;
- economic compensation;
- preservation of Thailand’s status as a principal Sphere power.

Historically, the Sarit–Thanom era created a close military-monarchical system, while King Bhumibol became increasingly important as an arbiter during major political crises. That provides a plausible institutional foundation for an alternate Thailand in which a royal-military establishment can remove or overrule a cabinet that has made compromise impossible. citeturn938415search6turn938415search8turn938415search3

The best direction is therefore:

> **The Malay–Bornean crisis helps force Thailand from a hardline annexationist military cabinet into a royal-arbitrated technocratic government.**

King Bhumibol does not personally negotiate every border article. He authorizes the change in direction, protects the new ministry from nationalist accusations, and presents indirect Thai guardianship as a higher form of kingship than permanent military administration.

The prime minister could be a Prem-like army technocrat, though the exact individual does not need to be fixed yet.

This gives Thailand its own political evolution:

- wartime nationalist expansion;
- postwar military administration;
- monarchical consolidation;
- crisis over the limits of the Thai national state;
- transition toward indirect imperial management.

# The war’s likely chronology

A useful working range would be **1973–1979**.

## 1973–1974: the charter crisis

Bornean assemblies reject federal centralization. Arrests, dissolutions, and police mutinies follow.

## 1974–1976: the Malay–Bornean War

The revolt spreads through Sarawak and North Borneo. The Malay government radicalizes. Communal violence and population displacement become central.

Japan attempts mediation while continuing to recognize the federal government.

## 1976–1977: strategic crisis

Fighting threatens major oil installations, ports, Japanese bases, and shipping routes. Malay forces begin measures Tokyo regards as politically indefensible. Bornean rebels demonstrate that they cannot be destroyed without a prolonged Japanese-backed war.

The issue reaches a full Sphere conference.

## 1977–1979: triangular settlement

Japan pressures Thailand, the Malay court, and the Bornean council toward the linked Borneo–Malaya settlement.

Japanese forces supervise ceasefires, disarmament zones, port security, and refugee corridors.

The Bornean Federation and Federated Kingdom of Malaya are recognized in stages.

# The zaibatsu during the crisis

The Japanese corporate houses initially favor the existing Bornean Malayan government.

They already possess:

- oil contracts;
- timber concessions;
- port agreements;
- corporate municipalities;
- relationships with Malay ministers and the Brunei court.

A Bornean revolution threatens every established agreement.

But the companies are also pragmatic. Once the old government can no longer guarantee production, they begin negotiating quietly with Bornean provincial authorities.

Their public position is continuity. Their operational position is survival.

A Japanese oil company may:

- continue paying contractual royalties to the recognized government;
- pay local security and labor costs to the Bornean authority controlling the field;
- evacuate Japanese families;
- request Japanese naval protection;
- prepare a new concession for whichever side wins.

This creates accusations from both camps that the corporations are prolonging the war or profiting from it.

After the settlement, most Japanese concessions survive. They are technically renegotiated with the Bornean Federation and Malayan kingdom, but Japan provides guarantees and compensation that protect the corporate houses.

The national map changes.

Japanese ownership does not.

That becomes another reason Tokyo later believes the corporate system works: the zaibatsu preserve economic continuity through a crisis that destroys an entire state.

# Reactions across the Sphere

The crisis divides the principal powers.

## The Philippines

The Philippines is likely sympathetic to Bornean self-government. Its own national story emphasizes Japanese recognition of an associated people rather than perpetual foreign administration.

## Manchukuo

Manchukuo is deeply nervous. Its government supports territorial continuity and insists that Borneo is an exceptional failed federation, not a precedent for Manchukuoan minorities.

## China

Nanjing supports cultural particularism in public but uses the crisis to criticize both Thai imperialism and Japanese inconsistency. China may offer itself as a moral voice without contributing much materially.

## Thailand

Thailand treats the matter as inseparable from the peninsula. It cannot tolerate a settlement that destroys the Malay state while leaving millions of Malays under Thai rule with no recognized homeland.

## The smaller frontier states

Tibet, Xinjiang, Mongolia, and Far Eastern Russia watch Japan’s behavior closely. The settlement reassures them that Japanese protection is not simply a promise to defend whichever government Tokyo happened to create in 1947.

# The foreign interpretation

American and German media present the war as proof that the Co-Prosperity Sphere is artificial.

They are not entirely wrong. Japan assembled Bornean Malaya for strategic convenience, and the state failed.

But the final settlement also gives Japan a defensible response:

- the war ended;
- the Borneans received a state;
- the Malays recovered a homeland;
- Thailand retained strategic protection;
- Singapore remained secure;
- no outside power entered the region.

Japan can argue that its system survived because it was capable of correcting its own founding mistake.

The American criticism that Japan cannot manage a divided multinational order would, as you noted, contain considerable unrecognized irony.

# Long-term consequences

The settlement does not create reconciliation.

By 2000:

- Borneans remember Malay rule as foreign domination;
- Malays remember Borneo as the country Japan allowed rebels to steal;
- Thai nationalists remember the peninsula settlement as an unnecessary concession;
- Bornean Malays remain caught between ancestral identity and Bornean citizenship;
- Malayan political movements occasionally demand Singapore;
- Kalimantan watches Bornean nationalism with suspicion;
- Japanese corporations remain economically dominant on both sides.

But the territorial question is settled well enough that another general war does not follow.

The Malay–Bornean War becomes the foundational example used in every later Sphere debate over nationality:

> Did Japan honor its principles, or did it improvise a settlement only after its original system collapsed?

Both interpretations remain politically viable.

# Working conclusion

The strongest direction is that Japan ultimately **does not enforce the survival of Bornean Malaya**.

It allows a Bornean Federation to emerge, but only as part of a wider settlement restoring a Malay homeland on the peninsula beneath Thai protection.

That outcome brackets the two destructive extremes.

Japan does not tell the Borneans that particularism ends wherever an existing treaty begins. It also does not tell the Malays that they must cease to possess any national state because their Bornean subjects revolted.

Instead:

> **Borneo becomes Bornean. Malaya becomes Malay. Thailand exchanges direct annexation for paramount protection. Japan pays much of the cost and guarantees the whole arrangement.**

The settlement is successful in the narrow strategic sense. It ends the war, preserves the Sphere, and gives each major national claim a political form.

But it also establishes a revealing limitation. Japan will recognize national particularism when it can fit that particularism into a new hierarchy of Japanese and Thai guarantees. The peoples receive states. They do not receive unrestricted freedom to decide where those states will stand.
