The note that I'm kind of making as we go through this is, there are a lot of various little princely states that exist all over the place. They're not solid, singular states on the same scale as Hindustan or Congress India. Rather, they are very small little states that exert significant autonomy, but the other larger states around them are so worried about each other that they aren't really working on trying to annex any of the smaller states. The Kashiwar Agency is also in the western states region, so to speak. And the Central Indian Agency is probably the one that most people would think of when they're trying to think of like, oh, the princely states. Almost all of these are independent, as they are also relatively associated with Hyderabad. Hyderabad is very powerful and is kind of the largest of the princely states, and exhibits a serious amount of influence on the central and western princely states. The TPS, which I will note is the Indian or the Telugu name for the movement. I can't remember the name of the movement properly, but it's not English name. I'm going to let you try to research and figure out what the name of TPS actually stands for, because it is in their native language. But that kind of exhibits a lot of control and kind of parallel governance inside of the central and eastern princely states. And the eastern princely states include things such as Afgara, Bamra, Hindol, etc. That's in the Orissa states region. The Chhattisgarh States Agency also breaks up. Much of the Azad Hind does kind of move in and take over spots, but again, its principal concern is the Congress India. And there is a certain understanding by the various princely states that if Azad Hind, Congress India, or Hindustan, like, beat the other two, everyone else is next. So, as much as the princely states are radically autonomous and very much insistent of their own independence, there's some general willingness to support whoever is weaker among the big three northern powers. And the communists exhibit or offer a fourth option that very few princely states are willing to really work with, because communists. But the communists effectively are usually fighting against the various princely states, which while the princely states are particularly divided and don't really work as one unanimous group, they are more powerful individually than the relatively small peasant forces or peasant revolutionaries that make up the communist branch of things. A few princely states do end up dissolving, being just outright taken over by the communists. However, that's relatively rare, in part because as soon as one or another princely state is outright taken by a communist force, the neighboring princely states now have a very clear target of who to attack. And Hyderabad is the kind of principal princely state that is willing to send forces across territory that isn't actually theirs in order to wipe out communist forces. Which creates a very odd position where, as much as they assert autonomy and independence, the princely states typically operate together and work together when opposed by one of the other four groups. This creates a very interesting tapestry throughout India. It is not a single coherent state. There is also a couple of former princely states that were annexed during the British Raj that also kind of effectively break free, as well as a few former kingdoms. This is a key thing to note, because what effectively occurs with India is a lot of it briefly returns to pre-British East India Company territories before very rapidly consolidating in a few places. And by rapidly consolidating, I mean on the scale of months or weeks, depending on how arbitrary the border system is and what the political circumstance is around that particular area. The rush out of India in 1947 is very much a mess, and it does leave a lot of relatively antiquarian politics a room to suddenly operate. But hopefully that kind of clarifies what I mean when I say the princely states. The princely states are not a federation, they are not a union, they are not even a small geographical location. They are a large number of individual rulers and states that exist all over the place, and are far from simple to address. Like looking at Rajkot or Gondal, they're not the same state, though they look like they should be because they're in the same general place. They're in the Kathiawar area. But they are independent states. And they are very insistent that they are independent states too. This also features as one of the more interesting parts about the arms shipments through the area, because in part because of how divided up and fragmented the region is, and because of the number of rulers and the likes, there is actually a very large market for military hardware. Because there's a lot of little independent states that want their own little munitions here and there.

iturn160497image0

This clarifies what “the princely states” means in the setting.

They are **not a fifth Indian bloc comparable to Azad Hind, Congress India, Hindustan, or the communist territories**. They are a dispersed political ecology: dozens of sovereign courts, protected rulers, subordinate chiefships, revived kingdoms, and treaty-bound estates occupying the spaces the larger claimant states have not been able to consolidate.

> **The princely states survive collectively without forming a collective state.**

They cooperate because they share enemies and vulnerabilities. They remain separate because sovereignty, dynasty, and local patrimony are the reason they exist at all.

# The Object 279 as an artillery-zone tank

The revised Object 279 justification works, with one important qualification.

It should not be described as able to withstand a **direct hit** from an extremely large artillery shell. A direct hit from heavy siege artillery would defeat almost any practical armored vehicle. Its intended role is to survive the environment created by a major barrage:

- heavy shell fragments;
- blast from near misses;
- collapsing earth;
- cratered and waterlogged ground;
- damaged roads;
- minefields and field obstacles;
- partial running-gear damage;
- concentrated antitank fire around a breach.

The historical Object 279 already combined extraordinary armor, a 130 mm gun, four tracks, low ground pressure, and a breakthrough role on terrain inaccessible to ordinary tanks. That makes the altered Indian rationale credible without needing the nuclear battlefield requirement. citeturn655402search1turn655402search3

In the Indian setting, it becomes an **artillery-storm assault tank**. Its curved hull is interpreted as reducing the effect of fragments and deflecting blast around the vehicle. The four-track system distributes its weight across churned ground and gives it some ability to remain mobile after limited running-gear damage.

The project still fails as a production vehicle because it is:

- too wide and heavy for many bridges;
- difficult to move by rail;
- extremely expensive;
- mechanically complicated;
- hard to recover if disabled;
- useful only on a narrow class of battlefield.

One prototype is enough.

The most flavorful arrangement would be that the **Hyderabadi Kirov émigré bureau designs and constructs it under commission for a Central Indian prince**, perhaps Gwalior. Hyderabad possesses the engineers and factory; the prince possesses the money, prestige interest, and immediate fear of a fortified-front assault.

It then becomes less a normal weapon than a dynastic strategic object. It appears in parades, participates in trials, and is kept near one especially important fortress sector. Its military value is uncertain, but any neighboring staff has to include it in planning.

That single vehicle says a great deal about the princely arms economy: a design rejected as too specialized by a large state can still find one ruler willing to pay for it.

# The historical agency map should not become the political map automatically

The British agencies were administrative devices for managing relations with the rulers. They were not federations, national states, or governments to which the individual princes had surrendered sovereignty.

That distinction matters when British paramountcy collapses.

Historically, there were roughly six hundred semi-autonomous princely kingdoms and states across British India. The precise count varies because the boundary between a sovereign state, protected chiefship, estate, and tributary territory was not always consistent. citeturn939069search12

In the alternate 1947 collapse, the agency headquarters disappear before replacement Indian institutions can consolidate them. The result is not that the Central India Agency becomes “Central India,” or that the Kathiawar Agency becomes one Kathiawar state. It means every ruler, minister, army commander, regent, and local political movement has to determine what the old relationship meant now that the British superior authority has vanished.

Some act as fully sovereign states.

Some seek protection from Hyderabad, Britain, Congress India, or another regional power.

Some are annexed within weeks.

Some accept a stronger neighboring prince as protector while retaining internal government.

Some former kingdoms or dynasties attempt restoration where a claimant, local administration, armed following, and treasury still exist. The name of an old kingdom alone is not enough.

The process therefore briefly resembles the pre-Company political map before rapidly condensing into a somewhat smaller—but still extraordinarily fragmented—system.

## A few naming cleanups

The Orissa state pronounced in dictation as “Afgara” is almost certainly **Athgarh**, also rendered Athagarh. Athgarh, Bamra, and Hindol were among the numerous states historically administered through the Orissa States Agency. The same eastern administrative world included states such as Mayurbhanj, Dhenkanal, Keonjhar, Talcher, Patna, Sonepur, Bastar, Kanker, Raigarh, and many others. citeturn939069search2

The southern administrative count also needs one technical cleanup. The Madras States Agency originally contained five states: Travancore, Cochin, Pudukkottai, Banganapalle, and Sandur. In 1939, Banganapalle and Sandur were transferred to the Mysore Residency, so late-colonial records list Travancore, Cochin, and Pudukkottai under Madras, with Banganapalle, Mysore, and Sandur under Mysore. citeturn384830search0turn384830search2

So the canon can certainly have four or more independent southern princely states inside the British-aligned system. But they should be selected explicitly rather than inherited from a supposed four-state Madras agency.

# The TPS name

The historical communist-led rebellion was commonly known as the **Telangana Peasant Armed Struggle**, or in Telugu transliteration, **Telangana Raithanga Sayudha Poratam**. It was not normally abbreviated TPS. citeturn760123search23turn349708search0

The cleanest in-setting solution is to distinguish the revolutionary movement from the state it eventually creates.

The wartime movement remains:

> **Telangana Raithanga Sayudha Poratam**  
> Telangana Peasant Armed Struggle

Once it establishes permanent government and expands beyond its original Telangana village zones, it reorganizes as:

> **Telangana Praja Samakhya**  
> తెలంగాణ ప్రజా సమాఖ్య  
> **TPS**

That translates naturally as the **Telangana People’s Federation**; *samakhya* carries the meaning of a federation. citeturn928581search0turn928581search2

This name fits the mature communist territory better than “People’s Republic.” TPS is not necessarily one centralized Telugu nation-state. It is a federation of:

- revolutionary village governments;
- Telangana districts;
- communist-controlled former princely territories;
- Bastar and central forest zones;
- allied tribal and peasant administrations;
- military regions operating under the party-army.

“Telangana” remains because that is where the revolution began and where its central party and military institutions were formed. But its later territory can include substantial non-Telugu populations with their own subordinate republics or autonomous zones.

That also gives TPS an internal contradiction. Telugu cadres may treat Telangana as the movement’s unquestioned political center. Bastar or Chhattisgarhi revolutionaries may ask why a supposedly internationalist federation still carries one regional name.

# The princely system’s three practical levels

There is no need to decide one exact number of princely states yet, because in-world governments would disagree over what counts as a state.

A useful three-level distinction is:

## Sovereign princely states

These possess their own:

- ruler;
- government;
- citizenship or subjecthood;
- courts;
- army;
- currency or banking arrangement;
- foreign relations;
- treaty network.

Hyderabad is the largest example. Rajkot and Gondal can both qualify despite their proximity and small size.

## Associated principalities

These retain domestic sovereignty but accept another ruler’s protection or strategic leadership.

They may depend upon Hyderabad, Rajputana, Gwalior, Britain, or a regional league for:

- foreign representation;
- heavy weapons;
- air defense;
- currency;
- access to a port;
- security against a large claimant state.

They are not provinces. But their ability to conduct fully independent foreign policy is narrow.

## Estates and chiefships

These preserve:

- hereditary rule;
- land and customary authority;
- local police;
- taxation;
- courts;
- sometimes a guard force.

They do not necessarily receive full international recognition. They may exist inside a larger prince’s defense system while remaining politically distinct enough that annexation would still provoke resistance.

This makes the map difficult to count. One atlas may show sixty independent states. Another legal register may show more than a hundred treaty governments. A dynastic almanac may list several hundred rulers and chiefships.

All can be correct under different definitions.

# Regional princely systems

## Hyderabad

Hyderabad is **first among the princes without being their emperor**.

Its power comes from:

- population;
- treasury;
- surviving ministries;
- industrial and military capacity;
- foreign arms relationships;
- the corridor through Warangal and Vijayawada to Machilipatnam;
- its willingness to deploy forces beyond its own territory.

Hyderabad does not formally command the Central Indian, western, or eastern princes. But it supplies:

- loans;
- military advisers;
- heavy weapons;
- aircraft repair;
- diplomatic representation;
- emergency expeditionary forces.

When a communist force destroys one small court, Hyderabad can send troops across two other states to prevent the revolutionary zone from consolidating.

That intervention is not entirely charitable. Hyderabad understands that every princely state destroyed by TPS brings the communist frontier closer to its own lands and communications.

So Hyderabad becomes the principal **security patron of princely India** while carefully avoiding a declaration that the other rulers are its subordinates.

## Rajputana

Rajputana develops closest to the pseudo-feudal arrangement you described.

It is not a unitary kingdom and probably not a federation in the modern sense. It is a **concert of Rajput courts** with a recognized hierarchy.

A plausible formal-functional arrangement would be:

- Udaipur or Mewar holds the highest ceremonial and dynastic precedence;
- Jaipur supplies the principal administrative and military center;
- Jodhpur, Bikaner, and the other courts retain wide internal sovereignty;
- common defense and external policy are negotiated through a permanent durbar.

Historically, Rajputana itself contained numerous distinct states rather than one preexisting Rajasthan government. citeturn160497image3

The Rajputana system can therefore act together against Hindustan or Congress India without ceasing to contain genuinely independent rulers.

A Jaipur commander may coordinate a regional army. He does not normally appoint the ministers of Jodhpur or Udaipur.

## Gwalior and Central India

Gwalior is large enough to become an independent military center, but the surrounding Central Indian states remain an intricate mosaic.

The system contains:

- Gwalior;
- Indore;
- Bhopal;
- Bundelkhand courts;
- Malwa states;
- smaller warrior and landed principalities;
- scattered enclaves.

Their borders are so broken that military passage is often more important than nominal adjacency.

A force may need three transit treaties to move from one friendly state to another. Arms dealers, railway companies, and diplomatic couriers therefore acquire unusual power.

This is also the best environment for one-off weapons such as the Object 279-derived assault tank. A ruler needs a weapon for one frontier, one road, or one fortress—not necessarily something suitable for a national army.

## Gujarat and Kathiawar

The western states are even more commercially fragmented.

The historical Kathiawar Agency contained roughly two hundred small princely states and estates, with Rajkot serving as the British political center. citeturn939069search32

In the alternate setting, Rajkot and Gondal remain distinct because neither accepts the argument that geographical proximity dissolves its dynasty or sovereignty. Larger states such as Bhavnagar, Nawanagar, Junagadh, and others form their own commercial and military relationships.

Ahmedabad may serve as the largest republican, commercial, or successor-state center of the western region without becoming sovereign over every Kathiawar court.

This creates a political economy built around:

- ports;
- textile production;
- banking;
- merchant houses;
- arms import;
- repair;
- transit between Sindh, Bombay, Rajputana, and Central India.

## The eastern states

The Orissa and Chhattisgarh princely regions sit directly against the revolutionary frontier.

This is where the princely system is least stable.

Some rulers survive behind fortified towns and foreign arms.

Some accept Azad Hind protection.

Some become Hyderabad clients.

Some are overthrown by TPS.

Some lose the countryside while retaining the palace, main town, and road system.

The frontier around Sambalpur and the Mahanadi is therefore not merely Azad Hind against TPS. It contains local princes, tribal authorities, communist village governments, Azad Hind garrisons, and Hyderabad-backed forces sharing the same operational space.

# The princes’ common strategic rule

The princely states do not need a shared ideology beyond survival.

Their implicit grand strategy is:

> **No one all-Indian claimant may be allowed to defeat the other two.**

If Azad Hind appears ready to destroy Congress India, several princes provide Congress with transit, intelligence, credit, or matériel.

If Congress appears likely to absorb Hindustan, they support Hindustan.

If Hindustan threatens to dominate the western and central states, Rajputana and the princes assist Congress or the Pakistani systems.

This does not make the princes loyal allies of whichever state they support. They are maintaining the balance.

Every major claimant understands that once it defeats its two principal rivals, the princely states become the next problem.

The princes understand the same thing.

That mutual recognition explains why even fiercely independent courts sometimes cooperate with rulers they dislike.

## Cooperation without federation

The princely system can maintain several common institutions without becoming a state.

A revived **Chamber of Princes**, or *Narendra Mandal*, is especially useful. Historically, the Chamber of Princes was established as a forum in which rulers could present their common interests without surrendering their separate authority. citeturn384830search19

Its alternate successor might handle:

- mutual recognition;
- transit;
- extradition;
- dynastic disputes;
- arms-purchase standards;
- railway access;
- common responses to communist conquest;
- mediation between princes.

It cannot impose taxes, command one army, or force a ruler to enter a war.

The Chamber is where princes agree that something must be done.

Hyderabad is often the state that actually does it.

# The communist–princely balance

The individual princely states are usually stronger than a local peasant revolutionary column. They possess:

- walls or fortified towns;
- trained guards;
- machine guns;
- armored cars or tanks;
- communications;
- money to hire troops.

TPS’s advantage is political depth.

It can operate through:

- village governments;
- peasant militias;
- forest zones;
- clandestine cells;
- land redistribution;
- agitation among a prince’s own soldiers.

A prince can defeat a column and still lose control of the villages around his capital.

But TPS also suffers from the princes’ fragmented geography. Capturing one state does not automatically open the whole region. It may instead place the revolution against three neighboring courts that had previously been neutral.

That gives the communist expansion a ratchet-like pattern:

1. TPS isolates one vulnerable ruler.
2. The state falls or loses its countryside.
3. Neighboring courts panic.
4. Hyderabad or another patron sends matériel and troops.
5. The communist advance stops at a newly organized princely line.

TPS gains territory in steps but rarely overruns the entire princely belt.

# Why the arms market becomes enormous

The princes create a market unlike the procurement system of a national army.

Congress India may order five hundred standardized armored vehicles.

A prince orders:

- twelve tanks;
- six aircraft;
- two radar sets;
- forty machine guns;
- a three-year ammunition contract;
- one foreign engineer to keep the whole collection working.

Another neighboring prince buys an entirely different package.

The result is not efficiency. It is **commercial opportunity**.

An arms merchant can sell the same design to ten rulers without any of them possessing enough buying power to demand exclusivity.

## The full commercial package

The successful dealer provides more than weapons.

He arranges:

- credit;
- commodity repayment;
- transport through several borders;
- mechanics;
- ammunition;
- training;
- spare parts;
- insurance;
- diplomatic introductions;
- bribery and transit fees.

The equipment may be German, Japanese, Russian-derived, British, American, or produced in Hyderabad.

The dealer’s real product is the ability to make it arrive.

## Why experimental designs enter service

A centralized government rejects a design because:

- it is too expensive;
- it cannot be standardized;
- it overlaps another vehicle;
- it would require a separate logistical chain.

A prince may accept it because he needs only eight.

That is how India acquires operational descendants of Soviet projects that historically remained prototypes.

The design does not have to win a national competition. It only needs to persuade one ruler that it is suited to his particular frontier.

This produces:

- one-off heavy tanks;
- small interceptor squadrons;
- unusual assault guns;
- imported radar with locally assembled missiles;
- armored trains;
- fortress artillery;
- bespoke royal-guard vehicles.

Many are poor investments.

A few become unexpectedly effective and are copied elsewhere.

# The political culture of princely sovereignty

The small courts are not pretending that their territory represents all of India.

Their claim is narrower and, in some ways, harder to disprove:

> “This dynasty governed this place before the British left, and no neighboring revolutionary government possesses a better right to it.”

A ruler of Gondal does not need to convince the population that Gondal ought to govern Delhi. He needs to convince it that Delhi, Lucknow, Calcutta, or Hyderabad has no right to govern Gondal.

That defensive legitimacy is often enough.

It also produces intensely local patriotisms. A soldier may fight for a state that appears microscopic on a continental map because that state contains:

- his ruler;
- his town;
- his caste or clan network;
- his regiment;
- his land;
- the court that pays him.

This helps explain why rapid conquest in 1947–48 is followed by slower borders. The obviously nonviable territories are absorbed quickly. The states that survive the first year have usually found a defensible combination of geography, dynasty, armed force, patron, and local loyalty.

# Development over time

## 1947–1949: the sovereign rush

British paramountcy disappears. Hundreds of rulers, ministers, councils, and local commanders issue declarations or assert inherited rights.

Large claimants absorb what they can reach quickly. Local wars settle obvious enclaves and undefended states.

## 1949–1956: the first sorting

Hyderabad, Rajputana, Gwalior, the western states, the southern British system, and the eastern princely belt emerge as recognizable political environments.

TPS destroys several vulnerable courts but provokes stronger anti-communist cooperation.

## 1956–1965: the balance system

The princes learn to support whichever of the major northern claimants is weakest.

The Chamber of Princes and regional durbars develop transit, procurement, and emergency-defense conventions.

During the Northern Indian War, princely support helps prevent any major claimant from converting local success into general victory.

## After 1965: fortified patrimonial survival

The princes stop expecting the Big Three to disappear soon.

They invest in:

- permanent armies;
- air defense;
- arms production;
- roads;
- water;
- fortified capitals;
- dynastic education;
- technical advisers.

Some become wealthy military-commercial states.

Others remain poor courts with one battalion and an old artillery park.

But the overall system endures because destroying it would require one Indian claimant to win the larger balance-of-power struggle first.

# Working canon

> **The princely states are not a federation, bloc, or geographically contiguous country. They are a dispersed system of sovereign kingdoms, associated principalities, protected chiefships, revived dynasties, and autonomous estates surviving across the Deccan, Rajputana, Central India, Gujarat, Kathiawar, Orissa, Chhattisgarh, Punjab, and the British-aligned south.**

> **Hyderabad is the largest and most influential princely power, but it is not suzerain over the others. It supplies arms, finance, technical assistance, diplomacy, and expeditionary forces, particularly against TPS, while the other rulers preserve their formal independence.**

> **Rajputana develops as a hierarchical concert of courts rather than a unitary state. The western states remain highly fragmented, with nearby polities such as Rajkot and Gondal insisting upon separate sovereignty. The eastern states form the most unstable princely frontier because TPS, Azad Hind, Hyderabad, and local rulers all exercise overlapping power.**

> **The princes share a balance-of-power interest in preventing Azad Hind, Congress India, or Hindustan from defeating the other two. They support the weakest major claimant when necessary, not because they accept its all-Indian claim, but because the final victor would turn next against princely independence.**

> **The communist state is formally the Telangana Praja Samakhya, or TPS, the Telangana People’s Federation. It descends from the historical Telangana Raithanga Sayudha Poratam but develops into a territorial federation of Telugu revolutionary districts, communist-controlled former princely states, Bastar and forest zones, and allied village republics.**

> **The princely system creates one of the world’s largest markets for small-batch military procurement. Arms merchants provide credit, transport, specialists, ammunition, and repairs to numerous rulers purchasing incompatible equipment in limited quantities. Hyderabad and other industrial courts become prototype and export centers, allowing experimental Russian-derived vehicles and aircraft to enter service without winning a national procurement competition.**

The princely states are therefore not leftover fragments waiting for the “real” Indian states to absorb them.

They are one of the principal reasons no real Indian state ever becomes strong enough to absorb the rest.

So if Balochistan is extended a little too far into Kandahar, Kalat very well may start attacking Balochistan just to see if they can take some territory. Sindh exists as the state on the outside of this little conflict that is independent enough that they kind of can do whatever they want. Sometimes they support Kalat, sometimes they support Balochistan. Most of the time, Sindh is selling weapons to everybody involved. The one north of them, though, in Sibi, are the Pakistani nationalists who are in a weak enough position they can't really enforce Pakistani nationalism on anyone. But that doesn't mean that they don't try. And Pakistani forces have on occasion moved in and taken Quetta, which is in north Balochistan, in an attempt to establish a urban center that they can solidly assert as theirs. There have also been instances where Pakistani nationalists will march into Harappa and attempt to take the city from, well, Khalistan. But Lahore very rarely is willing to accept that kind of encroachment. That is to kind of point out how messy the western Indian frontier is. The eastern Indian frontier has trenches and chemical warfare and, like, nation-states fighting. The western frontier is much more of a complicated mess. I will quickly correct an error in my naming of the areas. Baluchistan as a nation state exists as a combination of Makaran and Karan princely states, whereas the Kalat Khanate is in Kalat or Jahalawan, Sarawan, and Kechi locations. Lasbela is a position that Kalat occasionally takes but is technically one of the princely states that is part of Baluchistan. Chagai province is the province that Afghanistan takes that Baluchistan considers part of itself. Quetta Pishin, north of Quetta, is also a location that occasionally is taken by Afghanistan but is also one of the Pakistani locations that gets taken. The remaining components of the Chief Commissioner's province is what makes up the Pakistani nationalist combine state.

iturn366583image0

*Historical administrative map for orientation only. The alternate borders emerge from the collapse of British authority rather than following this map exactly.*

This clarifies the western frontier substantially. It should not look like a western extension of the Ganges trench system. The eastern and central Indian wars involve large successor states confronting one another across fortified fronts. The far west instead becomes a **mobile borderland war system** shaped by princes, tribal territories, strategic cities, foreign patrons, and governments whose claims are much larger than the land they actually control.

The governing model is:

> **Iran protects a coastal Baloch client. Afghanistan pushes south into the old British-administered frontier. Kalat claims the Baloch inheritance. Sindh finances whoever preserves the balance. The Pakistani rump claims nearly everything and possesses almost none of it.**

# Several historical corrections

## Afghanistan’s government

Afghanistan is ruled by **King Mohammad Zahir Shah**, not Mohammad Hashim Khan.

Hashim Khan was the royal prime minister until May 1946. His brother **Shah Mahmud Khan** was prime minister from 1946 until 1953, after which Mohammad Daoud Khan historically took office. citeturn108398search0turn108398search16turn108398search20

So the clean succession is:

- Zahir Shah as king throughout the initial crisis;
- Shah Mahmud as prime minister during the 1947 collapse;
- Daoud emerging in the early 1950s as the more assertive architect of Afghan frontier policy.

Daoud is particularly suitable for the setting because the historical Afghan government already challenged the post-1947 frontier through the idea of Pashtunistan, and Daoud later made that issue central to his premiership. citeturn971759search2turn971759search11turn971759search17

Hashim could remain prime minister beyond 1946 through a deliberate divergence, but it is not necessary. Shah Mahmud followed by Daoud gives the Afghan expansion a natural transition from opportunistic intervention to a more ideological frontier policy.

## The Baloch territories

The old British system contained two distinct political layers.

The directly administered Chief Commissioner’s Province included **Chagai, Quetta–Pishin, Sibi, Loralai, and Zhob**. Separate princely institutions included Kalat, Makran, Kharan, and Las Bela. citeturn108398search21turn108398search30

The traditional internal regions of Kalat are **Sarawan, Jhalawan, and Kachhi**. Kech belongs to the Makran region, so “Kechi” should not replace Kachhi in the Kalat list.

## Gwadar

Gwadar was historically an overseas possession of Muscat and Oman until Pakistan purchased it in 1958. It was not automatically part of Makran when British authority disappeared. citeturn108398search2turn108398search10turn108398search25

Therefore, putting the new Balochistan government in Gwadar requires one additional canonical event. The strongest route is an **Iranian-financed Gwadar transfer** during the late 1940s or early 1950s.

Iran purchases or otherwise negotiates the enclave from Oman and transfers it to the new Baloch state under conditions preserving:

- Iranian port access;
- Iranian naval and commercial privileges;
- limits on foreign basing;
- repayment through customs or mineral concessions.

That gives Balochistan its capital while making the state’s dependence on Tehran visible from the beginning.

# The five central western states

Moving from the Arabian Sea inland, five governments define the conflict.

## 1. The Baloch Confederated State

The state usually called **Balochistan** consists principally of:

- Makran;
- Kharan;
- Las Bela;
- associated coastal and tribal territories.

Its capital is Gwadar after the Omani transfer.

It should initially be a confederated princely state rather than a centralized nationalist republic. Makran, Kharan, and Las Bela have different ruling houses and local interests. Their common state exists because all three reject Kalat’s claim that they should return beneath the Khan.

The government controls:

- external diplomacy;
- the small national army;
- customs;
- common currency or banking;
- the Iranian security treaty;
- major ports and concessions.

The component rulers retain:

- land;
- customary law;
- local police;
- taxation arrangements;
- dynastic courts;
- much of ordinary administration.

This makes Balochistan a genuine national project but an administratively fragile one.

### Why Iran supports it

Iran’s support requires careful definition because Tehran also rules a substantial Baloch population of its own. A revolutionary pan-Baloch state claiming every Baloch district from Iran to Sindh would be unacceptable to the Shah.

Iran therefore supports a **bounded dynastic Balochistan**, not unrestricted Baloch nationalism.

The Baloch government must formally:

- recognize the Iranian frontier;
- renounce claims upon Iranian Sistan and Baluchestan;
- exclude anti-Iranian Baloch movements;
- accept Iranian military advisers and intelligence cooperation;
- coordinate foreign policy with Tehran.

Iran obtains a protected buffer and influence over Gwadar without legitimizing separatism inside Iran. Balochistan obtains money, weapons, fuel, officers, and diplomatic recognition that it could not produce alone.

The arrangement functions somewhat like Manchukuo’s relationship with Japan, though Iran possesses much less direct economic and institutional control than Japan does in Manchuria.

## 2. The Khanate of Kalat

Kalat is centered on:

- Kalat itself;
- Sarawan;
- Jhalawan;
- Kachhi;
- whatever neighboring districts its forces can hold or influence.

Its ruler in 1947 is **Ahmad Yar Khan**, who historically did declare Kalat independent before eventually acceding to Pakistan. citeturn108398search1turn108398search9

Kalat’s claim differs from Balochistan’s.

Balochistan says:

> The coastal and western Baloch states have united as one modern national country.

Kalat says:

> The Khanate is the historic center of Baloch political authority, and Makran, Kharan, and Las Bela are subordinate states that have broken their lawful relationship.

This makes their conflict both national and dynastic. Both claim to represent Baloch political unity. They disagree about where that unity originates.

Kalat’s central weakness is access.

Without secure possession of Makran or Las Bela, the khanate has poor independent access to the sea. It depends upon:

- Sindhi transit;
- temporary arrangements through Las Bela;
- roads through Sibi;
- arms supplied by brokers;
- occasional Afghan support.

That gives it a permanent incentive to attack outward.

Whenever Balochistan commits too much of its army against Afghanistan, Kalat attempts to recover:

- Las Bela;
- eastern Makran districts;
- roads toward Gwadar;
- strategically useful passes and wells.

Kalat rarely conquers the whole coastal state. It can repeatedly ensure that Balochistan cannot concentrate against Afghanistan.

## 3. The Afghan southern territories

Afghanistan’s initial expansion gives it control of:

- Chagai;
- much of Quetta–Pishin;
- Quetta itself during the stronger periods of Afghan occupation;
- perhaps portions of Zhob or frontier districts depending on the campaign.

The justification is mixed.

Afghanistan presents Quetta–Pishin and nearby Pashtun districts as part of the Pashtun national frontier. Chagai is harder to justify on ethnic grounds. Its value is strategic:

- it links Afghanistan toward Iran;
- protects approaches to Kandahar;
- gives depth around Quetta;
- prevents an Iranian-backed Baloch state from reaching the Afghan frontier uncontested;
- controls the Nushki and desert routes.

So the Afghan project is nationalist in its public language and imperial in its practical geography.

### Afghan administration

Kabul should not immediately integrate these territories as ordinary Afghan provinces.

The early system is closer to a **Southern Frontier Administration** under:

- an Afghan military governor;
- local Pashtun notables;
- tribal levies;
- retained municipal officials;
- military control over the railway and roads.

Quetta is especially difficult. It is a major administrative and military center with mixed communities and stronger modern institutions than the surrounding tribal districts. Afghan control there always requires a real garrison.

That is why Quetta changes hands while Chagai and Pishin remain more reliably within the Afghan sphere.

### Daoud’s role

Shah Mahmud accepts the initial occupation as a strategic consequence of British collapse.

Daoud later gives it a stronger ideological definition. He portrays Afghan control as the first stage in recovering the Pashtun lands divided by the Durand system. That increases Afghan pressure upon Peshawar, Waziristan, and the smaller frontier governments as well.

Afghanistan does not annex all of them. It uses:

- subsidies;
- road access;
- ammunition;
- recognition;
- royal marriages;
- troop demonstrations;
- border closures.

This is essentially landlocked gunboat diplomacy.

## 4. The Pakistan Emergency Government

The Pakistani state is not merely another local principality. It is a **government of national claim**.

Its controlled territory consists mostly of the remnants of the Chief Commissioner’s Province not held by Afghanistan:

- Sibi;
- Loralai;
- Zhob;
- adjoining military and tribal districts;
- perhaps portions of Quetta–Pishin during successful campaigns.

Its capital is Sibi, at least initially.

Sibi works better than its apparent size suggests because it is a transport hinge between Sindh, the Bolan approaches, Quetta, and the Punjab frontier. The Pakistan government inherits fragments of the colonial military, railway, and political infrastructure even while possessing little population or revenue.

Its political class consists of:

- Muslim League nationalists;
- displaced administrators;
- Muslim officers from the former Indian Army;
- refugees from Punjab, Sindh, Bengal, and the frontier;
- men committed to Pakistan as an idea rather than to Sibi as a homeland.

Its maps claim a country including some combination of:

- Lahore and Punjab;
- Karachi and Sindh;
- Peshawar and the frontier;
- Quetta and Balochistan;
- Kashmir;
- Bengali Muslim lands.

Its actual state is a dry inland military corridor.

That contrast makes it desperate and persistent.

### Pakistani offensives

The emergency government repeatedly attempts two symbolic operations.

One is the seizure of **Quetta**, because a state claiming Pakistan needs a recognizable provincial capital and military center.

The other is an eastward drive toward **Harappa** or another Punjabi city held by Khalistan, demonstrating that Pakistan remains a claimant to Punjab rather than merely a Baloch frontier regime.

These offensives rarely last. The Pakistan government lacks enough economic depth to hold distant territory once Khalistan, Afghanistan, Sindh, or Kalat concentrates against it.

But each temporary success keeps the national idea alive.

## 5. Sindh

Sindh is centered on Karachi and the lower Indus.

It is the least ideological of the western states and the most commercially useful.

Sindh possesses:

- Karachi;
- port and shipping infrastructure;
- banks and insurers;
- merchant houses;
- rail connections;
- repair yards;
- access to Arabian Sea trade;
- agricultural revenue from the lower Indus.

The Sindhi government has no interest in restoring Pakistan because any effective Pakistan would demand Karachi as its capital or principal port and subordinate Sindhi politics to a larger national project.

It therefore prefers a divided frontier.

Sindh’s policy is not to select one permanent ally. It is to prevent one neighbor from becoming dominant.

It may support:

- Kalat against Balochistan;
- Balochistan against Afghanistan;
- Pakistan against Khalistan;
- Khalistan against Pakistan;
- Afghanistan against an Iranian advance;
- Iran against an Afghan move toward the coast.

Most of the time, it sells to all of them.

# The Iran–Afghanistan rivalry

Iran and Afghanistan are the real outside powers of the western frontier.

Japan may recognize the region as belonging to its broad sphere by the Tehran Concord, but Japan does not manage this border directly. Iran and Afghanistan possess the nearby roads, intelligence networks, historical claims, troops, and clients.

Their competition has three dimensions.

## The coast

Iran wants an aligned government from Gwadar westward toward the Iranian frontier. It does not want Afghanistan or a restored Pakistan obtaining easy access to the Arabian Sea through Balochistan.

## Quetta and Chagai

Afghanistan wants strategic depth around Kandahar and a strong position in the former Pashtun and frontier districts. Iran sees Afghan control of Chagai as a direct threat to its client and its own eastern frontier.

## The local governments

Iran supports Balochistan.

Afghanistan may support Kalat, the Pakistan government, or selected frontier princes whenever doing so weakens the Iranian position. Kabul does not necessarily want any of those clients to become strong. It wants enough pressure to prevent Balochistan from turning north.

Neither Tehran nor Kabul normally wants a full Iranian–Afghan war.

They fight through:

- advisers;
- weapons;
- fuel;
- aircraft;
- intelligence;
- border forces;
- clients.

Direct Iranian and Afghan units occasionally exchange fire, but most campaigns remain formally wars among their protégés.

# Balochistan’s raids into Afghanistan

A permanent Baloch occupation of Kandahar or Farah would be implausible. Limited punitive raids are workable.

## Kandahar

Kandahar is the more natural objective.

Balochistan can push north from contested Chagai and Quetta routes, temporarily reaching the Kandahar approaches when:

- Afghanistan is fighting elsewhere;
- Iran supplies fuel and transport;
- Pakistani or Kalat forces are temporarily quiet;
- Afghan frontier units have been drawn east.

The objective is not annexation. It is to destroy depots, seize prisoners, disrupt roads, and demonstrate that Kabul cannot wage war entirely on Baloch territory.

## Farah

Farah is a more exceptional operation.

The practical route would run through or beside Iranian territory, with Tehran supplying staging, fuel, and intelligence. A Baloch force reaching Farah is therefore almost an Iranian proxy raid conducted under a Baloch flag.

It occurs rarely and carries a political message:

> Iranian support can bring the war around Afghanistan’s western flank.

The Baloch forces withdraw before Afghanistan can concentrate. Their temporary entry matters more than the ground occupied.

# The frontier polities around Peshawar and Waziristan

Not all of these should technically be called princely states.

The wider frontier contains several types of polity:

- hereditary princely states such as Swat, Dir, Chitral, and Amb;
- tribal agencies transformed into jirga-governed republics or confederacies;
- military chiefships;
- city-centered administrations;
- local religious or dynastic governments.

Waziristan in particular is better treated as a collection of tribal confederacies and armed districts than as one kingdom.

Peshawar may become a city-state or the center of a loose frontier government, but it cannot easily command all the surrounding highlands.

Afghanistan gains influence because these states require:

- ammunition;
- markets;
- road access;
- political recognition;
- protection against Pakistan, Khalistan, or one another.

They accept Afghan subsidies and sometimes Afghan garrisons without accepting outright annexation.

Kabul’s authority is therefore strongest along the main roads and weakest inside the more autonomous tribal districts.

# Khalistan, Kashmir, and Hindustan

Farther east, three arrangements connect this frontier system to the Northern Indian Long War.

## Khalistan

Khalistan is centered on Lahore and controls much of West Punjab.

It faces:

- Pakistan from the southwest;
- Hindustan from the east;
- Kashmir from the north;
- frontier states and Afghan influence beyond them.

Its quarrel with Kashmir should not be reduced to the idea that Kashmir is ethnically Sikh. It is not.

Khalistan’s claim is strategic and historical. It wants:

- the Jammu and Poonch approaches;
- control of roads into the mountains;
- Sikh military communities outside its current frontier;
- portions of the territorial inheritance associated with the old Lahore-centered Sikh kingdom.

Kashmir treats those claims as another attempt by a larger neighbor to turn it into a strategic appendage.

## Kashmir

Kashmir remains an independent state, with **Kotli** serving as its working capital.

Kotli makes sense as a wartime or successor capital even if it lacks the historic prestige of Srinagar or Jammu. Its location reflects which parts of the old princely state the new government actually controls.

Kashmir is often grouped geographically with the “Pakistani successors,” but it is not Pakistani in national identity or legal status.

## Hindustan

Hindustan controls Delhi and East Punjab, extending toward Amritsar and Dharamshala.

Its western military problem is therefore not one Pakistan. It is a chain of enemies and potential enemies:

- Khalistan;
- Kashmir;
- the Pakistan Emergency Government;
- the Peshawar and Waziristan polities;
- Sindh;
- Rajputana farther south.

That is why Hindustan cannot concentrate fully against Congress India.

# Nepal, Bhutan, and Sikkim

These three states form a different Himalayan system.

Nepal remains neutral and uses its independence to become the principal diplomatic meeting ground. Kathmandu conferences rarely produce permanent peace, but neither Congress India nor Azad Hind wishes to destroy the one capital where both can negotiate without visibly entering the other’s sphere.

Bhutan and Sikkim lean toward Azad Hind because:

- Calcutta is their nearest major economic center;
- Japanese guarantees can reach them through Azad Hind;
- Congress India and Hindustan offer less direct access;
- they need protection from absorption by any restored Indian state.

They remain sovereign rather than becoming Azad Hind provinces.

This produces a useful contrast.

The western frontier resolves disputes through raids, patrons, and temporary occupation.

The eastern Himalayan states preserve enough neutral or protected diplomacy that Kathmandu still hosts the fiction that a general Indian settlement might someday be negotiated.

# The style of war

The western frontier should look and operate differently from Patna.

There are fewer continuous fortification belts and more control points.

The decisive objects are:

- Quetta;
- Sibi;
- the Bolan and Khojak approaches;
- Chaman;
- Kandahar;
- Gwadar;
- Karachi;
- Peshawar;
- Lahore;
- rail junctions;
- passes;
- wells;
- fuel depots;
- airfields.

A successful campaign may advance hundreds of kilometers along one road while controlling almost nothing twenty kilometers away from it.

Armies rely heavily upon:

- motorized infantry;
- armored cars;
- light and medium tanks;
- mountain artillery;
- aircraft;
- tribal levies;
- hired transport;
- armed commercial convoys.

Heavy vehicles are useful around Quetta, Sibi, Karachi, Lahore, and the better roads. In the interior, possession of trucks, fuel, mechanics, and local guides matters more than possession of the most sophisticated tank.

The western frontier is consequently easier to penetrate and harder to hold.

A city can fall quickly. The attacking state then discovers that every road behind it passes through another ruler’s territory or within range of another militia.

# A working chronology

## 1947–1949: the Western Succession Crisis

British power disappears unevenly.

Afghanistan occupies Chagai and Quetta–Pishin. Kalat declares independence. Makran, Kharan, and Las Bela reject Kalat’s suzerainty and form the nucleus of Balochistan under Iranian support.

Sindh secures Karachi.

Muslim League officers and officials form the Pakistan Emergency Government around Sibi, Loralai, and Zhob.

Iran negotiates the transfer of Gwadar from Oman and provides it to Balochistan as the new capital and principal port.

## 1949–1955: the First Baloch Wars

Balochistan and Kalat fight over Las Bela, Makran, and the Kachhi approaches.

Afghanistan consolidates Quetta and Chagai.

Iran expands military aid to Balochistan. Sindh arms all sides. Pakistan launches its first unsuccessful Quetta campaigns.

## The later 1950s and 1960s: the Quetta cycle

Quetta changes hands or status more than once.

Balochistan conducts punitive raids toward Kandahar and, with Iranian support, occasionally toward Farah.

Kalat attacks Balochistan whenever the coastal army is committed north.

Pakistan conducts symbolic campaigns toward Quetta and Punjab.

No state obtains enough control to settle the frontier.

## After the 1960s: managed permanent conflict

The wars become smaller and more regular.

Borders are recognized diplomatically but tested militarily. Sindhi arms firms, Iranian and Afghan intelligence services, local princes, and commercial brokers become permanent parts of the political system.

## The Tehran Concord

By 1985, the Tehran Concord recognizes independent Afghanistan and the Pakistani successor states inside Japan’s broader strategic sphere. That recognition does not erase Iranian influence in Balochistan or make Japan the ordinary manager of the frontier.

Iran co-signs a system acknowledging that:

- the local states remain sovereign;
- Afghanistan will not receive an unrestricted path to the sea;
- Iran will not annex Balochistan;
- Japan will recognize the existing successor order rather than sponsor one restored Pakistan.

The western frontier becomes internationally settled without becoming locally peaceful.

# Working canon

> **The western successor system consists of an Iranian-backed Baloch Confederated State centered at Gwadar; the independent Khanate of Kalat controlling Sarawan, Jhalawan, and Kachhi; Afghan-held Chagai and Quetta–Pishin; a Pakistani emergency government based around Sibi, Loralai, and Zhob; and an independent Sindh centered upon Karachi.**

> **Gwadar does not automatically enter Balochistan in 1947. Iran negotiates its transfer from Oman and provides the port to its client under long-term Iranian military and commercial guarantees.**

> **Balochistan combines Makran, Kharan, Las Bela, and associated territories but remains internally confederal. It claims to be the modern Baloch national state. Kalat claims that the khanate is the historic center of Baloch sovereignty and that the coastal principalities are rebellious dependencies. Their war is therefore simultaneously national, dynastic, and territorial.**

> **Afghanistan is ruled by King Zahir Shah, with Shah Mahmud Khan as prime minister during the initial collapse and Daoud Khan later becoming the strongest advocate of the southern and Pashtun frontier. Afghanistan holds Chagai and much of Quetta–Pishin while exercising looser pressure over the Peshawar and Waziristan polities.**

> **The Pakistan Emergency Government claims the whole Muslim successor state but controls principally the surviving districts around Sibi, Loralai, and Zhob. It repeatedly attempts to seize Quetta and occasionally attacks toward Punjab, but it lacks the population and economy to reunify Pakistan.**

> **Sindh operates as the region’s commercial balance keeper. It sells arms, credit, shipping, repairs, and political support to competing states while preventing any one of them from acquiring enough power to absorb Karachi.**

The defining western image is not an endless concrete trench outside Patna.

It is a convoy leaving Karachi with rifles for Kalat, fuel purchased by Balochistan, spare parts ordered by Afghanistan, and paperwork issued by a Sindhi bank—while every government along the route insists that the others are illegitimate.

iturn250302image0turn250302image1turn250302image2turn250302image4

The use of cavalry works, provided it is understood as **modern mounted infantry rather than nineteenth-century shock cavalry**.

The real-world comparison you’re remembering is correct. Abdul Rashid Dostum’s Northern Alliance forces and the first American Special Forces teams used horses operationally in Afghanistan in 2001. They rode because the terrain, roads, and available transport made horses useful, then combined that mobility with modern radios, air support, and automatic weapons. citeturn797225search0turn797225search1turn797225search9

That gives the Western Indian Wars a distinctive military appearance:

> A rider carrying an AK-pattern rifle, radio batteries in one saddlebag, ammunition in the other, and a mortar section moving behind him on pack animals.

He is not expected to charge a machine-gun position with a saber. He rides to the battle, dismounts, and fights as infantry.

# The mounted war in the west

The western war system lacks the conditions that produced the fortified mechanized belt around Patna.

The states are smaller. Their tax bases are weaker. Roads are fewer and easier to disrupt. Fuel must often be imported. Armored vehicles exist, but usually in companies, squadrons, or isolated battalions rather than complete mechanized armies.

This leaves governments with three choices for moving infantry:

- walk;
- purchase and maintain trucks they often cannot afford;
- or use locally available horses.

Horses are not free. They require water, fodder, veterinary care, farriers, saddles, and remount systems. Drought or disease can cripple a mounted force almost as thoroughly as a fuel shortage cripples a truck column.

But the necessary skills and much of the supply already exist locally. A horse can also move across trails, broken ground, and secondary routes that a truck cannot use.

The advantage is therefore not tactical invulnerability. It is **operational mobility without complete dependence on industrial logistics**.

## How the mounted units fight

Western mounted forces divide into three broad types.

### Mounted rifles

These are the most common.

Mounted riflemen travel by horse, dismount before entering serious combat, and fight with:

- AK-pattern rifles;
- light machine guns;
- grenades;
- rocket launchers;
- light mortars;
- radios.

Pack animals carry ammunition and crew-served weapons. A few trucks transport workshops, medical equipment, heavier mortars, and fuel for radios or support vehicles.

### Frontier cavalry

These formations perform:

- reconnaissance;
- screening;
- pursuit;
- convoy escort;
- raiding;
- border patrol;
- suppression of isolated militias.

They may fire from horseback during pursuit or an ambush, but that is the exception rather than the principal doctrine.

### Tribal and princely contingents

These retain more personal and regional organization.

A prince, khan, tribal council, or local commander supplies a mounted regiment whose loyalty runs through its own officers rather than directly through a national army ministry.

These forces are cheap for the central government to maintain because part of their cost is carried by the locality. They are also politically unreliable. A mounted regiment that knows the roads and owns its horses can change sides with much of its combat power intact.

That is one reason the western wars remain difficult to settle.

# The remount economy

The prolonged wars prevent several regional horse populations from declining as rapidly as they otherwise might.

The Baluchi horse is historically associated with Balochistan, Sindh, and adjoining districts of Punjab. It is a relatively small regional riding horse rather than a massive European cavalry mount, which suits mounted rifles operating over dry country. citeturn463963search1turn463963search7

In setting, governments create military remount classifications rather than perfectly pure modern studbooks.

Balochistan and Kalat rely heavily on Balochi stock. Afghanistan and its frontier clients maintain Waziri and eastern Afghan riding strains, supplemented by animals traded from Central Asia. Khalistan draws upon Punjabi horses and imports from neighboring regions. Rajputana preserves Marwari and related western Indian breeding traditions.

The state becomes involved through:

- remount depots;
- subsidized stallions;
- veterinary schools;
- military purchasing fairs;
- branding and registration;
- emergency requisition.

This has a concrete civilian consequence. A rural family may breed horses principally because the army guarantees a purchaser. A commander may measure the strength of a frontier district not merely by its men, but by how many serviceable mounts it can provide after the harvest.

Raids often target remount herds. Capturing or scattering several hundred horses can immobilize a formation without defeating it in battle.

# The limits of cavalry

Mounted troops work because the western war is dispersed. They do not replace tanks, artillery, aircraft, or trucks where those systems can be concentrated.

A mounted column is badly vulnerable when:

- caught in open country by aircraft;
- forced against wire and machine guns;
- required to assault a fortified city;
- operating without water;
- separated from its fodder and remount train.

The horse also does not solve the ammunition problem. A mounted rifle battalion can move without gasoline, but its AKs, machine guns, mortars, and radios still require industrial supply.

So the characteristic western force is mixed.

A successful column may contain:

- mounted riflemen for movement and screening;
- trucks carrying ammunition and heavy weapons;
- several armored cars;
- one or two tanks;
- pack animals for country the trucks cannot cross;
- local guides and tribal auxiliaries.

The armored vehicles provide concentrated striking power. The cavalry lets that power find the enemy, move around him, and remain supplied beyond the main roads.

To a German officer, the arrangement looks anachronistic but not irrational. The oddity is not that horses exist. It is that a horse-mounted scout may report by Japanese radio to a commander whose reserve contains two Russian-derived tanks.

# The western settlement by the end of the 1960s

There should not be one clear victor. The stronger outcome is a redistribution in which nearly every state gains something important and loses something it considers essential.

## Balochistan

Balochistan eventually consists principally of:

- Makran;
- Kharan;
- Chagai;
- Gwadar and the western coast.

Recovering Chagai is an important strategic victory. It reconnects the state’s Iranian-backed western system with the Afghan frontier and prevents Kabul from holding the entire desert approach.

But Balochistan loses Las Bela to Kalat.

That becomes its principal national wound.

The government argues that Las Bela was a founding member of the Baloch confederated state and that Kalat’s occupation has separated eastern Baloch communities from the national project. Iranian maps and diplomatic language probably support Balochistan’s legal claim without committing Iran to an endless war for its recovery.

## Kalat

Kalat retains:

- Kalat;
- Sarawan;
- Jhalawan;
- Kachhi;
- Las Bela.

Las Bela transforms the khanate’s strategic position.

It does not immediately give Kalat a port comparable to Karachi or Gwadar. But it gives the state a coastal outlet, fishing settlements, smuggling routes, and the ability to develop a small commercial or military harbor.

Kalat is no longer entirely dependent upon Sindhi transit.

That allows it to purchase weapons more directly, offer concessions of its own, and claim that it—not the Iranian-sponsored government at Gwadar—is the viable center of Baloch political life.

Balochistan consequently views Las Bela not merely as lost land but as the territory that made its rival durable.

## The Pakistani nationalist state

The Pakistani national movement eventually secures most of the former Chief Commissioner’s Province except Chagai.

Its core includes:

- Quetta–Pishin;
- Sibi;
- Loralai;
- Zhob.

Quetta replaces Sibi as the effective capital once it can be held reliably.

This is a major Pakistani success. The government finally possesses:

- a recognized city;
- military depots;
- roads and rail connections;
- administrative buildings;
- an officer and refugee population;
- a territorial core larger than one desert emergency zone.

But the victory also reveals the limits of Pakistan.

It still does not control:

- Karachi;
- Lahore;
- Peshawar;
- Kashmir;
- Bengal;
- most of the Indus Valley.

It becomes a real state while remaining radically smaller than the Pakistan it claims to embody.

Its politics can therefore become even more revanchist after stabilization. The government no longer has to defend why it exists. It has to explain why it has not recovered the rest of the country.

## Afghanistan

Afghanistan is probably the largest strategic winner.

It does not permanently retain Chagai or Quetta. But it consolidates a sphere of influence over:

- Peshawar;
- the Khyber approaches;
- much of Waziristan;
- several frontier principalities and tribal confederacies.

This influence need not take the form of outright annexation.

Peshawar and the frontier states may retain their own rulers, councils, citizenship, and police while Kabul determines:

- foreign alignment;
- arms purchases;
- major roads;
- military access;
- relations with neighboring Indian states.

That gives Afghanistan a protected southeastern system without requiring it to administer every tribal district directly.

# Peshawar and the Indus trade

Peshawar gives Afghanistan access to the **Kabul–Indus corridor**, but not an effortless navigable route to the Arabian Sea.

The Kabul River runs through the Peshawar region and joins the Indus near Attock. It is also highly seasonal, so it cannot simply function as a continuous deep-water commercial highway from Kabul to Karachi. citeturn797225search11turn797225search26

Afghan exports therefore move through a mixed system:

- road and pack transport from the interior;
- storage and processing around Peshawar;
- road or rail movement toward Attock;
- river transport where practical;
- onward movement through Khalistani, Pakistani, or Sindhi territory;
- final export through Karachi.

The opium crop becomes important because it is high-value and comparatively compact. It can support expensive transport and multiple transit payments more easily than ordinary grain.

That makes Sindh indispensable.

Karachi receives customs revenue, banking business, shipping contracts, and commercial intelligence from Afghan trade. Sindh therefore has a strong interest in an Afghanistan powerful enough to trade but not powerful enough to dictate terms throughout the Indus Valley.

# Sindh’s position

Sindh wins economically rather than territorially.

It remains outside the principal conquest struggle while providing:

- weapons;
- ammunition;
- credit;
- repair;
- shipping;
- insurance;
- transit;
- brokerage.

Kalat’s acquisition of Las Bela alarms Karachi because it creates a second coastal actor near Sindh. But the new Kalat outlet remains too small to replace Karachi.

Sindh’s preferred outcome is a divided western frontier in which:

- Afghanistan needs access to Karachi;
- Kalat needs financial and technical services;
- Balochistan needs commercial routes beyond Iran;
- Pakistan needs arms;
- Khalistan needs downstream trade.

A united western state would threaten Sindhi independence. Permanent managed conflict enriches it.

# Khalistan’s southern frontier

One geographical correction is useful.

**Harappa is not a river port.** It is a town and archaeological site near the former course of the Ravi, west of Sahiwal, and it sits on the major Punjab railway system. citeturn490848search6turn490848search8turn490848search22

Its setting role should therefore be adjusted rather than removed.

Harappa becomes:

- Khalistan’s southern fortified rail town;
- an ammunition and grain depot;
- a symbolic city associated with the ancient Indus civilization;
- a recurring objective of Pakistani nationalist offensives.

The more important southern commercial and military hinge is **Multan**, with the wider lower-Punjab river and railway network behind it.

A major Pakistani offensive would normally have to move:

> Quetta–Sibi → Dera Ghazi Khan approaches → Multan corridor → Sahiwal and Harappa.

Reaching Harappa is therefore evidence of a deep and dangerous Pakistani penetration, not an ordinary crossing immediately outside Pakistan’s border.

That makes the repeated “Harappa campaigns” more meaningful. A Pakistani force that briefly raises its flag there can claim that the national army has returned to Punjab. Khalistan interprets the same event as proof that Pakistan will never accept the Sikh state’s existence.

## Does Khalistan claim Sibi?

There is no strong historical basis for presenting Sibi or Quetta as an ordinary recovered province of the Sikh Empire. The historic Sikh imperial system’s western centers were Peshawar and Multan, alongside Lahore and Kashmir. citeturn322302search5turn322302search7turn322302search9

Khalistan can still develop a claim, but it should be openly strategic rather than antique.

The argument would be:

- Pakistani forces repeatedly use Sibi as the base for incursions into southern Punjab;
- therefore Khalistan cannot be secure while Pakistan controls Sibi;
- Sibi and the approaches should be demilitarized, internationalized, or placed under Khalistani protection.

Hardline politicians may eventually convert that security demand into a territorial claim. But it is a twentieth-century frontier doctrine, not simply the restoration of Ranjit Singh’s borders.

# Rajputana and the Khalistani flank

Rajputana’s threat falls principally against Khalistan’s **southern Punjab and Multan approaches**, rather than directly against Lahore.

This matters because Khalistan cannot concentrate everything against Pakistan or Hindustan.

Its army has to cover:

- Hindustan and Amritsar to the east;
- Kashmir and the mountain approaches;
- Pakistan and the southern corridor;
- Rajputana-linked forces farther south.

Lahore may be the political center, but Multan and the southern railway system are the strategic hinge. Losing them would isolate Lahore from downstream trade and expose the state’s agricultural interior.

# The 1960s Western Indian Wars

The wars can remain continuous in memory while still being divided into recognizable campaigns.

## 1957–1960: the Quetta campaigns

Pakistan consolidates Sibi, Loralai, and Zhob and repeatedly contests Quetta–Pishin.

Afghanistan attempts to preserve a frontier administration around Quetta. Balochistan raids from Chagai. Kalat intervenes whenever either side appears overextended.

Pakistan eventually secures Quetta but cannot push far into Chagai or Kalat.

## 1960–1963: the Las Bela War

Kalat exploits Balochistan’s concentration against Afghanistan and seizes Las Bela.

Balochistan attempts several counteroffensives from Makran and Kharan but cannot sustain them while also defending Chagai and the Gwadar system.

Iran prevents the destruction of Balochistan but does not commit enough force to reconquer Las Bela.

The line freezes with Kalat on the coast.

## 1962–1966: the Peshawar consolidation

Afghanistan increases pressure upon Peshawar, Waziristan, and the frontier principalities.

Kabul does not need to conquer every district. It gains foreign-policy control, military access, and commercial privileges through subsidies and selective deployments.

This alarms:

- Kashmir;
- Khalistan;
- Pakistan;
- Sindh.

But none can dislodge Afghanistan without exposing itself elsewhere.

## 1964–1969: the Harappa and lower-Punjab campaigns

Pakistan conducts repeated eastward offensives intended to demonstrate that it remains an all-Pakistani state rather than a Quetta regime.

Most fail around the Indus and Multan approaches.

One or two reach Harappa, briefly occupying the railway town before Khalistani counterattacks and logistical collapse force withdrawal.

Khalistan responds with punitive operations toward the Sibi corridor. These attacks create the later Khalistani security claim without producing lasting occupation.

# Why no one wins

Every state encounters a different ceiling.

Afghanistan can dominate the frontier but cannot administer the whole Indus Valley.

Pakistan can hold Quetta and Sibi but cannot sustain deep operations toward Lahore.

Kalat can seize Las Bela but cannot conquer Makran and Gwadar.

Balochistan can recover Chagai with Iranian support but cannot destroy Kalat.

Khalistan can repel Pakistan but cannot eliminate it while also facing Hindustan, Kashmir, and Rajputana.

Sindh could finance a stronger army but would lose its commercial position if it openly tried to conquer its customers.

The mounted character of the war reinforces this balance. Cavalry permits raids, temporary occupations, and surprising penetrations. It does not provide the heavy logistics required to hold distant cities against organized counterattack.

The western frontier is therefore easier to cross than the Patna line and nearly as difficult to settle.

# Cultural consequence

The mounted-war tradition becomes a major part of regional identity.

Afghan, Pakistani, Baloch, Kalat, Khalistani, and frontier-state propaganda all develop images of the modern horse soldier.

But the reality is less romantic:

- horses die from thirst, disease, mines, and air attack;
- villages lose their work animals to requisition;
- remount officers decide which districts retain breeding stock;
- mounted columns seize grain and fodder from civilians;
- wounded riders may be days from a proper hospital.

The horse gives poor states mobility. It also transfers a large share of the war’s logistical burden onto rural households.

That is the better model than treating cavalry merely as a visual curiosity.

## Working canon

> **The Western Indian Wars retain extensive horse-mounted forces through the 1950s and 1960s. These formations are modern mounted rifles rather than traditional shock cavalry. They use horses for movement, reconnaissance, raiding, pursuit, and border patrol, then dismount to fight with AK-pattern rifles, machine guns, mortars, radios, and light antitank weapons.**

> **Local remount systems preserve Balochi and other regional horse populations. Governments operate breeding depots, veterinary services, purchasing fairs, and requisition systems. Mounted warfare remains viable because local states cannot afford full motorization and because much of the frontier lacks reliable roads and fuel distribution.**

> **By the end of the 1960s, Balochistan holds Makran, Kharan, Chagai, and Gwadar but loses Las Bela to Kalat. Kalat gains a narrow coastal outlet and becomes a more durable regional power. Pakistan consolidates Quetta–Pishin, Sibi, Loralai, and Zhob. Afghanistan gives up most direct claims to Quetta and Chagai but establishes decisive influence over Peshawar, Waziristan, and several frontier polities.**

> **Sindh remains independent and profits from Afghan trade, arms brokerage, finance, shipping, and the continued division of its neighbors. Khalistan holds Lahore and much of western Punjab but faces Hindustan in the east, Pakistan in the south, Kashmir in the north, and indirect Rajputana pressure against the Multan axis.**

> **Harappa is a fortified railway and symbolic frontier town rather than a river port. Pakistani forces occasionally reach or occupy it during deep lower-Punjab offensives, while Multan remains the more important southern commercial and operational hinge. Khalistani claims upon Sibi develop from modern security concerns rather than a straightforward historical Sikh territorial inheritance.**

The defining visual of the western war is therefore credible: a mounted rifle column moving through dust beside one aging tank, carrying modern automatic weapons toward a city that no state is strong enough to hold permanently.
