Britain’s starting position is far worse.

The existing canon gives Britain a 1948 Sterling and Commonwealth Reconstruction settlement based on blocked or converted overseas balances, exchange controls, reserve management, and a controlled sterling area. fileciteturn45file0 Britain retains a major financial system, but it also begins the postwar period defeated, indebted, dependent upon shipping, and burdened with enormous imperial and overseas sterling liabilities.

An immediate gold return would be nearly impossible.

Historical Britain’s 1947 attempt at broad sterling convertibility failed rapidly under pressure upon its reserves. Britain’s wartime and postwar exchange controls existed partly because London could not freely honor every external sterling claim in gold or dollars. citeturn272311search2turn272311search5turn272311search14

So Britain needs a staged return.

# IV. The British route back to gold

The cleanest development has four periods.

## 1948–1960: controlled sterling

The ordinary pound remains fiat and nonconvertible outside approved channels.

The sterling area uses:

- exchange controls;
- import licensing;
- blocked balances;
- Commonwealth reserve pooling;
- bilateral and multilateral clearing;
- preferential trade;
- gold or dollar settlement only for net external deficits.

Britain must first rebuild the merchant fleet, export industry, housing, power, ports, and strategic infrastructure. Gold convertibility before reconstruction would subordinate all of those needs to the defense of the exchange rate.

## 1960–1975: Gold Sterling Accounts

Britain begins creating a parallel external instrument before placing the ordinary pound on gold.

A working name would be the **Commonwealth Gold Sterling Account**.

These accounts are available to:

- Commonwealth central banks;
- Indian governments and princes;
- major commodity firms;
- licensed foreign banks;
- governments trading with Britain outside the sterling area.

They are denominated in sterling but backed by specified combinations of:

- British gold;
- pooled Commonwealth bullion;
- gold dollars;
- certified commodity export receipts;
- short-term commercial bills.

They are not ordinary banknotes. A British worker is still paid in domestic pounds.

This allows Hyderabad, Madras, Mysore, Sindh, or another Indian trader to accept a British claim without accepting unrestricted exposure to ordinary sterling.

It also gives Britain time to establish the accounting, assay, reserve, and clearing machinery required for eventual resumption.

## 1975–1982: the hard-account transition

By 1975, Britain regards physical reconstruction as essentially complete and possesses a mature high-value Sterling Commonwealth system. fileciteturn45file0

But Healey’s later soft budgets and producer controls make immediate full convertibility politically doubtful.

The Thatcher victory in 1980 creates the appropriate hard-account government. Her industrial policy already distinguishes between preserving strategic capacity and allowing ordinary firms to face harder commercial discipline.

A **Sterling Resumption Act** around 1981–82 could establish:

- a fixed external gold parity;
- legal redemption for approved international claims;
- reserve requirements for the Bank of England;
- strict limits on monetary financing of ordinary deficits;
- renewed freedom to own and trade bullion;
- a scheduled transition toward broader convertibility.

## 1986–1988: complete resumption

Full convertibility is completed only after the Falklands War and the associated financial strain.

That means Britain becomes the first great power after America to place its primary currency formally back on gold, but it does so over thirty or forty years rather than in one heroic act.

The final parity should be new.

Britain should not spend four decades forcing the economy back toward the pre-1914 $4.86 rate. That repeats the central error of 1925: treating an old nominal value as a moral obligation despite a changed domestic price level and economic structure. Britain’s historical gold-standard problem was closely connected to maintaining external parity through domestic deflation and high unemployment. citeturn272311search6turn272311search12

The restored pound is defined at a conservative gold weight reflecting the post-reconstruction economy.

A redenomination—ten old pounds becoming one new gold pound—is possible but not necessary. It is principally an accounting and political choice. Britain can simply define the existing pound at a new gold parity.

# V. What Britain gains

The gold pound gives Britain three advantages.

## Indian and Commonwealth trade

Indian cotton, food, minerals, tea, and other goods can be purchased with a currency the seller can redeem or use elsewhere.

British-aligned southern Indian states have an especially easy reason to accept sterling.

## London’s financial position

London becomes one of the major places where dollars, sterling, Indian gold certificates, and later Gold Yen can be exchanged and cleared.

Britain does not recover its nineteenth-century monetary supremacy. It becomes the **principal bridge market** between otherwise incompatible blocs.

## Political independence

A credible gold pound is harder for Germany, Japan, or America to dismiss as merely blocked imperial paper.

That strengthens the Sterling Commonwealth even where associated governments insist upon formal sovereignty.

The cost is equally real.

Britain accepts:

- tighter credit;
- less freedom to finance deficits;
- periodic deflationary pressure;
- greater exposure to gold withdrawals;
- political fights whenever employment and convertibility point in different directions.

# VI. Japan’s Gold Yen fits into this system

Japan’s established internal system remains a layered yen area. The ordinary yen is stabilized after the 1948 Imperial Financial Rectification, while intergovernmental imperial trade uses the Greater East Asia Clearing Yen. That clearing unit can be redeemed principally through Japanese production, not gold or unrestricted foreign assets. fileciteturn44file0 fileciteturn44file2

India is what forces Japan to create the separate **Indian Gold Settlement Yen**.

That means the world eventually contains three different Japanese monetary instruments:

- the domestic and inner-imperial yen;
- the Greater East Asia Clearing Yen;
- the Indian Gold Settlement Yen.

Only the third has a direct gold definition.

Japan does not make its entire domestic monetary system convertible. It walls the Gold Yen off behind approved trade transactions, licensed banks, and specific reserves.

That prevents an ordinary holder of domestic yen from buying Gold Yen at an artificial fixed rate and immediately emptying Japanese bullion reserves.

# VII. The emerging global system

This does not create one universal classical gold standard.

It creates a **gold clearing layer above several separate monetary blocs**.

The structure develops chronologically.

## 1949–1960: the solitary gold dollar

The United States dollar is the only major fully trusted gold-convertible currency.

It is accepted widely but not universally. Germany, Japan, Britain, and Italy restrict dollar use because they do not want their internal economies dollarized.

International trade remains highly bilateral and instrumental.

## 1960–1980: parallel hard accounts

Britain creates Gold Sterling Accounts.

India develops a dense network of princely, Hyderabad, Sindhi, Bombay, and other bullion certificates.

Commodity traders increasingly invoice contracts in weights of fine gold rather than one country’s currency.

The dollar remains the easiest common claim, but it is no longer the only one.

## 1981–1987: three hard gateways

Britain restores external gold sterling.

Japan creates the Indian Gold Settlement Yen after expanding into Hyderabad and princely India.

America enters commercial détente and passes the 1987 Reciprocal Commerce and Enterprise Act, opening ordinary consumer trade without abandoning strategic ownership and reciprocity rules. fileciteturn45file0

The conditions for broader multilateral trade finally exist.

## 1988–1995: the international bullion-clearing system

A working institution would be an **International Gold Settlement Convention** supported by clearing houses in:

- New York;
- London;
- Singapore;
- Hyderabad or Bombay;
- Zurich or another European bullion center.

The convention standardizes:

- gold fineness;
- vault certification;
- assay;
- insurance;
- bank guarantees;
- contract law;
- settlement deadlines;
- treatment of suspended convertibility;
- recognition of gold-denominated bills.

The system works through netting.

A British importer does not ship a gold bar to Japan for every machine purchase. British and Japanese banks record thousands of claims. At the end of the settlement period, only the net imbalance is paid in:

- bullion;
- gold dollars;
- gold sterling;
- Gold Yen;
- or another recognized gold claim.

That greatly reduces the quantity of physical metal that must move.

# VIII. An example of the new trade

A Hyderabadi merchant sells cotton to Britain.

The British buyer pays in Gold Sterling.

The merchant then purchases Japanese machine tools.

His bank transfers the Gold Sterling claim to a Japanese bank through the clearing system.

The Japanese bank may:

- retain sterling for future British purchases;
- exchange it for Gold Yen;
- redeem it through London;
- offset it against a British purchase of Japanese electronics.

No one has to accept ordinary sterling or ordinary yen.

And no gold necessarily leaves a vault unless the broader trade remains unbalanced.

That is the mechanism that restores **multilateral trade**.

Before this system, Hyderabad could sell to Britain and receive money principally useful in the British system. To buy from Japan, it might need a second bilateral export or an expensive bullion conversion.

After the system, the claim earned in one bloc can settle a purchase in another.

# IX. Germany’s response

Germany does not need to place the Einheitsmark or Verrechnungsmark on gold.

It is more likely to create a separate **Gold Export Mark** or simply permit German banks to issue gold-denominated export bills.

The domestic mark remains the instrument through which Berlin controls:

- wages;
- taxes;
- credit;
- investment;
- imperial clearing;
- internal prices.

But a Hyderabad buyer, American merchant, or Japanese company can insist that a German export contract be denominated in gold.

Germany accepts because the alternative is losing the sale.

This demonstrates the limit of “bad money drives out good.”

Inside Germany, the mark remains dominant because the state demands marks and German firms pay workers in marks.

Outside the German bloc, the seller or buyer may simply refuse it.

The mark does not drive out gold because it is never granted forced parity with gold in that market.

# X. The result is not free trade

Gold settlement solves one problem:

> **How can a seller in one bloc accept payment from a buyer in another bloc without becoming trapped inside the buyer’s currency system?**

It does not solve:

- tariffs;
- quotas;
- strategic embargoes;
- military rivalry;
- ownership restrictions;
- sanctions;
- shipping access;
- political distrust.

The global economy after 1990 is therefore more connected than it was in 1960, but it is not the liberalized global economy of our timeline.

A Japanese firm can sell a computer in Britain and receive gold-settled payment.

It still faces British reciprocity rules, local-content requirements, strategic-sector restrictions, and anti-dumping review.

The world gains a common **settlement grammar**, not a common market.

# XI. The principal consequences

## The dollar becomes the preferred reserve

The United States gains prestige, low-cost foreign financing, and broad demand for dollars.

But it must defend convertibility. A serious American inflation or deficit crisis becomes a gold crisis very quickly.

## Britain becomes the principal bridge

London regains importance because it clears American, Commonwealth, Indian, European, and Japanese claims.

The pound is important not because Britain rules world trade, but because Britain sits between several systems.

## Japan gains entry without surrendering monetary control

The Gold Yen allows Japanese companies to operate in India and trade with Britain or America without placing the ordinary yen on gold.

## India becomes unexpectedly central

India’s fragmentation and distrust created the practical need for universally acceptable gold settlement.

The region most incapable of producing one national currency becomes the laboratory that teaches the great blocs how to trade without one global currency.

## Domestic fiat currencies survive

The mark, ordinary yen, lira, baht, peso, and many Indian currencies continue circulating because governments demand taxes and pay salaries in them.

Gold currencies dominate savings, large contracts, and international settlement.

## Hard-currency debt becomes dangerous

A ruler or company earning weak domestic currency while owing gold faces an increasing real burden after devaluation.

Gold-denominated loans can therefore transfer:

- mines;
- ports;
- railways;
- customs receipts;
- company charters;

to foreign creditors after a crisis.

The system supports trade and also gives hard-currency banks enormous political power.

# Recommended canon chronology

**1933:** Roosevelt suspends ordinary domestic gold convertibility during the banking crisis.

**1934:** The dollar receives its revised official gold valuation.

**1947–1948:** Byrnes begins preparations for monetary resumption while preserving emergency controls.

**1949:** Dewey signs the Gold Dollar Restoration Act.

**1949–1951:** American convertibility is restored in stages at approximately the post-1934 parity rather than the old $20.67 rate.

**1948:** Britain creates the controlled Sterling Commonwealth system, blocks or restructures overseas balances, and retains exchange controls.

**1960s:** Britain introduces Commonwealth Gold Sterling Accounts for external and Indian trade.

**1981–1982:** The Sterling Resumption Act establishes a formal external gold parity.

**1986–1988:** Britain completes broader convertibility after the Falklands settlement.

**1986:** Japan regularizes the Indian Gold Settlement Yen.

**Late 1980s–early 1990s:** American, British, Japanese, Indian, and neutral banks build an international bullion-clearing network.

> **America has a gold currency. Britain restores a gold currency. Japan builds a gold trade currency. Germany retains a fiat imperial currency but accepts gold contracts abroad. India uses gold because it trusts no one’s political paper.**

And the resolution of the good-money paradox is:

> **The weak currencies remain dominant wherever governments can require their use. The hard currencies dominate wherever the recipient is free to say no.**

Yes. This changes one important conclusion from the previous pass:

> **Britain is not the first major power after America to return to gold. The Latin bloc creates the second major gold-currency area through the Latin scudo.**

And the scudo is not merely a clearing unit. It is the bloc’s actual common legal tender, broadly analogous to the euro in our timeline. The lira, peseta, Portuguese escudo, Occitan franc, and other participating currencies are converted into it and withdrawn.

That gives the mature international system two distinct kinds of gold money:

1. **actual gold-convertible currencies** used domestically—the dollar, Latin scudo, and eventually sterling;
2. **external gold-settlement currencies** used alongside domestic fiat systems—the Japanese Gold Yen and later German Goldmark.

That distinction lets international trade become multilateral without requiring Japan or Germany to put their domestic economies on gold.

# The Latin scudo

The gold backing solves the principal political problem created by a common Latin currency.

Italy is the dominant bloc power. Spain, Portugal, Occitania, and the other participants would reasonably hesitate to replace their currencies with something that the Italian government could inflate or manipulate unilaterally. A fixed gold definition gives them a guarantee outside Italian discretion.

The governing argument is:

> **The scudo belongs to the Latin community because no member government can create it at will.**

## Conversion from the national currencies

The conversion should not simply award each country scudi equal to the bullion physically held in its vaults. That would immediately starve countries with smaller reserves of money and credit.

Instead, the transition has three steps.

First, each national currency receives a negotiated gold valuation based on:

- domestic prices;
- outstanding currency;
- public debt;
- existing gold and foreign reserves;
- the state of its banking system.

Second, old notes and bank balances are converted into scudi at that rate.

Third, member governments transfer their gold reserves to a common **Latin Monetary Institute**, which becomes the issuer and redemption authority.

Countries whose currencies have been managed poorly receive less favorable conversion rates or must accept debt restructuring. That makes entry politically painful, but it prevents the new scudo from inheriting every previous inflation at face value.

## Gold coverage

The strongest version is that the **scudo monetary base**—notes, coin, and central-bank balances—is fully or almost fully covered by gold.

That does not mean every commercial bank deposit has an ounce-for-ounce bullion reserve. Banks can still extend credit and create deposits. But they must settle among themselves in scudi, and scudi remain redeemable at the Monetary Institute.

This creates a disciplined but not completely frozen banking system.

New gold entering an authorized bank can be exchanged for scudi. Scudi can likewise be presented for bullion, subject to ordinary assay, transport, and transaction fees.

## Working parity

The precise rate remains open, but a clean working value is:

> **50 Latin scudi = one troy ounce of gold.**

That makes one scudo worth:

- two Japanese Gold Yen under the proposed Japanese rate;
- half a restored British pound under the proposed sterling rate;
- seventy American cents under the $35 gold dollar.

It also gives the scudo a visibly substantial unit value without making ordinary pricing awkward.

The exact number could change without altering the institutional model.

## Domestic consequences

The gold scudo gives the Latin bloc:

- stable cross-border prices;
- elimination of exchange-rate disputes among members;
- a trusted common reserve;
- easier trade with America;
- an external symbol of bloc unity.

It also removes national devaluation as a safety valve.

A weak member cannot restore competitiveness by printing or devaluing its own currency. Adjustment has to occur through:

- lower wages or prices;
- fiscal transfers;
- migration;
- productivity;
- debt restructuring;
- direct investment from stronger members.

That produces recurring disputes over whether the scudo represents Latin solidarity or Italian-led monetary austerity.

# Why the scudo enables American–Latin trade

Once the United States restores the dollar at roughly **$35 per ounce**, the scudo and dollar have a stable gold cross-rate.

At the proposed parity:

> **$35 = 50 scudi = one ounce of gold.**

An American importer can pay in dollars. An Italian or Spanish bank can retain the dollars, redeem them for gold, or exchange them through the Latin Monetary Institute for scudi.

Likewise, an American exporter can accept scudi because the scudo represents a definite gold claim rather than blocked Italian or Spanish paper.

This does not create unrestricted free trade. Buchanan-era America and the Latin bloc still maintain tariffs, ownership rules, and strategic restrictions. But it removes the central monetary objection.

Neither side has to accumulate a currency useful only inside the other bloc.

That supplies the missing foundation for the previously established American–Italian trade relationship.

# The restored sterling system

Britain follows later.

A parity of:

> **£25 = one troy ounce**

works well as a post-reconstruction settlement. Combined with the other proposed rates, it produces:

> **£1 = $1.40 = 2 scudi = 4 Gold Yen.**

That is substantially below sterling’s old pre-1914 gold value, but that is desirable. Britain is not trying to reverse the entire monetary history of the twentieth century. It is establishing a credible new parity consistent with its postwar price and wage structure.

The likely sequence remains staged:

- gold-denominated external sterling accounts during the 1960s and 1970s;
- a formal resumption law in the early 1980s;
- full or nearly full convertibility around 1986–87.

Britain therefore becomes the third major gold-currency area after America and the Latin bloc.

The pound’s restoration is politically different from the scudo’s creation. The scudo uses gold to persuade several countries to accept one new currency. Britain uses gold to demonstrate that an old currency has completed its recovery.

# The Japanese Gold Yen

The Japanese instrument starts narrowly and then changes function.

## The Indian phase

Around 1987–88, Japanese banks regularize the **Indian Gold Settlement Yen** to conduct trade with Hyderabad, the princely states, Sindh, and other gold-oriented Indian markets.

Its purpose is initially regional:

- purchase Indian commodities;
- finance princely development;
- sell Japanese weapons and machinery;
- settle debts without forcing Indians to hold ordinary yen.

## The wider phase

Once sterling has returned to gold, Japanese banks realize the instrument can settle trade not only with India but with:

- Britain;
- the Latin bloc;
- America;
- neutral bullion markets;
- eventually Germany.

The word “Indian” gradually disappears from ordinary use.

By about 1990, it is normally called simply the:

> **Gold Yen**

Its formal legal name might remain something longer, but the short form is universal in banking and trade.

## Working parity

The cleanest value is the one you proposed:

> **100 Gold Yen = one troy ounce of gold.**

Each Gold Yen therefore represents one-hundredth of an ounce.

This is deliberately artificial. The issuing authority is not trying to connect the Gold Yen numerically to the ordinary yen. It is creating a convenient gold-accounting unit.

The exchange rate between ordinary yen and Gold Yen floats or is administratively quoted according to market conditions. There is no automatic rule that one ordinary yen equals one Gold Yen.

That legal separation is what protects the Bank of Japan.

A Japanese citizen cannot exchange unlimited domestic yen for Gold Yen at a fixed rate and drain the country’s bullion reserve.

Gold Yen are created only through:

- approved external trade;
- bullion deposits;
- convertible gold currencies;
- certified gold-denominated bills;
- authorized Japanese banking operations.

## An external currency, not ordinary money

The Gold Yen is normally used for:

- large contracts;
- banking reserves;
- commodity trade;
- arms purchases;
- international debt;
- inter-bloc settlement.

It does not ordinarily pay wages in Tokyo or buy groceries in Osaka.

A Japanese company earning Gold Yen sells them to an authorized bank for ordinary yen at the current exchange rate. The hard claim remains in the external banking system.

# The German Goldmark

Germany arrives last because it has the least initial incentive to cooperate.

The Einheitsblock is large enough that Germany can conduct most of its trade through:

- the Reichsmark;
- territorial currencies;
- the Einheitsmark system;
- the Verrechnungsmark clearing order;
- compulsory bilateral delivery arrangements.

Berlin therefore sees little reason to surrender monetary freedom merely to satisfy outsiders.

The pressure changes in the 1990s.

German exporters increasingly face foreign purchasers who are willing to buy German goods but unwilling to hold German clearing balances. A Japanese, British, American, or Indian buyer simply demands a gold invoice.

Germany then has two choices:

- accept foreign gold currencies and allow London, New York, Rome, or Singapore to intermediate German trade;
- create a German instrument and retain control of its own external settlement.

It chooses the second.

## Form

The **Goldmark** is not the Reichsmark restored to gold.

It is a separate external currency comparable to the Gold Yen. A more technical legal name might be *Goldverrechnungsmark*, but **Goldmark** is the natural public term. It also invokes pre-1914 German monetary prestige, which makes it politically attractive.

There is no automatic conversion between:

- Goldmarks;
- Reichsmarks;
- Einheitsmarks;
- Verrechnungsmarks.

German exporters receive Goldmarks and convert them through licensed banks. Domestic wages, taxes, and investment remain denominated in the existing German monetary system.

## Working parity

Germany would likely copy the Japanese denomination:

> **100 Goldmarks = one troy ounce of gold.**

This lets German banks enter the existing clearing network without creating another unnecessarily complex unit.

One Goldmark and one Gold Yen represent the same formal weight of gold. They may still trade at a small premium or discount to one another because of:

- redemption location;
- fees;
- transport;
- confidence in the issuing bank;
- temporary capital controls.

Equal gold content does not make every issuer equally convenient or trustworthy.

# The five-currency structure

A clean working system would therefore look like this:

| Currency | Type | Working gold parity | Ordinary domestic money? |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| U.S. dollar | National gold currency | $35 per ounce | Yes |
| Latin scudo | Common bloc gold currency | 50 scudi per ounce | Yes |
| Pound sterling | Restored national gold currency | £25 per ounce | Yes |
| Gold Yen | Japanese external settlement unit | 100 per ounce | No |
| Goldmark | German external settlement unit | 100 per ounce | No |

The rate structure produces several convenient relationships:

- £1 = 2 scudi;
- 1 scudo = 2 Gold Yen or Goldmarks;
- £1 = 4 Gold Yen or Goldmarks;
- 1 Gold Yen = 1 Goldmark by formal gold weight.

The dollar cross-rates are less neat, but they remain fixed through the common gold denominator.

# How global settlement works

The world does not need to ship bullion for every transaction.

Banks translate each claim into gold weight.

Suppose a British firm buys Japanese machinery worth ten ounces of gold. The contract can state any of the following:

- £250;
- 500 scudi;
- $350;
- 1,000 Gold Yen;
- 1,000 Goldmarks once the German unit exists.

The British and Japanese banks record the claim. Other trade runs in the opposite direction during the same settlement period.

At the end of the month or quarter, only the **net imbalance** has to be settled.

Settlement can occur through:

- physical gold;
- gold dollars;
- sterling;
- scudi;
- Gold Yen;
- Goldmarks;
- transferable claims on approved vaults.

This is what makes the system scalable. The amount of trade can be many times larger than the amount of metal physically moved.

# The system has three monetary levels

By the 1990s, world trade operates through three levels.

## Domestic currencies

These pay wages, taxes, rent, and ordinary purchases.

Examples include:

- ordinary yen;
- Reichsmarks and Einheitsmarks;
- baht;
- Indian local currencies;
- other national paper money.

Governments retain substantial control over them.

## Bloc clearing currencies

These settle trade inside political-economic systems.

Examples include:

- the Greater East Asia Clearing Yen;
- the Verrechnungsmark;
- internal Commonwealth accounts before complete sterling convertibility.

They are useful because the bloc guarantees access to its production, not because they represent gold.

## Gold currencies and settlement instruments

These settle trade between blocs whose governments do not trust one another’s domestic paper.

That upper layer consists of:

- dollar;
- scudo;
- sterling;
- Gold Yen;
- Goldmark;
- Indian and neutral bullion certificates.

This is not one world currency. It is a common method for translating several currencies into the same physical standard.

# Gresham’s law in this mature system

The system avoids the simplest Gresham problem because it does not legally declare ordinary yen and Gold Yen equal.

They are separate instruments with a market exchange rate.

The same is true of the Goldmark and domestic German money.

Inside Japan, people spend ordinary yen because:

- wages are paid in yen;
- taxes are due in yen;
- prices are listed in yen;
- ordinary citizens have little access to Gold Yen.

Inside international commerce, a seller may reject ordinary yen and demand Gold Yen.

So the result remains:

> **Fiat money dominates where the state defines the transaction. Gold money dominates where the recipient is free to define it.**

The scudo, dollar, and sterling are somewhat different because they are both domestic and gold money. Their governments accept the cost of allowing external confidence to constrain domestic policy.

Japan and Germany do not.

# The likely chronology

## 1949–1951

America restores dollar convertibility at about $35 per ounce.

## 1957–1962

The Latin Monetary Convention creates the gold-backed Latin scudo. Accounting conversion begins first; common notes and coin follow; the old national currencies are withdrawn over several years.

## The 1960s–1970s

The dollar and scudo form the first durable cross-bloc gold-trade axis. This supports later American–Latin commerce without broader dollarization.

Britain develops gold sterling accounts while retaining a controlled domestic pound.

## 1982–1987

Britain restores sterling in stages, settling around £25 per ounce.

## 1987–1990

Japan creates the Indian Gold Settlement Yen. Its use spreads beyond India, and it becomes commonly known as the Gold Yen.

## Approximately 1992–1995

Germany creates the Goldmark as the last great external gold-settlement instrument.

## The mid-1990s onward

Banks in New York, London, the Latin financial centers, Singapore, Hyderabad, and Berlin operate a mature multilateral bullion-clearing network.

# What changes in global trade

The scudo means the re-expansion of trade does not wait for Britain or Japan.

America and the Latin bloc can already conduct relatively secure cross-bloc trade during the 1960s and 1970s.

But the system becomes genuinely global only after three later events:

1. sterling becomes convertible;
2. Japan creates the Gold Yen;
3. Germany accepts the Goldmark.

That places all five major economic systems inside one settlement framework.

Trade remains strategic, protected, and politically managed. But a country can now sell to one bloc and use the resulting hard claim to purchase from another.

The world therefore moves from:

> **bilateral exchange between closed currency systems**

toward:

> **multilateral trade among protected economic blocs using gold as the common settlement language.**

# Revised canon formulation

> **The Latin scudo is the common circulating currency of the Latin bloc, comparable institutionally to the euro but backed by gold. Member currencies are converted into scudi at negotiated gold valuations and withdrawn. The Latin Monetary Institute pools member reserves, issues scudi, and guarantees convertibility at a fixed gold parity.**

> **The scudo becomes the second major gold currency after the restored American dollar and enables direct American–Latin trade well before Britain and Japan create their later hard-currency systems.**

> **Britain restores ordinary sterling to gold during the 1980s at a new postwar parity rather than the old pre-1914 rate. Japan then broadens the Indian Gold Settlement Yen into the general Gold Yen, defined as one hundred Gold Yen per troy ounce. The Gold Yen remains legally separate from the domestic yen and the Greater East Asia Clearing Yen.**

> **Germany adopts the Goldmark during the 1990s as a separate foreign-trade currency rather than converting the Reichsmark, Einheitsmark, or Verrechnungsmark to gold. The Goldmark is also defined at one hundred units per ounce, allowing direct entry into the established bullion-clearing system.**

The mature monetary order is therefore not a universal return to one classical gold standard.

It is a more politically fragmented arrangement:

> **America, Britain, and the Latin bloc put their actual money on gold. Japan and Germany put only the money they use with outsiders on gold.**

# The final Pacific order

The Japanese Pacific can be divided into four legal categories, moving outward from Japan.

## 1. Integral Japanese Micronesia

These are the older possessions Japan already regarded as part of its established imperial system:

- the Northern Marianas, excluding Guam;
- Palau;
- the Caroline Islands;
- the Marshall Islands;
- associated smaller Micronesian islands.

Historically, Japan’s South Seas Mandate covered the former German islands north of the equator, particularly the Marianas other than Guam, the Carolines, and the Marshalls. citeturn315540search4

In the alternate setting, victory removes the temporary character of the mandate. These territories cease to be administered as lands held for an international body and become permanent Japanese imperial territory.

Their inhabitants are legally Japanese. Micronesian identity survives as an ethnic, linguistic, regional, and ancestral category, not as citizenship in a separate Micronesian country.

This is where assimilation proceeds furthest.

## 2. The South Pacific imperial territories

Japan directly governs the later acquisitions:

- the Bismarck Archipelago;
- Bougainville and nearby islands;
- the Solomon Islands;
- the Santa Cruz Islands;
- Fiji;
- the New Hebrides, later called Vanuatu in our history;
- New Caledonia;
- Wallis and Futuna;
- the Gilbert Islands;
- the Ellice Islands;
- Nauru;
- Tahiti and the wider French Polynesian territories.

These are not associated states. They do not possess independent foreign policy, national citizenship, sovereign parliaments, or separate defense establishments.

Historically, these islands belonged to several distinct colonial systems: Fiji was British; the New Hebrides were jointly administered by Britain and France; New Caledonia and French Polynesia were French; the Gilbert and Ellice Islands were British; and Western Samoa was administered by New Zealand. citeturn315540search9turn412886search2turn412886search3turn412886search0turn412886search20

Japan is therefore not inheriting one ready-made Pacific colony. It is combining British, French, Australian, and mandate territories into a new Japanese oceanic administration.

## 3. Associated Papua New Guinea

Papua New Guinea is different.

The entire main island is unified beneath one national government. Japan combines the former Dutch western half with the former Australian-administered eastern territories. Historically, the Netherlands claimed western New Guinea as part of the Dutch East Indies, while the eastern side was divided between Papua and the former German New Guinea under Australian administration. citeturn387607search0turn315540search0

The unification is therefore a deliberate Japanese border revision.

Papua New Guinea becomes:

- a sovereign member of the Co-Prosperity Sphere;
- domestically self-governing;
- militarily dependent on Japan;
- heavily integrated into Japanese trade and finance;
- vulnerable to zaibatsu control;
- prohibited from admitting hostile bases or independently changing strategic alignment.

It is a real state, but not one with unrestricted strategic sovereignty.

## 4. The non-Japanese Pacific remnants

The Pacific remains interleaved rather than becoming a single Japanese ocean.

The United States retains:

- Hawaii;
- Guam;
- American Samoa;
- Wake;
- Midway;
- Johnston;
- the American-controlled Phoenix and Line Islands under the final setting;
- its other established central Pacific positions.

New Zealand retains Western Samoa, along with the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau. Australia retains Norfolk Island and its homeland. Tonga remains the independent Polynesian monarchy aligned with Britain and the Commonwealth.

Britain retains Pitcairn.

Chile retains Easter Island.

This creates American and Commonwealth islands embedded among Japanese routes rather than one clean line separating the blocs.

# Why New Guinea becomes one state

At first glance, unifying New Guinea appears inconsistent with Japan’s decision to divide the Indonesian archipelago into numerous particularist states.

But the conditions are different.

The southern archipelago contains large regional cultures, old courts, commercial centers, and islands capable of supporting recognizable governments. New Guinea contains an enormous number of local communities spread across mountains, valleys, river basins, forests, and coastal districts. Dividing the island strictly by ethnicity would produce hundreds of states or force Japan to arbitrarily place smaller peoples beneath somewhat larger ones.

So Tokyo uses a different rule:

> **In the Indonesian islands, geographic and national particularism produce several states. In New Guinea, extreme local particularism makes a geographic federation more workable than ethnic partition.**

Japan also has practical reasons for unification.

One Papuan state is cheaper to supervise than two large administrations inherited from Australia and the Netherlands. It prevents the western half from becoming part of one of the Indonesian states. It removes a potential Dutch or Australian claim. And it creates one buffer separating Australia from the Japanese Indonesian and Melanesian systems.

The unification can be presented as liberation from an arbitrary European line:

> The Europeans divided one island. Japan restored its natural territorial unity.

That argument has genuine appeal, even though Japan then retains many nearby islands as direct imperial possessions.

# The Papuan state

Papua New Guinea cannot operate as a strongly centralized unitary country.

Its government should be federal or highly regionalized.

## The central institutions

Port Moresby is the natural administrative capital.

It contains:

- the national government;
- Japanese embassy and military mission;
- central bank;
- defense and development ministries;
- principal foreign corporate offices;
- national legislative institutions.

Lae becomes the main commercial and industrial port of the eastern half.

The former Hollandia region becomes the western administrative center. Its eventual national name can remain open, since neither the Dutch colonial name nor a later Indonesian name necessarily survives.

The highlands require multiple regional governments because roads and communications cannot make Port Moresby’s authority immediate.

## The internal federation

The Papuan constitution likely contains three layers:

1. a national government responsible for diplomacy, currency, strategic transport, and common law;
2. large regional governments corresponding to geographic and administrative zones;
3. local councils, customary authorities, churches, and village institutions.

A **Council of Peoples** or comparable upper chamber would be useful. It gives smaller communities representation that a purely population-based assembly would not provide.

The lower chamber can represent population and districts.

The result is not ethnically perfect representation. That is impossible. It is an attempt to ensure that no one coastal or highland population can define the whole state.

## Papuan citizenship

Papua New Guineans possess Papuan citizenship, not Japanese nationality.

A Papuan born in Port Moresby cannot freely relocate to Osaka merely because both countries belong to the Sphere. He requires Japanese residence and employment permission like a Filipino, Vietnamese, or Manchukuoan.

Japanese residents in Papua New Guinea remain Japanese citizens. They may live around mines, ports, plantations, airfields, and company districts without becoming Papuan.

The Home and Return Mandate later allows Papuan citizens born abroad to return to Papua New Guinea. That right applies to the Papuan state, not to each individual valley or tribal district.

“Papuan” therefore becomes a political nationality layered above numerous local identities.

# Biak and the space program

Biak should remain Papuan territory rather than being removed into direct Japanese sovereignty.

Japan instead obtains an exceptionally long strategic lease.

The **Biak Space and Air District** can contain:

- the equatorial launch center;
- tracking stations;
- military airfields;
- communications;
- port facilities;
- Japanese housing;
- technical schools;
- corporate workshops;
- fuel and range infrastructure.

Papua New Guinea receives:

- rent;
- infrastructure;
- skilled employment;
- scholarships;
- transport investment;
- a share of associated commercial activity.

Japan controls actual launch security and strategic operations.

That makes Biak both the state’s greatest prestige project and the clearest evidence of limited sovereignty. Papua can place its flag at the entrance. Japanese authorities determine who may enter the launch complex.

The space center also gives Papua New Guinea unusual importance inside the Sphere. It is no longer merely a lightly populated resource state. It contains infrastructure Japan cannot casually lose.

# The zaibatsu in Papua New Guinea

Papua New Guinea is probably one of the states most vulnerable to corporate domination.

Its government has territory and resources but limited:

- capital;
- trained administrators;
- engineers;
- transport;
- tax collection;
- communications;
- domestic banking;
- industrial management.

Japanese companies can therefore enter not only as investors but as substitute institutions.

The principal economic sectors would include:

- mining;
- forestry;
- fisheries;
- plantation agriculture;
- hydropower;
- ports;
- aviation;
- telecommunications;
- construction;
- the Biak space complex.

Mining, agriculture, forestry, and fisheries are all plausible pillars of the Papuan economy. citeturn877954search2turn877954search8

A mining concession may require the company to build:

- the road;
- the port;
- the power station;
- worker housing;
- the hospital;
- the airstrip;
- the communications system;
- the local school.

The government then discovers that regulating the mine also means regulating the town, road, hospital, and power grid that only the company knows how to operate.

Papua is sovereign in law. Japanese firms increasingly control the practical links connecting its regions.

## Corporate politics

By the 1980s and 1990s, zaibatsu sponsorship becomes normal in Papuan politics.

A regional governor may depend upon one Japanese company for:

- construction;
- local employment;
- air transport;
- campaign communications;
- disaster relief;
- medical supplies.

The national government can challenge one concession. It cannot easily challenge every Japanese company at once.

Papua New Guinea consequently resembles the Indonesian states economically, but with one important difference: it is large enough to believe it ought eventually to control its own resources.

That produces a stronger resource-nationalist opposition than Japan encounters on many small islands.

# Direct rule in the South Pacific

Japan cannot administer the whole Pacific from one governor’s office.

The strongest arrangement is a **South Seas General Government** divided into four geographic administrations.

## 1. Micronesian Administration

**Headquarters:** Koror, with major naval authority at Truk and Saipan.

It governs:

- the Japanese Marianas;
- Palau;
- the Carolines;
- the Marshalls.

This is the oldest and most heavily Japanized region.

## 2. Central Pacific Administration

**Headquarters:** Tarawa, with major commercial and mining authority at Nauru.

It governs:

- the Gilbert Islands;
- the Ellice Islands;
- Nauru;
- associated central atolls.

Because the Gilbert and Ellice populations are culturally distinct, they receive separate district councils even though Japan refuses to create separate states.

## 3. Melanesian Administration

**Headquarters:** Rabaul.

It governs:

- the Bismarcks;
- Bougainville;
- the Solomons;
- Santa Cruz;
- the New Hebrides.

Rabaul becomes the Japanese military and commercial center north of Australia.

## 4. Southern and Eastern Pacific Administration

**Headquarters:** Suva.

It governs:

- Fiji;
- New Caledonia;
- Wallis and Futuna;
- French Polynesia.

Nouméa operates as a special naval and mineral district. Papeete has an eastern deputy governor because it is too distant for ordinary administration from Suva.

These civil administrations overlap with naval districts, but they are not identical. A naval commander controls defense and operations. A governor manages courts, taxation, schools, labor, health, and infrastructure.

# Nationality in the directly ruled islands

The direct-rule principle leaves one legal question that should now be fixed: are Fijians, Tahitians, Solomon Islanders, and the other new subjects foreigners under Japanese rule, or Japanese nationals?

The strongest fit with the earlier Korean, Formosan, and Micronesian canon is **staged incorporation**.

## The first stage

Immediately after 1947, the new island populations are Japanese imperial subjects under territorial law.

They do not possess foreign citizenship because no independent Fiji, Tahiti, Solomon Islands, or Vanuatu exists. But neither do they immediately exercise every right associated with Japanese citizenship in the home islands.

Their legal position resembles an outer imperial territory awaiting standardization.

## The second stage

During the 1960s and 1970s, Japan consolidates imperial nationality.

By 1985:

- a Fijian is legally Japanese;
- a Tahitian is legally Japanese;
- a Nauruan is legally Japanese;
- a Solomon Islander is legally Japanese;
- a Micronesian is legally Japanese.

Their older identities remain ethnic and regional categories.

This means they can legally migrate within the Japanese Empire. A Fijian may study in Tokyo, work in Yokohama, or serve in Korea without becoming a foreign resident.

The practical barriers remain substantial:

- cost;
- schooling;
- Japanese-language requirements;
- employment;
- discrimination;
- distance;
- company sponsorship.

But the movement is internal, not immigration.

That is also why these cultures face a risk closer to Korea’s than to the Philippines’.

## The return mandate does not help them in the same way

A Filipino born in Japan can claim assisted return to the Philippines.

A Fijian born in Japan cannot claim repatriation to a sovereign Fiji, because no such country exists. Fiji is already considered part of his national country: Japan.

He may receive regional-resettlement assistance to return to the islands, but that is domestic relocation, not the restoration of a foreign national people.

This becomes one of the strongest criticisms of Japanese cultural guardianship:

> Japan recognizes a Filipino as a member of another nation, but recognizes a Fijian only as a Japanese citizen with regional ancestry.

# The doctrine of viable statehood

Japan needs an official explanation for why Papua New Guinea receives a state while Fiji, Tahiti, and New Caledonia do not.

The likely doctrine is **national viability**.

A people receives associated statehood only if it can support:

- a durable central government;
- a tax base;
- internal communications;
- courts and police;
- national defense institutions;
- foreign representation;
- an economy capable of operating beyond permanent subsidy.

Population is one factor, but not the only factor.

Papua New Guinea qualifies because its territory, resources, population, and administrative burden justify a common government. Japan does not want to govern its vast interior directly.

A tiny atoll does not qualify because its entire government would depend upon Japanese shipping, finance, and defense.

That is the formal argument.

The objection is obvious.

Fiji, Tahiti, and New Caledonia are capable of supporting more domestic government than Tokyo admits. Japan keeps them because:

- Suva is a regional hub;
- Nouméa is strategically and economically valuable;
- Tahiti is the eastern relay;
- independent island governments would demand a voice in Sphere policy;
- bases would require negotiation rather than direct order;
- local ownership might threaten Japanese concessions.

So the actual rule is:

> **A territory receives statehood when Japan believes governing it indirectly is more useful than governing it directly.**

The viability doctrine is not entirely false. It is sufficiently flexible to protect Japanese interests.

# The Pacific economies

The direct territories fall into four economic groups.

## Strategic mineral islands

New Caledonia becomes the central nickel and metallurgical territory. Nauru remains heavily dependent upon phosphate. Both resources are historically central to their respective economies. citeturn877954search1turn877954search3

These are the islands where corporate rule becomes most conspicuous.

A mining firm can dominate:

- employment;
- shipping;
- land;
- electricity;
- water;
- housing;
- government revenue.

Nauru becomes the most extreme case. The population is denied sovereign statehood while Japanese extraction steadily consumes the physical island on which any future state would have to exist.

## Plantation and agricultural territories

Fiji supplies sugar and regional agricultural products. The New Hebrides, Solomons, and other tropical islands produce copra, timber, fisheries, and plantation goods. Fiji’s sugar industry provides a strong basis for that role. citeturn877954search0turn877954search4

Japanese companies control much of the processing, shipping, insurance, and export market even where land remains under customary or communal tenure.

## Naval and aviation territories

Some islands matter more as positions than as producers.

They provide:

- airfields;
- harbors;
- submarine facilities;
- weather stations;
- radio and cable relays;
- search-and-rescue bases;
- fuel storage;
- maritime patrol;
- missile and space tracking;
- ocean surveillance.

The Pacific empire is held together by information and transport more than by garrisons.

## Commercial and administrative hubs

Suva, Nouméa, Rabaul, Koror, Tarawa, and Papeete become regional centers.

They contain Japanese:

- banks;
- shipping houses;
- naval offices;
- courts;
- schools;
- hospitals;
- technical services;
- warehouses;
- corporate headquarters.

The smaller islands depend on these hubs for nearly every advanced service.

# Not every island is a fortress

Japan does not need a major battle fleet, armored garrison, or bomber base on every atoll.

The military network is hierarchical.

The major hubs are:

- Saipan and Tinian;
- Truk;
- Palau;
- Rabaul;
- Nouméa;
- Suva;
- Tarawa;
- Papeete.

A secondary island might have:

- a weather station;
- a short airstrip;
- a coastwatch detachment;
- a radio post;
- a small harbor;
- police;
- fuel or emergency stores.

Most islands are warning posts and logistical links rather than self-contained fortresses.

This reduces manpower requirements, but it makes shipping and aviation indispensable. A cyclone, dock strike, fuel shortage, or delayed supply ship can create a local crisis faster than a foreign attack.

Japan therefore develops a large South Seas service structure:

- inter-island passenger and cargo ships;
- flying boats and short-field aircraft;
- weather and cyclone warning;
- medical vessels;
- construction battalions;
- disaster-relief stores;
- radio technicians;
- mobile repair teams.

This is one of the ways Japanese direct rule provides genuine material value. It is also one of the ways the territories become incapable of functioning without Japan.

# Fiji, New Caledonia, and Tahiti

The three largest southern possessions develop different political textures.

## Fiji

Fiji becomes the administrative center of the southern ocean.

Its society contains indigenous chiefly institutions, Indo-Fijian agricultural and commercial communities, Japanese officials, and smaller foreign populations. Japan uses that internal diversity to argue against a sovereign Fijian national state.

Local rule operates through several parallel bodies:

- chiefly councils;
- municipal and commercial councils;
- religious institutions;
- labor organizations;
- the Japanese territorial government.

No one local institution is permitted to claim the whole country.

Suva becomes prosperous and important, but distinctly colonial. It is the place where islanders from throughout the South Pacific encounter the Japanese state.

## New Caledonia

New Caledonia is the most strategic southern possession.

Its nickel, port, proximity to Australia, and French-built institutions make it too valuable for Tokyo to hand to a local government.

Nouméa becomes:

- a naval base;
- metallurgical center;
- Japanese settler and corporate city;
- intelligence station facing Australia;
- headquarters for a special industrial district.

Kanak communities retain customary land and local councils outside designated mining and development zones. French settlers and technicians are divided between those who leave, those who retain protected residence, and those absorbed into the Japanese corporate order.

The independence question remains active because New Caledonia is large and wealthy enough that the viability argument is difficult to maintain honestly.

## Tahiti

Tahiti is Japan’s easternmost major possession.

Papeete is less important for raw materials than for:

- navigation;
- communications;
- fleet support;
- aviation;
- meteorology;
- tourism;
- later space tracking;
- the route toward Japanese commercial and naval access in Peru.

By the 1970s, Tahiti is the bridge between Japan’s Asian empire and its South American presence.

That makes its tiny population strategically disproportionate.

# Samoa and the American boundary

Western Samoa should remain under New Zealand.

There are three strong reasons.

First, taking it would place Japan directly beside American Samoa and create a recurring crisis with Washington.

Second, Japan already possesses Fiji and Tahiti. Samoa is useful, but not necessary enough to risk extending the war.

Third, leaving one substantial Polynesian society under New Zealand gives the final peace a visible boundary rather than transferring every British and Dominion island to Japan.

This creates a striking regional contrast.

Western Samoa is governed by New Zealand, perhaps with growing customary and constitutional autonomy.

American Samoa remains American.

Nearby Japanese Fiji, the Ellice Islands, and other territories remain directly imperial.

Samoan activists can therefore compare three systems within the same ocean:

- New Zealand trusteeship;
- American territorial rule;
- Japanese incorporation.

Tonga should likewise remain independent and British-aligned. Its monarchy gives it a preexisting sovereign structure that Japan can pressure without needing to abolish.

# Guam, the Line Islands, and the holes in the Japanese ocean

Guam becomes one of the strangest frontiers in the world.

It is an American island surrounded by Japanese Marianas. A traveler can move from Japanese Saipan to American Guam within the same island chain and cross between two different great-power systems.

The same broad pattern exists farther east.

Japanese Gilbert and Ellice territories sit near American Phoenix and Line possessions. American Samoa sits beside the New Zealand Samoan system. Japanese Tahiti lies farther east but does not erase the American routes connecting Hawaii, the Line Islands, and the South Pacific.

These possessions become:

- intelligence stations;
- signals posts;
- aviation relays;
- naval tripwires;
- propaganda showcases;
- smuggling routes;
- occasional sites of defection.

Japan and the United States both fortify carefully enough to deter attack and restrain themselves carefully enough to avoid making a local incident the beginning of the war they avoided in 1941.

A naming clarification will help future maps:

- **Christmas Island in the Indian Ocean** remains British.
- **Kiritimati**, historically also called Christmas Island, lies in the Line Islands and is American under this setting’s Pacific settlement.

# Timor and the Indian Ocean chain

Timor remains divided.

The western half belongs inside the Japanese-associated Eastern Lesser Sunda state. It is not necessarily direct Japanese territory, even though Japanese bases and companies are prominent.

Portuguese Timor survives in the east.

Japan pressures Lisbon for:

- basing;
- customs access;
- transit;
- commercial concessions;
- eventual cession.

Portugal refuses outright transfer.

Lisbon is stronger, has Latin-bloc backing, and regards abandoning Timor as a dangerous precedent for Angola, Mozambique, and the rest of its pluricontinental claims.

Timor therefore becomes another close imperial seam: a Japanese-associated western government beside a Portuguese eastern colony.

The Indian Ocean islands belong to another system.

Britain retains:

- Indian Ocean Christmas Island;
- the Cocos Islands;
- Ceylon;
- the Maldives;
- the Seychelles;
- links toward South Africa and Australia.

Christmas and Cocos are particularly important because they help connect the Cape route to Ceylon and Australia after the loss of the Raj and Mediterranean artery.

They are not minor decorative possessions. They are navigation, communications, aviation, and naval links in the Siege Commonwealth.

# The cultural contradiction

Japan’s Pacific system produces the clearest limit of its later cultural doctrine.

Tokyo says it protects:

- local languages;
- island customs;
- chiefly institutions;
- churches;
- traditional land systems;
- dances, music, and oral history.

By the 1980s, it may genuinely finance all of those things.

But it refuses to recognize the political conclusion that many island intellectuals draw from them:

> If we are a distinct culture worth preserving, why are we not a nation entitled to a state?

Japan’s answer is that culture does not automatically create viable sovereignty.

The island nationalist’s answer is that “viability” always seems to disappear where Japan wants a naval base, mine, phosphate concession, or administrative hub.

That conflict does not usually become a conventional war. The populations are too small and Japan controls the sea.

It appears through:

- church petitions;
- cultural congresses;
- student movements;
- strikes;
- independence societies;
- local-language newspapers;
- refusals to sell customary land;
- occasional sabotage;
- diaspora activism inside Japan.

Japan can repress the movement. It cannot completely answer it.

# Development over time

## 1942–1944: the short perimeter

Japan takes the resource and logistical core of Southeast Asia but avoids immediate overreach toward Fiji, Samoa, and New Caledonia.

## 1945–1947: the late Pacific expansion

As Britain, France, Australia, and the European empires lose the wider war, Japan occupies or receives isolated Pacific possessions that can no longer be defended coherently.

The United States, Australia, New Zealand, Portugal, and Chile retain specifically protected holdings.

## 1947–1955: territorial reorganization

Japan creates Papua New Guinea from the eastern Australian and western Dutch territories.

The Bismarcks, Bougainville, Solomons, Fiji, New Hebrides, New Caledonia, Gilbert and Ellice Islands, Nauru, and French Polynesia enter direct Japanese administration.

## 1955–1970: base and corporate development

Ports, airfields, mines, plantations, shipping, schools, hospitals, and communications expand.

Japanese settlement remains concentrated around strategic and corporate districts rather than spreading evenly across the islands.

## 1970–1985: incorporation and cultural guardianship

Direct island populations receive consolidated Japanese nationality.

Local languages, churches, customary authorities, and heritage institutions receive greater support, but no sovereign island states are created.

Papua New Guinea develops stronger domestic institutions while becoming increasingly dependent upon Japanese corporate finance and the Biak space system.

## By 2000

Papua New Guinea remains formally sovereign and corporately constrained.

The direct island territories are treated in Tokyo as ordinary parts of the Japanese imperial system, albeit remote and culturally distinctive ones.

Island nationalism persists because the difference between statehood and direct rule has never been explained in a way that does not ultimately return to Japanese convenience.

# Revised canon

> **Papua New Guinea consists of the entire main island of New Guinea, uniting the former Dutch western territory with the former Australian-administered east. It is a sovereign but strategically dependent member of the Co-Prosperity Sphere. Its government is federal or highly regionalized, while Japan controls external defense, possesses major bases and leases, and dominates infrastructure and resource development through the zaibatsu.**

> **The Bismarck Archipelago, Bougainville, the Solomons, Santa Cruz, Fiji, the New Hebrides, New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, the Gilbert and Ellice Islands, Nauru, Tahiti, and the wider French Polynesian territories remain direct Japanese imperial possessions. They do not become separate associated states.**

> **Older Micronesian possessions are incorporated most thoroughly and become heavily Japanized. The later South Pacific acquisitions initially possess separate territorial status but gradually enter a consolidated Japanese nationality system. Their peoples are legally Japanese by the 1970s–80s, while their older identities are treated as regional cultures rather than foreign nationalities.**

> **Japan justifies the distinction through a doctrine of national viability: associated statehood requires sufficient population, administration, revenue, communication, and defensive capacity. The doctrine contains practical truth but is applied selectively. Fiji, New Caledonia, and Tahiti remain directly ruled largely because their ports, resources, and positions are too useful for Tokyo to place behind another sovereign government.**

> **Western Samoa remains under New Zealand, American Samoa remains American, and Tonga remains an independent British-aligned monarchy. Guam and the American Phoenix and Line Islands create American enclaves within the wider Japanese Pacific. Portuguese Timor remains separate from the Japanese-associated western half of Timor. Indian Ocean Christmas Island and the Cocos Islands remain British components of the Cape–Ceylon–Australia route.**

The defining Pacific contrast is therefore simple:

> **Papua New Guinea receives a flag because Japan needs it to govern a continent-sized island. Fiji, New Caledonia, and Tahiti do not receive flags because Japan prefers to govern their ports itself.**
